Maxillary sinus; Infraorbital nerve
Frontal sinus; Supraorbital nerve
Maxillary sinus; Supraorbital nerve
Ethmoid sinus; Nasociliary nerve
correctOption: Maxillary sinus; Infraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: The sphenoid sinus is deep in the skull; its pain is usually referred to the vertex or occiput and it is not associated with dental pathology or cheek tenderness.

The maxillary sinus is intimately related to the roots of the molar teeth (explaining the tooth pain) and is innervated by the infraorbital nerve, which also supplies the skin of the cheek where tenderness is felt.
Frontal sinusitis causes pain in the forehead and vertex, supplied by the supraorbital nerve, and is not related to molar tooth infections.
While the maxillary sinus is correct, the supraorbital nerve supplies the frontal sinus and forehead, not the maxillary region.
The ethmoid sinuses are located between the nose and orbit; while the nasociliary nerve is involved in the region, ethmoiditis typically causes pain between the eyes, not in the cheek or teeth.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1776 (Book Page): The infraorbital nerve innervates the maxillary sinus, and in this case, pain is referred to the upper jaw, including the teeth. ... The maxillary sinus can be examined for tenderness by pressing the finger against the anterior wall of the maxilla below the inferior orbital margin.

category: Describe the course and distribution of olfactory nerve in reference to olfactory pathway
statement: A first-year medical student is studying the osteology of the skull base in relation to cranial nerve exits. Which specific bony feature provides the anatomical passage for the numerous bundles of the olfactory nerve (CN I) as they traverse from the nasal cavity into the cranial cavity?
options: Foramen magnum of the occipital bone
Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
Foramen rotundum of the sphenoid bone
Hypoglossal canal
Superior orbital fissure
correctOption: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
optionExplanations: The foramen magnum is the largest opening in the skull, transmitting the medulla oblongata, vertebral arteries, and spinal accessory nerve.

The cribriform plate is a sieve-like structure of the ethmoid bone that forms part of the roof of the nasal cavity. Its small perforations allow the olfactory nerve filaments (fila olfactoria) to pass from the olfactory epithelium to the olfactory bulb.
The foramen rotundum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid and transmits the maxillary nerve (V2), not the olfactory nerve.
The hypoglossal canal is situated in the occipital bone and transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to the muscles of the tongue.
The superior orbital fissure is a slit between the wings of the sphenoid that transmits CN III, IV, VI, and V1; it is not related to the olfactory pathway.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1493 (Book Page): The upper surface of the cribriform plate supports the olfactory bulbs, and the small perforations in the cribriform plate permit passage of the olfactory nerves.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: Following a thyroidectomy, a patient is observed to have a vocal fold that remains fixed in a position midway between abduction and adduction. What is the specific pathophysiological consequence of this unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
options: The vocal fold becomes hyper-resonant due to vocalis spasm.
The vocal fold is forced into maximal abduction.
The vocal fold assumes a median position due to cricothyroid activity.
The vocal fold is fixed just lateral to the midline.
The vocal fold is displaced superiorly into the laryngeal vestibule.
correctOption: The vocal fold is fixed just lateral to the midline.
optionExplanations: The vocalis muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve; therefore, a complete section would lead to flaccidity and atrophy, not spasm.
Maximal abduction is not possible because the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor of the vocal folds, is paralyzed in a recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion.
The median position is characteristically seen in partial lesions of the recurrent laryngeal nerve where abductor fibers are more severely affected than adductor fibers.

Correct. In a complete unilateral section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, all intrinsic muscles of the larynx on that side (except the cricothyroid) are paralyzed. This causes the vocal fold to sit in a 'cadaveric' or neutral position midway between abduction and adduction, just lateral to the midline.
Vocal folds are anchored by the vocal ligaments and laryngeal cartilages; a nerve lesion affects muscle tone and movement but does not cause superior vertical displacement into the vestibule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction. It lies just laterally to the midline.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Motor Innervation of the External Nose
statement: A patient is diagnosed with an isolated lesion of the facial nerve (CN VII) as it exits the stylomastoid foramen. Which of the following clinical signs would be most specifically related to the external nose?
options: Paralysis of the muscles that dilate or compress the nostrils.
Loss of general sensation over the bridge of the nose.
Inability to smell (anosmia) due to nerve compression.
Numbness over the lateral side of the nose.
Loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
correctOption: Paralysis of the muscles that dilate or compress the nostrils.
optionExplanations: Correct. The muscles of the external nose (nasalis, dilator naris) are muscles of facial expression and are supplied by the motor branches of CN VII.
General sensation over the bridge of the nose is mediated by the trigeminal nerve (V1), not the facial nerve.
Anosmia is related to the olfactory nerve (CN I), which is entirely distinct from the facial nerve.
Numbness over the side of the nose involves the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve, not the facial nerve.

While the facial nerve does mediate taste via the chorda tympani, this function is lost if the lesion is proximal to the stylomastoid foramen, but it is not a sign involving the external nose anatomy.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1764 (Book Page): The nasalis (compressor naris), dilator naris, and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi are the primary muscles of the external nose. All are facial muscles innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: Danger Triangle of the Face and Venous Drainage
statement: A 24-year-old patient presents with a deep infection in the 'danger area' of the face. If the infection spreads intracranially via the venous system, which of the following is the most likely anatomical pathway to the cavernous sinus?
options: Facial vein to the Retromandibular vein to the Sigmoid sinus
Facial vein to the Superior Ophthalmic vein through the Superior Orbital Fissure
Occipital vein to the Suboccipital plexus to the Transverse sinus
Superficial Temporal vein to the Maxillary vein through the Foramen Spinosum
Angular vein to the Pterygoid plexus through the Foramen Ovale
correctOption: Facial vein to the Superior Ophthalmic vein through the Superior Orbital Fissure
optionExplanations: The Retromandibular vein primarily drains toward the external and internal jugular systems and is not the direct route to the cavernous sinus.
Correct. The facial vein communicates with the superior ophthalmic vein at the medial angle of the eye, which then drains through the superior orbital fissure into the cavernous sinus.
The Occipital vein drains the back of the scalp and neck; it is not related to the 'danger area' of the face (nose/upper lip).
The Foramen Spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery; the Superficial Temporal vein drains into the retromandibular system.
While the facial vein connects to the pterygoid plexus via the deep facial vein, the standard 'danger triangle' route emphasized in clinical anatomy is via the ophthalmic veins.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1533 (Book Page): The facial vein is formed at the medial angle of the eye by the union of the supraorbital and supratrochlear veins (see Fig. 12.19D). It connects to the superior ophthalmic vein directly through the supraorbital vein. The facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus by way of the superior ophthalmic vein (see Fig. 12.28). This anastomosis is of great clinical importance because it provides a pathway for the spread of infection from the face to the cavernous sinus.

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Medial Nasal Wall
statement: Which specific structure constitutes the anterior-most portion of the medial wall of the nasal cavity?
options: Nasal bone
Cribriform plate
Septal cartilage
Perpendicular plate of ethmoid
Vomer
correctOption: Septal cartilage
optionExplanations: Nasal bones contribute to the bridge of the nose and the roof of the cavity, but are not part of the medial septal wall itself.
The cribriform plate is part of the ethmoid bone that forms the roof, not the anterior medial wall.
The nasal septum (medial wall) is composed of bone posteriorly and cartilage anteriorly. The septal cartilage is the flexible portion that forms the front of the septum.
The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the superior and posterior-superior parts of the septum, but not the anterior-most part.
The vomer forms the posterior and inferior bony portion of the nasal septum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1767 (Book Page): The septal cartilage forms the anterior part [of the medial wall].

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
statement: A patient presents with chronic unilateral nasal obstruction. Clinical examination reveals a significant septal deviation to the left. Which pathophysiological mechanism explains the common finding of mucosal thickening on the right lateral nasal wall in this individual?
options: Ischemic atrophy of the turbinates due to reduced airflow
Direct mechanical trauma from the deviated septal cartilage
Compensatory hypertrophy of the right conchae to regulate airflow
Sympathetic denervation of the right nasal mucosa
Decreased ciliary motility on the side of the deviation
correctOption: Compensatory hypertrophy of the right conchae to regulate airflow
optionExplanations: Reduced airflow typically leads to decreased mucosal activity, but not ischemic atrophy of the turbinates in the context of septal deviation.

Mechanical trauma only occurs on the side where the septum is deviated and makes contact with the lateral wall, not on the contralateral side showing thickening/hypertrophy at the lateral wall boundaries; also, the question specifies the right wall while the deviation is to the left (left septum-wall contact).

When the septum deviates to one side, the contralateral nasal cavity becomes larger. The lateral wall (conchae) often undergoes compensatory hypertrophy to increase surface area and regulate the moisture and temperature of the increased volume of air.
Septal deviation does not cause localized sympathetic denervation of the lateral nasal wall.
While ciliary motility might be affected by environmental factors, it is not the primary mechanism of wall structural changes opposite a deviation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1767 (Book Page): The septum rarely lies in the midline, thus increasing the size of one half of the nasal cavity and decreasing the size of the other.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Dermatomal Contrast of External Nose (V1 vs V2)
statement: Following a facial injury, a patient exhibits intact sensation on the bridge and crest of the nose but demonstrates localized anesthesia on the lateral ala and the skin of the cheek. This sensory contrast suggests a selective lesion to which specific nerve?
options: Infraorbital nerve
External nasal nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Supraorbital nerve
Infratrochlear nerve
correctOption: Infraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: The infraorbital nerve (a branch of V2) provides sensory supply to the side (ala) of the nose and the cheek; anesthesia in these specific areas confirms its involvement.
The external nasal nerve (V1) supplies the bridge and crest of the nose; sensation here was described as intact, ruling out a lesion of this nerve.
The zygomaticofacial nerve (V2) supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheek but does not extend its supply to the side of the nose (ala).
The supraorbital nerve (V1) supplies the skin of the forehead and the scalp up to the vertex, but it does not supply the lateral ala of the nose.
The infratrochlear nerve (V1) also supplies the bridge and crest; since these areas retain sensation, this nerve is not the site of the primary lesion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1765 (Book Page): The infratrochlear and external nasal branches of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) innervate the bridge and crest of the nose. The infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) supplies the side of the nose.

category: List the paranasal sinuses giving their locations, openings, neurovascular supply and clinical significance
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of Ethmoid Sinus Relations
statement: A 35-year-old patient with a severe upper respiratory tract infection presents with periorbital swelling and pain on eye movement. The physician suspects orbital cellulitis secondary to paranasal sinusitis. Which anatomical feature of the paranasal sinuses allows for the most direct spread of infection into the orbital cavity?
options: The proximity of the maxillary sinus floor to the molar teeth
The drainage of the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus
The thick bony septum of the sphenoid sinus
The extremely thin plate of bone separating the ethmoid sinuses from the orbit
The communication between the frontal sinus and the infundibulum
correctOption: The extremely thin plate of bone separating the ethmoid sinuses from the orbit
optionExplanations: The relationship between the maxillary sinus and the molar teeth is a common route for dental infections to enter the sinus, but it is not the primary route for sinus-to-orbital spread.
The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the eye to the nose; while it connects the regions, it is not the anatomical pathway for the spread of ethmoid-originating cellulitis into the orbit.
The sphenoid sinus is located within the body of the sphenoid bone, separated by a bony septum, but it is not the most common route for direct orbital spread compared to the ethmoid.

The ethmoid sinuses are separated from the medial wall of the orbit by the lamina papyracea, an exceptionally thin bony plate. This anatomical vulnerability allows infections to bypass typical barriers and enter the orbital fat.
While the frontal sinus is related to the roof of the orbit, the ethmoid sinus wall (lamina papyracea) is famously thin and presents the least resistance to the spread of infection.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1775 (Book Page): They [ethmoid sinuses] are separated from the orbit by an extremely thin plate of bone, and infection can readily spread from the sinuses into the orbit.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: A 22-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with a deep stab wound in the posterior triangle of the neck. On examination, he is unable to shrug his shoulder on the affected side, and there is visible wasting of the muscle between the neck and the shoulder. Which nerve has likely been lesioned?
options: Spinal part of the accessory nerve
Greater occipital nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Phrenic nerve
correctOption: Spinal part of the accessory nerve
optionExplanations: Correct. The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle superficially to supply the trapezius. Paralysis of the trapezius leads to an inability to shrug the shoulders and muscle wasting.
Incorrect. The greater occipital nerve is a sensory nerve (C2) to the scalp; its lesion causes sensory loss or neuralgia but no motor deficit like shoulder dropping.
Incorrect. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Lesion would cause hoarseness or voice changes, not muscle wasting in the neck/shoulder.
Incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles. Lesion would result in tongue deviation, not weakness of the trapezius muscle in the neck.
Incorrect. The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm. Lesion would cause respiratory symptoms (paralysis of half the diaphragm) but not affect shoulder shrugging.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve... the spinal root runs downward and laterally and enters the deep surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle... and then crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to supply the trapezius muscle... clinical examination of this nerve involves asking the patient to rotate the head... then, the patient is asked to shrug the shoulders, causing the trapezius muscles to come into action.

category: List the paranasal sinuses giving their locations, openings, neurovascular supply and clinical significance
statement: In which specific location does the maxillary sinus normally drain within the lateral wall of the nasal cavity?
options: The inferior meatus, guarded by a fold of mucous membrane
The superior meatus, below the superior concha
The hiatus semilunaris within the middle meatus
The summit of the bulla ethmoidalis
The sphenoethmoidal recess, above the superior concha
correctOption: The hiatus semilunaris within the middle meatus
optionExplanations: The inferior meatus is the site for the termination of the nasolacrimal duct, not the paranasal sinuses. It is protected by a mucosal fold to prevent air reflux.
The superior meatus receives the drainage from the posterior ethmoidal air cells, but it does not communicate with the maxillary sinus.
The maxillary sinus ostium is located in the hiatus semilunaris, which is a curved groove in the middle meatus situated inferior to the bulla ethmoidalis.
The bulla ethmoidalis is an elevation in the middle meatus formed by the middle ethmoidal air cells, which typically open on its upper border or surface, not the maxillary sinus.
The sphenoethmoidal recess is the specific drainage site for the sphenoid sinus, located at the highest and most posterior aspect of the nasal cavity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris.

category: Describe the course and distribution of olfactory nerve in reference to olfactory pathway
statement: During a neuroanatomy lecture, the mechanism of the olfactory pathway is discussed. Which of the following best describes the multi-step physiological course of the olfactory nerve fibers as they travel from the nasal cavity into the cranial cavity?
options: Fibers pass through the optic canal to synapse in the thalamus
Axons pass through the superior orbital fissure to the midbrain
The nerve descends through the palatine canal to join the maxillary nerve
Bundles of fibers traverse the foramen rotundum to reach the temporal lobe
Nerve bundles pass through the cribriform plate to enter the olfactory bulb
correctOption: Nerve bundles pass through the cribriform plate to enter the olfactory bulb
optionExplanations: The optic canal is reserved for the optic nerve (CN II) and ophthalmic artery; olfactory nerves do not use this passage.
The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, IV, V1, and VI; the olfactory nerve enters the anterior cranial fossa directly via the cribriform plate, not the orbit.
The olfactory nerve is a purely sensory ascending nerve and does not descend through the palatine canal or join the maxillary nerve's distribution.
The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2); it is not part of the olfactory nerve's course to the bulb.
Olfactory nerve fibers are organized into bundles that exit the nasal cavity through the perforations of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to synapse in the olfactory bulb.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1660 (Book Page): Bundles of these olfactory nerve fibers pass through the openings of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to enter the olfactory bulb in the cranial cavity.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
statement: A 40-year-old patient presents with a chronic ulcer on the ala of the nose. The biopsy reveals basal cell carcinoma. In planning the excision, the surgeon considers the blood supply to this specific area. Which artery provides the primary vascularization to the ala and the lower part of the nasal septum?
options: Ophthalmic artery
Ethmoidal artery
Internal carotid artery
Maxillary artery
Facial artery
correctOption: Facial artery
optionExplanations: The ophthalmic artery primarily supplies the bridge and crest of the nose via its terminal branches like the dorsal nasal artery.
The ethmoidal arteries (anterior and posterior) are branches of the ophthalmic artery and supply the internal nasal cavity and the dorsal bridge, not the lateral ala.
The internal carotid artery supplies the bridge of the nose indirectly through the ophthalmic artery, but the ala is an external carotid territory (facial artery).
While the maxillary artery provides supply to the nasal cavity (sphenopalatine artery), the external ala is primarily served by the facial system.
The facial artery provides specific branches (lateral nasal and superior labial) that are the main sources of blood for the ala and the inferior portion of the septum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1764 (Book Page)-1765: Branches from the facial artery supply the skin of the ala and the lower part of the septum.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Sensory Innervation of the External Nose
statement: During a sensory examination, a clinician notes reduced sensation along the side of a patient's nose. Which nerve is most likely involved in this deficit?
options: External nasal nerve
Nasopalatine nerve
Infraorbital nerve
Infratrochlear nerve
Zygomaticotemporal nerve
correctOption: Infraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: The external nasal nerve (V1) supplies the crest of the nose down to the tip, rather than the lateral side.
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the nasal septum and the anterior part of the hard palate, not the external skin of the nose.
The infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary division (V2), is specifically responsible for the sensory innervation of the side of the nose.
The infratrochlear nerve (V1) supplies the bridge and crest of the nose, not the lateral side.
The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the skin over the temple and does not provide sensation to the nasal region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1765 (Book Page): The infratrochlear and external nasal branches of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) innervate the bridge and crest of the nose. The infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) supplies the side of the nose.

category: List the paranasal sinuses giving their locations, openings, neurovascular supply and clinical significance
coreConcept: Anatomic Boundaries and Spread of Pathology
statement: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with a tumor originating in the ethmoid air cells. The clinician is concerned about the spread of the tumor into the orbital cavity. What anatomical feature of the ethmoid sinus makes this spread particularly likely?
options: The presence of the nasolacrimal duct within the sinus
The extremely thin plate of bone separating the sinus from the orbit
The shared nerve supply via the infraorbital nerve
The direct communication through the superior orbital fissure
The absence of a bony wall between the ethmoid and the orbit
correctOption: The extremely thin plate of bone separating the sinus from the orbit
optionExplanations: The nasolacrimal duct is located in the lacrimal bone and maxilla, opening into the inferior meatus, not within the ethmoid sinus.
The medial wall of the orbit is formed by the orbital plate of the ethmoid bone, which is so thin (lamina papyracea) that it offers little resistance to the spread of infection or neoplasm.
The ethmoid sinuses are supplied by ethmoidal nerves (V1), whereas the infraorbital nerve is a branch of V2; they do not share the same nerve supply.
The superior orbital fissure is a communication between the middle cranial fossa and the orbit, not between the ethmoid sinus and the orbit.
There is a bony wall (the lamina papyracea), but it is not absent; it is simply extremely thin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1775 (Book Page): The ethmoid bone houses three pairs of sinuses... They are separated from the orbit by an extremely thin plate of bone, and infection can readily spread from the sinuses into the orbit.

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
statement: Regarding the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity's lateral wall, what is the clinical significance of the structure that opens into this space?
options: It serves as the exit for the maxillary nerve.
It allows the drainage of tears from the conjunctival sac.
It acts as a resonator for the voice.
It contains the olfactory receptors for the sense of smell.
It provides a pathway for the frontal sinus to drain.
correctOption: It allows the drainage of tears from the conjunctival sac.
optionExplanations: The maxillary nerve branches (like the infraorbital) enter the cavity through other foramina (like the sphenopalatine foramen or infraorbital canal), not the inferior meatus.
Correct. The nasolacrimal duct, which carries tears from the eye, opens into the anterior part of the inferior meatus. This is why the nose 'runs' when a person cries.
The paranasal sinuses (Maxillary, Frontal, Sphenoid, Ethmoid) act as resonators, not the nasolacrimal duct.
The olfactory receptors are located in the roof and superior part of the cavity, not the inferior meatus.
The frontal sinus drains into the middle meatus via the infundibulum and hiatus semilunaris.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): The inferior meatus lies below the inferior concha and receives the opening of the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct, which is guarded by a fold of mucous membrane.

category: List the paranasal sinuses giving their locations, openings, neurovascular supply and clinical significance
statement: An elite surgeon is planning a transnasal approach to the sella turcica to resect a pituitary macroadenoma. To reach the hypophyseal fossa from the nasal cavity, which specific anatomical landmark must the surgeon traverse after passing the posterior roof of the nose?
options: Bulla ethmoidalis
Hiatus semilunaris
Inferior meatus
Sphenoethmoidal recess
Superior meatus
correctOption: Sphenoethmoidal recess
optionExplanations: The bulla ethmoidalis is a rounded swelling in the middle meatus formed by middle ethmoidal air sinuses; it is unrelated to the sphenoid bone or the sella turcica.
The hiatus semilunaris is a curved opening in the middle meatus that receives the maxillary sinus and frontal sinus via the infundibulum; it is too anterior and lateral for a pituitary approach.
The inferior meatus lies below the inferior concha and solely receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct; it does not provide access to the paranasal sinuses or the cranial base.

The sphenoethmoidal recess is the specific area above the superior concha where the sphenoid sinus opens. In transnasal surgery, the surgeon traverses the sphenoid sinus within the body of the sphenoid to enter the sella turcica.
The superior meatus is located below the superior concha and receives the openings of the posterior ethmoid sinuses, not the sphenoid sinus used in transnasal surgery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): [The sphenoethmoidal recess is a small area above the superior concha. It receives the opening of the sphenoid air sinus.]

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
statement: A patient presents with localized anesthesia on the skin of the lateral side of the nose, but sensation on the bridge and the tip of the nose remains intact. Which nerve is most likely involved in this sensory deficit?
options: Infraorbital nerve
Supraorbital nerve
Supratrochlear nerve
External nasal nerve
Infratrochlear nerve
correctOption: Infraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: The infraorbital nerve, a continuation of the maxillary division (V2), is specifically responsible for the sensory innervation of the side of the nose.
The supraorbital nerve (V1) supplies the skin of the forehead and the scalp up to the vertex, as well as the upper eyelid.
The supratrochlear nerve (V1) supplies the skin of the lower forehead and the medial aspect of the upper eyelid.
The external nasal nerve (V1) supplies the bridge and crest of the nose down to the tip; its loss would affect those areas, not the lateral side.
The infratrochlear nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic division (V1), supplies the bridge and medial part of the eyelids, not the side of the nose.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1765 (Book Page): The infratrochlear and external nasal branches of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) innervate the bridge and crest of the nose. The infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) supplies the side of the nose.

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: Skull Base Fractures and Nerve Deficits
statement: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a high-impact motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals leakage of cerebrospinal fluid and blood from the left external auditory meatus. He is unable to close his left eye tightly and has lost hearing in the left ear. Which anatomical region of the skull was most likely fractured?
options: Occipital condyles in the posterior cranial fossa
Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
Petrous part of the temporal bone in the middle cranial fossa
Greater wing of the sphenoid at the foramen rotundum
Orbital plate of the frontal bone
correctOption: Petrous part of the temporal bone in the middle cranial fossa
optionExplanations: Posterior cranial fossa fractures involving occipital condyles might affect the hypoglossal nerve, but would not typically cause bleeding from the ear or facial nerve palsy.
A cribriform plate fracture typically leads to CSF rhinorrhea (leakage through the nose) and anosmia, not ear symptoms.

Fractures of the middle cranial fossa often involve the petrous temporal bone, which contains the internal acoustic meatus housing CN VII (facial) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear), explaining the facial palsy, deafness, and CSF otorrhea.
The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2); its injury would cause mid-face anesthesia but not hearing loss or facial expression paralysis.
Fractures of the orbital plate of the frontal bone result in periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) and subconjunctival hemorrhage, not auditory meatus leakage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1498 (Book Page): Fractures of the middle cranial fossa are common... The seventh and eighth cranial nerves may be involved as they pass through the petrous part of the temporal bone. The leakage of cerebrospinal fluid and blood from the external auditory meatus is common.

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
statement: A patient with a chronic ethmoidal sinus infection develops symptoms of orbital cellulitis, including pain and swelling behind the eye. Which anatomical feature of the lateral nasal wall explains the rapid spread of infection in this case?
options: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid fails to fuse with the vomer, creating a gap
The thickness of the inferior concha prevents drainage, forcing pus into the orbit
The ethmoid sinuses are separated from the orbit by an extremely thin plate of bone
The nasolacrimal duct serves as a conduit for bacteria to travel from the inferior meatus to the globe
The sphenopalatine foramen provides a direct open channel to the orbital fat
correctOption: The ethmoid sinuses are separated from the orbit by an extremely thin plate of bone
optionExplanations: The perpendicular plate is part of the septum (medial wall) and its fusion with the vomer does not affect the lateral wall's relationship with the orbit.
The inferior concha is unrelated to the ethmoid sinus drainage and is located too inferiorly to influence orbital spread.

The 'lamina papyracea' (thin plate of the ethmoid bone) is the only barrier between the ethmoid air cells and the orbital cavity. Its paper-thin nature allows infections to erode through or spread via small vascular channels easily.
The nasolacrimal duct drains tears *from* the eye *to* the nose; it is not the primary route for ethmoid sinus infections to reach the orbit.
The sphenopalatine foramen connects the nasal cavity to the pterygopalatine fossa, not directly to the orbit.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1775 (Book Page): They [ethmoid sinuses] are separated from the orbit by an extremely thin plate of bone, and infection can readily spread from the sinuses into the orbit.

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Nasal Roof
statement: During a transsphenoidal surgical approach to the pituitary gland, the surgeon must traverse the nasal cavity to reach the sella turcica. Through which specific anatomical boundary of the nasal cavity is the entry into the sphenoid bone made?
options: The posterior-most sloping part of the roof (body of the sphenoid).
The anterior part of the medial wall (septal cartilage).
The anterior part of the floor (palatine process of the maxilla).
The lateral wall through the middle nasal concha.
The inferior meatus of the lateral wall.
correctOption: The posterior-most sloping part of the roof (body of the sphenoid).
optionExplanations: The posterior part of the roof of the nasal cavity is formed by the body of the sphenoid bone. In transsphenoidal surgery, the surgeon follows the roof posteriorly to pierce the sphenoid bone to reach the pituitary gland.
The septal cartilage is the anterior portion of the medial wall. While the septum is often deviated to the side during surgery, the entry point into the cranium is through the roof/sphenoid body.
The floor of the nasal cavity is too inferior and consists of the hard palate; it does not lead to the sphenoid bone or sella turcica.
The lateral wall contains the conchae and leads to the sinuses, but a lateral approach would not provide the direct midline path required for transsphenoidal surgery.
The inferior meatus is on the lateral wall and is the most inferior passage; it does not align with the sphenoid sinus or the sella turcica.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): The roof is narrow and is formed... posteriorly by the downward sloping body of the sphenoid. Page 1770 (Book Page): A convenient surgical path to the pituitary gland is a transnasal approach... The surgeon pierces the sphenoid, traverses the sphenoid air sinus, and enters the sella turcica from below.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
coreConcept: Hypoglossal Nerve Lesion and Genioglossus Action
statement: A patient presents with atrophy of the right side of the tongue and fasciculations. When asked to protrude the tongue, it deviates significantly to the right. Which cranial nerve lesion is most likely responsible for this clinical finding?
options: Left Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Right Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Left Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Right Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Right Trigeminal nerve (Mandibular division)
correctOption: Right Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory and taste to the posterior third of the tongue but does not control its motor protrusion.
The right hypoglossal nerve supplies the right genioglossus muscle. When paralyzed, the unopposed left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the side of the lesion (the right).
A left hypoglossal nerve lesion would cause the tongue to deviate to the left side because the healthy right genioglossus would push the tongue toward the weak left side.
Lesions of the glossopharyngeal nerve affect the gag reflex and taste on the posterior third, not the motor function of the genioglossus.

The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication, not the muscles of the tongue (except the mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric which are in the floor of the mouth).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The patient is asked to put out the tongue, and if a lesion of the nerve is present, it will be noted that the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side... One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue's deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Trigeminal Nerve Dermatomes of the Nose
statement: A 24-year-old boxer presents with an acute injury to the external nose. Physical examination reveals anesthesia over the bridge and crest of the nose extending to the tip. There is no loss of sensation on the cheeks or lateral sides of the nose. Which specific nerve division is involved in this deficit?
options: Maxillary division of Trigeminal nerve
Buccal branch of Facial nerve
Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve
Mandibular division of Trigeminal nerve
Zygomatic branch of Facial nerve
correctOption: Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve
optionExplanations: The maxillary division (V2) supplies the lateral side of the nose and upper lip; since sensation there is intact, V2 is not the primary lesion site.
The buccal branch of the facial nerve is motor to the buccinator and upper lip muscles, not sensory.
The ophthalmic division (V1) provides the infratrochlear and external nasal branches which are responsible for the bridge, crest, and tip of the nose.
The mandibular division (V3) supplies the lower face and chin, not the bridge or tip of the nose.
The zygomatic branch of the facial nerve is motor to the orbicularis oculi, not sensory to the nasal skin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1765 (Book Page): The infratrochlear and external nasal branches of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) innervate the bridge and crest of the nose.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
statement: Which muscle is responsible for the dilation of the nostrils during forced inspiration, and what is its innervation?
options: Levator labii superioris; Infraorbital nerve
Nasalis (compressor naris); Maxillary nerve
Nasalis (compressor naris); Facial nerve
Dilator naris; Ophthalmic nerve
Dilator naris; Facial nerve
correctOption: Dilator naris; Facial nerve
optionExplanations: Levator labii superioris acts mainly on the upper lip; while its 'alaeque nasi' portion assists the nose, its innervation is the facial nerve, and the infraorbital nerve is sensory, not motor.
The nasalis (compressor naris) functions to compress the nostrils, not dilate them, and it is innervated by the facial nerve, not the maxillary nerve.
The nasalis (compressor naris) is innervated by the facial nerve, but its action is to close or compress the nostrils, not dilate them.
While the dilator naris does dilate the nostrils, it is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII); the ophthalmic nerve (V1) provides only sensory fibers to the nose.
The dilator naris is the specific muscle for nostril dilation, and like all muscles of facial expression, it is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1764 (Book Page): The nasalis ( compressor naris ), dilator naris , and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi are the primary muscles of the external nose. All are facial muscles innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
statement: In contrasting the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, into which specific meatus does the posterior ethmoidal sinus drain, compared to the middle ethmoidal sinus?
options: Posterior into the Middle meatus; Middle into the Inferior meatus
Posterior into the Superior meatus; Middle into the Middle meatus (Bulla ethmoidalis)
Posterior into the Sphenoethmoidal recess; Middle into the Middle meatus
Posterior into the Superior meatus; Middle into the Infundibulum
Posterior into the Inferior meatus; Middle into the Superior meatus
correctOption: Posterior into the Superior meatus; Middle into the Middle meatus (Bulla ethmoidalis)
optionExplanations: The middle meatus receives the anterior and middle ethmoidal sinuses, and the inferior meatus is dedicated to the nasolacrimal duct.
Correct anatomical contrast. The posterior ethmoid cells drain into the superior meatus, while the middle ethmoid cells drain directly onto the bulla ethmoidalis in the middle meatus.
The sphenoethmoidal recess receives the sphenoid sinus, not the posterior ethmoidal sinus.
The infundibulum is the drainage pathway for the frontal sinus and anterior ethmoidal cells, not the middle ethmoidal cells.
The inferior meatus receives only the nasolacrimal duct, never any of the ethmoidal sinuses.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): The superior meatus lies below the superior concha. It receives the openings of the posterior ethmoid sinuses. The middle meatus lies below the middle concha. It has a rounded swelling called the bulla ethmoidalis that is formed by the middle ethmoidal air sinuses, which open on its upper border.

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: UMN vs LMN Facial Nerve Lesion
statement: A patient presents with a 'mask-like' paralysis of the entire right side of the face. Which clinical finding would most effectively distinguish this as a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve (Bell's Palsy) rather than an upper motor neuron (stroke-related) lesion?
options: Inability to close the right eye and loss of the forehead wrinkling on the right side
Hyperacusis due to paralysis of the tensor tympani muscle
Sagging of the angle of the mouth on the right side with preserved forehead movement
Loss of general sensation from the skin over the angle of the jaw and parotid gland
Deviation of the tongue to the right side upon protrusion
correctOption: Inability to close the right eye and loss of the forehead wrinkling on the right side
optionExplanations: In a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion, the entire ipsilateral half of the face is affected, including the forehead. This is because the LMN is the final common pathway for all facial expression on that side.

While hyperacusis can occur in facial nerve lesions due to stapedius muscle paralysis, the tensor tympani is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3). A facial nerve lesion does not affect the tensor tympani.
Sparing of the forehead is characteristic of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, as the forehead muscles receive bilateral innervation from both cerebral cortices.
The skin over the angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not the facial nerve, so this would not localize a facial nerve lesion.
Tongue deviation is a sign of a hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) lesion, not a facial nerve (CN VII) lesion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): An upper motor neuron lesion (involvement of the pyramidal tracts) will leave the upper part of the face normal because the neurons supplying this part of the face receive corticobulbar fibers from both cerebral cortices. However, in patients with a lower motor neuron lesion, all the muscles on the affected side of the face will be paralyzed.

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
statement: A 28-year-old male arrives at the Emergency Department following a traumatic head injury. He has clear fluid leaking from the nose (positive for beta-2 transferrin) and bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'). Based on the anatomical features of the skull base, which structure is most likely fractured?
options: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa
The greater wing of the sphenoid at the level of the foramen ovale
The petrous part of the temporal bone in the middle cranial fossa
The squamous part of the temporal bone at the pterion
The basilar part of the occipital bone near the foramen magnum
correctOption: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa
optionExplanations: The cribriform plate is the thin floor of the anterior cranial fossa; its fracture tears the meninges, leading to CSF rhinorrhea. The associated orbital plate fracture causes blood to track into the periorbital tissues, creating 'raccoon eyes'.
Fractures at the foramen ovale would affect the mandibular nerve (V3) but typically do not cause CSF rhinorrhea or raccoon eyes.
Fractures of the petrous temporal bone usually present with CSF otorrhea (fluid from the ear) and potentially CN VII or VIII deficits, not rhinorrhea.
Injury at the pterion commonly causes an epidural hematoma due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery but does not typically present with CSF rhinorrhea or raccoon eyes.
The basilar part of the occipital bone is in the posterior fossa; injuries here might cause 'Battle's sign' (ecchymosis over the mastoid) and affect lower cranial nerves (IX-XII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1498 (Book Page): Anterior Cranial Fossa Fractures. The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone may be damaged in fractures of the anterior cranial fossa... The patient will have bleeding from the nose (epistaxis) and leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nose (cerebrospinal rhinorrhea). Fractures involving the orbital plate of the frontal bone result in hemorrhage beneath the conjunctiva... causing exophthalmos.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Sequential Sensory Pathway of the External Nose
statement: Tracing the neurovascular pathway of a stimulus from the skin of the nasal tip to the central nervous system, which sequence correctly identifies the hierarchy of neural structures involved?
options: Nasal tip -> Infraorbital nerve -> Maxillary nerve -> Trigeminal ganglion
Nasal tip -> Infratrochlear nerve -> Nasociliary nerve -> Maxillary nerve
Nasal tip -> Lacrimal nerve -> Ophthalmic nerve -> Trigeminal ganglion
Nasal tip -> External nasal nerve -> Anterior ethmoidal nerve -> Nasociliary nerve -> Ophthalmic nerve
Nasal tip -> Buccal nerve -> Mandibular nerve -> Trigeminal ganglion
correctOption: Nasal tip -> External nasal nerve -> Anterior ethmoidal nerve -> Nasociliary nerve -> Ophthalmic nerve
optionExplanations: The infraorbital nerve is a branch of V2 and supplies the side of the nose, not the tip. Sensory fibers from the tip do not travel via the maxillary nerve.
The infratrochlear nerve supplies the bridge of the nose, not the tip. Additionally, the nasociliary nerve belongs to the ophthalmic division, not the maxillary nerve.
The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral part of the upper eyelid and the lacrimal gland; it has no sensory distribution to the nasal tip.

The sensory pathway for the nasal tip begins at the external nasal nerve, which is the cutaneous continuation of the anterior ethmoidal nerve. The anterior ethmoidal nerve is a branch of the nasociliary nerve, which is a major branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.
The buccal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division (V3) and supplies the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek, not the nasal tip.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1765 (Book Page): The external nasal nerve ... supplies the skin on the side of the nose down as far as the tip. [and] Page 1582 (Book Page): The nasociliary nerve ... ends by dividing into the anterior ethmoidal and infratrochlear nerves. ... The anterior ethmoidal nerve ... appears on the face as the external nasal branch.

category: List the paranasal sinuses giving their locations, openings, neurovascular supply and clinical significance
statement: An adult patient presents with acute sinusitis. Upon examination, the physician notes that the drainage of the largest paranasal sinus is obstructed. Where does this specific sinus typically open into the nasal cavity?
options: Inferior meatus
Infundibulum of the middle meatus
Hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus
Superior meatus
Sphenoethmoidal recess
correctOption: Hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus
optionExplanations: The inferior meatus receives the opening of the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct, not any of the paranasal sinuses.
The infundibulum is a funnel-shaped channel in the middle meatus that is continuous with the frontal sinus, rather than the maxillary sinus.
The maxillary sinus, which is the largest paranasal sinus, drains into the nasal cavity through the hiatus semilunaris located within the middle meatus.
The superior meatus receives the openings of the posterior ethmoid sinuses, not the maxillary sinus.
The sphenoethmoidal recess is a small area above the superior concha that specifically receives the opening of the sphenoid air sinus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
coreConcept: LMN vs UMN Facial Nerve Lesion
statement: A patient presents with a 'masklike' expression on one side of the face, inability to close the eye, and dribbling of saliva from the corner of the mouth. Which diagnostic contrast identifies this as a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve rather than an upper motor neuron lesion?
options: The muscles of the lower face are paralyzed.
The patient can still whistle but cannot smile.
Taste is preserved on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The muscles of the upper part of the face are paralyzed.
The lower eyelid is drooping on the affected side.
correctOption: The muscles of the upper part of the face are paralyzed.
optionExplanations: Paralysis of the lower face occurs in both UMN and LMN lesions because the lower face receives only contralateral UMN innervation.
Whistling requires the buccinator (facial nerve) and orbicularis oris; in a complete LMN lesion, the patient cannot whistle or smile on the affected side.

Taste preservation depends on the site of the lesion relative to the chorda tympani and is not the primary factor used to differentiate LMN from UMN cortical lesions in the clinical exam of facial muscles.

Correct. In an LMN lesion (e.g., Bell's palsy), the entire half of the face is affected including the forehead. In a UMN lesion, the forehead (upper face) is spared because the nucleus for the upper face receives bilateral cortical input.
Drooping of the lower eyelid can occur in both, though it is more pronounced in LMN lesions; however, it is not the definitive diagnostic differentiator.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1685 (Book Page): In patients with a lower motor neuron lesion, all the muscles on the affected side of the face will be paralyzed. . . . it should be remembered that the part of the facial nerve nucleus that controls the muscles of the upper part of the face receives corticobulbar fibers from both cerebral cortices. Therefore, in patients with an upper motor neuron lesion, only the muscles of the lower part of the face will be paralyzed.

category: Describe the course and distribution of olfactory nerve in reference to olfactory pathway
statement: A 25-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a severe head injury in a motorcycle accident. Examination reveals 'raccoon eyes' (periorbital ecchymosis) and a clear, watery discharge from the right nostril that tests positive for glucose. The patient also reports a total inability to smell. Which anatomical structure has most likely been fractured to cause this clinical presentation?
options: The perpendicular plate of the palatine bone
The sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
The lesser wing of the sphenoid bone
The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
The squamous part of the temporal bone
correctOption: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
optionExplanations: The palatine bone forms part of the hard palate and the lateral wall of the nasal cavity far posterior; its fracture would not typically lead to anosmia or anterior fossa CSF leaks.
Damage to the sella turcica is often associated with pituitary dysfunction or visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia) due to proximity to the optic chiasm, not nasal CSF leakage.
The lesser wing of the sphenoid forms the posterior boundary of the anterior cranial fossa; while near the optic canal, its fracture is less likely to cause anosmia than the central cribriform plate.
Fracture of the cribriform plate in the anterior cranial fossa tears the olfactory nerve filaments passing through it (causing anosmia) and the overlying meninges (causing CSF rhinorrhea).
Fractures of the temporal bone usually present with bleeding or CSF leakage from the ear (otorrhea) and potential damage to the facial or vestibulocochlear nerves, not anosmia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1498 (Book Page): The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone may be damaged in fractures of the anterior cranial fossa... The patient will have... leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nose (cerebrospinal rhinorrhea). Page 1682 (Book Page): Fractures of the anterior cranial fossa... may produce... loss of the sense of smell (anosmia).

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Vascular supply of the external nose
statement: A comparison of the arterial supply to the external nose reveals a dual origin from both the internal and external carotid systems. Which of the following vessels provides the primary supply to the bridge and crest of the nose?
options: Angular artery
Maxillary artery
Facial artery
Ophthalmic artery
Superior labial artery
correctOption: Ophthalmic artery
optionExplanations: The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery; while it is in the vicinity, the specific supply to the bridge is historically attributed to branches derived from the ophthalmic artery.
While the maxillary artery contributes to the external nose, it generally supplies the deeper structures or lateral aspects, whereas the ophthalmic system dominates the bridge and crest.
The facial artery primarily supplies the ala and the lower part of the septum via its labial and nasal branches.
The ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery, gives off the infratrochlear and external nasal branches that supply the bridge and crest of the nose.
The superior labial artery is a branch of the facial artery that specifically supplies the lower part of the nasal septum and the ala.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1764 (Book Page): Branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary arteries supply the skin of the external nose.

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
statement: The nasal cavity is divided into functional regions. In which specific location is the specialized olfactory mucous membrane, containing the receptors for smell, situated?
options: Within the nasal vestibule
Inside the maxillary sinus cavity
Along the floor of the nasal cavity
In the area above the superior concha
On the surface of the inferior concha
correctOption: In the area above the superior concha
optionExplanations: The nasal vestibule is lined with modified skin and coarse hairs (vibrissae) for filtering large particles, not for olfaction.
Paranasal sinuses are lined with respiratory mucoperiosteum and do not contain specialized sensory receptors for smell.
The floor of the nasal cavity is part of the respiratory region and consists of the hard palate; it does not contain olfactory receptors.
The olfactory region is limited to the uppermost part of the nasal cavity, including the roof, the superior concha, and the upper part of the septum.
The inferior concha is part of the respiratory region, which is specialized for warming and moistening air, not for smelling.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1767 (Book Page): A small olfactory region above the superior concha is lined with olfactory mucous membrane and contains nerve endings sensitive to the reception of smell.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: A patient diagnosed with Bell's palsy is found to have 'hyperacusis' (excessive sensitivity to loud sounds) on the affected side. This specific effect indicates that the lesion of the facial nerve is localized proximal to which anatomical branch?
options: The nerve to the stapedius
The posterior auricular nerve
The greater petrosal nerve
The chorda tympani
The temporal branch
correctOption: The nerve to the stapedius
optionExplanations: The nerve to the stapedius supplies the stapedius muscle, which dampens the vibrations of the stapes bone. When this nerve or its parent facial nerve (proximal to the branch) is damaged, the stapedius is paralyzed, resulting in uninhibited ossicular vibration and hyperacusis.
The posterior auricular nerve supplies muscles behind the ear and skin; it has no effect on the middle ear dampening mechanism.
The greater petrosal nerve is secretomotor to the lacrimal gland; its lesion causes a dry eye (xerophthalmia).
Damage to the chorda tympani results in loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and decreased salivation, not hyperacusis.
The temporal branch is a terminal branch that supplies the forehead muscles; a lesion here only affects facial expression, not sound sensitivity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1685 (Book Page): If the patient is excessively sensitive to sound in one ear ( hyperacusis ), the lesion probably involves the nerve to the stapedius.

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
statement: A 10-year-old child presents with persistent epiphora (overflow of tears) following a facial injury. A blockage of the nasolacrimal duct is suspected. To probe this duct, the physician must target its opening in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. Where exactly should the probe be directed?
options: The inferior meatus
The superior meatus
The sphenoethmoidal recess
The middle meatus
The atrium of the nasal cavity
correctOption: The inferior meatus
optionExplanations: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity. This opening is found in the anterior part of the meatus and is guarded by a mucosal valve (Hasner’s valve) to prevent air from entering the lacrimal system during nose blowing.
The superior meatus is located under the superior concha and receives the posterior ethmoidal air cells.
The sphenoethmoidal recess is the drainage site for the sphenoid sinus, located at the highest point of the nasal cavity.
The middle meatus receives most of the paranasal sinuses (frontal, anterior/middle ethmoidal, and maxillary) via the hiatus semilunaris and ethmoidal bulla.
The atrium is a shallow depression located just superior to the vestibule, leading into the middle meatus; it does not host any specific duct openings.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1766 (Book Page): The inferior meatus lies below the inferior concha and receives the opening of the lower end of the nasolacrimal duct, which is guarded by a fold of mucous membrane.

category: Describe the course and distribution of olfactory nerve in reference to olfactory pathway
coreConcept: Cerebrospinal Rhinorrhea and Cribriform Plate Trauma
statement: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals a clear fluid leaking from the nose and a total inability to perceive scents. Radiographic imaging confirms a fracture of the ethmoid bone. What is the most likely anatomical route for the fluid leakage observed?
options: From the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure into the nose
From the internal acoustic meatus through the petrosal bone into the pharynx
From the maxillary sinus through the hiatus semilunaris into the middle meatus
From the subarachnoid space through the cribriform plate into the nasal cavity
From the sphenoid sinus through the optic canal into the orbital cavity
correctOption: From the subarachnoid space through the cribriform plate into the nasal cavity
optionExplanations: The cavernous sinus contains venous blood; its rupture would lead to hemorrhage or vascular complications, not clear CSF rhinorrhea.
Internal acoustic meatus fractures would lead to CSF otorrhea (ear leakage) and involves the posterior/middle cranial fossa, not the anterior.
Maxillary sinus leakage usually involves blood or mucus, not clear CSF, and typically follows maxillary, not ethmoid, fractures.
A fracture of the cribriform plate often tears the dura and arachnoid mater, allowing CSF to flow from the subarachnoid space directly into the nasal cavity.
Optic canal involvement would present with visual loss and orbital symptoms, not rhinorrhea.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1498 (Book Page): The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone may be damaged in fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. This usually results in tearing of the overlying meninges ... and leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nose (cerebrospinal rhinorrhea).

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
statement: Which bony structures form the superior peripheral elements of the external nose skeleton?
options: Lacrimal bone and nasal bone
Palatine bone and sphenoid
Zygomatic bone and maxilla
Nasal bones and frontal processes of the maxillae
Ethmoid and vomer
correctOption: Nasal bones and frontal processes of the maxillae
optionExplanations: While the nasal bone is correct, the lacrimal bone is located within the medial wall of the orbit and is not a peripheral element of the external nose skeleton.
The palatine bone and sphenoid are located in the posterior nasal cavity and skull base, respectively; they do not contribute to the external nasal skeleton.
The zygomatic bone forms the cheek prominence and lateral orbital margin but does not form the peripheral skeleton of the external nose.
According to the anatomical features of the external nose, its bony skeleton is formed by the nasal bones, the frontal processes of the maxillae, and the frontal bone.
The ethmoid and vomer are deep bones that form the internal nasal septum, not the external peripheral framework of the nose.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1764 (Book Page): The nasal bones, the frontal processes of the maxillae, and the nasal part of the frontal bone are the peripheral bony elements.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: A patient suffers a penetrating wound to the lower neck that severs the phrenic nerve. What is the most likely clinical observation regarding the effect of this lesion?
options: Deviation of the uvula to the side of the lesion
Dilation of the pupil on the affected side
Loss of sensation in the skin over the angle of the mandible
Inability to adduct the vocal folds during speech
The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax by abdominal pressure
correctOption: The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax by abdominal pressure
optionExplanations: Uvular deviation is a sign of a vagus nerve (CN X) lesion, specifically affecting the muscles of the soft palate.
Pupillary dilation is controlled by the sympathetic system; miosis (constriction) occurs in sympathetic lesions, while CN III lesions cause dilation.
Sensation over the angle of the mandible is provided by the great auricular nerve (C2-C3), not the phrenic nerve.
Vocal fold adduction is controlled by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the phrenic nerve.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. Paralysis causes that half of the diaphragm to become flaccid; the positive pressure from the abdominal viscera then pushes it superiorly into the thoracic cavity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve is of considerable clinical importance because it is the sole nerve supply to the muscle of the diaphragm. ... If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: A patient undergoes a thyroidectomy and subsequently presents with a voice that is not greatly affected but has difficulty reaching high pitches. On examination, a unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve is suspected. What is the expected anatomical position of the affected vocal fold?
options: The vocal fold is fixed in the adducted midline position
The vocal fold assumes a position of maximal abduction
The vocal fold vibrates sporadically with no fixed position
The vocal fold assumes a position midway between abduction and adduction
The vocal fold is retracted into the laryngeal ventricle
correctOption: The vocal fold assumes a position midway between abduction and adduction
optionExplanations: The adducted midline position is characteristic of a partial section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, where abductors are more affected than adductors.
Maximal abduction is only achieved during deep inspiration and requires a functioning posterior cricoarytenoid muscle.
Vocal folds do not vibrate sporadically without neuro-muscular tension; they remain in a fixed paralyzed position based on the extent of the nerve damage.
In a complete section, all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid are paralyzed, causing the fold to rest in a neutral 'midway' position.
The vocal folds are structural ligaments that cannot be retracted into the ventricle, which is a space, not a contractile mechanism.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction.

category: List the paranasal sinuses giving their locations, openings, neurovascular supply and clinical significance
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with severe pain over the forehead and the vertex of the skull, accompanied by nasal congestion. Physical examination reveals tenderness when pressure is applied upward beneath the medial end of the superior orbital margin. Which sinus is most likely involved, and why is the pain felt at the vertex?
options: Maxillary sinus; due to referred pain via the infraorbital nerve
Ethmoid sinus; due to referred pain via the anterior ethmoidal nerve
Sphenoid sinus; due to referred pain via the posterior ethmoidal nerve
Maxillary sinus; due to shared drainage in the hiatus semilunaris
Frontal sinus; due to referred pain via the supraorbital nerve
correctOption: Frontal sinus; due to referred pain via the supraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: Maxillary sinus pain is typically referred to the upper jaw and teeth via the infraorbital nerve, not the forehead or vertex.
While ethmoid sinuses can be tender, the specific referred pain to the vertex and the palpation point under the orbital margin specifically target the frontal sinus.
Sphenoid sinusitis typically causes deep-seated pain or pain referred to the temple or occiput, but it is not palpated at the orbital margin.
Although the frontal and maxillary sinuses share drainage areas (middle meatus), the primary source of forehead/vertex pain and the specific tenderness site is the frontal sinus.
The frontal sinus is innervated by the supraorbital nerve (V1). This nerve also supplies the forehead and scalp up to the vertex, leading to referred pain in those regions during inflammation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1776 (Book Page): The frontal sinus can be examined by pressing the finger upward beneath the medial end of the superior orbital margin... The supraorbital nerve innervates the frontal sinus and also supplies the skin of the forehead and scalp as far back as the vertex. It is, therefore, not surprising that patients with frontal sinusitis have pain referred over this area.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Skeletal Framework of the External Nose
statement: A medical student is examining the skeletal framework of the external nose during a gross anatomy session. Which specific bony elements constitute the peripheral boundaries of this structure's superior portion?
options: Greater wing of the sphenoid, lacrimal bone, and nasal bones
Nasal bones, frontal processes of the maxillae, and the nasal part of the frontal bone
Zygomatic bone, inferior conchae, and the alveolar process of the maxilla
Palatine bone, horizontal plate of maxilla, and the nasal bones
Vomer, perpendicular plate of ethmoid, and septal cartilage
correctOption: Nasal bones, frontal processes of the maxillae, and the nasal part of the frontal bone
optionExplanations: The greater wing of the sphenoid is located in the middle cranial fossa and lateral wall of the orbit, while the lacrimal bone forms part of the medial orbital wall; neither contributes to the external peripheral framework of the nose.

According to the anatomical description of the external nose, the superior skeletal framework is established by the bilateral nasal bones, the upward-extending frontal processes of the maxillae, and the nasal part of the frontal bone which articulates with the nasal bones at the root.

The zygomatic bone forms the cheek prominence, and the inferior conchae are independent bones located within the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. The alveolar process carries the teeth and does not form the external nose bridge.
The palatine bone and the horizontal plate of the maxilla form the hard palate (the floor of the nasal cavity), not the external nasal framework seen on the face.

The vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid are internal bony components that form the posterior and superior parts of the nasal septum, respectively, rather than the external peripheral bony framework. The septal cartilage is a hyaline structure, not a bone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1764 (Book Page): Several bones and cartilages make up the skeleton of the external nose. The nasal bones, the frontal processes of the maxillae, and the nasal part of the frontal bone are the peripheral bony elements.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: A patient suffers a deep laceration in the posterior triangle of the neck. On clinical examination, the patient is unable to shrug their shoulders on the affected side. This indicates a lesion of which nerve?
options: Great auricular nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Spinal accessory nerve
Cervical sympathetic trunk
Phrenic nerve
correctOption: Spinal accessory nerve
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve is a purely cutaneous sensory branch from the cervical plexus (C2, C3).
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles and does not affect the shoulder girdle.
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the trapezius; its paralysis results in an inability to shrug and a dropped shoulder.
The sympathetic trunk lesion causes Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis) but does not affect skeletal muscle power for shrugging.
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; its lesion causes respiratory compromise but not shoulder muscle paralysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): the accessory nerve controls the movements of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles... Then, the patient is asked to shrug the shoulders, causing the trapezius muscles to come into action. Page 1681 (Book Page): The trapezius muscle is paralyzed... and the shoulder will drop.

category: Give their anatomical features and neurovascular supply
statement: A patient presents with signs of meningitis shortly after a severe purulent infection of the nasal cavity. Pathophysiologically, through which specific anatomical route is it most likely for the infection to have spread to the anterior cranial fossa?
options: Through the hiatus semilunaris into the maxillary sinus
Via the foramen rotundum along the maxillary nerve
Along the sheaths of the olfactory nerves via the cribriform plate
Through the sphenopalatine foramen into the pterygopalatine fossa
Via the nasolacrimal duct to the conjunctival sac
correctOption: Along the sheaths of the olfactory nerves via the cribriform plate
optionExplanations: The hiatus semilunaris is an opening into the paranasal sinuses within the lateral wall; infection here leads to sinusitis, which is a localized infection.
The foramen rotundum carries the maxillary nerve from the middle cranial fossa, but it is not the primary route for ascending infections from the nasal respiratory mucosa.
The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone contains numerous small perforations for olfactory nerve fibers; their meningeal sheaths provide a direct potential pathway for pathogens to reach the brain.
The sphenopalatine foramen connects the nasal cavity to the pterygopalatine fossa, which is extracranial and not a primary route for meningitis.
The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the eye to the inferior meatus; while infection can spread here, it leads to dacryocystitis, not typically meningitis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1770 (Book Page): It is possible for organisms to ascend to the meninges of the anterior cranial fossa along the sheaths of the olfactory nerves through the cribriform plate and produce meningitis.

category: Give the effects of its lesions
statement: A 50-year-old male presents with a progressive loss of vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination is normal, but visual field testing reveals a loss of the lateral halves of the fields of vision in both eyes (bitemporal hemianopia). A pituitary tumor is suspected. Where is the lesion located?
options: Optic chiasma
Optic nerve
Optic tract
Lateral geniculate body
Optic radiation
correctOption: Optic chiasma
optionExplanations: The optic chiasma contains decussating fibers from the medial retinas (responsible for lateral/temporal vision). Compression here by a pituitary tumor causes bitemporal hemianopia.
A lesion of the optic nerve causes total blindness in the ipsilateral eye, not a hemianopia affecting both eyes.
A lesion of the optic tract causes a homonymous hemianopia, where the same side of the visual field (e.g., both left halves) is lost in both eyes.
The lateral geniculate body is a relay station; a lesion here would cause homonymous hemianopia, similar to an optic tract lesion.
The optic radiation carries information to the visual cortex; damage here typically causes homonymous hemianopia or quadrantanopia, depending on the extent of the lesion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1683 (Book Page): Bitemporal hemianopia is a loss of the lateral halves of the fields of vision of both eyes (i.e., loss of function of the medial half of both retinas). This condition is most commonly produced by a tumor of the pituitary gland exerting pressure on the optic chiasma.

category: Describe the anatomical features and neurovascular supply of external nose
coreConcept: Nerve Course of the External Nasal Nerve
statement: Regional anesthesia for surgical repair of a laceration at the bridge of the nose requires blocking the external nasal nerve. To reach the skin, this nerve must emerge between which two anatomical structures?
options: Frontal bone and nasal bone
Septal cartilage and vomer
Lateral nasal cartilage and ala nasi
Nasal bone and upper nasal cartilage
Maxilla and zygomatic bone
correctOption: Nasal bone and upper nasal cartilage
optionExplanations: The junction of the frontal and nasal bones forms the root of the nose, but the external nasal nerve does not emerge to the surface here.
The septal cartilage and vomer are internal midline structures that form the nasal septum, not the exit point for cutaneous nerves of the bridge.
The lateral nasal cartilage and ala nasi are distal components of the nasal framework; the nerve emerges more superiorly near the bony-cartilaginous junction.
The external nasal nerve descends on the deep surface of the nasal bone before passing between the lower border of the bone and the upper nasal cartilage to become cutaneous.
The maxilla and zygomatic bone form the inferior and lateral orbital margins; this area is associated with the infraorbital nerve, not the external nasal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The external nasal nerve leaves the nose by emerging between the nasal bone and the upper nasal cartilage.

category: Describe the boundaries of nasal cavity: nasal septum, lateral wall of nose, roof and floor
statement: A 22-year-old medical student is examining a dried skull and identifies the vomer bone. Which specific anatomical boundary of the nasal cavity is primarily formed by the vomer in its posteroinferior portion?
options: The medial wall of the nasal cavity
The sphenoethmoidal recess
The lateral wall of the nasal cavity
The roof of the nasal cavity
The floor of the nasal cavity
correctOption: The medial wall of the nasal cavity
optionExplanations: The medial wall is the nasal septum, which is a midline structure dividing the cavity into two halves. It is formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid superiorly, the vomer posteroinferiorly, and the septal cartilage anteriorly.
The sphenoethmoidal recess is a small area located superior to the superior concha on the lateral wall, providing a site for the sphenoid air sinus to drain.
