The lingual nerve is a sensory nerve; its lesion causes loss of sensation but does not cause motor wasting or wrinkling of the tongue muscles.
Salivary gland inflammation (sialadenitis) might cause swelling in the floor of the mouth but would not cause neurogenic wasting and wrinkling of the tongue musculature.
Muscle wasting and wrinkling (atrophy) are classic signs of a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion. In the tongue, this signifies a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve or its nucleus on the ipsilateral side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Autonomic Supply of the Oral Cavity
statement: During a surgical procedure in the submandibular triangle, the submandibular ganglion is accidentally damaged. What is the most likely neurological deficit regarding the tongue?
options: Paralysis of the hyoglossus and styloglossus muscles.
Complete loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds.
Inability to perceive bitter taste on the vallate papillae.
Impaired secretion from glands in the oral floor and sublingual gland.
Loss of general sensation in the posterior third.
correctOption: Impaired secretion from glands in the oral floor and sublingual gland.
optionExplanations: Motor supply to the hyoglossus and styloglossus is provided by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which does not involve the submandibular ganglion.

Taste fibers for the anterior two-thirds pass through the lingual nerve but do not synapse in the submandibular ganglion; they have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion. Secretomotor fibers are what synapse here.
Bitter taste on the vallate papillae is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which relates to the otic ganglion for parotid secretion, not the submandibular ganglion.

The submandibular ganglion is a parasympathetic relay station. Postganglionic fibers from this ganglion provide secretomotor supply to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands and minor glands in the floor of the mouth.
General sensation for the posterior third is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and is entirely independent of the submandibular ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Submandibular Ganglion... Postganglionic secretomotor fibers pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which nerve provides the primary general somatic afferent (GSA) innervation—carrying sensations such as touch, pain, and temperature—to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
Vagus nerve
Facial nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue.
The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), is the primary carrier of general sensation (GSA) for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The vagus nerve provides sensory innervation to the extreme posterior part of the tongue and the epiglottis, but not the anterior two-thirds.
The facial nerve (via chorda tympani) provides special sensory (taste) innervation to the anterior two-thirds, not general sensation.
The hypoglossal nerve is a motor nerve and does not provide cutaneous or mucosal general sensation to the tongue surface.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Anterior two thirds: Lingual nerve branch of the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (general sensation)

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Components of Neck Block Dissection
statement: A surgeon is performing a radical 'block dissection' of the neck for a patient with metastatic lingual carcinoma. According to clinical anatomy, which structure is purposefully removed en bloc to ensure all regional and terminal lymphatics are cleared, while sparing the carotid arteries and vagus nerve?
options: The external carotid artery and the facial nerve
The internal jugular vein and the submandibular salivary gland
The sublingual salivary gland and the lingual artery
The parotid gland and the masseter muscle
The hypoglossal nerve and the stylohyoid muscle
correctOption: The internal jugular vein and the submandibular salivary gland
optionExplanations: The facial nerve and carotid arteries are vital structures that the surgeon specifically attempts to preserve during the dissection.
Radical neck dissection involves the removal of the internal jugular vein, the deep cervical lymph nodes, and the submandibular salivary gland to eliminate all possible metastatic pathways.
The sublingual gland is not part of a standard radical neck dissection unless the primary tumor in the floor of the mouth is being excised simultaneously.
The parotid gland is only partially involved in superior neck dissections and the masseter muscle is unrelated to the lymphatic chains of the neck triangle.
The hypoglossal nerve is usually preserved unless directly involved in cancerous deposits; the stylohyoid is not a primary target for nodal clearance.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): This procedure involves the removal en bloc of the internal jugular vein, the fascia, the lymph nodes, and the submandibular salivary gland.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: The chorda tympani nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers and special sensory taste fibers. To which anatomical structure does it provide preganglionic input before its postganglionic fibers eventually reach the sublingual gland?
options: Submandibular ganglion
Otic ganglion
Geniculate ganglion
Ciliary ganglion
Pterygopalatine ganglion
correctOption: Submandibular ganglion
optionExplanations: The submandibular ganglion is the synapse site for the chorda tympani's parasympathetic fibers; postganglionic fibers then supply the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The otic ganglion receives preganglionic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve for parotid gland secretion.
The geniculate ganglion is a sensory ganglion for the facial nerve; it contains the cell bodies for taste fibers but does not serve as a parasympathetic relay station.
The ciliary ganglion receives preganglionic fibers from the oculomotor nerve (CN III) for pupillary constriction and accommodation.
The pterygopalatine ganglion receives preganglionic fibers from the greater petrosal nerve (CN VII) for lacrimation and nasal/palatal gland secretion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Embryology of the Tongue and Thyroid
statement: The foramen cecum, located at the apex of the sulcus terminalis, is a clinical landmark representing the site of origin for which embryological structure?
options: The parotid duct
The second pharyngeal arch
The tuberculum impar
The thyroglossal duct
The lateral lingual swellings
correctOption: The thyroglossal duct
optionExplanations: The parotid duct develops from ectoderm in the vestibule of the mouth, not from the dorsal surface of the tongue.
The second pharyngeal arch contributes to the tongue but does not originate from the foramen cecum; the foramen is the site of the thyroglossal duct.
The tuberculum impar is a median swelling that forms part of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; the foramen cecum is behind it.
The thyroid gland begins as an endodermal thickening at the foramen cecum and descends into the neck via the thyroglossal duct.
Lateral lingual swellings are paired structures from the first arch that form the body of the tongue; they are located anterior to the foramen cecum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): The apex of the sulcus projects backward and is marked by a small pit, the foramen cecum. The foramen cecum is an embryologic remnant and marks the site of the upper end of the thyroglossal duct.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which of the following describes the pericervical collar of lymph nodes?
options: Nodes located exclusively along the anterior jugular vein.
A vertical chain of nodes inside the carotid sheath.
A group of nodes located behind the pharynx.
The terminal group of nodes in the root of the neck.
A ring of nodal groups at the junction of the head and neck.
correctOption: A ring of nodal groups at the junction of the head and neck.
optionExplanations: Nodes along the anterior jugular vein are the anterior cervical nodes, which are a regional cervical group below the collar.
The vertical chain inside the carotid sheath refers to the deep cervical nodes, not the pericervical collar.
Nodes behind the pharynx are the retropharyngeal nodes; they are regional deep nodes but not part of the superficial pericervical ring.
The terminal group of nodes refers to the deep cervical chain near the jugular trunks, not the collar.
The pericervical collar is a horizontal-like ring comprising the submental, submandibular, parotid, mastoid, and occipital nodes at the head-neck junction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1654 (Book Page): (1) a pericervical collar that extends from below the chin to the back of the head... arranged roughly in a ring around approximately the junction of the head and neck.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which of the following muscles of the tongue is the only one to remain functional in a patient with a confirmed isolated complete bilateral lesion of the hypoglossal nerves?
options: Superior longitudinal intrinsic muscle
Hyoglossus
Styloglossus
Genioglossus
Palatoglossus
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: All intrinsic muscles of the tongue (longitudinal, transverse, and vertical) are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve and would be paralyzed.
Hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed.
Styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed.
Genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed.
Correct. The palatoglossus is technically a muscle of the soft palate and is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagal fibers), making it the only tongue muscle not innervated by CN XII.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Note: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A dentist is performing a difficult extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar. If the nerve closely related to the medial surface of the mandible in this region is injured, what would be the expected sensory deficit?
options: Loss of sensation to the soft palate.
Loss of general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Paralysis of the mylohyoid and anterior digastric muscles.
Numbness of the skin over the angle of the jaw.
Loss of taste to the posterior third of the tongue.
correctOption: Loss of general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
optionExplanations: Sensation to the soft palate is provided by the lesser palatine nerves (V2) and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the lingual nerve.

The Lingual nerve (V3) passes very close to the medial aspect of the mandibular third molar. Its injury results in loss of general sensation (numbness) to the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth.
The nerve to the mylohyoid (a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve) supplies these muscles, not the lingual nerve.
The skin over the angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not the lingual nerve.
Taste to the posterior third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which is not in close proximity to the mandibular third molar.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): Lingual Nerve Injury: The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Final Lymphatic Pathway of the Neck
statement: In the anatomical progression of lingual carcinoma, what is the final common lymphatic trunk that collects lymph from the deep cervical nodes before it enters the venous system at the brachiocephalic vein junction?
options: Right lymphatic duct
Subclavian trunk
Jugular trunk
Bronchomediastinal trunk
Thoracic duct
correctOption: Jugular trunk
optionExplanations: The right lymphatic duct may receive the right jugular trunk, but the jugular trunk is the immediate vessel arising from the deep cervical nodes.
The subclavian trunk drains the upper limb and is not the primary conduit for lingual lymph.
The jugular trunk is the terminal vessel for all head and neck lymph; it is formed by the union of efferents from the deep cervical chain.
The bronchomediastinal trunk drains the thoracic viscera, not the head and neck structures.
The thoracic duct receives the left jugular trunk, but the trunk itself is the specific vessel formed by the efferents of the deep cervical nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The efferent lymph vessels from the deep cervical nodes join to form the jugular trunks

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Zonal Drainage of the Tongue
statement: A 55-year-old tobacco chewer presents with a malignant ulcer on the very tip of his tongue. In a primary clinical evaluation of metastatic spread, which group of lymph nodes must the clinician palpate first as the direct primary drainage site for this specific location?
options: Jugulodigastric lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is part of the deep cervical chain and is the primary station for the posterior third of the tongue and the palatine tonsil, not the anterior tip.
The submandibular nodes receive drainage from the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the nose, and the cheeks, but they are secondary to the submental nodes for the tip of the tongue.
The retropharyngeal nodes are situated behind the pharynx and primarily drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube; they are not involved in the primary drainage of the oral part of the tongue.

The submental lymph nodes, located in the submental triangle just below the chin, are the primary and most immediate lymphatic station for the tip of the tongue, the lower incisors, and the central part of the lower lip.
The parotid nodes drain the scalp, auricle, and eyelids; they do not receive direct lymphatic channels from any part of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During an oral examination of a patient with suspected lingual malignancy, you note a significant swelling of the lymph node located below and behind the angle of the jaw. This specific node is most accurately identified as the:
options: Occipital node
Submental node
Mastoid node
Jugulodigastric node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: Occipital nodes are on the back of the skull, nowhere near the mandible's angle.
The submental node is located in the midline below the chin, not at the angle of the jaw.
Mastoid nodes are behind the ear, superior and posterior to the angle of the jaw.
The jugulodigastric node is the most superior node in the deep cervical chain and is found just below and behind the angle of the mandible; it is the primary terminal node for the tongue.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is located much lower in the neck, where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Regarding the physiological pathway of taste, where are the cell bodies of the neurons that receive taste impulses from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue located?
options: Submandibular ganglion
Trigeminal (Semilunar) ganglion
Inferior ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Superior ganglion of the vagus nerve
Geniculate ganglion
correctOption: Geniculate ganglion
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The submandibular ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion where preganglionic fibers synapse; it does not contain sensory cell bodies.
Incorrect. The trigeminal ganglion contains cell bodies for general sensation (V1, V2, V3), not taste.
Incorrect. The inferior ganglion of CN IX contains cell bodies for taste from the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
Incorrect. The superior/inferior ganglia of the vagus handle sensation from the larynx and pharynx, not taste from the anterior tongue.
Correct. Taste from the anterior two-thirds is carried by the chorda tympani (CN VII). The cell bodies for these primary sensory neurons are located in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1713 (Book Page): The taste fibers are the peripheral processes of the cells in the geniculate ganglion.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a dissection, the genioglossus muscle is identified. What is the primary action of this muscle when both the right and left sides contract simultaneously?
options: Transverse narrowing of the tongue body.
Elevation of the posterior part of the tongue.
Depression of the tongue toward the hyoid bone.
Protrusion of the tongue out of the mouth.
Retraction of the tongue into the oral cavity.
correctOption: Protrusion of the tongue out of the mouth.
optionExplanations: Transverse narrowing of the tongue is an action of the intrinsic muscles of the tongue, which are not attached to bone.
Elevation of the posterior tongue is primarily the function of the palatoglossus and styloglossus muscles.
Depression of the tongue is the primary action of the hyoglossus muscle.
The genioglossus is known as the 'safety muscle' of the tongue; bilateral contraction pulls the tongue forward, resulting in protrusion.
Retraction is performed by the styloglossus and hyoglossus muscles acting together.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1728 (Book Page): Protrusion: Genioglossus muscles on both sides acting together.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: The chorda tympani nerve, while traveling with the lingual nerve, provides which functional modality to the submandibular and sublingual glands?
options: General sensory fibers to the gland capsules
Postganglionic sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibers
Somatomotor fibers for glandular contraction
Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers directly from the brainstem
Preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers
correctOption: Preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers
optionExplanations: General sensation for the glands is not the primary function of the chorda tympani; its main roles are taste and parasympathetic supply.
Sympathetic fibers reach the glands via plexuses on arteries (e.g., facial artery), not via the chorda tympani.
Salivary glands are not under somatomotor (voluntary) control; they are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.
Parasympathetic fibers leaving the brainstem are always preganglionic in the cranial nerves; they must synapse in a peripheral ganglion (submandibular) to become postganglionic.
The chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that must synapse in the submandibular ganglion before supplying the glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Afferent Limb of the Gag Reflex
statement: A patient presents with a loss of the 'gag reflex' on the right side. When the posterior third of the tongue is touched, no sensation is felt and no gagging occurs. Which nerve provides the afferent limb of this reflex for the tongue?
options: Facial nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
Vagus nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The facial nerve (CN VII) provides taste to the anterior two-thirds, but does not participate in the sensory limb of the gag reflex from the tongue.
Incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue and does not carry sensory information for reflexes.

Correct. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue. It acts as the afferent (sensory) limb for the gag reflex when that area is stimulated.
Incorrect. The lingual nerve (V3) supplies the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third where the gag reflex is initiated.
Incorrect. The vagus nerve (CN X) provides the efferent (motor) limb of the gag reflex via the pharyngeal muscles, and sensory only to the extreme base/vallecula.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch [of IX] carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which clinical procedure is the standard diagnostic criterion used by a physician to specifically test the integrity of the lower motor neurons supplying the tongue?
options: Applying sugar and salt to the anterior part of the tongue.
Testing general sensation with a cotton wisp on the tongue tip.
Touching the posterior pharyngeal wall to elicit a gag reflex.
Asking the patient to protrude the tongue and observing for deviation.
Asking the patient to say 'Ah' and observing the uvula.
correctOption: Asking the patient to protrude the tongue and observing for deviation.
optionExplanations: Applying sugar/salt tests the taste pathways (CN VII and IX), which are sensory, not the motor neurons (CN XII).
Testing general sensation evaluates the trigeminal nerve (V3 - lingual nerve) or the glossopharyngeal nerve, not the motor supply.
The gag reflex tests CN IX (afferent) and CN X (efferent); it does not evaluate the hypoglossal nerve.
Protrusion of the tongue is the definitive test for CN XII (hypoglossal nerve). Any weakness or lesion results in deviation toward the affected side.
Observing the uvula while saying 'Ah' tests the vagus nerve (CN X) supply to the soft palate, not the tongue muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The patient is asked to put out the tongue, and if a lesion of the nerve is present, it will be noted that the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which muscle of the tongue would remain functional if the hypoglossal nerve were completely severed at the hypoglossal canal?
options: Superior longitudinal muscle
Hyoglossus
Palatoglossus
Styloglossus
Genioglossus
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: The superior longitudinal muscle is an intrinsic muscle of the tongue; all intrinsic muscles are supplied by CN XII and would be paralyzed.
The hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed.
The palatoglossus is the only tongue muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (specifically via the vagus nerve, CN X). It would remain functional in an isolated CN XII lesion.
The styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed.
The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Note: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A patient with carcinoma of the tongue develops an enlarged node near the point where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. This node is specifically associated with drainage from which part of the tongue?
options: Pharyngeal wall
Sides of the anterior two-thirds
Hard palate
Tongue (general drainage)
Tip of the tongue
correctOption: Tongue (general drainage)
optionExplanations: Pharyngeal wall drainage typically involves the retropharyngeal and other deep cervical nodes, but the jugulo-omohyoid is not its primary specific marker.
The sides of the anterior two-thirds drain first to submandibular nodes, though they eventually reach the deep cervical chain including the jugulo-omohyoid.
The hard palate drains via the greater palatine and nasopalatine nerves to the deep cervical nodes, but the jugulo-omohyoid is specifically cited for lingual drainage.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a key deep cervical node specifically identified in anatomical texts as being primarily associated with drainage from the tongue.
The tip drains primarily to submental nodes before reaching deeper levels; it does not go directly to the jugulo-omohyoid node.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Boundaries of Lingual Lymphatic Watersheds
statement: Which anatomical landmark serves as the dividing line between the lymphatic drainage systems that go to the submandibular nodes versus those that drain directly to the deep cervical nodes?
options: Sulcus terminalis
Foramen cecum
Plica fimbriata
Frenulum of the tongue
Vallate papillae
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The sulcus terminalis is the V-shaped groove that anatomically divides the tongue into the anterior two-thirds (oral part) and the posterior third (pharyngeal part). This boundary also demarcates different lymphatic pathways: the anterior part drains to submental/submandibular nodes, while the posterior part drains directly to deep cervical nodes.
The foramen cecum is a small pit at the apex of the sulcus terminalis marking the site of the embryonic thyroglossal duct; though a landmark, the entire sulcus is the dividing line.
The plica fimbriata is a fringed fold lateral to the lingual vein on the inferior surface and does not represent a major boundary for lymphatic drainage classification.

The lingual frenulum is a midline fold on the undersurface of the tongue; while it is near the submandibular duct openings, it does not serve as a primary watershed for the change in nodal drainage tiers.
Vallate papillae are large papillae located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis; while they help identify the border, the sulcus itself is the defined anatomical divider.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts. Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular... Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Organization of Head and Neck Lymphatics
statement: Which specific group of lymph nodes is described as forming a 'pericervical collar' at the junction of the head and neck, acting as regional filters before lymph reaches the deep terminal group?
options: Tracheal and Laryngeal nodes
Submandibular, Submental, and Parotid nodes
Deep Cervical nodes only
Retropharyngeal and Buccal nodes
Infraclavicular and Axillary nodes
correctOption: Submandibular, Submental, and Parotid nodes
optionExplanations: Tracheal and laryngeal nodes are regional nodes of the neck proper, located more inferiorly than the pericervical collar.
The pericervical collar consists of the submental, submandibular, parotid, mastoid, and occipital nodes, which encircle the head-neck junction.
Deep cervical nodes are the terminal group into which the regional nodes and the collar ultimately drain; they are not part of the initial collar.
Retropharyngeal nodes are deep neck nodes, and while buccal nodes are facial, they are not categorized as part of the primary pericervical ring.
Infraclavicular and axillary nodes are associated with the upper limb and breast, not the head and neck lymphatic collar system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1654 (Book Page): The lymph nodes of the head and neck... are arranged in three groups: (1) a pericervical collar... (3) a deep terminal group... Page 1655 (Book Page): [Lists Occipital, Mastoid, Parotid, Submandibular, and Submental in the collar].

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Correlates of the Jugulodigastric Node
statement: A clinical examiner palpates a tender, enlarged lymph node located just below and behind the angle of the mandible. Which specific lingual anatomical structure is this node primarily responsible for draining?
options: The sublingual fold
The mandibular incisors
The skin over the chin
The apex of the tongue
The palatine tonsil and tongue
correctOption: The palatine tonsil and tongue
optionExplanations: The sublingual fold drains into the submandibular and submental nodes.
The mandibular incisors drain into the submental nodes.
The skin of the chin drains into the submental nodes.
The apex (tip) drains to the submental nodes, located more anteriorly and medially.
The jugulodigastric node, found at Level II, is a deep cervical node primarily associated with the tonsils and the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 62-year-old tobacco user presents with a non-healing ulcer on the lateral border of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging reveals a 3cm metastasis in the deep cervical chain. To effectively treat this via radical 'block' neck dissection, which structure is meticulously preserved by the surgeon while removing the lymphatics?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Submandibular salivary gland
Internal jugular vein
Common carotid artery
correctOption: Common carotid artery
optionExplanations: While often attempted to be saved, the text notes the hypoglossal nerve is frequently sacrificed if it is involved in the cancerous deposits during a block dissection.
The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is part of the tissue removed during a block dissection to ensure a clean surgical margin around the nodes.
The submandibular salivary gland is removed en bloc because the submandibular lymph nodes are intimately associated with its capsule and parenchyma.
In a standard block dissection (radical neck dissection), the internal jugular vein is routinely sacrificed/removed to ensure all surrounding lymphatic tissue is excised.
The carotid arteries (common, internal, and external) are vital structures that are carefully preserved by the surgeon unless directly invaded by an unresectable mass.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): The carotid arteries and the vagus nerve are carefully preserved. It is often necessary to sacrifice the hypoglossal and vagus nerves, which may be involved in the cancerous deposits.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: When assessing the potential for contralateral nodal spread in a case of tongue carcinoma, which anatomical feature of the tongue's lymphatic system is the most significant correlate?
options: Direct drainage into the thoracic duct from the tongue base
Drainage into the external jugular venous system
The decussation of lymphatic vessels across the midline
The presence of the lingual tonsil at the base
The lack of valves in lingual lymphatic vessels
correctOption: The decussation of lymphatic vessels across the midline
optionExplanations: Lymph from the tongue must pass through at least one lymph node (usually deep cervical) before entering the jugular trunks, which then join the thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct.
Tongue lymphatics drain into the deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular system.

The lymphatics from the central and posterior parts of the tongue often cross the midline (decussation). This anatomical correlate means a lesion on one side of the midline can present with metastases in the lymph nodes of the opposite side of the neck.
The lingual tonsil is a collection of lymphoid tissue, but it is not the anatomical 'pathway' or 'correlate' that facilitates contralateral spread.
Lymphatic vessels do have valves; while the text mentions emissary veins are valveless, tongue lymphatics follow standard unidirectional flow unless obstructed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes... In patients with bilateral spread, a bilateral block dissection may be necessary.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: In the neuro-pharmacological regulation of salivary flow, preganglionic parasympathetic fibers destined for the submandibular and sublingual glands travel through a specific cranial nerve before joining the lingual nerve. If these fibers are interrupted before they join the lingual nerve, what other tongue-related function is simultaneously lost?
options: Motor control of the styloglossus muscle.
Taste sensation from the vallate papillae.
General sensation from the posterior third of the tongue.
Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
correctOption: Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
optionExplanations: Motor control of the styloglossus is provided by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which is anatomically distinct from the chorda tympani.
Taste from the vallate papillae is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), despite their location being slightly anterior to the sulcus terminalis.
General sensation from the posterior third is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

The chorda tympani (CN VII) carries both preganglionic parasympathetic fibers for salivation and special sensory (taste) fibers for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. A lesion proximal to its junction with the lingual nerve destroys both.
General sensation from the anterior two-thirds is carried by the lingual nerve itself (V3), not the chorda tympani fibers that join it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The chorda tympani nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa... The chorda tympani fibers carry taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and also give off preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular ganglion.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Genioglossus Action in CN XII Palsy
statement: During a clinical evaluation, a patient is found to have atrophy and wrinkling of the right half of the tongue. What is the physiological mechanism explaining why the tongue deviates to the right during protrusion?
options: The right hyoglossus muscle fails to depress the tongue, causing it to curl toward the midline.
The left genioglossus muscle pulls the left side of the tongue forward, while the right side remains stationary.
The right styloglossus muscle becomes hyperactive and pulls the tongue back and to the right.
Bilateral contraction of the intrinsic muscles is required for protrusion; without the right side, the left side fails to engage.
The right palatoglossus muscle, supplied by the vagus nerve, overcompensates for the loss of hypoglossal innervation.
correctOption: The left genioglossus muscle pulls the left side of the tongue forward, while the right side remains stationary.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While the hyoglossus is involved in depression, its dysfunction does not explain the characteristic deviation seen in protrusion.

Correct. Protrusion is a 'pushing' action. The healthy left genioglossus pushes the left base of the tongue forward. Since the right side lacks this forward push, the tongue pivots toward the stationary (paralyzed) right side.
Incorrect. Atrophy indicates a lower motor neuron lesion where muscles lose tone; they do not become hyperactive.
Incorrect. Protrusion is primarily the function of the extrinsic genioglossus muscles, not just intrinsic muscles, and the healthy side does still engage, causing the deviation path.
Incorrect. The palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus) and primarily elevates the root of the tongue; it cannot compensate for the genioglossus in protrusion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Functional Components of the Glossopharyngeal Nerve
statement: The general sensation of the posterior third of the tongue is mediated by the same nerve that provides taste to the same region. This nerve is also responsible for the sensory limb of the pharyngeal (gag) reflex. Which nerve is it?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
Vagus nerve
Chorda tympani
Lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue muscles.
The vagus nerve is primarily the efferent (motor) limb of the gag reflex and provides sensation to the extreme posterior tongue/epiglottic area, but not the general posterior 1/3.
The chorda tympani provides taste only to the anterior two-thirds.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation only to the anterior two-thirds.
Correct. The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and is the afferent nerve for the gag reflex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste). Page 1686 (Book Page): Testing Glossopharyngeal Nerve Integrity... evaluate by testing the patient’s general sensation and that of taste on the posterior third of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: In a complete transection of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which muscle of the tongue would remain functional due to its different embryological origin and nerve supply?
options: Verticalis
Hyoglossus
Styloglossus
Genioglossus
Palatoglossus
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: The verticalis is an intrinsic tongue muscle. All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve and would be affected by its lesion.
Hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed in a CN XII lesion.
Styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed in a CN XII lesion.
Genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it would be paralyzed in a CN XII lesion.
Palatoglossus is technically a muscle of the soft palate and the tongue. It is the only tongue muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve fibers), not the hypoglossal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Muscular branches to all the muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: In the classification of the tongue for lymphatic drainage mapping, which region is characterized by drainage that specifically targets the submental lymph nodes?
options: Extreme tip of the tongue
Valleculae and epiglottis
Lateral margins of the body
Dorsum of the posterior third
Posterior third (root)
correctOption: Extreme tip of the tongue
optionExplanations: The tip of the tongue is the only lingual region whose primary lymphatic drainage is directed toward the submental lymph nodes.
The valleculae and epiglottis are related to the laryngeal and pharyngeal drainage systems, which primarily target the deep cervical nodes.
The lateral margins drain into the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical chain.
The dorsum of the posterior third follows the general drainage of the root, which is directly to the deep cervical nodes.
The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, bypassing all superficial regional groups.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which of the following is the terminal group of lymph nodes in the neck that receives lymph from all regional nodes of the head and neck?
options: Mastoid nodes
Parotid nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Submental nodes
Submandibular nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Mastoid nodes are regional nodes located behind the ear, serving the scalp and auricle; they are not terminal nodes.
Parotid nodes are regional nodes for the lateral face and scalp; they are not terminal for the entire head and neck.
The deep cervical nodes, located along the internal jugular vein, are the final common pathway for all lymphatic drainage from the head and neck before entering the venous system.
Submental nodes are regional nodes for the chin and tip of the tongue, representing a first-level filter rather than a terminal group.
Submandibular nodes are regional nodes that drain specific areas like the face and tongue; they then empty into the deep cervical chain.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): They [Deep cervical nodes] receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Conceptual Application of Deep Cervical Anatomy
statement: A surgeon performing a block dissection of the neck for a patient with lingual carcinoma intends to remove the 'principal node' associated with the tongue's lower drainage. Which node should be identified near the intermediate tendon of the omohyoid muscle?
options: Tracheal node
Jugulodigastric node
Submandibular node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
Anterior cervical node
correctOption: Jugulo-omohyoid node
optionExplanations: Tracheal nodes are located alongside the trachea and primarily drain the thyroid and larynx rather than the tongue.
The jugulodigastric node is located much higher in the neck, specifically below the posterior belly of the digastric muscle near the angle of the jaw.
Submandibular nodes are located in the submandibular triangle, superficial to the deep fascia, and are not part of the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.

The jugulo-omohyoid node is a specific member of the deep cervical chain located near the point where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein; it is a key landmark in tongue cancer surgery.
Anterior cervical nodes are superficial and follow the anterior jugular veins; they are not the primary target for deep lingual metastatic spread.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 65-year-old chronic smoker presents with a firm, fixed, 3 cm ulcer on the right lateral margin of the tongue. On examination, a hard, painless lymph node is palpated just below and behind the angle of the mandible. Which specific node is most likely involved in this metastatic presentation?
options: Jugulodigastric node
Mastoid node
Submental node
Occipital node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is known as the 'principal node of the tongue' in some contexts and is located specifically below and behind the angle of the mandible, making it the primary site for palpable metastasis from the tongue.
Mastoid nodes are retroauricular and receive drainage from the scalp and ear; they are not standard sites for lingual carcinoma metastasis.
The submental node is located in the midline below the chin and drains the tip of the tongue; it would not be found behind the angle of the mandible.
Occipital nodes are located at the back of the skull and drain the posterior scalp; they are anatomically unrelated to lingual lymphatic pathways.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a deep cervical node located lower in the neck near the omohyoid muscle, usually involved in drainage from the tongue but less associated with the angle of the jaw.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A lesion of the lingual nerve occurring in the infratemporal fossa BEFORE it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve would result in which specific deficit?
options: Loss of salivary secretion from the parotid gland
Loss of general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue only
Loss of motor control to the genioglossus muscle
Loss of general sensation and taste to the anterior two-thirds
Loss of taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue only
correctOption: Loss of general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue only
optionExplanations: Parotid secretion is controlled by the glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve, not the lingual nerve or chorda tympani (which supply the submandibular/sublingual glands).
The lingual nerve itself carries general somatic afferent fibers. If severed before the chorda tympani joins it, only general sensation is lost.
The genioglossus is a motor muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, not the lingual nerve.
This combined loss would only occur if the lesion were distal to the point where the chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve.
Taste is carried by the chorda tympani; if the lingual nerve is injured before they join, taste fibers (which are currently still in the facial nerve/canal) would be spared.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... fibers carry general sensation from the mucous membrane of the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The chorda tympani nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: In the physiological pathway for taste, where are the cell bodies of the first-order neurons located for the fibers that supply the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
options: Superior cervical ganglion
Otic ganglion
Geniculate ganglion
Inferior ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Trigeminal ganglion
correctOption: Geniculate ganglion
optionExplanations: The superior cervical ganglion is a sympathetic ganglion and does not contain sensory or taste cell bodies.
The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion for the parotid gland; it is not a sensory ganglion.
The facial nerve (CN VII) mediates taste for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani. The first-order sensory neurons for this pathway are located in the geniculate ganglion.
The inferior ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) contains cell bodies for taste and sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
The Trigeminal ganglion contains the cell bodies for general sensation (touch/pain) for the anterior tongue via the lingual nerve, but not for taste.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1671 (Book Page): On reaching the medial wall of the middle ear... the nerve swells to form the sensory geniculate ganglion. Page 1713 (Book Page): The taste fibers are the peripheral processes of the cells in the geniculate ganglion.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: The sensory-motor coordination required to prevent biting the tongue during mastication involves several nerves. Which nerve provides the sensory feedback (proprioception) for the muscles of facial expression which help keep the cheek and tongue in proper alignment?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Cervical plexus
Hypoglossal nerve
Facial nerve
Trigeminal nerve
correctOption: Trigeminal nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides sensation to the posterior tongue and pharynx but is not the primary carrier for facial muscle proprioception.
The cervical plexus (C2-C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the jaw and the neck, and proprioception for the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, not the mimetic muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (XII) is the motor nerve to the tongue muscles. It does not provide sensory feedback for the facial muscles (like the buccinator).
The facial nerve (VII) provides the motor supply to the muscles of facial expression, but the text notes that proprioceptive fibers from these muscles pass through the trigeminal nerve.
While the trigeminal nerve (V) is primarily known for general sensation (touch/pain) of the face and tongue, it also carries proprioceptive fibers from the facial muscles to the CNS.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1527 (Book Page): These nerves not only supply the skin of the face but also supply proprioceptive fibers to the underlying muscles of facial expression.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which extrinsic muscle of the tongue is the anatomical exception, being supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) rather than the hypoglossal nerve?
options: Palatoglossus
Styloglossus
Hyoglossus
Genioglossus
Chondroglossus
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: The palatoglossus is technically a muscle of the soft palate as well as the tongue; it is the only tongue muscle not supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
The styloglossus retracts the tongue and is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
The hyoglossus depresses the tongue and is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
The genioglossus is the main protrusor of the tongue and is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
The chondroglossus is a small part of the hyoglossus and follows the general rule of hypoglossal innervation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): All the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Anatomically, why can an infection or carcinoma at the side of the tongue cause enlargement of the submandibular lymph nodes even if the primary lesion is purely intra-oral?
options: Because the tongue is directly fused to the submandibular salivary gland
Because the submandibular nodes are located superficial to the submandibular gland just below the jaw
Because the submandibular nodes are located within the tongue substance
Because the lingual nerve acts as a conduit for lymphatic fluid
Because the lymph vessels from the lateral tongue pierce the mylohyoid muscle to reach these nodes
correctOption: Because the submandibular nodes are located superficial to the submandibular gland just below the jaw
optionExplanations: The tongue and the submandibular gland are separate structures separated by muscles like the hyoglossus and mylohyoid.
The submandibular nodes are located just below the lower margin of the mandible, superficial to the submandibular gland, making them easily palpable when enlarged due to lingual pathology.
Lymph nodes are not found within the muscular substance of the tongue; they are regional structures.
Nerves are not conduits for lymphatic fluid; lymph travels through specific lymphatic vessels.
While lymph vessels do travel through the floor of the mouth, the primary reason for node palpability is their external location relative to the mandible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submandibular nodes: Located superficial to the submandibular salivary gland just below the lower margin of the jaw, they receive lymph from... the anterior two thirds of the tongue (except the tip)

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Terminal Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue
statement: According to the pericervical collar and regional cervical group classification, what is the terminal lymphatic destination for all lymph originating from any part of the tongue?
options: Submental lymph nodes
Superficial cervical lymph nodes
Deep cervical lymph nodes
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Submental nodes are regional nodes for the tip and eventually drain into the deep cervical group.
Superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein and drain into the deep cervical nodes; they are not the terminal group.
The deep cervical nodes form a vertical chain along the internal jugular vein and serve as the final common pathway for all head and neck lymph, including the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx; they are not the terminal pathway for lingual drainage.
Submandibular nodes are regional nodes for the anterior body and eventually drain into the deep cervical group.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The deep cervical nodes... receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a block dissection of the neck for a metastasizing lingual carcinoma, the surgeon removes the internal jugular vein, submandibular gland, and cervical fascia. Which of the following structures must be meticulously preserved to maintain essential neurovascular function?
options: Carotid arteries
Submandibular salivary gland
Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Deep cervical lymph nodes
Internal jugular vein
correctOption: Carotid arteries
optionExplanations: The carotid arteries (common, internal, and external) are essential for cerebral and facial blood supply and must be preserved unless directly invaded by the tumor.
The submandibular gland is removed during the procedure as it is closely associated with the submandibular lymph nodes that drain the tongue.
The investing layer of fascia is removed as part of the en bloc resection to ensure all lymphatic channels within the fascial planes are captured.
The deep cervical lymph nodes are the primary target for removal in this surgery to treat or prevent metastasis.
The internal jugular vein is typically removed en bloc during a radical neck dissection to ensure all associated lymphatics are cleared.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): The carotid arteries and the vagus nerve are carefully preserved.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Combined Cranial Nerve Lesions of the Tongue
statement: A patient presents with a deep penetrating wound to the upper neck. Clinical examination reveals the tongue deviates to the right upon protrusion, and there is a total loss of both taste and general sensation on the posterior one-third of the tongue. Which combination of nerves has most likely been damaged?
options: Right Hypoglossal and Right Glossopharyngeal nerves
Right Vagus and Right Glossopharyngeal nerves
Left Hypoglossal and Right Glossopharyngeal nerves
Right Hypoglossal and Right Chorda Tympani nerves
Right Hypoglossal and Right Lingual nerves
correctOption: Right Hypoglossal and Right Glossopharyngeal nerves
optionExplanations: Correct. Tongue deviation to the right indicates a right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) lesion. Loss of taste and sensation on the posterior third identifies a right glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) lesion.
The vagus nerve supplies only the palatoglossus muscle (motor) and very minor sensory fibers near the epiglottis, but it is not responsible for the primary sensation of the posterior third.
The tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion; therefore, a right-sided deviation indicates a right-sided CN XII lesion, not left-sided.
The chorda tympani supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds, not the posterior third.
The lingual nerve supplies the anterior two-thirds, not the posterior third, of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste). Page 1681 (Book Page): The hypoglossal nerve... innervates the muscles of the tongue... and therefore controls the shape and movements of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Functional Modalities of the Chorda Tympani
statement: A lesion involving the chorda tympani nerve as it travels through the middle ear would affect which of the following physiological processes associated with the tongue?
options: Somatic pain perception on the tip of the tongue.
Salivary secretion from the submandibular and sublingual glands.
Salivary secretion from the parotid gland.
The cough reflex initiated by touching the posterior tongue.
The ability to detect bitter taste on the vallate papillae.
correctOption: Salivary secretion from the submandibular and sublingual glands.
optionExplanations: Somatic pain on the tip of the tongue is carried by the general sensory fibers of the lingual nerve (branch of CN V3).
The chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that synapse in the submandibular ganglion to provide secretomotor supply to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
Parotid gland secretion is controlled by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve.
The cough reflex and sensory information from the extreme posterior tongue/epiglottic region are mediated by the vagus nerve (CN X).
Bitter taste on the vallate papillae is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the chorda tympani.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Anatomically, the foramen cecum on the dorsal surface of the tongue serves as an important landmark between which two areas of differing nerve supply?
options: The areas supplied by the Facial nerve and the Vagus nerve
The tip of the tongue and the lateral margins
The area of general sensation (V3) and the area of taste (CN VII)
The areas of the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles
The oral part (anterior 2/3) and the pharyngeal part (posterior 1/3)
correctOption: The oral part (anterior 2/3) and the pharyngeal part (posterior 1/3)
optionExplanations: The foramen cecum marks the divide between areas supplied by V3/CN VII (anterior) and CN IX (posterior), not Facial/Vagus.
The tip and lateral margins are both within the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
General sensation and taste are both found in the anterior 2/3 and the posterior 1/3; the foramen cecum does not separate these two modalities.
Intrinsic and extrinsic muscles are intermingled and both are mostly supplied by CN XII; they are not separated by the foramen cecum.
The foramen cecum and sulcus terminalis represent the developmental and neurological boundary between the anterior two-thirds (oral part) and posterior one-third (pharyngeal part).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts. The apex of the sulcus projects backward and is marked by a small pit, the foramen cecum.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which specific physiological step is required for taste sensations from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue to reach the central nervous system?
options: Passage through the geniculate ganglion
Transmission via the lesser petrosal nerve
Relay through the otic ganglion
Synapse in the submandibular ganglion
Bypassing the facial canal in the temporal bone
correctOption: Passage through the geniculate ganglion
optionExplanations: The cell bodies for taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue are located in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve within the temporal bone.
The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve for the parotid gland, not taste from the tongue.
The otic ganglion is involved in the parasympathetic supply to the parotid gland; it is not part of the taste pathway for the anterior tongue.
The submandibular ganglion is a site for parasympathetic synapse (secretomotor), but taste fibers (sensory) pass through it or nearby without synapsing.
Taste fibers do not bypass the facial canal; they enter it via the chorda tympani and travel within it to reach the geniculate ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains taste fibers from the mucous membrane covering the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The taste fibers are the peripheral processes of the cells in the geniculate ganglion.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which muscle of the tongue is the only one supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve) rather than the hypoglossal nerve?
options: Styloglossus
Hyoglossus
Genioglossus
Palatoglossus
Verticalis
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
Incorrect. The hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
Incorrect. The genioglossus is the main 'safety' muscle of the tongue, supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
Correct. The palatoglossus is anatomically a muscle of the tongue but embryologically and functionally part of the soft palate group, thus supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X).
Incorrect. The verticalis is an intrinsic muscle of the tongue, which are all supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Note: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which nerve supplies the taste buds of the vallate papillae, which are located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The internal laryngeal nerve supplies a small area of taste at the extreme base of the tongue/epiglottis, but not the vallate papillae.
Incorrect. The lingual nerve carries only general sensation (touch/pain) and serves as a vehicle for taste, but is not the source of taste fibers for the vallate papillae.
Incorrect. The greater petrosal nerve (CN VII) is secretomotor to the lacrimal gland and carries taste from the palate, not the tongue.
Incorrect. The chorda tympani supplies the fungiform papillae on the anterior 2/3, but stops at the vallate papillae.

Correct. Despite being on the oral part (anterior to the sulcus terminalis), the vallate papillae are embryologically related to the third arch and thus supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1734 (Book Page): Remember that the circumvallate papillae are situated on the mucous membrane just anterior to the sulcus terminalis and that their taste buds are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which of the following regional lymph node groups is correctly matched with its specific drainage area of the tongue, crucial for the clinical evaluation of lingual carcinoma?
options: Occipital nodes — Sublingual fold
Submandibular nodes — Posterior third of the tongue
Submental nodes — Lateral border of the tongue
Deep cervical nodes — Direct drainage from the posterior third
Mastoid nodes — Apex of the tongue
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes — Direct drainage from the posterior third
optionExplanations: Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp. The sublingual fold and the floor of the mouth drain into the submental or submandibular nodes depending on the specific location.
The posterior third drains directly to the deep cervical nodes, bypassing the submandibular group. The submandibular nodes receive lymph from the lateral anterior two-thirds.
The submental nodes drain the tip (apex) of the tongue, not the lateral borders. The lateral borders drain into the submandibular nodes.

This is a correct match. The posterior third of the tongue (the pharyngeal part) has lymphatic vessels that drain directly into the deep cervical chain, specifically targeting nodes like the jugulodigastric.
Mastoid nodes drain the scalp and the ear. The apex (tip) of the tongue drains into the submental nodes located in the submental triangle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a block dissection of the neck for metastatic lingual carcinoma, which of the following structures is traditionally removed to ensure oncological clearance of the deep cervical nodes?
options: Phrenic nerve
Common carotid artery
Internal carotid artery
Vagus nerve (CN X)
Internal jugular vein
correctOption: Internal jugular vein
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve is located deep to the prevertebral fascia and is carefully protected to maintain diaphragmatic function.
The common carotid artery is never removed in a standard block dissection as it is the primary blood supply to the brain.
The carotid arteries (internal and common) are vital structures that are carefully preserved during neck dissection unless directly invaded by tumor.
The vagus nerve is usually preserved; its sacrifice is only considered if it is directly involved in the cancerous deposit, which is not the standard 'en bloc' protocol.
In a radical neck dissection, the internal jugular vein is removed along with the deep cervical lymph nodes, fascia, and submandibular gland to ensure complete removal of lymphatic tissues.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): This procedure involves the removal en bloc of the internal jugular vein, the fascia, the lymph nodes, and the submandibular salivary gland.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Jugular Foramen Syndrome and Cranial Nerve IX/X/XI
statement: A 68-year-old male is diagnosed with a tumor at the base of the skull involving the jugular foramen. On examination, he exhibits wasting of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, hoarseness, and loss of the gag reflex. Regarding the tongue, what additional finding is most consistent with this specific neurological deficit?
options: Wrinkling and atrophy of the tongue on the left side
Loss of general sensation to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue
Loss of taste and sensation to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue
Paralysis of the palatoglossus muscle with deviation to the left
Deviation of the tongue to the right on protrusion
correctOption: Loss of taste and sensation to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue
optionExplanations: Atrophy and wrinkling are signs of a CN XII lesion. CN XII is protected by the strong bony walls of the hypoglossal canal and is usually spared in jugular foramen lesions.
Anterior sensation is via the lingual nerve (V3), which exits the foramen ovale, not the jugular foramen.
The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, and XI. A lesion here will damage CN IX, leading to loss of taste and sensation on the posterior third of the tongue.
While the palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X), deviation of the tongue itself is governed by CN XII, and the palate would deviate away from the side of a CN X lesion.
Tongue deviation indicates CN XII damage. The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1496 (Book Page): The jugular foramen... transmits the following structures in anteroposterior sequence: the inferior petrosal sinus; the 9th, 10th, and 11th cranial nerves; and the large sigmoid sinus.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with difficulty in taste and sensation after the surgical extraction of an impacted lower third molar. Anatomically, why is the lingual nerve particularly vulnerable during this specific dental procedure?
options: It is closely related to the medial surface of the mandible near the last molar tooth.
It lies superficial to the buccinator muscle near the molar.
It passes through the mandibular foramen with the inferior alveolar nerve.
It exits the mental foramen immediately adjacent to the molar root.
It loops under the submandibular duct in that specific region.
correctOption: It is closely related to the medial surface of the mandible near the last molar tooth.
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve passes just medial to the alveolar process of the mandible, specifically near the third molar, making it susceptible to injury during dental surgery in that area.
The lingual nerve lies deep in the submandibular region/infratemporal fossa, not superficial to the buccinator.
The lingual nerve does not enter the mandibular foramen; it remains medial to the mandible while the inferior alveolar nerve enters the canal.
The mental nerve exits the mental foramen (usually near the premolars), not the lingual nerve, and it is located on the lateral surface of the mandible.
While the lingual nerve does loop under the submandibular duct, this occurs further forward in the floor of the mouth, not at the immediate site of the third molar extraction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): Lingual Nerve Injury... Here, it is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A patient presents with a malignant lesion at the extreme tip of the tongue. To which group of lymph nodes would the metastatic cells first migrate?
options: Jugulodigastric lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is the 'main' node for the tonsil and the general tongue body, but it is considered a secondary or deep cervical station for the tip, not the initial one.

The submental lymph nodes are the primary first-order nodes for the tip of the tongue and the central part of the lower lip. Malignancies here typically follow this direct pathway before moving to deeper cervical chains.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube; they are not part of the oral cavity or tongue drainage system.
The submandibular nodes receive drainage from the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but they are not the primary first-tier drainage for the central tip.
Parotid nodes receive lymph from the scalp, eyelids, and auricle; they do not play a role in the lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Pathway of the Chorda Tympani
statement: The chorda tympani carries essential fibers for tongue function. In addition to taste for the anterior two-thirds, which physiological process is directly mediated by the secretomotor fibers it distributes?
options: Parotid gland secretion
Mucus production in the nasopharynx
Submandibular and sublingual gland secretion
Lacrimal gland tear production
Sweat production on the cheek skin
correctOption: Submandibular and sublingual gland secretion
optionExplanations: Parotid secretion is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the tympanic plexus, lesser petrosal nerve, and otic ganglion.
Nasopharyngeal mucus is supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion via branches of the maxillary nerve (V2), mediated by the greater petrosal nerve (VII).
The chorda tympani (from CN VII) provides the parasympathetic drive for both the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands via the submandibular ganglion.
Lacrimal secretion is mediated by the greater petrosal nerve (another branch of CN VII) via the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the chorda tympani.
Sweat production on the face is mediated by sympathetic fibers traveling with branches of the trigeminal nerve, or abnormally in Frey's syndrome by the auriculotemporal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1713 (Book Page): The chorda tympani... carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that reach the submandibular ganglion and are there relayed to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which anatomical structure serves as the primary boundary between the sensory territories of the lingual nerve and the glossopharyngeal nerve on the tongue?
options: Lingual frenulum
Plica fimbriata
Epiglottis
Foramen cecum
Sulcus terminalis
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The lingual frenulum is a midline fold on the undersurface of the tongue; it does not mark the boundary between anterior and posterior sensory territories.
The plica fimbriata is a fringed fold on the inferior surface of the tongue, lateral to the lingual veins; it is not a territory boundary for nerve supply.
The epiglottis is posterior to the tongue; the sensory supply to the region between the tongue and epiglottis is provided by the internal laryngeal nerve.
The foramen cecum is the apex of the sulcus terminalis; while it is part of the boundary, the entire sulcus is the dividing line for innervation.
The sulcus terminalis is the V-shaped groove that separates the anterior two-thirds (innervated by CN V3 and CN VII) from the posterior third (innervated by CN IX).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts... The sulcus divides the tongue into the anterior two thirds (oral part; body) and the posterior third (pharyngeal part; root).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A lesion of the hypoglossal nerve results in characteristic deviation of the tongue upon protrusion. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological mechanism responsible for this physical sign?
options: The genioglossus of the unaffected side pushing the tongue toward the paralyzed side.
The palatoglossus muscle on the affected side pulling the tongue posteriorly.
Spasm of the intrinsic muscles on the affected side causing curvature.
Atrophy of the hyoglossus muscle causing a rotational shift toward the unaffected side.
Unilateral contraction of the styloglossus pulling the tongue toward the normal side.
correctOption: The genioglossus of the unaffected side pushing the tongue toward the paralyzed side.
