Based on the specific nodal location, which part of the tongue is most classically associated with primary drainage to this 'jugulo-omohyoid' node?
options: The dorsal surface of the hard palate
The floor of the mouth only
The pharyngeal part of the tongue exclusively
The tongue (as a whole, but it is a specifically associated terminal relay)
Only the extreme apex of the tongue
correctOption: The tongue (as a whole, but it is a specifically associated terminal relay)
optionExplanations: The palate drains via the greater palatine and nasopalatine routes to the submandibular or deep cervical nodes, but the jugulo-omohyoid is specifically linked to the tongue.
The floor of the mouth drains to the submental and submandibular nodes; the jugulo-omohyoid is a higher-tier node that receives lymph from these primary sites and the tongue.
The pharyngeal part (posterior 1/3) drains directly to the deep cervical nodes, often reaching the jugulodigastric node first, but the jugulo-omohyoid serves the tongue broadly as a deep relay.

While the jugulodigastric node is the 'sentinel' for the tonsil and tongue, the jugulo-omohyoid node (located lower in the chain) is classically described as being specifically associated with the lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
The apex (tip) drains to submental nodes first; the jugulo-omohyoid node is a more distal relay for the entire tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A medical student is performing a cranial nerve examination. When asked to test the motor innervation of the tongue, the student recalls that one specific nerve is responsible for the movement of both the intrinsic and nearly all extrinsic muscles. Which of the following nerves is primarily responsible for these motor functions?
options: Lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Facial nerve
Vagus nerve
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and is purely sensory for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; it does not provide motor fibers to tongue muscles.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory and taste innervation to the posterior third of the tongue but only supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle in the neck, not the tongue muscles.

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is the primary motor nerve for the tongue, supplying all intrinsic muscles and extrinsic muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus) with the sole exception of the palatoglossus.
The facial nerve (CN VII) provides taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani but does not provide motor innervation to the tongue muscles themselves.
The vagus nerve (CN X) provides motor supply to the palatoglossus muscle via the pharyngeal plexus, but it does not supply the bulk of the tongue's motor apparatus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The hypoglossal nerve is a motor nerve. ... Muscular branches to all the muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which anatomical landmark serves as the dividing line between the anterior two-thirds and the posterior one-third of the tongue, and also represents the embryological site of the thyroglossal duct origin?
options: Sulcus terminalis
Epiglottic valeculla
Plica fimbriata
Lingual frenulum
Palatoglossal arch
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The sulcus terminalis is the V-shaped groove on the dorsum of the tongue. Its apex contains the foramen cecum, the site of the embryonic origin of the thyroid gland via the thyroglossal duct.
The valleculae are depressions located between the posterior part of the tongue and the epiglottis.
The plica fimbriata is a fringed fold located on the inferior surface of the tongue, lateral to the lingual frenulum.
The lingual frenulum is a midline fold on the inferior surface of the tongue that anchors it to the floor of the mouth.
The palatoglossal arch is the fold of mucous membrane covering the palatoglossus muscle, forming the oropharyngeal isthmus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts. The apex of the sulcus... is marked by a small pit, the foramen cecum... [which] marks the site of the upper end of the thyroglossal duct.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Dissociation of Sensation and Taste on the Tongue
statement: A patient presents with a 'burning' sensation on the anterior portion of the tongue. However, upon testing, taste perception (sweet/salty) is perfectly intact, but the patient cannot feel the touch of a cotton wisp on the same area. Which nerve is specifically damaged?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Superior laryngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
Mandibular division of Trigeminal nerve (V3)
Chorda tympani
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve serves the posterior third, not the anterior portion.
The superior laryngeal nerve is sensory to the larynx and does not provide innervation to the tongue.

The lingual nerve carries fibers for general sensation. If damaged at a point where it does not yet carry chorda tympani fibers (or if only the V3 component is affected), touch is lost while taste remains.
While the lingual nerve is a branch of V3, V3 damage would involve more extensive deficits including the muscles of mastication and sensation to the lower teeth/chin.
The chorda tympani carries taste; if it were damaged, taste would be lost, but general sensation (touch) would be preserved.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Anterior two thirds: Lingual nerve branch of the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (general sensation) and chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (taste).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of Terminal Lymph Nodes
statement: In a radical neck dissection for lingual carcinoma, the surgeon must remove the vertical chain of deep cervical nodes. These nodes are anatomically found embedded within which connective tissue structure?
options: Prevertebral fascia
Carotid sheath
Pretracheal fascia
Buccopharyngeal fascia
Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
correctOption: Carotid sheath
optionExplanations: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles and forms the floor of the posterior triangle; the deep cervical nodes lie anterior to this layer within the carotid sheath.

The deep cervical lymph nodes are located within the carotid sheath, alongside the internal jugular vein and common carotid artery. This is why the carotid sheath is a critical area during oncological surgery of the neck.
Pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid, parathyroid, and trachea; it does not house the terminal deep cervical nodes.
Buccopharyngeal fascia covers the outer surface of the pharyngeal constrictor muscles; it contains retropharyngeal nodes but not the terminal deep cervical chain.
The investing layer splits to enclose the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid but the deep cervical nodes are found deeper, within the carotid sheath condensation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The deep cervical nodes form a vertical chain... within the carotid sheath, from the base of the skull to the root of the neck.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Terminal Lymphatic Chain of the Neck
statement: Which group of lymph nodes serves as the final common pathway (terminal group) for all lymph originating from the tongue, regardless of whether it was first filtered by submental or submandibular nodes?
options: Superficial cervical nodes
Laryngeal nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Anterior cervical nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein and drain into the deep cervical nodes; they are not the terminal group.
Laryngeal nodes are specific to the larynx and are not involved in lingual drainage.
The deep cervical nodes, forming a chain along the internal jugular vein, are the final terminal group for all lymph vessels of the head and neck, including those from the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and are not part of the standard drainage pathway for the tongue.
Anterior cervical nodes drain the skin of the front of the neck and do not receive the primary or secondary lingual drainage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sentinel Deep Cervical Lymphadenopathy in Lingual Malignancy
statement: A 58-year-old male with a history of heavy smoking presents with a hard, fixed, ulcerated mass on the right lateral margin of the oral part of his tongue. He has a palpable, firm, 2cm node at the level of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, deep to the sternocleidomastoid. Which specific node is most likely involved?
options: Jugulo-omohyoid node
Buccal node
Mastoid node
Submental node
Parotid node
correctOption: Jugulo-omohyoid node
optionExplanations: The jugulo-omohyoid node is a deep cervical node located near the omohyoid muscle (lower neck, but related to the hyoid level) that specifically receives drainage from the tongue. In lateral margin cancers, lymph may bypass the submandibular nodes and drain directly into these deep cervical nodes.
Buccal nodes are superficial facial nodes on the buccinator muscle; they drain the cheek and upper lip, eventually passing to submandibular nodes, but do not directly receive lingual lymph.
Mastoid nodes are retroauricular and serve the scalp and ear; they are never involved in primary lingual carcinoma drainage pathways.
Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue and the center of the lower lip; they would not be the primary palpable deep cervical finding for a lateral oral tongue lesion.
Parotid nodes drain the upper face and scalp; they are anatomically unrelated to the lymphatic pathway of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a physical examination, a patient is asked to protrude their tongue. The tip of the tongue deviates significantly to the right side. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this finding?
options: The right genioglossus is paralyzed, and the normal left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the affected side.
Spasm of the right styloglossus muscle pulling the tongue toward the midline.
Bilateral weakness of the hyoglossus muscles resulting in medial collapse.
Atrophy of the left intrinsic muscles causing a lack of support on the right side.
Paralysis of the left genioglossus muscle allowing the right muscle to pull the tongue to the right.
correctOption: The right genioglossus is paralyzed, and the normal left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the affected side.
optionExplanations: The genioglossus muscle's primary action is to protrude the tongue by pushing it forward. In a unilateral CN XII lesion, the healthy muscle pushes the tongue forward and toward the paralyzed side because the paralyzed side offers no resistance.
The styloglossus muscle retracts and elevates the tongue; it does not protrude it and its spasm would not cause the classic protruded deviation seen in lower motor neuron lesions.
The hyoglossus muscle depresses the tongue. Its bilateral weakness would affect the ability to flatten the tongue but would not cause lateral deviation during protrusion.
While atrophy occurs in long-standing lesions, the deviation is primarily a functional result of the genioglossus muscle's action (pushing) rather than a loss of intrinsic support.
If the left genioglossus were paralyzed, the right genioglossus would push the tongue toward the left side, not the right.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A surgeon is performing an extraction of an impacted lower third molar. During the procedure, the nerve passing deep to the superior constrictor muscle near the posterior border of the mylohyoid line is accidentally severed. What will be the clinical consequence for the tongue?
options: Loss of both general sensation and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Inability to protrude the tongue in the midline
Loss of general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue only
Isolated loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Loss of taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue only
correctOption: Loss of both general sensation and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve at the site of the third molar already carries both general sensory fibers (V3) and taste fibers (from chorda tympani). Damage here results in the loss of both modalities for the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.
Tongue protrusion is a motor function of the hypoglossal nerve, which is located deeper and more inferiorly than the lingual nerve in the submandibular region.
General sensation for the posterior third is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which follows a different course toward the pharynx and posterior tongue root.
Taste alone would only be lost if the chorda tympani were severed before it joined the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa.
The posterior third of the tongue is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is not the nerve typically endangered during a third molar extraction in this specific anatomical plane.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve passes forward... Here, it is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Secretomotor Function of the Chorda Tympani
statement: A patient presents with dry mouth (xerostomia) and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. The physician suspects a lesion of the chorda tympani nerve. Which of the following secretomotor pathways is interrupted in this patient?
options: Preganglionic fibers from the inferior salivary nucleus to the otic ganglion.
Postganglionic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion to the lacrimal gland.
Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion to the sublingual gland.
Postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
Preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
correctOption: Preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
optionExplanations: The inferior salivary nucleus is the origin for the glossopharyngeal nerve's parasympathetic component (CN IX), which targets the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
The secretomotor pathway to the lacrimal gland involves the greater petrosal nerve (CN VII) and the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the chorda tympani.

While sympathetic fibers do reach salivary glands, the primary secretomotor (fluid-producing) drive is parasympathetic. The chorda tympani lesion specifically halts the parasympathetic preganglionic input.
Secretomotor supply to the parotid gland is provided by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the otic ganglion, not the chorda tympani.

The chorda tympani (CN VII) carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that join the lingual nerve to synapse in the submandibular ganglion. These provide the secretomotor drive for the submandibular and sublingual glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a clinical evaluation for lingual carcinoma, the physician palpates a specific node located below and behind the angle of the jaw. This node is classically associated with the tonsils but is also a primary site for lingual drainage. What is the anatomical name of this node?
options: Submental node
Mastoid node
Jugulodigastric node
Prelaryngeal node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: Submental nodes are midline structures located inferior to the chin, far from the angle of the mandible.
Mastoid nodes are retroauricular and serve the scalp and ear, not the deep structures of the oropharynx.
The jugulodigastric node is the 'principal' node of the tongue and tonsil, located where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein.
Prelaryngeal nodes (Delphian nodes) are located in front of the larynx and are associated with thyroid and laryngeal drainage, not the tongue.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is situated further down the neck, near the omohyoid muscle, and while it drains the tongue, it is not the primary 'tonsillar' node at the angle of the jaw.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: An ENT surgeon is performing a neck dissection for lingual cancer. After clearing the submental and submandibular nodes, the surgeon follows the efferent vessels to the 'terminal' station for all lymph in the head and neck. What is this final nodal group?
options: Occipital nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Tracheal nodes
Parotid nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: The occipital nodes are the most posterior regional nodes of the pericervical collar; they drain into the deep cervical nodes.
The deep cervical nodes, located along the internal jugular vein, represent the 'final common pathway' for all lymph from the head and neck before it enters the jugular trunks.
Tracheal nodes are regional nodes for the trachea and thyroid; they are part of the vertical chain but not the overarching terminal group for the tongue.
The parotid nodes are regional nodes for the scalp and eyelids; they drain into the deep cervical chain rather than being the terminal station themselves.
The retropharyngeal nodes are a regional group draining specific areas like the nasopharynx; they are not the terminal collection point for the entire head.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): They [Deep cervical nodes] receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which cranial nerve provides the motor supply to both the intrinsic and most of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue?
options: Vagus nerve (CN X)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve supplies only one tongue muscle, the palatoglossus, through the pharyngeal plexus; it is not the primary motor nerve for the tongue mass.
The facial nerve provides special sensory (taste) innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani but is not responsible for tongue muscle movement.
The trigeminal nerve provides general sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the lingual nerve but does not provide motor supply to the tongue muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is the primary motor nerve for the tongue, innervating all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles with the sole exception of the palatoglossus.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides both general and special sensory innervation to the posterior third of the tongue but only supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle in the pharynx, not tongue muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Note: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: In the surgical management of a midline carcinoma of the tongue, the examiner emphasizes the risk of 'contralateral nodal metastasis'. Which anatomical feature of the tongue's lymphatic system provides the mechanistic basis for this risk?
options: The drainage of the entire tongue into the submental nodes.
The presence of valveless emissary veins connecting to the cavernous sinus.
The communication between the lingual artery and the facial artery.
The decussation of lymphatic vessels across the median fibrous septum.
The connection of the sublingual gland to the deep cervical fascia.
correctOption: The decussation of lymphatic vessels across the median fibrous septum.
optionExplanations: Only the tip drains to the submental nodes; the rest of the tongue has a more complex, multi-nodal drainage pattern.
Emissary veins connect the scalp and intracranial sinuses; they are not involved in the lymphatic spread of lingual cancer.
Arterial communications explain blood supply but not the pathway of metastatic spread, which is primarily lymphatic.

While a median fibrous septum exists, the lymphatic vessels, especially from the central part and the posterior third, often cross the midline or drain bilaterally into the deep cervical nodes of both sides.
Glandular connections to fascia do not dictate the primary routes of lymphatic metastasis in lingual carcinoma.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1725 (Book Page): A median fibrous septum divides the tongue into right and left halves. [Contextual anatomical correlate of bilateral drainage].

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Following a deep neck laceration, a patient is asked to protrude their tongue. The tip of the tongue deviates significantly to the right side. What is the precise pathophysiological mechanism explaining this clinical finding?
options: Hyperactivity of the right styloglossus muscle pulling the tongue laterally.
Spasm of the right hyoglossus muscle causing retraction to the ipsilateral side.
The normal left genioglossus muscle pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed right side.
The left genioglossus muscle is paralyzed, preventing protrusion on the left.
Bilateral paralysis of the intrinsic longitudinal muscles.
correctOption: The normal left genioglossus muscle pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed right side.
optionExplanations: The styloglossus muscle retracts and elevates the tongue. It does not play a primary role in the midline protrusion or the specific deviation seen during the forward extension of the tongue.
The hyoglossus muscle depresses the tongue. Nerve lesions typically result in flaccid paralysis and atrophy rather than spasm in the acute phase of a peripheral nerve injury.

In a Lower Motor Neuron lesion of CN XII, the genioglossus muscle (which protrudes the tongue) on the affected side fails to contract. The contralateral intact genioglossus continues to push its half of the tongue forward and medially, resulting in the tip pointing toward the side of the lesion.
If the left genioglossus were paralyzed, the tongue would deviate to the left side, as the intact right genioglossus would push the tongue toward the weak left side.
Bilateral paralysis would result in an inability to protrude the tongue at all and potential airway obstruction, rather than a unilateral deviation to one side of the mouth.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient suffers from a lesion of the facial nerve at the level of the geniculate ganglion. In addition to facial paralysis, what specific sensory deficit related to the tongue will be present?
options: Loss of taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue
Loss of taste from the epiglottis and extreme posterior tongue
Loss of general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue
Loss of general sensation (pain/touch) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Total loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
correctOption: Total loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
optionExplanations: Taste for the posterior 1/3 is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which does not pass through the geniculate ganglion.
Taste from the epiglottic region is carried by the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), which is unrelated to the geniculate ganglion.
General sensation from the posterior 1/3 is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the facial nerve.
General sensation from the anterior 2/3 is carried by the lingual nerve (V3), not the facial nerve. It remains intact in a facial nerve lesion.
The geniculate ganglion contains the cell bodies for taste fibers from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue. A lesion here or proximal to it destroys the taste pathway carried via the chorda tympani.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The taste fibers are the peripheral processes of the cells in the geniculate ganglion... The chorda tympani contains taste fibers from the mucous membrane covering the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Jugular Foramen Syndrome and CN IX
statement: A 55-year-old male presents with a large tumor at the base of the skull involving the jugular foramen. Examination reveals a total loss of the gag reflex, loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue, and significant wasting of the trapezius muscle. Which nerve supplying the tongue is primarily involved in this constellation of symptoms?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Lingual nerve (V3)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) exits via the jugular foramen along with CN X and XI. It provides taste and general sensation to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue and forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
The lingual nerve arises from V3 and supplies the anterior 2/3 of the tongue; it does not pass through the jugular foramen.
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) exits via various foramina (superior orbital fissure, rotundum, ovale) but none involve the jugular foramen or posterior tongue taste/trapezius function.
The facial nerve (CN VII) exits via the internal acoustic meatus and stylomastoid foramen; its taste contribution is limited to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) leaves through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen; while it supplies tongue muscles, it doesn't cause loss of taste on the posterior third or trapezius wasting.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): The glossopharyngeal nerve... leaves the skull by passing through the jugular foramen... Lingual branch carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Terminal Nodal Group of the Head and Neck
statement: What is the final terminal group of lymph nodes in the neck through which all lymph from the tongue must pass before entering the blood?
options: Deep cervical nodes
Mastoid nodes
Submandibular nodes
Submental nodes
Occipital nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: The deep cervical nodes are the final common pathway for all lymphatic drainage from the head and neck, including the tongue.
Mastoid nodes are regional nodes for the scalp and do not participate in the terminal drainage of the tongue.
Submandibular nodes are regional (pericervical collar) nodes that drain into the deep cervical chain.
Submental nodes are regional nodes for the tongue tip that must subsequently drain into the submandibular or deep cervical nodes.
Occipital nodes are regional nodes for the posterior scalp and are not part of the terminal chain for lingual lymph.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): They [deep cervical nodes] receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the majority of the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue?
options: Facial nerve (CN VII)
Vagus nerve (CN X)
Lingual nerve (V3)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
optionExplanations: The facial nerve provides taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani, but it does not provide motor supply to the tongue itself.
The vagus nerve provides motor fibers to the palatoglossus muscle only (via the pharyngeal plexus), but the rest of the tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII.
The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and provides only general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory and taste innervation to the posterior third of the tongue and motor supply to the stylopharyngeus, but not to the tongue muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve is the primary motor nerve for all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, with the sole exception of the palatoglossus muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The hypoglossal nerve thus innervates the muscles of the tongue (except the palatoglossus) and therefore controls the shape and movements of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Surgical Correlates of Radical Neck Dissection
statement: In the management of advanced lingual carcinoma, surgeons often perform a 'block dissection' of the neck. Which anatomical structure's relationship to the deep cervical nodes necessitates its frequent removal during this procedure?
options: Vagus nerve
Internal jugular vein
Facial nerve
Subclavian artery
External jugular vein
correctOption: Internal jugular vein
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve is a vital cranial nerve within the carotid sheath that is preserved unless directly invaded by cancerous deposits, unlike the dispensable internal jugular vein in unilateral dissections.
The deep cervical nodes are embedded in the carotid sheath and form a chain along the internal jugular vein; hence, the vein is removed to ensure complete clearance of nodal tissue.
The facial nerve is carefully preserved whenever possible to avoid facial paralysis, as it is not the primary conduit for lingual lymphatic spread.
The subclavian artery is a vital structure in the root of the neck and is not routinely removed, as lymphatics of the tongue do not primarily cluster around it.
The external jugular vein is more superficial and associated with superficial cervical nodes, which are not the terminal targets in deep lingual cancer spread.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): This procedure involves the removal en bloc of the internal jugular vein, the fascia, the lymph nodes, and the submandibular salivary gland.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: In the clinical staging of a carcinoma at the center (midline) of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, which nodal group is at highest risk for 'bilateral' involvement compared to a lesion at the lateral edge?
options: Occipital nodes
Buccal nodes
Mastoid nodes
Submandibular nodes
Parotid nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: Occipital nodes are at the back of the head and are unrelated to the tongue.
Buccal nodes are found in the cheek and drain the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek, not the tongue.
Mastoid nodes drain the scalp and are not associated with any part of the tongue.
Lesions in the midline of the tongue can drain to the submandibular lymph nodes on both the right and left sides, unlike lateral lesions which usually drain ipsilaterally.
Parotid nodes drain the face and lateral scalp, not the midline tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes [Clinical Correlation: Midline structures drain bilaterally]

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Chorda Tympani Relationship
statement: A surgeon is performing an extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar. If the lingual nerve is accidentally severed at this specific anatomical site, what combined sensory deficit will the patient most likely exhibit?
options: Loss of general sensation only to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue
Loss of taste only to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue
Loss of secretomotor function to the parotid gland
Loss of both general sensation and taste to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue
Loss of motor control to the genioglossus and hyoglossus muscles
correctOption: Loss of both general sensation and taste to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue
optionExplanations: While the lingual nerve provides general sensation, it is typically joined by the chorda tympani (taste) in the infratemporal fossa before reaching the third molar region.
The posterior 1/3 of the tongue is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which is not typically at risk during a routine third molar extraction.
Secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland are carried by the auriculotemporal nerve from the otic ganglion (CN IX), not the lingual nerve.

At the level of the mandibular third molar, the lingual nerve already contains the taste fibers from the chorda tympani; thus, a lesion here results in loss of both touch and taste for that side of the tongue.
Motor control is provided by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which runs deeper and more inferiorly than the lingual nerve in the submandibular region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The chorda tympani nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa... The lingual nerve fibers carry general sensation from the mucous membrane of the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The chorda tympani fibers carry taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which specific deep cervical lymph node, located near the omohyoid muscle, is frequently identified in clinical anatomy as being primarily associated with the drainage of the tongue?
options: Retropharyngeal node
Occipital node
Jugulodigastric node
Buccal node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
correctOption: Jugulo-omohyoid node
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes are situated behind the pharynx and do not drain the tongue.
Occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp and have no relation to the lingual lymphatic system.
While the jugulodigastric node drains the tongue, the question specifies the node located near the omohyoid muscle.
Buccal nodes are superficial nodes in the cheek, far from the deep omohyoid region.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a specific member of the deep cervical chain that sits at the junction of the omohyoid and internal jugular vein, specifically draining the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Mechanism of Tongue Deviation in Hypoglossal Nerve Palsy
statement: Following a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve on the right side, why does the tongue deviate to the right when the patient is asked to protrude it?
options: The right styloglossus muscle pulls the root of the tongue backward and to the right.
The right hyoglossus muscle fails to depress the tongue, causing it to elevate and shift.
The left genioglossus muscle is unopposed and pulls the left side of the tongue forward.
The intrinsic muscles on the left side contract more forcefully, pushing the tongue right.
The right palatoglossus muscle is hyperactive, shifting the tongue to the ipsilateral side.
correctOption: The left genioglossus muscle is unopposed and pulls the left side of the tongue forward.
optionExplanations: The styloglossus muscle retracts and elevates the tongue; it does not contribute to the forward protrusion required for clinical testing of CN XII.
The hyoglossus is a depressor of the tongue; its paralysis causes wasting but does not explain the lateral deviation during protrusion.

The genioglossus is the primary protrusor. Each muscle pulls its respective side forward. If the right is paralyzed, the left genioglossus acts alone, pushing the base of the tongue forward and causing the tip to deviate toward the stationary, paralyzed (right) side.
While intrinsic muscles are paralyzed, their role is in changing the shape of the tongue, not the primary directional movement of protrusion controlled by the extrinsic genioglossus muscle.
The palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X), not the hypoglossal nerve, and acts to elevate the root of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a neurological exam, a physician applies a cotton wisp to the posterior third of the tongue and observes no response. Which nerve is specifically responsible for general sensation in this region?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve
Facial nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve (CN X) provides sensation to the vallecula and the region around the epiglottis, just posterior to the tongue proper.
The facial nerve (CN VII) is responsible for taste in the anterior two-thirds but does not provide general sensation to any part of the tongue.
The hypoglossal nerve is exclusively motor to the tongue muscles and carries no significant general sensory fibers from the lingual mucosa.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both general somatic sensation (touch/pain) and special sensation (taste) to the posterior third of the tongue.
The lingual nerve (CN V3) provides general sensation only to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, ending at the sulcus terminalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Final Lymphatic Drainage of Head and Neck
statement: What is the terminal destination for all lymphatic vessels originating from the various anatomical regions of the tongue in the context of lingual carcinoma spread?
options: Submandibular lymph nodes
Buccal lymph nodes
Deep cervical lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Superficial cervical lymph nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Submandibular nodes are intermediate collectors for the lateral tongue but not the final terminal group.
Buccal nodes are facial nodes that do not serve as a terminal destination for the tongue's lymphatic system.
Regardless of whether the lymph starts at the tip, sides, or root of the tongue, it all eventually converges into the deep cervical lymph nodes.
Submental nodes are intermediate collectors for the tip of the tongue but not the final terminal group.
Superficial cervical nodes drain the skin of the neck and do not receive deep drainage from the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is unique because it travels through two different cranial nerves before reaching the brainstem. Which of the following correctly traces the step-by-step pathway of these special sensory fibers from the tongue to the geniculate ganglion?
options: Lingual nerve then Chorda tympani
Inferior alveolar nerve then Auriculotemporal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve then Tympanic plexus
Chorda tympani then Lingual nerve
Greater petrosal nerve then Maxillary nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve then Chorda tympani
optionExplanations: Taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue first travel within the lingual nerve (branch of V3) and then leave it to join the chorda tympani (branch of VII), which carries them to the geniculate ganglion.
The inferior alveolar and auriculotemporal nerves are branches of the mandibular nerve but do not carry taste fibers from the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve handles taste for the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
The fibers start in the tongue and travel in the lingual nerve first; they 'jump' into the chorda tympani later in the infratemporal fossa while heading toward the brain.
The greater petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland and some taste from the palate, not the anterior tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve... joins the lingual nerve... It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The taste fibers are the peripheral processes of the cells in the geniculate ganglion.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: UMN vs LMN Lesions in Cranial Nerves
statement: A patient presents with sudden onset of tongue deviation to the left. On examination, there is no evidence of muscle atrophy or fasciculations, but the patient also has weakness of the lower left quadrant of the face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Right-sided Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion
Left-sided Glossopharyngeal nerve lesion
Bilateral Vagus nerve paralysis
Left-sided Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion
Left-sided Hypoglossal nerve (LMN) injury
correctOption: Right-sided Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion
optionExplanations: A Right UMN lesion (e.g., stroke) causes contralateral (left) tongue deviation and contralateral (left) lower facial weakness. Atrophy is absent in UMN lesions.
A glossopharyngeal lesion would not cause tongue deviation or facial weakness; it would manifest as loss of the gag reflex and posterior tongue sensation.
Vagus paralysis would cause dysphagia and uvula deviation, but not the specific combination of isolated tongue deviation and quadrant-specific facial palsy.
A Left UMN lesion would cause deviation of the tongue to the right and weakness of the right lower face due to the decussation of corticobulbar tracts.
An LMN lesion of the left CN XII would cause deviation to the left, but it must be accompanied by muscle wasting and wrinkling, which are absent here.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): An upper motor neuron lesion (involvement of the pyramidal tracts) will leave the upper part of the face normal... Page 1685 (Book Page): in patients with an upper motor neuron lesion, only the muscles of the lower part of the face will be paralyzed.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Landmark of Deep Cervical Nodes
statement: Which anatomical structure serves as the primary landmark along which the deep cervical lymph nodes are arranged?
options: Superficial temporal artery
Facial artery
External jugular vein
Anterior jugular vein
Internal jugular vein
correctOption: Internal jugular vein
optionExplanations: The superficial temporal artery is located on the scalp and is related to the parotid and preauricular nodes, not the deep cervical chain.
The facial artery is related to submandibular and buccal nodes but does not define the vertical chain of the deep cervical system.
The external jugular vein is the landmark for the superficial cervical nodes, which drain the skin over the angle of the jaw.
The anterior jugular vein is associated with the anterior cervical nodes, which drain the superficial tissues of the front of the neck.
The internal jugular vein, located within the carotid sheath, acts as the central axis for the deep cervical nodal chain, which receives all lymph from the head and neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The deep cervical nodes form a vertical chain along the course of the internal jugular vein, within the carotid sheath, from the base of the skull to the root of the neck

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient suffers a lesion of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) as it exits the jugular foramen. Which of the following sensory deficits would be most characteristic of this specific nerve injury?
options: Loss of taste and general sensation on the posterior one-third of the tongue.
Anesthesia of the tip of the tongue only.
Isolated loss of taste on the vallate papillae only.
Loss of taste only on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Loss of general sensation only on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
correctOption: Loss of taste and general sensation on the posterior one-third of the tongue.
optionExplanations: CN IX is unique because it carries both general somatic sensation and special sensory (taste) fibers for the posterior one-third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae.
The tip of the tongue is supplied by the lingual nerve (general sensation) and chorda tympani (taste), both of which are independent of CN IX.
While the vallate papillae are supplied by CN IX, the entire posterior third (including areas without vallate papillae) would lose both sensation and taste.
Taste on the anterior two-thirds is provided by the chorda tympani (VII), which is separate from the glossopharyngeal nerve.
General sensation on the anterior two-thirds is provided by the lingual nerve (V3), which is not affected by a CN IX lesion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 70-year-old female presents with a non-healing, painful mass at the base of the tongue (posterior third). Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging reveals enlarged lymph nodes within the carotid sheath. During a block dissection, which of the following structures must the surgeon carefully preserve while removing the internal jugular vein and the associated lymph nodes?
options: The carotid arteries and the vagus nerve
The submandibular salivary gland
The fascia of the investing layer
The external palatine vein
The deep cervical lymph nodes
correctOption: The carotid arteries and the vagus nerve
optionExplanations: In a radical neck dissection for lingual carcinoma, the carotid arteries and the vagus nerve are vital structures within the carotid sheath that must be spared if they are not directly invaded.
The submandibular salivary gland is actually removed during a radical block dissection to ensure all associated lymph nodes are cleared.
The investing layer of fascia is part of the 'en bloc' removal to ensure that the lymphatics contained within the fascial compartments are taken.
The external palatine vein is usually ligated or removed as it is superficial and not a vital structure requiring preservation in major neck surgery.
The deep cervical lymph nodes are the target of the removal; preserving them would defeat the purpose of the oncological surgery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): The aim of the operation is removal of all the lymph tissues on the affected side of the neck. The carotid arteries and the vagus nerve are carefully preserved.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Motor Innervation of Extrinsic Tongue Muscles
statement: In the process of deglutition, the tongue's root is pulled upward and backward to push a food bolus into the pharynx. Which nerve provides the motor supply to the extrinsic muscle primarily responsible for this retracting and elevating action?
options: Vagus nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Facial nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Mandibular nerve
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The Vagus nerve (via pharyngeal plexus) only supplies the palatoglossus among the tongue muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus) except the palatoglossus.
The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and carries taste, but does not provide motor innervation to the tongue muscles.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is sensory to the posterior tongue but motor only to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
The mandibular nerve (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication, not the muscles of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Styloglossus: Action: Draws tongue upward and backward. Nerve supply: Hypoglossal nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Bilateral Lymphatic Drainage and Midline Carcinoma
statement: When comparing the lymphatic spread of a carcinoma located on the lateral margin of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue versus a midline lesion, which anatomical contrast is most accurate regarding nodal involvement?
options: Lateral lesions drain to the retropharyngeal space, while midline lesions drain to the buccal nodes.
Lateral lesions drain to the occipital nodes, while midline lesions drain to the submental group.
Lateral lesions drain only to submental nodes, while midline lesions drain to parotid nodes.
Lateral lesions bypass the submandibular nodes, whereas midline lesions always involve the mastoid nodes.
Lateral lesions drain to submandibular and deep cervical nodes, whereas midline lesions may show bilateral spread.
correctOption: Lateral lesions drain to submandibular and deep cervical nodes, whereas midline lesions may show bilateral spread.
optionExplanations: The retropharyngeal space is associated with the nasopharynx, not the anterior tongue. The buccal nodes drain the cheek, not the primary musculature of the tongue.

The occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp. While the submental group is involved in tongue drainage, it is restricted to the tip, not the entire midline of the anterior two-thirds which involves submandibular/deep cervical groups on both sides.
Lateral lesions do not primarily use submental nodes (which are for the tip), and midline lingual lesions never drain to the parotid nodes, which serve the face and scalp.
Lateral lesions specifically utilize the submandibular nodes as an intermediate step. Midline lesions have no anatomical connection to the mastoid nodes, which are located behind the auricle.

Lymphatic vessels from the lateral margins of the tongue typically drain to the ipsilateral submandibular and deep cervical nodes. However, because the tongue's lymphatic plexus crosses the midline, central or midline lesions can drain to both sides of the neck, necessitating bilateral clinical evaluation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes. [Page 1657 (Book Page): Clinical Notes] In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes... In patients with bilateral spread, a bilateral block dissection may be necessary.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with 'pseudobulbar palsy' following a bilateral stroke. On examination, the tongue is stiff, small, and difficult to move, but there is no evidence of muscle wasting or wrinkling. How does this differ from 'bulbar palsy' caused by a lesion of the hypoglossal nuclei?
options: Pseudobulbar palsy involves the chorda tympani, resulting in loss of taste.
Pseudobulbar palsy results in the tongue deviating to the side of the stronger stroke.
Bulbar palsy involves lower motor neurons, resulting in muscle wasting and fasciculations.
Bulbar palsy is characterized by hyperactivity of the genioglossus muscle.
Bulbar palsy exclusively affects the sensory nerves of the tongue, leaving motor function intact.
correctOption: Bulbar palsy involves lower motor neurons, resulting in muscle wasting and fasciculations.
optionExplanations: Pseudobulbar palsy refers to corticobulbar tract lesions affecting motor control; it does not primarily involve the chorda tympani or taste pathways.

In UMN lesions, the tongue may deviate away from the side of a unilateral cortical lesion, but pseudobulbar palsy is usually bilateral and characterized by a 'stiff' tongue rather than simple deviation.

Bulbar palsy is a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of cranial nerves (like XII). It presents with wasting, wrinkling (atrophy), and fasciculations. Pseudobulbar palsy is an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, showing spasticity without wasting.
Bulbar palsy involves paralysis and loss of tone/bulk in the tongue muscles; it does not feature hyperactivity.
Bulbar palsy is a motor deficit affecting the nuclei or axons of the motor cranial nerves; it is not a sensory nerve condition.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1685 (Book Page): In patients with a lower motor neuron lesion, all the muscles on the affected side... will be paralyzed... Page 1687 (Book Page): the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: What is the primary sensory innervation for taste sensation at the level of the vallate papillae of the tongue?
options: Lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
Vagus nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds, which does not include the vallate papillae.

The vallate papillae, although located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis, are embryologically and neuroanatomically part of the posterior third and are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the muscles of the tongue and provides no sensory or taste innervation.
The chorda tympani provides taste to the anterior two-thirds, ending at the sulcus terminalis and sparing the vallate papillae.
The vagus nerve (CN X) provides taste from the extreme root of the tongue and epiglottic area via the internal laryngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch [of IX] carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient experiences a clumsy extraction of an impacted lower third molar. Post-operatively, they complain of a 'numb tongue' on the side of the extraction. Which nerve was likely injured and what specific sensory deficit is expected?
options: Chorda tympani nerve; loss of taste only
Mylohyoid nerve; loss of motor control
Inferior alveolar nerve; loss of taste
Glossopharyngeal nerve; loss of general sensation
Lingual nerve; loss of general sensation and taste
correctOption: Lingual nerve; loss of general sensation and taste
optionExplanations: An injury specifically to the chorda tympani in the middle ear would cause taste loss only, but at the third molar site, the fibers are part of the lingual nerve.
The mylohyoid nerve is motor to the mylohyoid and anterior digastric; it does not provide sensation to the tongue.
The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the teeth and chin; its injury would cause numbness of the lip and teeth, not the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is located further posteriorly and is not typically at risk during a third molar extraction.

The lingual nerve passes very close to the medial aspect of the third molar. Injury here affects both general sensation (from V3) and taste (from the chorda tympani, which has already joined the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): Lingual Nerve Injury: The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: In the multi-step physiological pathway of lymph from the tongue to the heart, what is the structure formed by the union of efferent vessels from the deep cervical nodes?
options: Bronchomediastinal trunks
Ansa cervicalis
Subclavian trunks
Jugular trunks
Thoracic duct on the right side
correctOption: Jugular trunks
optionExplanations: Bronchomediastinal trunks drain the thoracic viscera, including the lungs and mediastinum. They are distinct from the jugular trunks that specifically serve the head and neck lymphatic drainage.
The ansa cervicalis is a nerve loop from the cervical plexus (C1-C3) that supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. It is part of the nervous system and has no role in the lymphatic drainage pathway.
Subclavian trunks drain the upper limbs, not the head and neck. They are formed by the efferents of the axillary nodes and join the lymphatic ducts separately from the jugular trunks.

This is correct. The efferent vessels leaving the deep cervical chain converge at the root of the neck to form the jugular trunks, which then deliver lymph into the large veins or the thoracic/right lymphatic ducts.

The thoracic duct is on the left side, not the right. On the right, the jugular trunk typically drains into the right lymphatic duct or directly into the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The efferent lymph vessels from the deep cervical nodes join to form the jugular trunks.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a radical neck dissection for lingual carcinoma, the surgeon identifies a prominent lymph node situated close to where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. According to anatomical landmarks, this node is primarily associated with the drainage of which structure?
options: The tongue
The nasopharynx
The parotid gland
The scalp above the ear
The external auditory meatus
correctOption: The tongue
optionExplanations: The jugulo-omohyoid node is a specific member of the deep cervical chain. It is located at the junction of the internal jugular vein and the omohyoid muscle and is functionally dedicated to the lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
The nasopharynx drains primarily to the retropharyngeal nodes and then to the upper deep cervical nodes, not specifically the jugulo-omohyoid node.
The parotid gland drains into the parotid lymph nodes, which are located on or within the gland itself, not the lower jugulo-omohyoid node.
The scalp above the ear drains into the mastoid (retroauricular) nodes and parotid nodes, part of the pericervical collar, before reaching the deep cervical chain.
The external auditory meatus drains to the mastoid and parotid nodes. The jugulo-omohyoid node is too inferior and specialized for tongue drainage to be its primary site.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Bilateral Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Base
statement: When comparing the lymphatic spread of lingual carcinoma, why is a lesion located in the posterior third of the tongue generally considered to have a poorer prognosis regarding metastatic spread compared to the anterior two-thirds?
options: The posterior third drains into smaller, less accessible nodes
The posterior third lacks a primary nodal relay in the neck
The posterior third has fewer lymphatic vessels overall
The posterior third drains exclusively to the submental group
The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes bilaterally
correctOption: The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes bilaterally
optionExplanations: The nodes associated with the posterior third are the deep cervical group, which are the largest and most significant terminal nodes in the neck.
The posterior third has a very robust primary nodal relay—the deep cervical chain—specifically the jugulodigastric node.
The posterior third is highly vascular and has a dense lymphatic network, increasing the risk of early and rapid spread.
The submental group only drains the tip; the posterior third bypasses all superficial nodes and enters the deep chain directly.

The posterior third (root) of the tongue drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes. Because lymphatic vessels in the midline and posterior regions often cross the midline, carcinoma here can metastasize to both sides of the neck simultaneously.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the primary motor nerve responsible for the intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue. Which nerve is the correct answer?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Vagus nerve (CN X)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Mandibular division of Trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
optionExplanations: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory and taste innervation to the posterior third of the tongue but does not provide motor supply to its muscles.
Vagus nerve (CN X) provides motor innervation only to the palatoglossus muscle via the pharyngeal plexus; it does not supply the other intrinsic or extrinsic muscles.
The facial nerve (CN VII) carries taste fibers via the chorda tympani but does not provide motor innervation to the tongue muscles themselves.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is the sole motor provider for all intrinsic muscles and all extrinsic muscles of the tongue, with the specific exception of the palatoglossus.
The mandibular nerve (V3) provides general sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds via the lingual nerve and motor innervation to muscles of mastication, not the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The hypoglossal nerve thus innervates the muscles of the tongue (except the palatoglossus) and therefore controls the shape and movements of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A physician notes that a patient’s tongue has become atrophied and wrinkled on the left side over several months. Which specific muscle’s paralysis is primarily responsible for the failure to protrude the left side of the tongue?
options: Right Genioglossus
Left Palatoglossus
Left Hyoglossus
Left Genioglossus
Left Styloglossus
correctOption: Left Genioglossus
optionExplanations: The right genioglossus is intact (as the atrophy is on the left) and would be the muscle responsible for pushing the tongue toward the left side.
The palatoglossus elevates the root of the tongue but is not involved in protrusion; it is also innervated by the vagus nerve.
The hyoglossus depresses and retracts the tongue, it does not protrude it.
Correct. The genioglossus is the primary protrusor of the tongue. If the left genioglossus is paralyzed, the left side of the tongue cannot be pulled forward.
The styloglossus retracts and elevates the tongue, it does not protrude it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Figure 12.80... One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a carotid endarterectomy in the carotid triangle, a surgeon accidentally damages a nerve crossing the internal and external carotid arteries. Postoperatively, the patient displays wasting and wrinkling of the right half of the tongue. What additional clinical sign is expected?
options: Deviation of the tongue to the right upon protrusion
Deviation of the tongue to the left upon protrusion
Loss of the gag reflex on the right side
Inability to sense hot or cold on the anterior tongue
Loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue
correctOption: Deviation of the tongue to the right upon protrusion
optionExplanations: Damage to the right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) results in ipsilateral paralysis. Upon protrusion, the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion (right). Long-term lesions lead to atrophy (wasting) and wrinkling.
The tongue deviates to the paralyzed side, not the healthy side, because the healthy side's genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side.
The gag reflex afferent limb is the glossopharyngeal nerve. CN XII has no sensory or reflex-afferent component.
Thermosensation on the anterior tongue is carried by the lingual nerve (V3), not the hypoglossal nerve (XII).
Taste on the posterior third is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is located deeper and higher than the typical crossing of CN XII over the carotids in the carotid triangle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The hypoglossal nerve... passes downward and forward in the neck and crosses the internal and external carotid arteries to reach the tongue... In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: How does the lymphatic drainage of a lingual carcinoma located in the posterior third (pharyngeal part) of the tongue contrast with a lesion located in the anterior two-thirds?
options: The posterior third involves only unilateral nodes, whereas the anterior two-thirds always involves bilateral nodes.
The posterior third drains to the submandibular nodes, whereas the anterior two-thirds drains directly into the internal jugular vein.
The posterior third drains to the submental nodes, whereas the anterior two-thirds drains to the deep cervical nodes.
The posterior third drains to the parotid nodes, whereas the anterior two-thirds drains to the mastoid nodes.
The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, whereas the anterior two-thirds typically involves regional nodes like the submandibular group first.
correctOption: The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, whereas the anterior two-thirds typically involves regional nodes like the submandibular group first.
optionExplanations: Actually, the posterior third is more likely to show bilateral drainage due to the lack of a strong midline barrier in its lymphatic network.
The anterior two-thirds uses submandibular nodes; lymph does not drain directly into the internal jugular vein but into the nodes surrounding it.
The submental nodes drain the tip (anterior), not the posterior third; the deep cervical nodes are terminal for both but primary only for the posterior third.
Neither the parotid nor mastoid nodes are involved in the primary lymphatic drainage of any portion of the tongue.

The posterior third of the tongue (root) is unique in that its lymphatics drain directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, often bilaterally, bypassing the more superficial regional nodes used by the anterior part.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Tip
statement: Which specific group of lymph nodes initially receives drainage from the tip of the tongue?
options: Submandibular lymph nodes
Occipital lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Submandibular lymph nodes primarily drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the upper lip, and lateral parts of the lower lip, but not the apex/tip of the tongue.
Occipital lymph nodes are located at the back of the skull and receive drainage from the posterior scalp; they have no anatomical communication with the oral cavity or tongue.

The submental lymph nodes, located in the submental triangle, are the primary first-level nodes for the tip of the tongue, the central part of the lower lip, and the floor of the anterior part of the mouth.
Parotid nodes receive lymph from the lateral face, eyelids, and external auditory meatus; they do not participate in the drainage of the tongue.
Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes drain the scalp above the ear and the auricle; they are not involved in the lymphatic pathways of the lingual region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of the Jugulodigastric Node
statement: A 62-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a non-healing, firm ulcer on the base of his tongue. On examination, a large, painless, fixed node is palpated just below and behind the angle of the mandible. Vitals: BP 135/85 mmHg, Pulse 82 bpm; Labs: Hb 11.5 g/dL. Which specific node is most likely involved in this metastatic spread?
options: Jugulodigastric node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
Submental node
Supraclavicular node
Mastoid node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is the 'sentinel' node for the posterior tongue and tonsil, characteristically located at the level where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is also associated with the tongue but is located lower in the neck, near the omohyoid muscle, whereas this mass is at the angle of the jaw.
The submental node drains the tip of the tongue, which is anatomically distant from the base (posterior third) described in the case.
Supraclavicular nodes are at the root of the neck; while they represent the final common pathway, they are not the first-order nodes for the tongue base.
Mastoid nodes are behind the ear and do not receive lymph from the tongue base.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Mechanics of Tongue Protrusion in Nerve Lesions
statement: A patient presents with a lower motor neuron lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve. When asked to protrude the tongue, it deviates to the right. Which physiological mechanism best explains this finding?
options: Paralysis of the left hyoglossus muscle
Unopposed action of the left genioglossus muscle
Overactive contraction of the right palatoglossus muscle
Unilateral contraction of the right styloglossus muscle
Spasm of the right intrinsic longitudinal muscles
correctOption: Unopposed action of the left genioglossus muscle
optionExplanations: The hyoglossus muscle depresses the tongue. If the left hyoglossus were paralyzed, it would not explain deviation toward the right during protrusion.
Protrusion is driven by the genioglossus muscles. If the right side is paralyzed, the left genioglossus acts alone, pushing the tongue forward and toward the inactive (right) side.
The palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus nerve, and its primary action is to elevate the root of the tongue, not to drive protrusion or horizontal deviation.
The styloglossus muscle functions to retract and elevate the tongue, not to protrude it; its unilateral contraction would not cause protrusion-associated deviation.
Intrinsic muscles change the shape of the tongue (curling, flattening) but are not the primary drivers of the midline protrusion/deviation seen in nerve testing.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with an advanced carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue. Anatomically, why is a 'block dissection' of the neck on only the ipsilateral side often insufficient for this specific site?
options: Because the posterior third is supplied by the external carotid artery which has high pressure.
Because the lymphatic vessels of the posterior third frequently cross the midline to the opposite deep cervical nodes.
Because the posterior third is derived from the first pharyngeal arch.
Because the lingual nerve provides a pathway for perineural spread to the brainstem.
Because the posterior third drains primarily to the submental nodes in the midline.
correctOption: Because the lymphatic vessels of the posterior third frequently cross the midline to the opposite deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Vascular supply (arterial) does not determine the direction of primary lymphatic metastasis, which follows low-pressure lymph channels.
The posterior third of the tongue has extensive lymphatic cross-communication. Carcinoma in this region often metastasizes to the deep cervical lymph nodes on both sides of the neck simultaneously.
The posterior third is derived from the third pharyngeal arch, not the first, though embryology is less relevant than the adult lymphatic anatomy here.
While perineural spread occurs, 'block dissection' is a surgical procedure for lymphatic control; the inadequacy refers to the missed contralateral lymph nodes.
The posterior third drains to the deep cervical nodes, not the submental nodes (which serve the tip).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes. [Context of complex drainage].

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Tracing the lymphatic pathway of a lateral tongue lesion, the lymph usually passes through the submandibular nodes. Which anatomical landmark marks the divide where the drainage shifts from these regional nodes to the direct deep cervical nodes?
options: Foramen cecum
Vallate papillae
Plica fimbriata
Lingual frenulum
Sulcus terminalis
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The foramen cecum is the apex of the sulcus terminalis; it is a single point rather than the boundary line (sulcus) that separates the oral and pharyngeal parts.
The vallate papillae are located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis; while they mark the location, the sulcus itself is the defined anatomical divide.
The plica fimbriata is a fold on the undersurface of the tongue lateral to the frenulum and has no significance as a lymphatic divide.

The lingual frenulum is a midline fold on the undersurface; while it helps define the floor of the mouth, it is not the boundary between the regional and direct deep cervical drainage of the tongue's dorsum.
