The sulcus terminalis is the critical anatomical landmark. Anterior to it (the oral tongue), drainage is generally regional (submental/submandibular). Posterior to it (the pharyngeal tongue), drainage is direct to the deep cervical nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts... [Page 1730 (Book Page)] Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 24-year-old dental student is studying the sensory innervation of the oral cavity. Which nerve is primarily responsible for providing general somatic sensation (touch and pain) to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
options: Lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), carries general somatic afferent fibers for touch, pain, and temperature from the oral part of the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both general and special (taste) sensation to the posterior third of the tongue.
The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), is responsible for special sensory (taste) fibers to the anterior two-thirds, not general sensation.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is a purely motor nerve supplying the intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue; it has no sensory distribution to the mucosa.
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of the larynx and a small area of the tongue base near the epiglottis, but not the anterior two-thirds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Anterior two thirds: Lingual nerve branch of the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (general sensation) and chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (taste)

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A lesion occurs in the facial nerve within the facial canal, proximal to the origin of the chorda tympani but distal to the geniculate ganglion. Which functional loss regarding the tongue would be most characteristic of this specific 'step' in the nerve's course?
options: Loss of taste sensation from the vallate papillae
Loss of general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Loss of motor control over the genioglossus muscle
Loss of general somatic sensation from the posterior third of the tongue
correctOption: Loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
optionExplanations: The vallate papillae, despite being in the anterior-looking portion of the tongue, are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

General sensation from the anterior two-thirds is provided by the lingual nerve (V3). These fibers do not travel in the facial nerve canal; they only join the chorda tympani in the infratemporal fossa.

The chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic and taste fibers. A lesion proximal to its branching point from the facial nerve will result in an ipsilateral loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Motor control of the tongue is provided by the hypoglossal nerve, which is unaffected by facial nerve lesions.
General sensation from the posterior third is the responsibility of the glossopharyngeal nerve, not the facial nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve arises from the facial nerve in the facial canal... It contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a surgical staging for lingual carcinoma, the surgeon must understand the sequence of lymph flow. If a malignancy is located on the side of the tongue, what is the most likely sequential destination of lymph before it enters the jugular trunk?
options: Submental nodes then to submandibular nodes.
Superficial parotid nodes then to retropharyngeal nodes.
Deep cervical nodes then to submental nodes.
Submandibular nodes then to deep cervical nodes.
Buccal nodes then to mastoid nodes.
correctOption: Submandibular nodes then to deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Submental nodes receive lymph from the tip of the tongue and do not typically drain into the submandibular nodes as part of the side-of-tongue pathway.
Neither parotid nor retropharyngeal nodes are standard intermediate stations for lymphatic drainage originating from the lateral tongue.
The flow of lymph is from the tongue to the deep cervical nodes, not the other way around; deep cervical nodes are the terminal group.

Lymph from the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue flows first to the submandibular nodes and subsequently to the deep cervical nodes, which form the final common pathway before the jugular trunk.
Buccal nodes drain the cheek, and mastoid nodes drain the scalp; they are not involved in the lingual lymphatic chain.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Bilateral Lymphatic Drainage of Midline Lingual Structures
statement: Carcinomas involving the central midline region of the tongue are associated with a higher risk of bilateral neck metastasis. Which anatomical feature of the lingual lymphatic system best explains this clinical observation?
options: Midline structures only drain into the ipsilateral deep cervical chain via the lingual vein.
The submental nodes only communicate with the contralateral submandibular nodes.
Lymphatic vessels from the center of the tongue decussate or drain to nodes on both sides of the neck.
The central part of the tongue lacks valves in its lymphatic vessels, allowing retrograde flow.
The midline of the tongue is drained solely by the thoracic duct, bypassing regional nodes.
correctOption: Lymphatic vessels from the center of the tongue decussate or drain to nodes on both sides of the neck.
optionExplanations: Midline structures do not follow a strictly ipsilateral (same side) drainage pattern; they often exhibit cross-over drainage, which is why bilateral neck dissection is often considered.

Submental nodes receive lymph from the center but they drain primarily into the submandibular or deep cervical nodes; they are not limited to communicating only with contralateral submandibular nodes.

Lymphatic drainage from central structures like the midline of the tongue is often bilateral. Vessels from the center can cross the midline or communicate with nodes on both sides of the neck (submental and deep cervical), facilitating the spread of carcinoma to both sides.
While lymphatic vessels generally contain valves to ensure unidirectional flow, the clinical concern in the midline is the anatomical distribution of vessels to both sides, not a lack of valves.
The thoracic duct is the terminal lymphatic vessel for the left side of the body but is not a primary drainage site for the tongue; lymph must pass through regional and deep cervical nodes first.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submental nodes... drain lymph from the tip of the tongue... center part of the lower lip. Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which anatomical structure serves as the dividing landmark between the anterior two-thirds (oral part) and the posterior one-third (pharyngeal part) of the tongue, where sensory nerve supply changes?
options: Epiglottis
Plica fimbriata
Frenulum
Sulcus terminalis
Vallate papillae
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The epiglottis is a cartilaginous structure posterior to the tongue that protects the laryngeal inlet; it is not a part of the tongue's dividing surface.
The plica fimbriata is a fringed fold of mucous membrane located on the lateral side of the lingual frenulum on the undersurface.
The frenulum is a midline fold of mucous membrane on the undersurface of the tongue connecting it to the floor of the mouth.
The sulcus terminalis is a V-shaped groove on the dorsal surface that marks the embryological and neuroanatomical boundary between the oral (anterior 2/3) and pharyngeal (posterior 1/3) portions.
While the vallate papillae lie immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis, the sulcus itself is the defined boundary between the two regions.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: When a patient with a lower motor neuron lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve is asked to protrude the tongue, the tip deviates to the right side. What is the precise pathophysiological mechanism for this observation?
options: The hyoglossus muscle on the right side fails to depress the tongue.
The right styloglossus muscle pulls the tongue to the ipsilateral side.
The intrinsic muscles on the right side undergo spastic contraction.
The palatoglossus muscle on the left side rotates the tongue clockwise.
The left genioglossus muscle is unopposed and pulls the normal side forward.
correctOption: The left genioglossus muscle is unopposed and pulls the normal side forward.
optionExplanations: The hyoglossus depresses the tongue; while it may be paralyzed, its dysfunction does not explain the horizontal deviation seen during protrusion.
The styloglossus muscle is responsible for the retraction and elevation of the tongue, not its protrusion.
Lower motor neuron lesions result in flaccid paralysis, wasting, and wrinkling of the muscle, not spastic contraction.
The palatoglossus muscle elevates the root of the tongue but does not significantly contribute to the midline protrusion or deviation in CN XII lesions.

The genioglossus muscle is the primary protrusor. In a unilateral lesion, the healthy muscle on the opposite side contracts, pushing that half of the tongue forward. Since the paralyzed side remains fixed, the tongue pivots and deviates toward the weak side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue's deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Lymph from a carcinoma at the tip of the tongue first reaches the submental nodes. To which node group does the lymph typically travel next in the hierarchical chain of the neck?
options: Mastoid nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Parotid nodes
Occipital nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Mastoid nodes are located behind the ear and do not receive lymph from the submental region.
Retropharyngeal nodes are located behind the pharynx and serve the nasopharynx area, not the submental pathway.
Submental nodes are regional nodes that eventually pass their lymph to the deep cervical nodes, which serve as the terminal chain for the neck.
Parotid nodes are not part of the tongue's drainage hierarchy.
Occipital nodes are located on the back of the head and drain the posterior scalp.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submental nodes... drain into the submandibular or deep cervical nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: The Sentinel Node of the Tongue
statement: A 60-year-old male presents with a firm, painless mass located just below and behind the angle of the mandible. Clinical examination reveals a primary lesion on the pharyngeal part of the tongue. Which specific sentinel node is most likely involved in this clinical presentation?
options: Mastoid node
Jugulodigastric node
Supraclavicular node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
Buccal node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: The mastoid (retroauricular) nodes drain the scalp and auricle; they have no role in lingual carcinoma metastasis.
The jugulodigastric node, found at the level of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle, is the primary 'tonsillar' or 'lingual' node for the posterior portion of the tongue.

The supraclavicular nodes are terminal nodes in the root of the neck; their involvement usually indicates advanced, late-stage spread rather than primary sentinel involvement from the posterior tongue.
While the jugulo-omohyoid node is associated with the tongue, it is located lower in the neck near the omohyoid muscle and typically receives lymph from the anterior two-thirds.
Buccal nodes are small nodes occasionally found on the cheek over the buccinator; they drain the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek, not the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A patient with long-standing carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue presents with hoarseness and a deviated uvula. Which anatomical complication during a block dissection would best explain these multi-cranial nerve symptoms if they occurred post-operatively?
options: Sacrifice of the hypoglossal nerve and internal jugular vein
Compression of the sympathetic trunk behind the carotid sheath
Accidental sectioning of the cervical branch of the facial nerve
Involvement and sacrifice of the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath
Surgical trauma to the pharyngeal plexus and recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Involvement and sacrifice of the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath
optionExplanations: Sacrifice of the hypoglossal nerve causes tongue deviation but not hoarseness or uvula deviation (which are vagal/pharyngeal plexus functions).
Sympathetic trunk injury would result in Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis), not laryngeal or palatal paralysis.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve supplies the platysma; its loss would not cause hoarseness or palatal issues.

The vagus nerve (CN X) provides motor supply to the soft palate and the larynx. Sacrifice of this nerve during a block dissection for advanced lingual carcinoma (if involved in nodal masses) results in paralysis of the larynx (hoarseness) and the soft palate (uvula deviation).

While surgical trauma is possible, 'sacrifice' of the vagus nerve () is a recognized necessity in advanced cancer and explains both hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal) and uvula deviation (pharyngeal branches).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): It is often necessary to sacrifice the hypoglossal and vagus nerves, which may be involved in the cancerous deposits.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: The lymphatic drainage of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is classified into which of the following groups based on its lateral margins?
options: Submandibular and deep cervical
Pharyngeal and tracheal
Mastoid and parotid
Submental and occipital
Retropharyngeal and laryngeal
correctOption: Submandibular and deep cervical
optionExplanations: The lateral sides (margins) of the anterior 2/3 of the tongue drain primarily to the submandibular and deep cervical groups.
Pharyngeal and tracheal nodes are deep visceral nodes for the respiratory and digestive tubes, not the tongue musculature.
Mastoid and parotid nodes are related to the ear and scalp/face, respectively.
Submental nodes drain the tip; occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp, not the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx; laryngeal nodes drain the larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Clinical Localization of Hypoglossal Nerve Lesions
statement: A physician is performing a neurological assessment on a patient. When the patient is asked to protrude the tongue, the tip points significantly to the left. The left side of the tongue also shows significant atrophy. What is the most likely location of the lesion?
options: Right lingual nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
Right hypoglossal nerve
Left glossopharyngeal nerve
Left facial nerve
correctOption: Left hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve provides sensory innervation to the tongue; it does not control tongue movement or muscle bulk.
Correct. Atrophy and deviation to the left indicate a lower motor neuron lesion of the left hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
A right-sided lesion would cause the tongue to deviate to the right, not the left.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is involved in taste and sensation of the posterior 1/3 and the gag reflex, but not tongue protrusion.
The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and taste to the anterior 2/3, but it has no motor control over tongue protrusion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): if a lesion of the nerve is present, it will be noted that the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side (see Fig. 12.80)... In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with restricted movement of the tongue. Upon examination, it is found that the only muscle of the tongue not paralyzed is the one responsible for elevating the root of the tongue and narrowing the oropharyngeal isthmus. Which nerve provides the motor innervation to this specific spared muscle?
options: Mandibular Nerve (V3)
Hypoglossal Nerve (CN XII)
Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)
Facial Nerve (CN VII)
Vagus Nerve (CN X)
correctOption: Vagus Nerve (CN X)
optionExplanations: The mandibular nerve (V3) provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the lingual nerve and motor supply to the muscles of mastication, but not tongue muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and all extrinsic muscles of the tongue (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) except for the palatoglossus.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue and motor supply to the stylopharyngeus muscle, but does not innervate tongue muscles.

The facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the chorda tympani, but provides no motor supply to tongue musculature.

The palatoglossus muscle is the only muscle of the tongue that is not supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; instead, it receives its motor supply from the cranial part of the accessory nerve via the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): Muscular branches to all the muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a biopsy of a carcinoma located on the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the surgical team discusses the potential routes of embolic malignancy. Which path represents the standard anatomical progression for lymph from this region?
options: To the submental nodes and then to the submandibular nodes.
To the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes.
Directly to the jugulodigastric node bypassing all regional nodes.
To the paratracheal nodes and then to the thoracic duct.
To the occipital nodes and then to the superficial cervical chain.
correctOption: To the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: The submental nodes specifically drain the tip and central structures; the lateral sides bypass these to reach the submandibular group.

Lymph from the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds typically flows to the submandibular nodes first, or in some cases directly to the deep cervical nodes, eventually reaching the jugulo-omohyoid node.
Direct drainage to the jugulodigastric node is more characteristic of the posterior third of the tongue (root) rather than the lateral margins of the oral part.
The paratracheal nodes drain the trachea and thyroid gland; the tongue's lymph does not enter this pathway.
The occipital nodes are part of the pericervical collar for the scalp and have no anatomical connection to the oral cavity or lingual drainage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Cranial Nerve Foramina and Tongue Deficits
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with loss of the gag reflex, loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue, and deviation of the uvula to the right. When she protrudes her tongue, it deviates to the left. At which anatomical site is a single lesion most likely to explain these multiple deficits?
options: Jugular foramen
Internal acoustic meatus
Foramen rotundum
Hypoglossal canal
Apex of the petrous temporal bone
correctOption: Jugular foramen
optionExplanations: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX (posterior tongue taste/gag sensory), CN X (uvula/gag motor), and CN XI. In clinical practice, large lesions here often involve the nearby hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) as it exits its canal.
The internal acoustic meatus transmits CN VII and CN VIII; lesions here would cause facial paralysis and deafness, not tongue deviation or loss of gag reflex.
The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2), which provides sensation to the midface and palate but does not affect tongue motor or posterior taste.
A lesion isolated to the hypoglossal canal would only cause tongue deviation; it would not explain the loss of the gag reflex or uvular deviation.
The apex of the petrous bone is related to the trigeminal ganglion and the abducens nerve; it does not contain the nerves responsible for the tongue or pharyngeal symptoms described.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1498 (Book Page): In fractures involving the jugular foramen, the 9th, 10th, and 11th cranial nerves may be damaged. The strong bony walls of the hypoglossal canal usually protect the hypoglossal nerve from injury. [Note: Clinical context implies a large lesion extending to include XII or a posterior fossa tumor].

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A clinical examination of a patient with suspected lingual carcinoma involves palpating the 'jugulo-omohyoid' node. Which specific portion of the tongue's drainage is this node most classically associated with according to regional neck anatomy?
options: The very tip of the tongue only.
The nasopharynx and auditory tube.
The posterior pharyngeal third exclusively.
The hard palate and maxillary teeth.
The tongue (as a major primary or secondary station).
correctOption: The tongue (as a major primary or secondary station).
optionExplanations: The tip drains to the submental nodes first. The jugulo-omohyoid node is a deeper, lower station in the chain.
Nasopharyngeal drainage is directed toward the retropharyngeal nodes and the upper deep cervical nodes, not specifically the jugulo-omohyoid node.
The posterior third drains primarily to the jugulodigastric node, although all lingual lymph eventually reaches the deep cervical chain.
The hard palate and maxillary teeth drain primarily to the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical chain, but they are not the primary association for the omohyoid station.
In anatomical texts, while the jugulodigastric is the 'tonsillar' node, the jugulo-omohyoid is frequently identified as the specific node for the tongue's drainage, particularly the anterior part.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Tip
statement: An elite surgeon is planning the resection of a squamous cell carcinoma located at the extreme tip of the tongue. To address the first echelon of lymphatic spread, which group of lymph nodes must be prioritized for biopsy?
options: Paratracheal nodes
Submandibular nodes
Retroauricular nodes
Jugulodigastric nodes
Submental nodes
correctOption: Submental nodes
optionExplanations: Paratracheal nodes are associated with the trachea and thyroid gland, not lingual drainage.
Submandibular nodes primarily receive lymph from the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the tip.
Retroauricular nodes drain the scalp and auricle; they have no role in the lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
The jugulodigastric node is associated with the tonsil and the general tongue body, but it is not the first-line node for the tip.
According to the anatomical correlates of the tongue, the lymph vessels from the tip of the tongue pass to the submental lymph nodes, making them the primary drainage site.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Lingual Nerve
statement: A 32-year-old male undergoes a difficult extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar. Post-operatively, he complains of 'numbness' on the right side of the anterior tongue and a loss of taste on that same side. Which anatomical structure was most likely injured during the procedure?
options: Superior laryngeal nerve near the hyoid bone
Lingual nerve as it passes the third molar tooth
Glossopharyngeal nerve as it enters the pharynx
Hypoglossal nerve in the submandibular triangle
Chorda tympani before it joins the lingual nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve as it passes the third molar tooth
optionExplanations: The superior laryngeal nerve is involved in laryngeal sensation and cricothyroid motor supply; it has no role in anterior tongue sensation or taste.

The lingual nerve passes just medial to the mandibular third molar. If injured here, it causes loss of general sensation (lingual fibers) and taste (chorda tympani fibers already joined), leading to the patient's symptoms.
Damage to the glossopharyngeal nerve would affect the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds, and would typically occur higher in the neck or at the jugular foramen.
An injury to the hypoglossal nerve would cause motor paralysis and deviation of the tongue, not a loss of general sensation or taste.
While the chorda tympani carries taste, injuring it before it joins the lingual nerve would spare general sensation; the patient's numbness indicates lingual fiber involvement as well.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient is unable to detect a bitter solution applied to the very back of their tongue. Which nerve is likely to have a lesion affecting its sensory distribution in this specific area?
options: Facial nerve
Lingual nerve
Vagus nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The facial nerve provides taste to the anterior two-thirds via the chorda tympani.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation only to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The vagus nerve provides taste sensation from the extreme posterior part of the tongue (near the epiglottis) but the majority of the posterior third is glossopharyngeal.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, including the area of the vallate papillae.
The hypoglossal nerve is exclusively motor to the tongue muscles and has no sensory or taste function.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1734 (Book Page): the glossopharyngeal nerve provides both general sensation and taste to [the posterior third]. Page 1726 (Book Page): The large vallate papillae lie alongside the sulcus terminalis.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Deep Cervical Nodes as Terminal Lymphatic Filters
statement: Which specific deep cervical node is considered the terminal filter for lymph coming from the submental and submandibular regional groups during the drainage of the tongue body?
options: Jugulodigastric node
Submandibular node
Occipital node
Deep cervical nodes
Mastoid node
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is a specific node *within* the deep cervical chain, but the question asks for the group name for all regional efferents.
Submandibular nodes are regional (intermediate) nodes, not the terminal deep cervical group.
Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp, not the tongue.
The deep cervical lymph nodes represent the final nodal group that all lingual lymph must pass through before entering the jugular trunks.
Mastoid nodes drain the ear and scalp.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): Deep Cervical Nodes... receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 28-year-old male undergoes a difficult surgical extraction of a deeply impacted right mandibular third molar. Postoperatively, he complains of a 'burnt' sensation and a complete loss of touch on the right half of his tongue's anterior portion. He also mentions that food tastes 'metallic' or 'bland' on that same side. Which anatomical structure was most likely injured during the procedure?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen
Hypoglossal nerve in the submandibular triangle
Maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa
Lingual nerve as it relates to the mylohyoid line
Chorda tympani nerve within the middle ear
correctOption: Lingual nerve as it relates to the mylohyoid line
optionExplanations: Injury at the jugular foramen would affect the posterior third of the tongue and would likely be accompanied by deficits in nerves X and XI.
The hypoglossal nerve is deeper and more inferior in the submandibular region; its injury would cause motor loss (deviation), not the sensory and taste loss described.
The maxillary nerve supplies the upper jaw and palate; it has no role in the sensory or taste innervation of the tongue.

The lingual nerve passes just medial to the mandibular third molar. Because it carries both general sensation from V3 and taste fibers from the chorda tympani (VII), a lesion here abolishes both modalities on the anterior two-thirds of the ipsilateral tongue.
While the chorda tympani carries taste, it does not carry general sensation; an injury in the middle ear would not explain the loss of touch and 'burnt' feeling.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with 'Anosmia' following a fracture of the cribriform plate. On testing the tongue, the physician notes that the patient can still perceive taste on the most posterior part of the tongue near the epiglottis. Which nerve provides the sensory pathway for this specific region?
options: Maxillary division of Trigeminal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Internal laryngeal branch of the Vagus nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal branch of the Vagus nerve
optionExplanations: The Maxillary nerve (V2) provides sensation to the palate and upper teeth, but it does not provide sensory innervation to any part of the tongue.
The Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is purely motor to the tongue muscles and has no sensory or taste function.
The Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the posterior third of the tongue up to the sulcus terminalis, but the extreme root near the epiglottis is served by a different nerve.
The Greater petrosal nerve (branch of CN VII) provides parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland and taste from the soft palate, not the tongue root.
The internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the Vagus, CN X) provides general sensation and taste to the root of the tongue, the vallecula, and the epiglottis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1755 (Book Page): Laryngopharynx (around the entrance into the larynx): Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a clinical examination for tongue cancer, the physician identifies an enlarged, firm node specifically located below and behind the angle of the jaw. This node is anatomically identified as the jugulodigastric node. Why is this significant for the tongue?
options: It marks the point where the submandibular duct enters the oral cavity.
It is the primary site of drainage for the tip of the tongue only.
It is the node that primarily drains the parotid gland and external ear.
It is a specific deep cervical node primarily concerned with the drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.
It is a superficial node that drains the skin of the chin and lower lip.
correctOption: It is a specific deep cervical node primarily concerned with the drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.
optionExplanations: The entry of the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) into the oral cavity is at the sublingual papilla near the frenulum, which is not related to the nodal anatomy of the jugulodigastric region.
The tip of the tongue drains first to the submental nodes, not the jugulodigastric node directly, although lymph eventually reaches the deep cervical chain.
Parotid lymph nodes (preauricular and deep) drain the parotid gland; the jugulodigastric node is primarily linked to the pharyngeal and lingual structures.

The jugulodigastric node is a prominent member of the deep cervical chain. It is strategically located near where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein and is a major 'sentinel' for malignancies of the tongue and tonsil.
The jugulodigastric is a deep node (within the carotid sheath), not a superficial node. Superficial nodes drain the skin, whereas deep nodes drain the viscera like the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: In the surgical management of lingual carcinoma, a 'block dissection' of the neck is often performed. According to the anatomical layout of the neck's lymphatic system, which vessel serves as the primary landmark for the vertical chain of the deep cervical nodes that must be removed?
options: Superficial temporal vein
External jugular vein
Facial artery
Internal jugular vein
Anterior jugular vein
correctOption: Internal jugular vein
optionExplanations: The superficial temporal vein drains the scalp and parotid region; it is far superior and superficial to the primary metastatic route of lingual carcinoma.
The external jugular vein is associated with the superficial cervical nodes, which drain the skin over the angle of the jaw, not the deep structures like the tongue.
The facial artery is a landmark for the submandibular nodes and facial muscles, but it does not track the vertical chain of the deep cervical nodes.

The internal jugular vein, located within the carotid sheath, is the central axis for the deep cervical lymph nodes. Radical neck dissections focus on removing the lymphoareolar tissue along this vein.
The anterior jugular vein drains the superficial tissues of the front of the neck and is not a landmark for the deep terminal nodes of the head and neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The deep cervical nodes form a vertical chain along the course of the internal jugular vein, within the carotid sheath, from the base of the skull to the root of the neck

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Functional Dissociation of Lingual and Chorda Tympani Fibers
statement: During a sensory evaluation of the tongue, a patient is found to have lost general tactile sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the left side, yet taste perception in the same area remains perfectly intact. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Lingual nerve distal to its junction with the chorda tympani
Glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen
Chorda tympani nerve in the middle ear
Hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone
Lingual nerve proximal to its junction with the chorda tympani
correctOption: Lingual nerve proximal to its junction with the chorda tympani
optionExplanations: A distal lesion (after the junction) would destroy both the general sensory fibers (V3) and the taste fibers (VII), resulting in complete sensory loss in that quadrant.
A lesion of the glossopharyngeal nerve would affect the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
A lesion of the chorda tympani in the middle ear would cause loss of taste and salivation but would spare general sensation carried by the lingual nerve.
The hypoglossal canal transmits CN XII, which is purely motor; a lesion here would cause paralysis and wasting of the tongue without sensory deficits.
The lingual nerve carries only general sensation until it is joined by the chorda tympani. A proximal lesion would selectively abolish general sensation while taste (joining later) remains intact.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve fibers carry general sensation from the mucous membrane of the anterior two thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth. The chorda tympani fibers carry taste from the anterior two thirds... joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a clinical anatomy lecture, the professor emphasizes that although the hypoglossal nerve is the 'nerve of the tongue,' one muscle in the tongue's anatomical region is a notable exception. Which muscle of the tongue is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
options: Genioglossus
Styloglossus
Verticalis
Palatoglossus
Hyoglossus
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it is responsible for protrusion.
The styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it retracts and elevates the tongue.
The verticalis is an intrinsic muscle of the tongue; all intrinsic muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.
The palatoglossus is technically a muscle of the soft palate and the tongue; it is the only muscle of the tongue supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (Vagus nerve, CN X).
The hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; it depresses the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Note: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with a carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue. Why is this specific location associated with a higher risk of early systemic involvement compared to the anterior tongue?
options: Lymphatics of the posterior third bypass the deep cervical chain.
The posterior third drains primarily to the submental and submandibular nodes.
The posterior third has no cross-midline lymphatic communications.
The posterior third drains exclusively to the superficial cervical nodes.
The posterior third drains directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes, often bilaterally.
correctOption: The posterior third drains directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes, often bilaterally.
optionExplanations: On the contrary, the posterior third drainage is directly into the deep cervical chain, which is the final common pathway for head and neck cancers.
The submental and submandibular nodes are intermediate stations for the tip and sides of the anterior two-thirds, not the posterior third.
The posterior tongue is notorious for having cross-midline decussating lymphatics, which is why contralateral or bilateral nodal metastasis is common.
Superficial cervical nodes drain the skin of the neck; they are not the primary conduits for deep visceral structures like the tongue.

The posterior third of the tongue lacks the intermediate filtering stages (like submental or submandibular nodes) seen in the anterior tongue. It drains directly to the deep cervical nodes and frequently does so bilaterally due to the lack of a midline barrier, facilitating rapid spread.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Components of the Chorda Tympani Nerve
statement: A patient with a lesion in the infratemporal fossa presents with dry mouth and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but maintains normal tactile sensation there. Which nerve is specifically affected?
options: Chorda tympani nerve
Mental nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Lingual nerve
correctOption: Chorda tympani nerve
optionExplanations: The chorda tympani carries taste fibers for the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers for the submandibular and sublingual glands. A selective lesion here spares the general sensation carried by the V3 component of the lingual nerve.
The mental nerve is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve supplying the skin of the chin and lower lip, with no role in tongue sensation or taste.
The greater petrosal nerve is responsible for lacrimation and nasal secretions; it does not supply the tongue.
The auriculotemporal nerve provides sensation to the temple and parotid region and carries secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland, not the submandibular/sublingual glands or tongue.
The lingual nerve carries both general sensation (V3) and taste/parasympathetics (VII). If the lingual nerve itself were lesioned, tactile sensation would be lost as well.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani... contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: The deep cervical lymph nodes represent the final common pathway for all lymph from the head and neck. In the context of lingual carcinoma, these nodes are anatomically sequestered within which structure?
options: Buccopharyngeal fascia
Investing layer of deep fascia
Carotid sheath
Pretracheal fascia
Prevertebral fascia
correctOption: Carotid sheath
optionExplanations: The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the constrictor muscles of the pharynx and is not the primary sheath for the deep cervical nodes.
The investing layer encircles the neck and splits for muscles like the sternocleidomastoid but is more superficial than the nodal chain.
The carotid sheath is a condensation of fascia that encloses the internal jugular vein and the deep cervical lymph nodes, making it the primary anatomical container for metastatic spread.
The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland and trachea; it does not contain the deep cervical nodal chain.
The prevertebral fascia covers the muscles of the floor of the neck; it is posterior to the deep cervical nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The deep cervical nodes form a vertical chain along the course of the internal jugular vein, within the carotid sheath

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lower Motor Neuron Lesion of CN XII
statement: A 58-year-old male undergoes a radical neck dissection for the treatment of a malignant tumor in the submandibular region. Post-operatively, the physician notes that the patient's tongue is wrinkled and wasted on the right side. When the patient is asked to protrude the tongue, it deviates sharply to the right. Additionally, the patient has no difficulty swallowing or speaking. Which structure was most likely sacrificed during the surgery?
options: Right Hypoglossal nerve
Right Chorda tympani nerve
Right Lingual nerve
Right Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Right Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Right Hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies the motor innervation to the tongue. A lower motor neuron lesion, such as that occurring during surgery in the submandibular triangle, leads to ipsilateral atrophy (wasting/wrinkling) and deviation to the same side during protrusion due to the unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus.
The chorda tympani carries taste and parasympathetic fibers. While its loss would affect taste and salivation, it would not result in skeletal muscle atrophy or motor deviation of the tongue body.
A lesion of the lingual nerve causes sensory loss (anesthesia) and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but does not cause muscle wasting or deviation during protrusion.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid). Its injury causes hoarseness but does not affect tongue movement or appearance.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is responsible for sensation and taste on the posterior third of the tongue and the gag reflex; its injury would not lead to tongue wasting or deviation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side... the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: How does the lymphatic drainage of the posterior third of the tongue differ anatomically from the anterior two-thirds?
options: It passes through the parotid nodes before the neck.
It drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes.
It drains exclusively into the submandibular nodes.
It drains directly into the submental nodes.
It bypasses all cervical nodes to reach the thoracic duct.
correctOption: It drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes.
optionExplanations: The parotid nodes do not serve any part of the tongue; they are limited to the lateral face and scalp.

Lymph from the posterior third of the tongue (behind the sulcus terminalis) passes directly to the deep cervical nodes, including the jugulodigastric node, because of its midline location and proximity to the pharynx.
Submandibular nodes primarily serve the anterior two-thirds (sides); the posterior third typically bypasses these superficial nodes.
Only the tip of the tongue drains to the submental nodes; the posterior third is too distal and deep for this pathway.
All lymph from the head and neck must pass through at least one nodal group, typically the deep cervical chain, before entering the jugular trunks and thoracic duct.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: In a clinical setting, how is the sensory integrity of the glossopharyngeal nerve specifically differentiated from that of the facial nerve regarding tongue innervation?
options: Observing the direction of tongue protrusion
Testing the motor strength of the buccinator muscle
Testing taste on the posterior one-third
Testing taste on the anterior two-thirds
Testing general sensation on the anterior two-thirds
correctOption: Testing taste on the posterior one-third
optionExplanations: Observing the direction of protrusion tests the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not the sensory nerves.
The motor strength of the buccinator is a test for the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which is unrelated to tongue sensation.
Taste and general sensation on the posterior third of the tongue are mediated solely by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
Taste on the anterior two-thirds is a function of the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani.
General sensation on the anterior two-thirds is a function of the lingual nerve (V3).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1686 (Book Page): Testing Glossopharyngeal Nerve Integrity... evaluation by testing the patient’s general sensation and that of taste on the posterior third of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with a visible wrinkling and wasting of the right side of the tongue. During the physical examination, the physician asks the patient to protrude the tongue. To which side will the tip of the tongue most likely deviate if there is a lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve?
options: To the left side (unaffected side)
To the right side (paralyzed side)
The tongue will retract instead of protruding
Straightforward with no deviation
The tongue will oscillate between both sides
correctOption: To the right side (paralyzed side)
optionExplanations: Deviation to the unaffected side is incorrect. The mechanics of the genioglossus muscle require it to push the tongue out; a functional muscle on one side will push the tongue toward the weak side.

The correct answer. In a lower motor neuron lesion of CN XII, the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion because the contralateral genioglossus muscle is unopposed and pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed side.
The tongue is still capable of protrusion via the intact contralateral genioglossus, though it will be asymmetrical.
Straightforward protrusion is impossible if one genioglossus is paralyzed, as the balanced 'push' from both sides is lost.
Oscillation or fasciculation might occur, but the primary clinical sign for localization is the direction of deviation upon protrusion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side (see Fig. 12.80). This can be explained as follows. One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Pathway of the Lateral Tongue
statement: In the progression of lingual carcinoma involving the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, what is the most common multi-step mechanistic pathway of lymphatic spread before reaching the terminal deep cervical nodes?
options: Direct drainage into the submental nodes followed by the jugulodigastric nodes.
Retrograde flow into the parotid nodes before entering the internal jugular chain.
Primary drainage into the retropharyngeal nodes via the pharyngeal wall.
Direct drainage into the supraclavicular nodes bypassing the cervical chain.
Drainage into the submandibular nodes followed by the deep cervical nodes.
correctOption: Drainage into the submandibular nodes followed by the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: The tip drains to submental nodes, but the lateral margins primarily utilize the submandibular station as the first step in the pathway.
Lymph flow in the head and neck is generally orthograde toward the deep cervical chain; the parotid nodes are not part of the lingual drainage circuit.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, whereas the tongue's lateral drainage is directed inferiorly toward the submandibular region.
Bypassing the deep cervical chain to reach supraclavicular nodes is not the standard physiological pathway for lingual lymphatics.

Anatomically, the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue drain into the submandibular lymph nodes. From there, the lymph follows the efferent vessels to the deep cervical nodes, which serve as the terminal collection point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior third of the tongue, carrying both general sensation and taste fibers?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve
Chorda tympani
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Lingual nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve (X) provides sensation to the small region at the very base of the tongue near the epiglottis, but not the posterior third proper.
The chorda tympani (VII) provides only taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the primary nerve for the posterior third of the tongue, handling both general sensory and taste modalities.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is purely motor to the tongue muscles and has no sensory or taste function for any portion of the tongue.
The lingual nerve (V3) provides only general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1731 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a long-standing lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the hypoglossal nerve. Beyond the characteristic deviation of the tongue during protrusion, which of the following clinical findings would most likely be observed on the affected side?
options: Hypertrophy of the intrinsic muscles
Wrinkling and wasting of the tongue surface
Loss of the gag reflex upon stimulation
Excessive salivation from the submandibular gland
Loss of taste sensation on the posterior third
correctOption: Wrinkling and wasting of the tongue surface
optionExplanations: Muscles undergo atrophy (wasting), not hypertrophy, when their motor nerve supply is severed in an LMN lesion.
Wasting (atrophy) of the muscle mass and subsequent wrinkling of the overlying mucous membrane are classic signs of chronic LMN denervation of the tongue.
The gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal (afferent) and vagus (efferent) nerves; the hypoglossal nerve does not participate in this reflex loop.
Salivation is controlled by the autonomic components of the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves; the hypoglossal nerve is purely somatic motor.
Taste on the posterior third is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is not part of a hypoglossal nerve lesion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue
statement: In the context of lingual carcinoma involving the lateral borders of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, which of the following best describes the multi-step anatomical pathway lymph takes to reach the deep cervical chain?
options: Drainage to submandibular nodes followed by drainage into the deep cervical nodes.
Drainage to submental nodes then to the parotid nodes and finally the jugular trunk.
Direct drainage into the thoracic duct via the transverse cervical lymphatics.
Retrograde flow from the submandibular gland to the facial nodes before reaching the deep chain.
Direct drainage to the supraclavicular nodes skipping the submandibular station.
correctOption: Drainage to submandibular nodes followed by drainage into the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: The lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue typically drain first to the submandibular nodes, which then act as a conduit to the deep cervical lymph nodes along the internal jugular vein.
The submental nodes drain the tip, not the sides; furthermore, parotid nodes are not part of the standard lingual lymphatic pathway.
Lymph from the right side of the head and neck typically enters the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct, and only after passing through the deep cervical chain.
Lymphatic flow in the head and neck is generally anterograde toward the deep cervical chain; retrograde flow to facial nodes is not a standard physiological or metastatic pathway.
Drainage from the lateral sides of the tongue typically follows a sequential pathway through the submandibular nodes rather than a direct skip to the supraclavicular nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 55-year-old male with a history of a glomus jugulare tumor presents with dysphagia and loss of sensation on the posterior 1/3 of the tongue. Imaging shows the tumor has compressed the structures in the jugular foramen. Which nerve's sensory function is specifically being tested at the posterior third of the tongue?
options: CN VII (Facial)
CN XI (Accessory)
CN XII (Hypoglossal)
CN X (Vagus)
CN IX (Glossopharyngeal)
correctOption: CN IX (Glossopharyngeal)
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The facial nerve exits via the internal acoustic meatus and stylomastoid foramen, not the jugular foramen.
Incorrect. CN XI is a motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; it has no sensory distribution to the tongue.
Incorrect. CN XII exits via the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen, and it is a motor nerve, not sensory for the posterior tongue.
Incorrect. While CN X exits the jugular foramen and causes dysphagia, its sensory contribution to the tongue is limited to the extreme base/epiglottic area, not the posterior third.

Correct. CN IX (Glossopharyngeal) exits the skull via the jugular foramen. It is responsible for all sensation (general and taste) for the posterior third of the tongue; its compression explains the sensory loss.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1496 (Book Page): [The jugular foramen] transmits the following structures in anteroposterior sequence: the inferior petrosal sinus; the 9th, 10th, and 11th cranial nerves.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Sensory Exception of the Vallate Papillae
statement: A physician is examining a patient's tongue and notes the presence of large vallate papillae. He explains that although these papillae are located anterior to the sulcus terminalis, their taste buds are innervated by a specific nerve. Which nerve is this?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
Chorda tympani
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is a purely motor nerve and does not carry any sensory or taste fibers for the vallate papillae or any other part of the tongue.
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies a very small area of the tongue base near the epiglottis for general sensation/taste, distal to the vallate papillae.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides taste and general sensation to the posterior third and extends anteriorly across the sulcus to supply the vallate papillae.
The lingual nerve provides only general sensation to the anterior two-thirds, not taste; it does not supply the vallate papillae.
The chorda tympani provides taste to the anterior two-thirds, but specifically excludes the vallate papillae despite their anatomical location anterior to the sulcus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1734 (Book Page): Remember that the circumvallate papillae are situated on the mucous membrane just anterior to the sulcus terminalis and that their taste buds are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which group of lymph nodes serves as the final terminal collection point for all lymphatic drainage originating from the tongue before the lymph enters the jugular trunks?
options: Submental nodes
Anterior cervical nodes
Submandibular nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Superficial cervical nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Submental nodes are a first-order regional group for the tip of the tongue but must eventually drain into the deep cervical chain.
Anterior cervical nodes drain the skin of the front of the neck and are not a terminal group for the tongue's deep lymphatic system.
Submandibular nodes are a first-order regional group for the sides of the tongue and face but must eventually drain into the deep cervical chain.
The deep cervical nodes, forming a chain along the internal jugular vein, are the ultimate destination for all lymph from the head and neck, including every region of the tongue.
Superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein and drain the skin; they eventually empty into the deep cervical nodes rather than the jugular trunks directly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): They [Deep Cervical Nodes] receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 62-year-old male with a history of heavy tobacco use presents with a biopsy-confirmed squamous cell carcinoma on the lateral border of the tongue, approximately 3 cm posterior to the tip. Examination reveals a hard, fixed mass just below the body of the mandible. Which specific anatomical node is most likely involved?
options: Submandibular lymph node
Occipital lymph node
Jugulodigastric node
Laryngeal lymph node
Anterior cervical lymph node
correctOption: Submandibular lymph node
optionExplanations: The submandibular nodes are situated superficial to the submandibular gland, directly under the body of the mandible. They are the primary intermediate drainage site for the lateral margins of the oral (anterior 2/3) tongue, fitting the clinical description perfectly.
The occipital nodes are located at the back of the skull and drain the posterior scalp. They are not involved in the drainage of the oral cavity or the tongue.

While the jugulodigastric node is a deep cervical node that receives lymph from the tongue, it is located below and behind the angle of the jaw. A mass specifically 'below the body of the mandible' is the classic location for submandibular nodes.
Laryngeal nodes are located in front of the larynx and drain the laryngeal structures. They are not primary or secondary drainage sites for the anterior portions of the tongue.
Anterior cervical nodes lie along the anterior jugular veins and drain the skin of the front of the neck. They do not receive deep lymphatic drainage from the tongue's musculature.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes. Page 1655 (Book Page): [Submandibular nodes] Located superficial to the submandibular salivary gland just below the lower margin of the jaw, they receive lymph from... the anterior two thirds of the tongue (except the tip).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a cranial nerve examination, a physician observes that a patient's tongue appears wrinkled and smaller on the left side compared to the right. Which clinical term and associated nerve lesion best describe this finding?
options: Ageusia; Facial nerve lesion
Atrophy; Hypoglossal nerve lesion
Anesthesia; Lingual nerve lesion
Hypertrophy; Glossopharyngeal nerve lesion
Dysphagia; Vagus nerve lesion
correctOption: Atrophy; Hypoglossal nerve lesion
optionExplanations: Ageusia is the loss of taste. A facial nerve lesion (chorda tympani) causes loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds but does not affect the motor size or wrinkling of the tongue.
Atrophy (wasting) of the tongue muscles is a hallmark of a chronic lower motor neuron lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The loss of trophic motor input leads to muscle fiber shrinkage.
Anesthesia is the loss of sensation. While a lingual nerve lesion causes anesthesia, it does not lead to skeletal muscle wasting of the tongue.
Hypertrophy refers to an increase in muscle size; the description 'wrinkled and smaller' signifies muscle wasting (atrophy).
Dysphagia refers to difficulty swallowing, often related to CN IX or CN X, but it does not cause localized wrinkling or wasting of the tongue body.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: In the classification of the lymphatic system of the head and neck, which nodal group serves as the final terminal station for all lymph originating from the tongue before it enters the venous circulation?
options: Occipital nodes
Submandibular nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Submental nodes
Mastoid nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Occipital nodes are part of the pericervical collar located at the back of the head. They drain the posterior scalp and have no anatomical or functional connection to the tongue.
Submandibular nodes are regional nodes that drain the anterior part of the tongue (except the tip). They are an intermediate station and must eventually pass their lymph to the deep cervical nodes.

The deep cervical nodes are the terminal group for the entire head and neck. Regardless of whether lymph starts in the tip, sides, or posterior third of the tongue, it must ultimately pass through this vertical chain.
Submental nodes are regional nodes for the tip of the tongue and the floor of the mouth. They are not a terminal group; their efferents drain into the submandibular or deep cervical groups.
Mastoid nodes are regional nodes for the scalp and ear. Like the occipital nodes, they do not participate in the lymphatic drainage of the oral cavity or the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 62-year-old male smoker presents with a firm, fixed, 2 cm ulcer on the right lateral border of the tongue and a palpable, non-tender 1.5 cm lymph node just below and behind the angle of the mandible. Given the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma spread, which specific deep cervical node is most likely involved?
options: Jugulo-omohyoid node
Buccal node
Mastoid node
Supraclavicular node
Jugulodigastric node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: The jugulo-omohyoid node is also associated with the tongue but is located lower in the neck near the omohyoid muscle, usually receiving drainage after more superior nodes.
Buccal nodes are superficial nodes in the cheek that drain the skin and mucous membranes of the face, not the deep lingual tissues.
Mastoid nodes drain the scalp and ear, not the tongue.
Supraclavicular nodes are typically involved in late-stage spread or from primary tumors below the clavicle (e.g., Virchow's node), not as the primary site for lingual carcinoma.
The jugulodigastric node, located at the level of the greater cornu of the hyoid and behind the angle of the jaw, is the primary sentinel-like node for the tongue and tonsils.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient exhibits loss of both taste and general sensation specifically on the posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae. Which nerve lesion is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Lingual nerve distal to the joining of chorda tympani
Mandibular division of Trigeminal nerve (V3) at the foramen ovale
Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve
Facial nerve (CN VII) at the stylomastoid foramen
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
optionExplanations: The Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is unique because it carries both special sensory (taste) and general sensory fibers for the posterior third of the tongue. It also supplies the vallate papillae, which are located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis.
The Lingual nerve (V3) only handles general sensation for the anterior two-thirds. Even when joined by the chorda tympani, it does not supply the posterior third or the vallate papillae.

A lesion at the foramen ovale would affect the entire mandibular nerve, causing sensory loss in the lower face and anterior tongue and motor loss of mastication, but it spares the posterior third of the tongue (CN IX).
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the vallecula and the small area of the tongue root near the epiglottis, but not the entire posterior third or the vallate papillae.
A facial nerve lesion at the stylomastoid foramen would cause facial paralysis but would not affect taste to the tongue because the chorda tympani branches off higher up in the facial canal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Multi-stage Lymphatic Flow of the Tongue
statement: Lymphatic fluid from the tip of the tongue follows a multi-step pathway to reach the venous system. What is the correct sequence of this drainage based on anatomical planes?
options: Tip -> Submental nodes -> Deep cervical nodes -> Jugular trunks
Tip -> Submandibular nodes -> Deep cervical nodes -> Jugular trunks
Tip -> Mastoid nodes -> Superficial cervical nodes -> Internal jugular vein
Tip -> Buccal nodes -> Parotid nodes -> Deep cervical nodes
Tip -> Deep cervical nodes -> Submental nodes -> Thoracic duct
correctOption: Tip -> Submental nodes -> Deep cervical nodes -> Jugular trunks
optionExplanations: Lymph from the tip first enters the submental nodes (regional). From there, it drains into the deep cervical chain (terminal). The efferents of the deep cervical chain form the jugular trunks, which then enter the venous system.
The submandibular nodes drain the sides of the anterior tongue, not the tip. The tip specifically utilizes the submental group as its first station.
Mastoid nodes and superficial cervical nodes (which follow the external jugular vein) are not the primary pathways for the deep muscular drainage of the tongue tip.
Buccal and parotid nodes are not part of the lymphatic pathway for the tongue. Parotid nodes drain the upper face and scalp.
This sequence is backward. Lymph flows from superficial regional nodes (submental) to deep terminal nodes (deep cervical), not the other way around.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Tip: Submental lymph nodes. Page 1656 (Book Page): [Deep Cervical Nodes] They receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes... The efferent lymph vessels from the deep cervical nodes join to form the jugular trunks.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with a persistent, painful growth on the lateral border of the anterior two-thirds of her tongue. Examination reveals a firm, 2cm mass. Vitals: BP 122/80 mmHg, Pulse 74 bpm. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. If this tumor metastasizes sequentially, through which nodal group would it likely pass before reaching the deep cervical chain?
options: Occipital nodes
Parotid nodes
Submandibular nodes
Submental nodes
Laryngeal nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: Occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp and have no anatomical relevance to lingual malignancies.
Parotid nodes drain the scalp and face; they do not receive lymph from the lateral tongue.
The anatomical drainage for the lateral tongue (anterior 2/3) flows first into the submandibular nodes before progressing to the deep cervical nodes.
Submental nodes are reserved for the tip of the tongue; lateral lesions bypass them.
Laryngeal nodes drain the larynx; they are not involved in the primary or secondary drainage of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Innervation of the Posterior Third of the Tongue
statement: A patient with a skull base fracture involving the jugular foramen shows a loss of taste and general sensation specifically over the posterior third of the tongue. Which nerve has been affected to produce these specific sensory deficits?
options: Vagus nerve
Lingual nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Facial nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve (CN X) provides taste sensation to the extreme posterior part of the tongue (epiglottic region) via the internal laryngeal nerve, but not the entire posterior third.
The lingual nerve (V3) provides only general sensation (not taste, unless joined by chorda tympani) and only to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue muscles and does not carry any sensory or taste fibers from the tongue surface.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is unique in that its lingual branch carries both general somatic sensation and special visceral sensation (taste) from the posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae.
The facial nerve (via chorda tympani) provides taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third, and does not provide general sensation to the tongue surface at all.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch [of IX] carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which anatomical mechanism explains why a carcinoma located in the central part of the tongue dorsum may present with metastatic nodes in both the right and left submandibular regions?
options: Lymphatic vessels from the central part frequently cross the midline to the opposite side.
The lingual artery carries malignant cells to both sides of the neck via retrograde flow.
Central lesions always drain first to the submental nodes before bifurcating.
Gravity causes lymph to settle in the submandibular fossa bilaterally.
The tongue lacks a median fibrous septum, allowing unrestricted lymph flow.
correctOption: Lymphatic vessels from the central part frequently cross the midline to the opposite side.
optionExplanations: The central portion of the tongue has a rich plexus of lymphatic vessels that can cross the midline, allowing malignant cells to migrate to lymph nodes on either the ipsilateral or contralateral side.
Lymphatic spread is the primary route for lingual carcinoma; hematogenous spread via the lingual artery is less common and would not follow nodal drainage patterns.
Only the tip drains to the submental nodes; central lesions drain toward the submandibular or deep cervical nodes.
Lymphatic flow is directed by pressure gradients and valves, not by gravity settling in specific fossae.
The tongue actually possesses a median fibrous septum, but lymphatic vessels are known to cross this barrier, especially in the posterior and central regions.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage] Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes. [Context of bilateral drainage for central/posterior structures]
