category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Topography of the Tongue Apex
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with a suspicious lesion at the very apex (tip) of the tongue. In reference to the anatomical lymphatic drainage of the tongue, which initial lymph node group should the clinician palpate first for potential metastasis?
options: Occipital lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Tracheal lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Occipital nodes are part of the pericervical collar located on the back of the skull; they drain the posterior scalp and do not receive primary or secondary lingual lymph.

The submental lymph nodes, located in the submental triangle below the chin, are the primary first-order nodes for the lymph vessels draining the tip of the tongue, the floor of the anterior mouth, and the central lower lip.
Parotid lymph nodes are located on or within the parotid gland and primarily receive drainage from the scalp, eyelids, auricle, and external auditory meatus, rather than the tongue.

Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes are situated behind the ear over the mastoid process and receive lymph from the scalp above the ear and the external meatus, making them irrelevant for lingual carcinoma.
Tracheal or paratracheal nodes are regional nodes in the neck that receive lymph from the trachea and thyroid gland, sitting far from the primary drainage pathway of the tongue's apex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a physical examination, a neurologist notes that a patient has lost both taste and general sensation strictly on the posterior one-third of the tongue. The gag reflex is also absent on the same side. Which nerve is most likely compromised?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
Chorda tympani
Lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor and does not carry sensory or taste fibers.
The chorda tympani provides taste specifically to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue only.
The lingual nerve only serves the anterior two-thirds of the tongue for general sensation.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is unique in providing both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue. It also provides the sensory limb for the gag reflex.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensation to the larynx and the area around the epiglottis, but not the posterior third of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae). The glossopharyngeal nerve thus assists swallowing and promotes salivation. It also conducts sensation from the pharynx.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Metastatic Pathway of Lateral Lingual Carcinoma
statement: A malignancy located on the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue follows a specific metastatic pathway. Which mechanism best describes the standard lymphatic progression for this region?
options: Direct flow into the thoracic duct via the internal jugular vein.
Bilateral drainage to the retropharyngeal nodes via the pharyngeal plexus.
Primary drainage to the paratracheal nodes bypassing the superficial collar.
Sequential drainage to the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes.
Direct drainage to the submental nodes followed by the jugulo-omohyoid node.
correctOption: Sequential drainage to the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Lymph must pass through several nodal filters (submandibular and deep cervical) before entering the venous system; direct entry is anatomically impossible.
The retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the oral tongue.
Paratracheal nodes receive lymph from the trachea and thyroid; lingual lymphatics do not utilize this pathway.
Lymph from the lateral borders of the anterior two-thirds typically drains first to the submandibular nodes and subsequently to the deep cervical nodes.
The submental nodes specifically receive drainage from the tip, not the lateral sides of the anterior two-thirds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 48-year-old female is diagnosed with a midline carcinoma on the dorsum of the tongue. Clinical examination reveals bilateral enlargement of the submandibular lymph nodes. What anatomical characteristic of lingual lymphatics explains this finding?
options: The facial artery provides a retrograde lymphatic path
The tongue lacks a median fibrous septum
The submandibular gland has no capsule
Lymphatic vessels from the center of the tongue cross the midline
All lingual lymph drains into the thoracic duct first
correctOption: Lymphatic vessels from the center of the tongue cross the midline
optionExplanations: Lymphatic flow is generally unidirectional; the facial artery is a vascular supply and does not provide a physical pathway for lymph or bilateral spread.
The tongue does have a median fibrous septum (Page 1725), but lymphatic vessels can still communicate across the central regions of the musculature.
The submandibular gland is indeed enclosed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia (Page 1747); this does not explain bilateral drainage patterns.
Lymphatic vessels from the central part of the tongue often cross the midline or bifurcate, allowing a midline tumor to spread to lymph nodes on both sides of the neck.
Lymph from the head and neck only reaches the thoracic duct (left) or right lymphatic duct after passing through the deep cervical chain; it is never the first tier.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1725 (Book Page): A median fibrous septum divides the tongue into right and left halves. [Note: Clinical application of midline crossing in lingual carcinoma is a standard anatomical correlate of the drainage listed on Page 1730 (Book Page)].

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient reports a total inability to perceive bitterness and saltiness on the back part of their tongue. Testing confirms loss of both taste and general touch sensation on the posterior third. Damage to which nerve most likely explains this global deficit of the posterior tongue?
options: Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)
Internal Laryngeal Nerve
Greater Petrosal Nerve
Chorda Tympani Nerve
Lingual Nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is unique because it carries both general sensation and taste for the posterior third of the tongue. A single lesion to this nerve accounts for the loss of both sensory modalities in that region.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides some taste and general sensation to the epiglottic region and the extreme posterior part of the tongue, but the majority of the posterior third is CN IX.
The greater petrosal nerve is involved in lacrimation and taste from the palate, but it does not supply the tongue directly.
The chorda tympani provides taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
The lingual nerve supplies the anterior two-thirds of the tongue for general sensation, not the posterior third.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Metastatic Mechanism of Lateral Tongue Carcinoma
statement: A patient presents with a malignant lesion on the lateral border of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Which mechanistic pathway describes the standard progression of lymphatic metastasis for this specific anatomical site?
options: Ipsilateral drainage into submandibular nodes and then to deep cervical nodes.
Direct and immediate bilateral spread into the retropharyngeal nodes.
Direct drainage into the submental nodes followed by bilateral deep cervical involvement.
Retrograde flow into the sublingual glands followed by drainage into the facial nodes.
Selective drainage into the parotid nodes before entering the jugular system.
correctOption: Ipsilateral drainage into submandibular nodes and then to deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Lesions on the sides of the anterior two-thirds (the body) typically drain first into the submandibular nodes and subsequently into the deep cervical nodes, often following an ipsilateral path unless the lesion crosses the midline.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the anterior tongue.
Only the tip of the tongue drains into the submental nodes; lateral lesions bypass these for the submandibular group.
Lymph flow is antegrade toward the neck nodes; it does not involve the sublingual glands or parotid-region facial nodes in this context.
The parotid nodes drain the scalp and eyelids; they are not part of the lingual lymphatic circuit.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a clinical evaluation for lingual carcinoma, the physician notes an enlarged node situated close to where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. Which specific region of the tongue is most associated with this nodal station?
options: The pharyngeal part of the tongue
The entire tongue, but specifically associated with the 'tongue' node
The ventral surface of the tongue
The foramen cecum only
The circumvallate papillae only
correctOption: The entire tongue, but specifically associated with the 'tongue' node
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal part (posterior third) drains broadly to the deep cervical nodes, including both the jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid stations.

The jugulo-omohyoid node is clinically recognized as the 'tongue node' because it receives drainage from the entire organ, either directly from the posterior third or as a second-order station from the anterior part.
The ventral surface follows the general drainage of the anterior two-thirds (body) of the tongue into submandibular and then deep cervical nodes.
The foramen cecum is an embryological remnant (thyroglossal duct origin) and does not have an isolated lymphatic drainage pattern separate from the posterior third.
The circumvallate papillae are landmarks for the sulcus terminalis; they drain with the posterior third, but the question asks for the specific 'tongue node' association.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 45-year-old male is admitted following a deep penetrating stab wound to the upper carotid triangle of the neck. On examination, the tongue deviates to the left upon protrusion. The left side of the tongue appears wrinkled and wasted. There is no loss of taste or general sensation on either the anterior or posterior portions of the tongue. Which structure was most likely severed?
options: Left Chorda tympani
Left Lingual nerve
Left Hypoglossal nerve
Left Internal laryngeal nerve
Left Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Left Hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The chorda tympani carries taste and parasympathetic fibers. Injury results in loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds and reduced salivation, not motor wasting.
The lingual nerve is sensory. Severing it would cause loss of general sensation in the anterior two-thirds but would not cause deviation or muscle wasting.
Wasting, wrinkling, and deviation toward the side of the injury (left) are classic signs of a Lower Motor Neuron lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensory supply to the tongue base near the epiglottis; it does not have any motor control over the tongue's intrinsic or extrinsic muscles.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is primarily sensory for the posterior tongue. Its injury would cause taste and sensation loss in the posterior third, not motor deviation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side... the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Which specific group of lymph nodes in the pericervical collar is located superficial to the submandibular salivary gland and receives lymph from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (except the tip)?
options: Mastoid nodes
Submandibular nodes
Parotid nodes
Submental nodes
Buccal nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: The mastoid nodes are posterior to the ear and drain the scalp and auricle.
The submandibular nodes are the primary regional station for the lateral portions of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, as well as the upper lip and the lateral parts of the lower lip.
The parotid nodes are located on or within the parotid gland and do not receive drainage from the tongue; they drain the lateral face and scalp.
The submental nodes are located in the submental triangle, not superficial to the submandibular gland, and they drain the tip of the tongue.
Buccal nodes are facial nodes located on the cheek; they drain the buccal mucosa and skin but not the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submandibular nodes: Located superficial to the submandibular salivary gland just below the lower margin of the jaw, they receive lymph from... the anterior two thirds of the tongue (except the tip)

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with a lower motor neuron lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). When asked to protrude the tongue, in which direction will the tip of the tongue deviate?
options: Toward the right (paralyzed) side
Toward the left (unaffected) side
Upward toward the hard palate
Straight forward with no deviation
Retracted back into the oropharynx
correctOption: Toward the right (paralyzed) side
optionExplanations: Correct. In a CN XII lesion, the genioglossus muscle on the healthy side acts normally to pull that side of the tongue forward, while the paralyzed side remains stationary. This imbalance causes the tip to point toward the side of the lesion.
Incorrect. The tongue does not deviate to the unaffected side; it is pushed toward the weak side by the functional muscle of the opposite side.
Incorrect. Upward movement involves the styloglossus and palatoglossus; it is not the primary diagnostic sign for a CN XII nerve lesion during protrusion testing.
Incorrect. Protrusion straight forward requires the balanced, bilateral contraction of both genioglossus muscles, which is absent in a unilateral lesion.
Incorrect. Retraction is performed by the styloglossus and hyoglossus; while they may be affected, the clinical hallmark of protrusion is deviation, not simple retraction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Drainage of the Pharyngeal Part of the Tongue
statement: A 50-year-old female is diagnosed with an invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue (Stage T3). Which clinical observation regarding her lymphatic spread would be most consistent with the known anatomical drainage of this region?
options: The carcinoma will bypass all cervical nodes to reach the axillary nodes.
The buccal nodes will be the first site of palpable disease.
Nodal involvement is likely found in the deep cervical chain, potentially bilaterally.
Metastasis to the submental nodes (Level IA) occurs first due to gravity.
Spread is limited to the superficial cervical nodes along the external jugular vein.
correctOption: Nodal involvement is likely found in the deep cervical chain, potentially bilaterally.
optionExplanations: Tongue lymphatics do not communicate with the axillary system; the terminal destination is the jugular trunks in the neck.
Buccal nodes are facial; they do not receive lymph from the root of the tongue.
Carcinoma of the posterior third (pharyngeal part) drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, and because of the anatomical midline decussation in the root, bilateral spread is common.
Submental nodes drain the tip; gravity does not dictate lymphatic flow, which is guided by anatomical vessels.
Superficial cervical nodes drain skin; the tongue is a deep structure draining to the deep cervical nodes within the carotid sheath.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Filters of the Oral Tongue
statement: In the pericervical collar of lymph nodes, which specific group serves as a primary relay for lymph originating from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (excluding the tip)?
options: Mastoid nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Submandibular nodes
Occipital nodes
Parotid nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: Mastoid nodes drain the scalp and auricle; they are not connected to the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and vertebral column, located behind the pharynx.
Submandibular nodes are the primary regional nodes for the lateral margins and dorsum of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp and have no role in lingual drainage.
Parotid nodes receive lymph from the lateral face and scalp, not the oral cavity proper.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submandibular nodes... receive lymph from... the anterior two thirds of the tongue (except the tip).

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with a lower motor neuron lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve. During examination, when the patient is asked to protrude their tongue, it deviates to the right side. What is the precise pathophysiological mechanism behind this specific deviation?
options: Bilateral failure of the palatoglossus muscles to elevate the root
Paralysis of the contralateral hyoglossus muscle
Unopposed contraction of the contralateral genioglossus muscle
Spasm of the ipsilateral intrinsic longitudinal muscles
Hyperactivity of the ipsilateral styloglossus muscle
correctOption: Unopposed contraction of the contralateral genioglossus muscle
optionExplanations: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the vagus nerve and functions to elevate the posterior tongue; its dysfunction would result in sagging of the soft palate rather than tongue deviation during protrusion.
The hyoglossus muscle primarily depresses the tongue. Paralysis of the contralateral muscle would affect depression, not the direction of protrusion.

The genioglossus muscle is responsible for tongue protrusion. In a unilateral lesion, the healthy contralateral muscle continues to push its side of the tongue forward and toward the midline, but because the ipsilateral muscle is inert, the tongue 'points' toward the side of the lesion.
Intrinsic muscles change the shape of the tongue; a spasm would cause distortion but not the directional deviation during protrusion caused by extrinsic muscle imbalance.
The styloglossus muscle functions to retract and elevate the tongue; its hyperactivity would not cause protrusion or the characteristic deviation seen in CN XII palsy.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue's deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Direct Deep Cervical Drainage of the Pharyngeal Tongue
statement: A 62-year-old female presents with dysphagia and is found to have a malignant mass at the root (posterior third) of the tongue. Unlike the oral part, carcinoma of the posterior third is more likely to present with early deep cervical lymphadenopathy because:
options: The posterior third only drains into the suboccipital venous plexus.
The posterior third is drained by the facial vein which carries cancer cells to the parotid nodes.
Lymph from the posterior third must pass through the submental nodes first.
The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, bypassing superficial regional nodes.
The posterior third is less vascular, forcing lymph into deeper pathways.
correctOption: The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, bypassing superficial regional nodes.
optionExplanations: While the occipital vein drains to the suboccipital plexus, the lymphatic system of the tongue is distinct and leads to the cervical nodal chains, not the posterior scalp drainage sites.
Venous drainage does not typically carry lymph to the parotid nodes; furthermore, the parotid nodes do not serve as drainage sites for the tongue.
The submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue; the posterior third does not drain into the submental or submandibular regional groups.

Anatomically, the lymph vessels from the posterior third (root) of the tongue pass directly to the deep cervical nodes (especially the jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid nodes). This direct pathway allows for early nodal involvement in the neck without preceding superficial nodes.
The posterior third of the tongue is highly vascular (lingual artery, etc.), and the early metastasis is due to direct lymphatic pathways, not a lack of vascularity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia. During a clinical evaluation, the physician tests for taste and general sensation. Which specific anatomical features are most likely to show impaired sensation if the glossopharyngeal nerve is dysfunctional?
options: Filiform papillae on the tongue tip
Vallate papillae anterior to the sulcus terminalis
Fungiform papillae on the lateral margins
Gingival mucosa of the lower incisors
Skin over the angle of the mandible
correctOption: Vallate papillae anterior to the sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: Filiform papillae are mechanical receptors located on the anterior 2/3 and are supplied by the lingual nerve (V3).

The vallate (circumvallate) papillae, although physically located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis, are embryologically and neuroanatomically associated with the posterior third and supplied by CN IX.
Fungiform papillae are located on the anterior 2/3 and their taste buds are supplied by the chorda tympani (CN VII).
The gingival mucosa of the lower incisors is supplied by the mental nerve and incisive branches of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not the trigeminal or glossopharyngeal nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1734 (Book Page): Remember that the circumvallate papillae are situated on the mucous membrane just anterior to the sulcus terminalis and that their taste buds are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Metastasis of Lingual Carcinoma
statement: A patient with carcinoma on the lateral border of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is likely to have metastatic spread to which primary nodal groups?
options: Retropharyngeal and laryngeal nodes
Parotid and submental nodes
Tracheal and mastoid nodes
Submental and submandibular nodes
Submandibular and deep cervical nodes
correctOption: Submandibular and deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, while laryngeal nodes drain the larynx; they do not receive lymph from the oral tongue.
Parotid nodes drain the scalp and eyelids; they are never involved in the primary lymphatic pathway of the tongue's lateral borders.
Tracheal nodes are associated with the thyroid and trachea; mastoid nodes are associated with the ear. Neither group is part of the lingual drainage system.
While submental nodes drain the tip, the lateral sides specifically bypass these and drain first into submandibular nodes and then the deep cervical chain.
The lymphatic vessels from the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue pass to the submandibular nodes and the deep cervical nodes (specifically the jugulo-omohyoid node).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoes an evaluation of oral motor function. During the examination, it is noted that while most muscles of the tongue are functioning normally, the palatoglossus muscle is paralyzed. Which nerve is responsible for the motor innervation of this specific muscle?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Lingual nerve (V3)
Chorda tympani (CN VII)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Pharyngeal plexus (CN X fibers)
correctOption: Pharyngeal plexus (CN X fibers)
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both general and taste sensation to the posterior third of the tongue but does not provide motor innervation to the tongue muscles.
The lingual nerve is a sensory branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve and does not provide motor innervation to the tongue musculature.

The chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that carries taste fibers for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers, but it is not a motor nerve for tongue muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor supply to all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, such as the genioglossus and hyoglossus, but specifically excludes the palatoglossus.

The palatoglossus is technically a muscle of the soft palate and the tongue; it is the only tongue muscle innervated by the pharyngeal plexus, specifically via the cranial root of the accessory nerve traveling with the vagus nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Muscular branches to all the muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Contrast: Tongue Body vs. Root
statement: When contrasting the lymphatic drainage of the anterior two-thirds (body) and the posterior one-third (root) of the tongue, which diagnostic finding is most indicative of a carcinoma originating in the posterior third?
options: Presence of skip-metastasis to the superficial parotid nodes.
Direct and early involvement of the deep cervical lymph nodes.
Isolated swelling of the buccal nodes without cervical involvement.
Initial metastasis confined strictly to the submental triangle.
Primary drainage into the anterior jugular venous system without nodal filtration.
correctOption: Direct and early involvement of the deep cervical lymph nodes.
optionExplanations: Parotid nodes are not involved in the drainage of the posterior third of the tongue.
Unlike the anterior two-thirds, which often drains through intermediate nodes (submandibular/submental), the posterior third (root) drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes.
Buccal nodes drain the cheek; they are occasionally involved in facial drainage but are not the primary target for the posterior tongue.
The submental nodes drain the tip, which is part of the anterior two-thirds, not the posterior third.
Lymph must always filter through lymph nodes before entering the venous system; it does not bypass nodal filtration.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Base of Skull Foramina and Nerve Lesions
statement: A 55-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a high-velocity motor vehicle accident. Radiology reveals a fracture through the right hypoglossal canal. On clinical examination, the patient shows clear deviation of the tongue to the right upon protrusion. If the fracture also extended to involve the jugular foramen, which additional tongue-related deficit would most likely be present?
options: Bilateral paralysis of the genioglossus muscles
Loss of sensation to the cheek and lower lip
Loss of taste on the right posterior third
Deviation of the uvula to the right side
Loss of general sensation on the right anterior two-thirds
correctOption: Loss of taste on the right posterior third
optionExplanations: Tongue paralysis would remain unilateral (on the side of the fracture) unless both hypoglossal canals were compromised.
Sensation to the cheek and lower lip is provided by branches of the mandibular nerve (V3), which exits through the foramen ovale.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) exits via the jugular foramen. Its lingual branch provides taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue; thus, a lesion here would abolish these modalities.
The vagus nerve (CN X) exits the jugular foramen and supplies the soft palate; a lesion results in the uvula deviating to the *opposite* (healthy) side, which would be the left side in this case.
General sensation on the anterior 2/3 is provided by the lingual nerve (V3), which exits the skull via the foramen ovale, not the jugular foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Lingual branch [of IX] carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue... [and] Page 1496 (Book Page): The jugular foramen ... transmits ... the 9th, 10th, and 11th cranial nerves.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: When comparing a malignancy on the lateral margin of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue with a malignancy of the posterior third, which anatomical distinction is most significant regarding their immediate lymphatic drainage?
options: Lateral lesions drain to the submental nodes, whereas posterior lesions drain to the parotid nodes.
Lateral lesions drain to the submandibular nodes, whereas posterior lesions drain directly to deep cervical nodes.
Lateral lesions drain to the occipital nodes, whereas posterior lesions drain to the mastoid group.
Lateral lesions drain to the retropharyngeal nodes, whereas posterior lesions drain to the submandibular group.
Lateral lesions bypass all regional nodes, whereas posterior lesions must pass through the submental group.
correctOption: Lateral lesions drain to the submandibular nodes, whereas posterior lesions drain directly to deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Submental nodes only drain the tip, and parotid nodes do not drain the tongue at all.
The anterior sides drain sequentially (submandibular then deep cervical), while the posterior third drains directly to the deep cervical chain, a critical distinction for surgical staging.
Occipital and mastoid nodes drain the scalp and have no anatomical connection to the tongue's lymphatic system.
Retropharyngeal nodes are involved in pharyngeal drainage, and submandibular nodes do not receive lymph from the posterior third of the tongue.
No lingual lesion bypasses nodes; furthermore, posterior lesions never drain into the submental group.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes; Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty moving the tongue. During examination, the physician notes that all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue are functioning except for the palatoglossus muscle. Which nerve is most likely responsible for the innervation of this specific muscle?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus
Chorda tympani (CN VII)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Lingual nerve (V3)
correctOption: Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus
optionExplanations: The Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue and supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle, but not the palatoglossus.

The palatoglossus muscle is structurally a muscle of the tongue but is functionally and embryologically related to the soft palate; it is supplied by the cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) via the vagus nerve (CN X) through the pharyngeal plexus.

The Chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that carries taste fibers for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

The Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is the primary motor nerve for the tongue, supplying all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles except the palatoglossus. A lesion here would affect the majority of the tongue's mobility.

The Lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), provides general somatic sensation (touch, pain, temperature) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not motor supply.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Muscular branches to all the muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Direct vs. Indirect Lymphatic Drainage of Lingual Segments
statement: When comparing the lymphatic drainage of the pharyngeal part (posterior third) of the tongue with the oral part (anterior two-thirds), which anatomical contrast is most significant regarding carcinoma spread?
options: The anterior part drains to the occipital nodes, while the posterior part drains to the mastoid nodes.
The anterior two-thirds possesses no lymphatic vessels, unlike the highly vascularized posterior third.
The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, bypassing superficial regional nodes.
The posterior third drains only unilaterally, whereas the anterior two-thirds drains bilaterally.
The posterior third drains exclusively to the submental nodes, whereas the anterior part drains to the deep cervical nodes.
correctOption: The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, bypassing superficial regional nodes.
optionExplanations: Neither lingual segment drains to the occipital or mastoid nodes, as these are located on the scalp and posterior head.
Both parts of the tongue are highly vascularized and possess extensive lymphatic networks necessary for immune surveillance.
The posterior third of the tongue drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, which often results in earlier systemic involvement in base-of-tongue cancers.
Midline structures in both segments can drain bilaterally; unilateral drainage is not a distinguishing feature of the posterior third.
This is inverted; the tip drains to submental nodes, but the posterior third drains directly to deep cervical nodes.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with a 'burning' sensation and severe lancinating pain triggered by swallowing, located deep in the throat and the back of the tongue. This clinical picture is most suggestive of a lesion or neuralgia involving which nerve?
options: Vagus nerve (Superior laryngeal branch)
Trigeminal nerve (Mandibular division)
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Facial nerve (Chorda tympani branch)
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Superior laryngeal nerve pain typically involves the larynx and may cause coughing or voice changes, but not specific triggers at the back of the tongue.
Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) usually affects the face (cheeks, jaw), not the deep throat or the posterior third of the tongue.

The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior third of the tongue and the oropharynx. Neuralgia of this nerve causes intense pain in these areas, often triggered by swallowing.
The hypoglossal nerve is motor; a lesion would cause paralysis and atrophy, not paroxysmal lancinating sensory pain.
The chorda tympani is involved in taste and salivation; dysfunction leads to ageusia (loss of taste) or xerostomia, not lancinating pain.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): The glossopharyngeal nerve... conducts sensation from the pharynx and the back of the tongue...

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: Which specific anatomical landmark marks the junction between the anterior two-thirds (oral part) and the posterior one-third (pharyngeal part) of the tongue, effectively delineating the territories of different sensory nerve supplies?
options: Plica fimbriata
Median fibrous septum
Sulcus terminalis
Lingual frenulum
Glossoepiglottic fold
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The plica fimbriata is a fringed fold located lateral to the lingual vein on the undersurface of the tongue.
The median fibrous septum is an internal structure that divides the tongue muscles into right and left halves.
The sulcus terminalis is the V-shaped groove on the dorsal surface that separates the oral part (CN V and VII) from the pharyngeal part (CN IX).
The lingual frenulum is a midline fold on the inferior surface of the tongue connecting it to the floor of the mouth.
The glossoepiglottic folds (median and lateral) connect the posterior tongue to the epiglottis, forming the boundaries of the valleculae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Direct Primary Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Apex
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with a suspicious lesion localized strictly to the apex (tip) of the tongue. Based on anatomical lymphatic mapping, which group of lymph nodes should be palpated first for potential metastasis?
options: Submental lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
Occipital lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Jugulodigastric lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: The tip of the tongue is the only lingual region that specifically drains into the submental nodes located in the submental triangle.
Submandibular nodes primarily drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the isolated tip.
Occipital nodes are located at the back of the skull and drain the posterior scalp; they are irrelevant to oral cavity malignancies.
Parotid nodes drain the scalp, auricle, and eyelids; they have no anatomical communication with the lingual lymphatic system.
Jugulodigastric nodes are part of the deep cervical chain and usually receive secondary drainage from the tongue rather than primary drainage from the tip.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: Why is the prognosis for a carcinoma located on the posterior third of the tongue generally considered more grave in terms of surgical access and nodal spread compared to the tip of the tongue?
options: Because it drains to the parotid nodes, leading to immediate facial nerve paralysis.
Because the posterior third is only supplied by the facial artery, which limits drug delivery.
Because it lacks lymphatic drainage, causing internal necrosis and sepsis.
Because it drains directly to the deep cervical nodes and is often bilateral.
Because it drains solely to the submental nodes which are difficult to excise.
correctOption: Because it drains directly to the deep cervical nodes and is often bilateral.
optionExplanations: The tongue does not drain to parotid nodes; facial nerve paralysis occurs due to parotid tumors, not tongue tumors.
The posterior third is supplied by multiple arteries including the lingual and ascending pharyngeal; blood supply does not dictate nodal spread.
The posterior third has very rich lymphatic drainage directly to deep nodes, which facilitates rapid metastasis.
Carcinoma of the posterior third is aggressive because lymph drains directly to the deep cervical nodes (bypassing superficial ones) and often crosses the midline (bilateral spread).
The posterior third does not drain to the submental nodes; they are easily accessible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with a loss of general sensation over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but taste sensation remains intact. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
options: Lingual nerve proximal to the junction with chorda tympani
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
Lingual nerve distal to the junction with chorda tympani
correctOption: Lingual nerve proximal to the junction with chorda tympani
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve carries general somatic afferent fibers. If damaged proximal to where the chorda tympani joins it, only general sensation is lost, as taste fibers have not yet entered the nerve bundle.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is purely motor to the tongue muscles and has no sensory role; its lesion results in motor paralysis.
The chorda tympani is responsible for taste sensation only on the anterior two-thirds; its lesion would cause loss of taste, not general sensation.
If the lingual nerve is damaged distal to the junction, both general sensation and taste (carried by the chorda tympani) would be lost simultaneously.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Anterior two thirds: Lingual nerve branch of the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (general sensation) and chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (taste).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a squamous cell carcinoma involving the very tip of the tongue. According to the anatomical principles of lymphatic drainage, which group of lymph nodes is the first-order site for metastatic spread from this specific location?
options: Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes are located behind the pharynx and primarily drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the anterior tongue.
The submandibular nodes drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but they are not the primary site for the tip itself.
Parotid nodes receive lymph from the scalp, auricle, and eyelids, not from the internal oral structures like the tongue tip.
Mastoid nodes are posterior to the ear and drain the scalp and external auditory meatus; they have no role in lingual drainage.
Anatomically, the tip of the tongue is the only portion of the organ that specifically drains into the submental triangle nodes, located below the chin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 62-year-old patient presents with difficulty swallowing and a loss of the gag reflex on the right side. During testing, they are found to have a loss of both bitter and sweet taste perception on the posterior third of the tongue. A lesion in which foramen is most likely?
options: Internal acoustic meatus
Jugular foramen
Hypoglossal canal
Foramen rotundum
Foramen ovale
correctOption: Jugular foramen
optionExplanations: The internal acoustic meatus transmits CN VII and VIII. This would cause facial paralysis and hearing loss/vertigo, but not the symptoms described.

The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, and XI. A lesion here (Vernet Syndrome) affects the glossopharyngeal nerve (posterior tongue taste/sensation and afferent gag) and vagus nerve (efferent gag/swallowing).
The hypoglossal canal transmits only the hypoglossal nerve (XII), which would cause tongue deviation but not loss of taste or the gag reflex.
Foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2), which supplies the midface and palate but not the posterior tongue or gag reflex.
Foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), which provides sensation to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue, but does not control the gag reflex or posterior taste.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1496 (Book Page): The jugular foramen... transmits the following structures in anteroposterior sequence: the inferior petrosal sinus; the 9th, 10th, and 11th cranial nerves.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: When assessing a patient with carcinoma of the tongue, the clinician must distinguish between specific deep cervical nodes. Which of the following best describes the anatomical contrast between the jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid nodes in tongue drainage?
options: The jugulodigastric node drains the submental region, while the jugulo-omohyoid drains the submandibular region.
The jugulodigastric node is a superficial node, whereas the jugulo-omohyoid is part of the deep terminal group.
The jugulodigastric node is associated with the posterior third, while the jugulo-omohyoid node is only for the tip.
The jugulodigastric node is mainly for the tonsil and tongue, while the jugulo-omohyoid node is exclusively associated with the tongue.
The jugulodigastric node is located at the carotid bifurcation, while the jugulo-omohyoid node is in the posterior triangle.
correctOption: The jugulodigastric node is mainly for the tonsil and tongue, while the jugulo-omohyoid node is exclusively associated with the tongue.
optionExplanations: Submental drainage eventually reaches deep cervical nodes, but the jugulo-omohyoid node is not restricted to submandibular inputs. These nodes represent different vertical levels of the same terminal deep cervical chain.

Both the jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid nodes are members of the deep cervical group. They are terminal nodes situated along the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath, not superficial nodes.

Both nodes are involved in the terminal drainage of various parts of the tongue. The jugulo-omohyoid node specifically receives lymph from the tongue, but it is not limited to the tip; it is a critical station for various lingual pathways.

This is the correct functional distinction. The jugulodigastric node, found below the angle of the mandible, has a broader drainage area including the palatine tonsil, whereas the jugulo-omohyoid is more specifically recognized for its tongue associations.

The jugulo-omohyoid node is located deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle near the intermediate tendon of the omohyoid muscle, which is in the anterior triangle, not the posterior triangle. The jugulodigastric is higher up.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node... is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue. The jugulo-omohyoid node... is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 30-year-old patient presents with a 'jugular foramen syndrome' caused by a glomus jugulare tumor. The physician notes loss of the gag reflex and loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue. Additionally, the patient has difficulty shrugging the shoulder. Which finding regarding the tongue's motor function is most likely in this patient?
options: The tongue deviates to the side of the lesion on protrusion.
The tongue cannot be retracted due to hyoglossus paralysis.
The tongue remains in the midline on protrusion.
The tongue shows fasciculations and atrophy on the contralateral side.
The tongue deviates to the opposite side of the lesion on protrusion.
correctOption: The tongue remains in the midline on protrusion.
optionExplanations: Deviation to the side of the lesion occurs only if the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is involved. CN XII exits via the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen.
Retraction is a motor function of the styloglossus and hyoglossus (CN XII); it would not be affected by a pure jugular foramen lesion.

The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, and XI. A tumor here affects these three nerves (causing loss of gag reflex, taste on posterior 1/3, and trapezius weakness). Since CN XII exits through a separate bony canal (hypoglossal canal), motor function of the tongue is typically spared, and the tongue stays in the midline.
Fasciculations and atrophy are signs of CN XII damage, which is not part of the standard jugular foramen contents.
Deviation to the opposite side is not a feature of lower motor neuron lesions of the tongue nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1499 (Book Page): The strong bony walls of the hypoglossal canal usually protect the hypoglossal nerve from injury. [Context: discussing fractures of the posterior fossa and jugular foramen].

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Terminal Nodal Echelons of the Head and Neck
statement: In the context of lingual carcinoma, which group of nodes acts as the final 'terminal' filter for all lymphatic drainage from the tongue before it enters the jugular trunks?
options: Submental nodes
Superficial cervical nodes
Anterior cervical nodes
Submandibular nodes
Deep cervical nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Submental nodes are regional nodes for the tip of the tongue; like the submandibular nodes, they are intermediary and not the terminal group.

Superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein and drain the skin over the angle of the jaw; they eventually drain into the deep cervical nodes but are not the terminal group for lingual lymph.
Anterior cervical nodes are a regional group for the superficial tissues of the front of the neck and do not serve as the terminal destination for deep lingual drainage.
Submandibular nodes are regional nodes; while they drain the tongue, their efferents must pass into the deep cervical nodes before reaching the venous circulation.

The deep cervical nodes form a vertical chain along the internal jugular vein. They receive lymph from all other regional head and neck groups (pericervical collar and superficial nodes) and are the final filter before the lymph enters the jugular trunks.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The deep cervical nodes... receive lymph from all the groups of regional nodes and as such are the terminal group of nodes in the neck.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Chorda Tympani vs. Lingual Nerve Dissociation
statement: A 32-year-old male is brought to the ER after a trauma to the infratemporal fossa. Examination reveals a loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the right side, along with decreased salivation from the right submandibular gland. However, general sensation (pain/touch) on the same part of the tongue is intact. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen
Facial nerve at the internal acoustic meatus
Chorda tympani nerve before it joins the lingual nerve
Lingual nerve in the floor of the mouth
Mandibular nerve (V3) just below the foramen ovale
correctOption: Chorda tympani nerve before it joins the lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the posterior third of the tongue. Damage here would not affect the anterior two-thirds or the submandibular gland (it affects the parotid).

A lesion at the internal acoustic meatus would affect CN VII and CN VIII, causing facial paralysis, deafness, and loss of taste/salivation. It is too proximal and would involve much more than just tongue taste.

The Chorda tympani carries only taste (VII) and parasympathetic fibers. If it is damaged before joining the Lingual nerve (V3), taste and salivation are lost, but general sensation (carried by the Lingual nerve) remains intact.

A lesion of the Lingual nerve in the floor of the mouth would result in the loss of *both* taste and general sensation because the chorda tympani fibers have already joined the lingual nerve at this point.

A lesion of V3 at the foramen ovale would cause loss of general sensation in the anterior tongue and lower teeth, and potentially taste if the chorda tympani joined it immediately, but it wouldn't spare general sensation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve... joins the lingual nerve... contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Bilateral Lymphatic Spread of Lingual Malignancy
statement: Carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue is often associated with a poorer prognosis than the anterior tongue. What anatomical feature of its lymphatic drainage contributes to this?
options: Lymphatics must cross the parotid gland before the neck.
It drains to superficial nodes that are easily missed.
It possesses bilateral drainage, facilitating contralateral metastasis.
It has no lymphatic drainage, leading to local necrosis.
The lymphatics are confined to a single side of the neck.
correctOption: It possesses bilateral drainage, facilitating contralateral metastasis.
optionExplanations: The parotid gland is not part of the tongue's lymphatic pathway; drainage goes directly to the deep cervical chain in the neck triangle.
Posterior tongue lymph drains to the deep cervical nodes (internal jugular chain), which are deep and can be difficult to palpate until significantly enlarged.
The posterior third of the tongue has significant lymphatic crossover, meaning a tumor on one side can readily metastasize to lymph nodes on the opposite side of the neck.
The tongue has a very rich lymphatic supply; lack of drainage is not the issue, rather the efficiency of spread is the clinical problem.
Unlike the sides of the anterior tongue which have more unilateral tendencies initially, the posterior part is highly prone to bilateral nodal involvement.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): In patients with bilateral spread, a bilateral block dissection may be necessary.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoes a neurological examination where the physician notes a lack of motor function in several muscles of the tongue. However, one specific muscle remains functional because it is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus rather than the hypoglossal nerve. Which muscle is this?
options: Palatoglossus
Hyoglossus
Styloglossus
Vertical intrinsic muscle
Genioglossus
correctOption: Palatoglossus
optionExplanations: The palatoglossus is the only tongue muscle not supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; instead, it receives motor innervation from the pharyngeal plexus via the vagus nerve (CN X).
The hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); its primary action is to depress the tongue.
The styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); it acts to retract and elevate the tongue.
The intrinsic muscles (superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical) are all supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to alter the shape of the tongue.
The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); it is responsible for protruding the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Note: the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with an invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue. Unlike the anterior two-thirds, why is carcinoma in this region associated with a higher risk of early, deep metastatic involvement?
options: It drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, often bilaterally.
It drains exclusively to the submental nodes which are difficult to palpate.
The posterior third lacks any organized lymphatic drainage system.
Lymph from this area must pass through the parotid gland before the neck.
The posterior third drains into the superficial cervical nodes along the external jugular vein.
correctOption: It drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, often bilaterally.
optionExplanations: The posterior third of the tongue (pharyngeal part) drains directly into the deep cervical lymph nodes, specifically the jugulodigastric node. Crucially, these channels often cross the midline, leading to bilateral metastasis.
The submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue, not the posterior third; furthermore, submental nodes are relatively accessible to palpation in the midline.
The posterior third has a very rich and organized lymphatic network that facilitates the rapid spread of malignant cells to deep nodal stations.
The parotid nodes do not receive lymph from the tongue; parotid drainage is limited to the lateral face, scalp, and external ear.
The superficial cervical nodes drain the skin of the angle of the jaw; lingual drainage is deep to the investing fascia, following the internal jugular vein (deep cervical chain).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: The Jugulo-omohyoid Node in Lingual Malignancy
statement: A 62-year-old chronic smoker presents with a persistent, painful ulcer on the right lateral margin of his tongue. Clinical examination reveals a fixed, hard mass located at the junction of the internal jugular vein and the omohyoid muscle. Based on the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma, which specific lymph node is likely involved?
options: Jugulodigastric node
Submental node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
Mastoid node
Supraclavicular node
correctOption: Jugulo-omohyoid node
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is concerned with the tongue but is located higher, behind the angle of the jaw, near the digastric muscle.
The submental node is in the submental triangle (Level IA) and would not be found at the IJV/omohyoid junction.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is located where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein and is specifically noted as being mainly associated with the drainage of the tongue.
The mastoid node is retroauricular and drains the scalp/ear, not the tongue.
Supraclavicular nodes are involved in late-stage spread or distant malignancies (Virchow's node), not the primary echelon for lateral tongue drainage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Chorda Tympani Relationship
statement: A dentist performs a clumsy extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar, resulting in a nerve lesion in the infratemporal fossa. The patient subsequently reports a loss of both general sensation and taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. At which location was the nerve most likely damaged?
options: The lingual nerve proximal to its junction with the chorda tympani.
The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve at the foramen ovale.
The glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen.
The lingual nerve distal to its junction with the chorda tympani.
The chorda tympani before it enters the petrotympanic fissure.
correctOption: The lingual nerve distal to its junction with the chorda tympani.
optionExplanations: If the lingual nerve were damaged proximal to its junction with the chorda tympani, general sensation would be lost, but taste (conveyed by chorda tympani) would remain intact.
A lesion at the foramen ovale would involve the entire mandibular nerve (V3), affecting muscles of mastication and sensation to the lower face, which is more extensive than the symptoms described.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds, so its injury would not match the reported deficits.

The lingual nerve is frequently injured near the third molar. Because the chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa, a lesion at the third molar level destroys both the general sensory fibers (from V3) and the taste fibers (from CN VII) carried within the common nerve trunk.
Damage to the chorda tympani alone would result in loss of taste and secretomotor function to the submandibular/sublingual glands, but general sensation (Lingual nerve) would be preserved.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Clinical Topography of Deep Cervical Lymph Nodes
statement: A 62-year-old heavy smoker presents with an indurated ulcer on the right lateral border of the tongue and a palpable, non-tender mass at the level of the omohyoid muscle crossing the internal jugular vein. Which specific node is likely involved, and what is its clinical significance?
options: The Jugulodigastric node; it is the primary terminal node for the pharyngeal part of the tongue.
The Mastoid node; it suggests the cancer has spread through the external auditory meatus.
The Submental node; it indicates the tumor has crossed the midline from the right side.
The Buccal node; it implies the tumor has invaded the buccinator muscle.
The Jugulo-omohyoid node; it is a deep cervical node associated with tongue drainage.
correctOption: The Jugulo-omohyoid node; it is a deep cervical node associated with tongue drainage.
optionExplanations: While the jugulodigastric node is associated with the tongue and tonsils, it is located higher up, near the angle of the jaw, not at the omohyoid level.
Mastoid nodes are superficial and drain the scalp; they do not receive lymph from the tongue.
The submental node drains the tip of the tongue and is located in the midline below the chin, not deep near the omohyoid.
Buccal nodes are found in the cheek and drain the cheek and lips; they are not the primary deep nodes for lateral lingual margins.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a deep cervical node located where the omohyoid crosses the internal jugular vein and is specifically associated with lingual drainage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Bilateral Drainage Mechanism of the Tongue Root
statement: In the mechanistic spread of lingual carcinoma, why do lesions of the posterior third of the tongue often present with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy even when the primary tumor appears unilateral?
options: Metastasis occurs primarily via the lingual artery to the contralateral side.
Lymphatic vessels from the root of the tongue frequently decussate or cross the midline.
The posterior third drains exclusively into the thoracic duct, bypassing regional nodes.
The presence of valves in the lingual lymphatics encourages retrograde bilateral flow.
The root of the tongue contains no intrinsic lymphatics, relying on the pharyngeal plexus.
correctOption: Lymphatic vessels from the root of the tongue frequently decussate or cross the midline.
optionExplanations: Lymphatic spread is the primary route for carcinoma; arterial spread (hematogenous) occurs in advanced stages but does not explain the early bilateral nodal pattern.
Carcinoma of the posterior third is dangerous because the lymphatic drainage of this region is often bilateral, as vessels cross the midline to reach the deep cervical nodes on both sides.
Lymph always drains through cervical trunks before reaching the thoracic duct; it cannot bypass regional nodes.
Lymphatic vessels have valves to ensure unidirectional flow; they do not promote retrograde spread.
The root of the tongue has a very rich lymphatic network, which is why it metastasizes so effectively.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes. [Contextual anatomical correlate: Posterior third drainage is frequently bilateral due to midline crossing].

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Hypoglossal Nerve Lesion and Tongue Deviation
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with a history of a deep neck wound in the carotid triangle. On examination, when the patient is asked to protrude his tongue, the tip deviates significantly to the right side. Which nerve has most likely been transected?
options: Left Lingual nerve
Right Hypoglossal nerve
Right Glossopharyngeal nerve
Right Vagus nerve
Left Hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: Right Hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve provides general somatic sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but carries no motor fibers to the tongue muscles.

The hypoglossal nerve supplies the motor innervation to the tongue muscles. In a unilateral lesion, the action of the intact contralateral genioglossus muscle is unopposed, pushing the tongue toward the side of the lesion (the paralyzed side).
The Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory and taste innervation to the posterior third of the tongue but does not control the muscles responsible for protrusion.
The Vagus nerve (CN X) only supplies the palatoglossus muscle of the tongue; a lesion would not cause deviation of the tongue tip during protrusion, which is primarily a function of the genioglossus.
A lesion of the left hypoglossal nerve would cause the tongue to deviate to the left side because the healthy right genioglossus would push the tongue toward the weak left side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The patient is asked to put out the tongue, and if a lesion of the nerve is present, it will be noted that the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side (see Fig. 12.80). This can be explained as follows. One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A pathologist is examining the dorsal surface of a tongue during an autopsy. They use a specific anatomical landmark to distinguish between the oral part (anterior two-thirds) and the pharyngeal part (posterior one-third). Which of the following represents this landmark?
options: Frenulum linguae
Median fibrous septum
Sulcus terminalis
Plica fimbriata
Labiogingival lamina
correctOption: Sulcus terminalis
optionExplanations: The frenulum linguae is a midline fold on the inferior surface of the tongue, not the dorsal surface.
The median fibrous septum is an internal structure that divides the tongue into right and left halves, not anterior and posterior parts.
The sulcus terminalis is the V-shaped groove on the dorsal surface that separates the oral anterior 2/3 from the pharyngeal posterior 1/3.
The plica fimbriata is a fringed fold located on the inferior surface of the tongue, lateral to the lingual vein.
The labiogingival lamina is an embryological structure involved in the separation of the lips and gums.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1726 (Book Page): A V-shaped sulcus, the sulcus terminalis, divides the mucous membrane of the upper surface of the tongue into anterior and posterior parts.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Specific Lymph Nodes of Lingual Drainage
statement: A 62-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a persistent, firm, 2cm ulcer on the right lateral border of his tongue. On physical examination, his vitals are stable (BP 130/85, Pulse 78), but a palpable, non-tender, fixed 1.5 cm lymph node is noted in the neck, located deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the level where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. Which specific node is most likely involved?
options: Mastoid node
Parotid node
Jugulodigastric node
Submental node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
correctOption: Jugulo-omohyoid node
optionExplanations: Mastoid nodes are retroauricular and drain the scalp and external ear; they are not involved in lingual carcinoma metastasis.
Parotid nodes are located on or in the parotid gland and do not receive primary or secondary lymph from the tongue's lateral margins.
The jugulodigastric node is located higher in the neck, below and behind the angle of the mandible, and is associated more with the tonsils and posterior tongue.
The submental node is located in the midline below the chin and drains the tip, not the lateral border, and is far superior to the omohyoid crossing.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a specific deep cervical node located where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. It is a classic terminal station for lymph from the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A clinician is comparing the metastatic risks of carcinomas located on different parts of the tongue. Why is a lesion on the posterior third of the tongue considered to have a different anatomical correlate compared to the anterior two-thirds?
options: It lacks lymphatic drainage entirely, spreading only through the bloodstream.
It drains directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes, bypassing regional superficial groups.
It follows the course of the external jugular vein to the superficial cervical nodes.
It drains to the submental nodes first, increasing the chance of early detection.
It drains into the parotid nodes, causing early facial nerve palsy.
correctOption: It drains directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes, bypassing regional superficial groups.
optionExplanations: The tongue has an extremely rich lymphatic network, and the posterior third is no exception. Spread to lymph nodes is a primary route for lingual carcinoma, rather than being purely hematogenous.

This is correct. While the anterior two-thirds of the tongue typically drains into submental or submandibular regional nodes first, the posterior third (pharyngeal part) drains directly into the deep cervical nodes.
The posterior third of the tongue is deep and its lymphatics follow the internal jugular vein (deep cervical nodes), not the external jugular vein, which is associated with superficial drainage.
The submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue, not the posterior third. Drainage from the posterior third is more occult and direct to deep stations, often leading to later clinical detection.
The parotid nodes do not drain any part of the tongue. Facial nerve palsy is associated with parotid gland pathology, not lingual carcinoma metastasis to the deep neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 65-year-old chronic tobacco user presents with a 2.5 cm malignant ulcer on the left lateral border of his tongue. Physical examination reveals a palpable, hard, non-tender mass in the left submandibular triangle and another smaller node along the internal jugular vein. Based on the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma spread, what is the most likely pathological staging of these nodes?
options: The submandibular mass is a first-order metastasis from the lateral tongue.
The internal jugular node is an anterior cervical node involved in skin drainage.
The submandibular mass represents primary parotid spread.
The node along the internal jugular vein is a direct spread from the tip of the tongue.
The palpable nodes indicate spread to the pericervical collar exclusively.
correctOption: The submandibular mass is a first-order metastasis from the lateral tongue.
optionExplanations: This is the correct anatomical interpretation. The lateral borders of the anterior two-thirds drain first to the submandibular nodes. Their enlargement in the presence of a lateral lingual ulcer is highly suggestive of metastatic disease.

Nodes along the internal jugular vein are deep cervical nodes, which receive all lymph from the head and neck. Anterior cervical nodes are superficial and follow the anterior jugular veins, draining the skin of the neck front.
Lingual carcinoma does not spread to the parotid nodes as a primary or secondary site. Parotid nodes drain the scalp, temple, and eyelids, which are distinct from the lingual lymphatic pathways.

While the tip of the tongue can drain to the submental and then deep cervical nodes, the primary ulcer in this case is on the lateral border, not the tip, making lateral-to-submandibular-to-deep-cervical the likely path.

The deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein are terminal nodes, not part of the pericervical collar. The pericervical collar nodes (like submandibular) are regional, while the deep chain is the final station.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Circuitry of the Anterior Tongue
statement: In the physiological loop of lymphatic return from the tongue, lymph from the submental nodes must pass through which specific pathway to reach the venous circulation?
options: To the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes.
Directly into the sublingual vein at the frenulum.
To the parotid nodes and then the retromandibular vein.
Directly to the thoracic duct via the lingual nerve sheath.
Through the anterior jugular vein into the external jugular vein.
correctOption: To the submandibular nodes and then to the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Lymph from the tip of the tongue enters the submental nodes, then moves to the submandibular nodes, and finally reaches the terminal deep cervical chain.
Lymph does not enter the venous system at the sublingual vein; it must pass through the jugular trunks first.
The parotid nodes do not participate in the submental/lingual drainage loop.
Nerves do not serve as primary conduits for bulk lymphatic flow to the thoracic duct.
Lymphatics and veins are separate systems; lymph reaches the veins only at the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins via the lymphatic/thoracic ducts.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1654 (Book Page): Pericervical collar nodes [including submental]... basicially, the tissues drain into the nodal group located most closely [then to deep cervical].

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve vs. Chorda Tympani Functional Anatomy
statement: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with a tumor in the infratemporal fossa that has damaged the lingual nerve proximal to where it is joined by the chorda tympani.
