Which of the following sensory deficits would be most accurately expected in this patient regarding the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
options: Loss of general sensation only, with taste preserved
Isolated loss of sensation to the vallate papillae
Loss of general sensation and taste on the posterior third
Loss of both general sensation and taste
Loss of taste only, with general sensation preserved
correctOption: Loss of general sensation only, with taste preserved
optionExplanations: Correct. If the lingual nerve is damaged proximal to its junction with the chorda tympani, only the V3 fibers (general sensation) are affected; the taste fibers (VII) have not yet joined the nerve and would be spared.
The vallate papillae are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for both taste and general sensation.
The posterior third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the lingual nerve.
This would only happen if the lesion were distal to the junction where the chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve.
This is incorrect because the lingual nerve itself (CN V3) is responsible for general sensation, not taste.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The chorda tympani nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa. The lingual nerve fibers carry general sensation from the mucous membrane of the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The chorda tympani fibers carry taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: During a surgical resection of a carcinoma located at the junction of the oral and pharyngeal parts of the tongue, which deep neck node must be carefully cleared due to its association with the omohyoid muscle and lingual drainage?
options: Laryngeal node
Superficial parotid node
Tracheal node
Retroauricular node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
correctOption: Jugulo-omohyoid node
optionExplanations: Laryngeal nodes are located in front of the larynx and drain the larynx itself.
Superficial parotid nodes drain the scalp, temple, and eyelids, not the deep structures of the tongue.
Tracheal nodes are located alongside the trachea and primarily drain the trachea and thyroid gland.
Retroauricular nodes are the same as mastoid nodes and drain the scalp and auricle.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a specific deep cervical node associated with the omohyoid muscle that receives lymph from the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulo-omohyoid node, which is situated close to the omohyoid muscle, is mainly associated with drainage of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of the Jugulodigastric Node
statement: A 65-year-old male presents with a firm, ulcerated lesion on the right posterior third of the tongue and a palpable 2 cm mass below and behind the right angle of the mandible. Which specific lymph node is most likely involved in this metastasis?
options: Buccal node
Jugulodigastric node
Submental node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
Occipital node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: Buccal nodes are superficial nodes on the cheek (buccinator muscle) and drain the facial skin and mucous membrane, not the posterior tongue.

The jugulodigastric node (the sentinel node of the tongue) is located at the level where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein, receiving primary lymph from the posterior tongue and tonsil.
The submental node is located centrally under the chin and drains the tip of the tongue; it is anatomically distant from the angle of the mandible.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is also associated with the tongue but is located lower in the neck, near the omohyoid muscle, and typically receives drainage from the anterior tongue.
Occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp and are located at the base of the skull posteriorly, far from the lymphatic pathway of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Spread from Lateral Tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a carcinoma involving the lateral margin of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Pathophysiologically, what is the most common sequential lymphatic pathway for the spread of these malignant cells before they reach the terminal deep cervical chain?
options: Directly to the jugulodigastric node bypassing all regional groups
Paratracheal nodes followed by supraclavicular nodes
Submandibular nodes then to the deep cervical nodes
Submental nodes followed by submandibular nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes followed by internal jugular vein involvement
correctOption: Submandibular nodes then to the deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Direct drainage to the jugulodigastric node is more characteristic of the posterior third and the tonsillar region, whereas the lateral margins usually follow a regional relay.
Paratracheal nodes are associated with the thyroid gland and neighboring structures, not the anterior tongue's lymphatic system.
The sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue drain into the submandibular lymph nodes, which subsequently drain into the deep cervical lymph nodes along the internal jugular vein.
The submental nodes are specific to the tip and lower incisors; the lateral margins bypass these and drain to the submandibular group first.
Retropharyngeal nodes receive lymph from the nasopharynx and auditory tube; they do not serve as a primary relay for the anterior tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with dysphagia and a deviated uvula. During examination, the physician notes that the patient's palatoglossus muscle is paralyzed on the left side, though all other tongue movements (protrusion, retraction) are intact. Which nerve is likely damaged?
options: Left mandibular nerve
Left glossopharyngeal nerve
Left vagus nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
Left lingual nerve
correctOption: Left vagus nerve
optionExplanations: The mandibular nerve (V3) provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication, but not to the tongue or palate muscles.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory and taste fibers to the posterior third but only supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle in the pharynx.
The palatoglossus is technically a muscle of the soft palate and the tongue; it is the only tongue muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (primarily via the vagus nerve, CN X).
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue except for the palatoglossus.
The lingual nerve is a sensory nerve (V3) and does not provide motor innervation to the tongue muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all the tongue muscles, except one, the palatoglossus (supplied by vagus fibers in the pharyngeal plexus).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Anatomical Contrast in Lingual Lymphatic Drainage
statement: When comparing the lymphatic prognosis of a carcinoma located on the posterior third of the tongue versus the anterior two-thirds, which anatomical contrast is most significant for surgical planning?
options: The anterior two-thirds lacks connection to the jugulo-omohyoid node, which is exclusive to the posterior third.
The anterior two-thirds has higher rates of bilateral drainage compared to the strictly unilateral posterior third.
The posterior third drains exclusively to the submental nodes, whereas the anterior drains to the deep cervical nodes.
The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, whereas the anterior drainage often involves intervening regional nodes.
The posterior third utilizes the buccal nodes as a primary station, unlike the anterior portion.
correctOption: The posterior third drains directly into the deep cervical nodes, whereas the anterior drainage often involves intervening regional nodes.
optionExplanations: The jugulo-omohyoid node is specifically associated with the drainage of the tongue, including the anterior portions, and is not exclusive to the posterior third.
The posterior third of the tongue actually has a significant tendency for bilateral drainage due to the midline crossing of vessels, making it more dangerous than the anterior lateral margins.
This is factually reversed; the tip (anterior) drains to submental nodes, while the posterior third drains to deep cervical nodes.

Carcinoma of the posterior third is often more aggressive and spreads faster because it drains directly into the deep cervical nodes (terminal group) without being filtered by intervening pericervical collar nodes like the submandibular group.
Buccal nodes are located in the cheek and drain the cheek and upper lip; they are not primary stations for any part of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Genioglossus Action in CN XII Lesion
statement: A patient with a suspected lower motor neuron lesion of the hypoglossal nerve is asked to protrude their tongue. The tip of the tongue deviates significantly to the right side. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this clinical finding?
options: The right styloglossus is hyperactive, pulling the tongue toward the side of the lesion.
The left genioglossus is paralyzed, allowing the unopposed right genioglossus to push the tongue to the right.
The right genioglossus is paralyzed, allowing the unopposed left genioglossus to pull the tongue to the right.
The right palatoglossus is paralyzed, causing the tongue to fail in midline protrusion.
The intrinsic muscles on the left side are wasted, causing a mechanical tilt toward the right.
correctOption: The right genioglossus is paralyzed, allowing the unopposed left genioglossus to pull the tongue to the right.
optionExplanations: The styloglossus muscle retracts and elevates the tongue; it is not the primary muscle involved in protrusion or the specific midline deviation observed during protrusion.
If the left genioglossus were paralyzed, the tongue would deviate to the left, as the right side would be the only one protruding forward.

The genioglossus muscle acts to protrude the tongue. If the right nerve is lesioned, the right genioglossus is paralyzed. The left genioglossus, being functional, protrudes the left side of the tongue forward and toward the midline, resulting in the tip deviating to the weak (right) side.
The palatoglossus is involved in elevating the root of the tongue and is supplied by the vagus nerve, not the hypoglossal nerve; its lesion would not cause this specific deviation on protrusion.
While wasting of intrinsic muscles occurs in chronic LMN lesions, the active deviation during protrusion is primarily a result of the extrinsic genioglossus muscle's unilateral action.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Tip
statement: A 52-year-old male presents with a persistent, firm ulcer on the absolute apex of his tongue. In evaluating for metastatic spread of lingual carcinoma, which group of lymph nodes should the surgeon palpate as the primary first-order site of drainage for this specific location?
options: Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes are located in the prevertebral region and drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube. They do not serve as a primary or secondary site for the anterior portions of the tongue involved in this clinical scenario.

Mastoid nodes, also known as retroauricular nodes, are located behind the ear and drain the posterior scalp and external auditory meatus. They are part of the pericervical collar but are not involved in the lymphatic pathway of the tongue.

Submandibular lymph nodes are incorrect because they primarily drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the tip. While they are a major site for lingual cancer spread, they are not the immediate primary site for lesions located at the absolute apex.

Parotid lymph nodes receive lymph from the lateral part of the face, eyelids, and scalp above the parotid gland. They do not receive direct lymphatic drainage from any portion of the tongue and are thus irrelevant to lingual carcinoma spread.

Submental lymph nodes are the correct primary drainage site for the tip of the tongue. They are located in the submental triangle between the two anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and collect lymph from the midline structures of the floor of the mouth and the tongue apex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient presents with a loss of both general sensation and taste on the posterior one-third of the tongue. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
Chorda tympani
Lingual nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor and does not carry any sensory or taste fibers from the tongue surface.
The chorda tympani carries taste fibers specifically for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the lingual nerve.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation only to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides some sensory fibers to the most posterior part of the tongue near the epiglottis, but the main supply for the posterior third is CN IX.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is unique in providing both general sensory and taste (special sensory) innervation to the posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1731 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste)

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Pathways of the Tongue
statement: Which of the following describes the anatomical pathway through which carcinoma of the lateral margin of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue spreads to the deep cervical nodes?
options: Retrograde flow through the lingual vein directly into the internal jugular bulb.
Direct drainage exclusively into the submental nodes then to the paratracheal nodes.
Primary drainage into the mastoid nodes before entering the jugulodigastric chain.
Drainage into the submandibular nodes followed by the deep cervical nodes.
Bilateral drainage into the retropharyngeal nodes prior to the carotid sheath.
correctOption: Drainage into the submandibular nodes followed by the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: Lymphatic spread occurs through lymphatic vessels, not through venous retrograde flow in the lingual vein.
The tip, not the sides, drains to submental nodes; paratracheal nodes primarily serve the trachea and thyroid.
Mastoid nodes are specialized for the scalp and ear; they are not part of the drainage pathway for any part of the tongue.
The lateral margins of the anterior tongue drain sequentially to the submandibular nodes and subsequently to the deep cervical chain, though some vessels may go directly to deep cervical nodes.
Retropharyngeal nodes receive lymph from the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the anterior tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve Injury in Oral Surgery
statement: A 28-year-old female undergoes a difficult extraction of a horizontal impacted lower third molar. Post-operatively, she complains of a complete loss of touch and temperature on the right side of the anterior tongue, as well as an inability to taste food on that same side. Which nerve was most likely damaged during the procedure?
options: Right Glossopharyngeal nerve
Right Lingual nerve
Right Hypoglossal nerve
Right Inferior Alveolar nerve
Right Facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
correctOption: Right Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Damage to the glossopharyngeal nerve would affect the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.

Correct. The lingual nerve passes very close to the medial aspect of the third molar. At this point, it already contains both general sensory fibers (V3) and taste fibers (from chorda tympani), explaining the loss of both modalities.
Incorrect. A hypoglossal nerve injury would result in motor paralysis and deviation, not sensory loss of touch and taste.
Incorrect. The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the teeth and the chin (via the mental nerve), not the sensory mucous membrane of the tongue.

Incorrect. While the facial nerve carries taste, a lesion at the stylomastoid foramen is distal to the origin of the chorda tympani, and would cause facial paralysis without affecting taste or lingual sensation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): [The lingual nerve] is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: The Jugulodigastric Node and Lingual Malignancy
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a tumor in the posterior third of the tongue. Clinical examination reveals an enlarged, non-tender, stony-hard lymph node located at the level of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, just behind the angle of the mandible. Which anatomical node is this, and why is it significant in lingual carcinoma?
options: Parotid node; it indicates spread to the salivary glands.
Jugulodigastric node; it is the most common site for metastasis from the tongue and tonsil.
Mastoid node; it indicates spread to the cutaneous tissues.
Occipital node; it indicates retrograde lymphatic flow.
Submental node; it is the primary site for posterior drainage.
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node; it is the most common site for metastasis from the tongue and tonsil.
optionExplanations: Parotid nodes are located within the parotid gland (preauricular) and do not drain the posterior third of the tongue.

The jugulodigastric node (also called the 'tonsillar node') is part of the upper deep cervical chain. It is located where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein, making it the primary drainage site for the posterior tongue and tonsils.
Mastoid nodes are behind the ear and drain the scalp/auricle. They have no anatomical relevance to the deep lymphatic pathways of the posterior tongue.
Occipital nodes are at the back of the head. Lymphatic flow from the tongue is toward the deep cervical chain, not posteriorly to the scalp.
The submental node is in the midline under the chin and drains the tip of the tongue. It is not located behind the angle of the mandible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with a deep penetrating wound to the upper carotid triangle of the neck. On examination, when asked to stick out his tongue, it deviates significantly to the right. There is also visible wasting and wrinkling of the right half of the tongue. No sensory deficits are noted on the tongue. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
options: Right hypoglossal nerve in the neck
Left hypoglossal nerve in the neck
Right chorda tympani in the middle ear
Left glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen
Right lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa
correctOption: Right hypoglossal nerve in the neck
optionExplanations: A lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve causes paralysis of the right intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles. The tongue deviates to the side of the lesion (the right) due to the unopposed action of the left genioglossus.
A lesion of the left hypoglossal nerve would cause the tongue to deviate to the left, which contradicts the clinical finding of right-sided deviation.
The chorda tympani carries taste and parasympathetic fibers; a lesion would lead to loss of taste on the anterior tongue but no motor deviation.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is primarily sensory to the posterior tongue and motor to the stylopharyngeus; a lesion would not cause the tongue to deviate on protrusion.
The lingual nerve is sensory; a lesion here would cause loss of general sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but would not cause motor deviation or muscle wasting.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The patient is asked to put out the tongue, and if a lesion of the nerve is present, it will be noted that the tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side... In patients with long-standing paralysis, the muscles on the affected side are wasted, and the tongue is wrinkled on that side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Direct Deep Cervical Drainage of the Pharyngeal Tongue
statement: Metastatic spread from a carcinoma involving the posterior third of the tongue differs significantly from the anterior two-thirds. Which nodal group receives lymph directly from the pharyngeal part of the tongue, often bypassing more superficial regional groups?
options: Deep cervical nodes
Superficial cervical nodes
Buccal nodes
Submandibular nodes
Submental nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: The posterior third of the tongue (pharyngeal part) drains directly into the deep cervical chain, specifically targeting the jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid nodes, which facilitates rapid deep metastasis.
Superficial cervical nodes follow the external jugular vein and drain the skin over the angle of the jaw, whereas the tongue requires deep fascial pathways along the internal jugular vein.
Buccal nodes are small nodes located on the buccinator muscle that drain the cheek and upper lip; they do not participate in lingual drainage.
Submandibular nodes primarily act as first-tier filters for the lateral anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue, not the posterior third.
Submental nodes are specialized for the tip of the tongue and central chin area, showing no clinical involvement in posterior lingual malignancies.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient complains of numbness on the left side of the tongue following the extraction of a deeply impacted lower third molar. The dentist suspects a nerve lesion. Which nerve is most likely involved due to its anatomical proximity to the last molar tooth?
options: Lingual nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Chorda tympani
Inferior alveolar nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve runs on the medial surface of the mandible, very close to the roots of the third molar. It provides general sensation to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.
The hypoglossal nerve lies deeper in the neck and enters the tongue from below the submandibular gland, far from the alveolar margin of the molars.
The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa, but the primary clinical concern for tongue sensation in this area is the main trunk of the lingual nerve itself.
The inferior alveolar nerve is located within the mandibular canal. While its injury causes numbness of the lower lip/chin (via the mental nerve), it does not supply the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is located more posteriorly in the oropharynx and is not typically at risk during a routine third molar extraction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve passes forward into the submandibular region from the infratemporal fossa... Here, it is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A surgeon is performing a selective neck dissection for a lateral tongue carcinoma. The dissection is focused on the submandibular triangle. Based on the anatomical sequence of lymph flow, which specific nodes are being targeted before they reach the deep cervical chain?
options: Retropharyngeal nodes
Submental nodes
Submandibular nodes
Jugulodigastric nodes
Paratracheal nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes are located behind the pharynx and are irrelevant to the drainage of the anterior tongue.
Submental nodes primarily serve the tip of the tongue and the central lower lip; they are not the primary station for lateral border drainage.
The lateral borders of the anterior two-thirds (the body) drain first into the submandibular nodes located in the digastric triangle before progressing to the deep cervical nodes.
The jugulodigastric nodes are part of the deep cervical chain and represent the next station (second-order) after the submandibular nodes for the anterior tongue.
Paratracheal nodes are located alongside the trachea and receive drainage from the thyroid gland, not the oral tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a neurological evaluation, a patient exhibits a loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but general sensation (touch and temperature) in the same area remains perfectly intact. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
options: Lingual nerve in the submandibular region
Chorda tympani nerve proximal to its junction with the lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen
Hypoglossal nerve in the hypoglossal canal
Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve at the foramen ovale
correctOption: Chorda tympani nerve proximal to its junction with the lingual nerve
optionExplanations: A lesion of the lingual nerve in the submandibular region would result in loss of both general sensation and taste, as the chorda tympani fibers have already joined the lingual nerve by this point.

The chorda tympani carries taste fibers for the anterior 2/3. If it is lesioned before joining the lingual nerve, only taste is lost. General sensation remains because the lingual nerve (carrying V3 fibers) is unaffected.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) handles taste and general sensation for the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is purely motor; its lesion affects tongue movement and muscle bulk but does not affect any sensory modalities (taste or touch).
A lesion at the foramen ovale would affect all branches of the mandibular nerve, including general sensation from the tongue and motor supply to muscles of mastication.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains taste fibers from the mucous membrane covering the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The nerve leaves the middle ear through the petrotympanic fissure and enters the infratemporal fossa, where it joins the lingual nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Tip
statement: A 50-year-old patient presents with a small, indurated ulcer on the absolute tip of the tongue. Based on the anatomical lymphatic drainage patterns, which group of lymph nodes should the clinician palpate first for primary metastasis?
options: Submandibular lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Submandibular nodes primarily drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the upper lip, and the lateral parts of the lower lip, but not the central tip. While they are regional, they are not the primary site for the tongue's apex.
Parotid nodes receive drainage from the scalp, auricle, and eyelids. They are not involved in the lymphatic pathway of the tongue or the oral floor.
Mastoid nodes, also known as retroauricular nodes, drain the posterior scalp and the external auditory meatus. They have no anatomical connection to the lingual lymphatic system.

The submental nodes are located in the submental triangle and specifically receive primary lymph from the tip of the tongue, the central lower lip, and the floor of the anterior mouth. They are the first-tier filter for malignancies at the tongue's apex.
Retropharyngeal nodes are deep nodes located behind the pharynx that drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube. They do not receive direct or primary drainage from the anterior segments of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage of Tongue] Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: During a clinical assessment of a patient with suspected cranial nerve damage, the physician finds that general sensation is lost on the posterior third of the tongue. Which nerve is most likely involved, and what other modality is likely lost in the same region?
options: Hypoglossal nerve; loss of motor control and taste.
Vagus nerve; loss of taste and proprioception.
Glossopharyngeal nerve; loss of both general sensation and taste.
Chorda tympani; loss of taste only.
Lingual nerve; loss of general sensation only.
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve; loss of both general sensation and taste.
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor (except for C1 proprioceptive fibers) and does not carry taste or general sensation from the tongue mucosa.
The vagus nerve (CN X) provides taste sensation to the extreme posterior part of the tongue/epiglottic region, but the primary sensory nerve for the posterior third is CN IX.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is unique in that it provides both general sensation and taste sensation to the posterior third of the tongue (including the vallate papillae).
The chorda tympani provides taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, whereas the posterior third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste)

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage Territories of the Tongue
statement: A 52-year-old patient is diagnosed with a small malignant lesion located at the extreme tip of the tongue. Based on the anatomical patterns of lymphatic flow, which lymph nodes are the primary site for the initial metastatic spread from this specific location?
options: Parotid lymph nodes
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Parotid nodes receive lymph from the scalp, eyelids, and external auditory meatus; they are not involved in the primary lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes are situated behind the pharynx and primarily drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, whereas lingual drainage follows a more superficial and then deep cervical path.
The submental lymph nodes, located in the submental triangle, are the primary first-order stations for the tip of the tongue, the central part of the lower lip, and the floor of the anterior mouth.
Mastoid nodes, or retroauricular nodes, are responsible for drainage from the scalp above the ear and the auricle, having no anatomical connection to lingual carcinoma spread.
Submandibular lymph nodes primarily drain the lateral sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but not the extreme tip, which bypasses them to reach the submental group.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): [Lymph Drainage] Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve vs. Chorda Tympani Innervation
statement: A lesion of the lingual nerve occurs in the infratemporal fossa before it is joined by the chorda tympani. Which sensory deficit will be isolated to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
options: Loss of both general sensation and taste sensation
Loss of proprioception but intact thermoreception
Loss of general sensation with intact taste sensation
Loss of all sensation including the vallate papillae
Loss of taste sensation with intact general sensation
correctOption: Loss of general sensation with intact taste sensation
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This would occur only if the lesion was distal (after) the junction of the chorda tympani with the lingual nerve.
Incorrect. General sensation includes pain, temperature, and touch; there is no physiological mechanism for isolated loss of proprioception in a total lingual nerve trunk lesion.

Correct. The lingual nerve proper carries general sensation (touch, pain, temperature). If severed before the chorda tympani joins it, only general sensation is lost; taste fibers (CN VII) are still separate and unaffected.
Incorrect. The vallate papillae are located anterior to the sulcus terminalis but are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the lingual nerve.
Incorrect. Taste is carried by the chorda tympani; if the lesion is in the lingual nerve before the junction, taste remains intact as those fibers haven't joined the nerve path yet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve fibers carry general sensation from the mucous membrane of the anterior two thirds of the tongue... The chorda tympani nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 58-year-old patient presents with a deep-seated carcinoma in the posterior third of the tongue. Contrast the clinical prognosis of this lesion versus one on the tip of the tongue based on lymphatic anatomy.
options: The tip has a worse prognosis because it bypasses the deep cervical chain.
The posterior third has a worse prognosis due to direct and bilateral deep cervical drainage.
Both have similar prognoses because they both drain into the submental nodes.
The tip has a worse prognosis due to direct drainage into the jugular trunk.
The posterior third has a better prognosis because its lymph is filtered by the submandibular nodes.
correctOption: The posterior third has a worse prognosis due to direct and bilateral deep cervical drainage.
optionExplanations: The tip does not bypass the deep cervical chain; it simply has more intermediate stations (submental and submandibular) before reaching it.
Posterior third lesions are more clinically aggressive because their lymphatics drain directly and often bilaterally to the deep cervical nodes, allowing for early, occult contralateral spread.
The tip drains to submental nodes, whereas the posterior third drains to deep cervical nodes; their drainage patterns are entirely distinct.
The tip of the tongue drains into submental nodes first, which are easily accessible and provide a 'buffer' before reaching the deep chain.
The posterior third bypasses the submandibular nodes, meaning there is no 'filtration' in the superficial nodal groups, leading to faster deep spread.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient undergoes a procedure where the glossopharyngeal nerve is accidentally compressed. While the tongue's motor functions remain intact, the patient loses a specific reflex loop involving the tongue. Which of the following explains the physiological disruption?
options: Loss of the afferent limb of the pharyngeal (gag) reflex
Loss of the ability to protrude the tongue
Hyper-reactivity of the sublingual salivary glands
Loss of the efferent limb of the corneal reflex
Paralysis of the palatoglossus muscle
correctOption: Loss of the afferent limb of the pharyngeal (gag) reflex
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides the sensory (afferent) limb for the gag reflex from the posterior third of the tongue and the oropharynx. Compression prevents the detection of the stimulus, thus abolishing the reflex.
Protrusion is a motor function of the hypoglossal nerve, which is not affected by a glossopharyngeal lesion.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland, but the sublingual and submandibular glands are supplied by the facial nerve.
The corneal reflex involves the ophthalmic nerve (afferent) and the facial nerve (efferent).
The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus, not by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1686 (Book Page): Touching the lateral wall of the pharynx with a spatula may test the pharyngeal reflex. ... Sensory fibers [of IX] innervate the posterior one third of the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Contralateral Lymphatic Spread in Lingual Carcinoma
statement: A 70-year-old patient presents with a malignant lesion on the right lateral border of the tongue. Despite the unilateral nature of the lesion, the physician orders a bilateral neck examination. Which anatomical fact regarding the posterior portion of the tongue justifies this precaution?
options: Lymph from the posterior third can drain directly to the deep cervical nodes of either side
The posterior third of the tongue drains into the submental nodes which are midline
Lymphatic vessels from the posterior tongue are less numerous than the anterior
The lateral margins of the tongue always have crossed drainage
The lingual artery provides a pathway for contralateral nodal seeding
correctOption: Lymph from the posterior third can drain directly to the deep cervical nodes of either side
optionExplanations: While the anterior two-thirds tends to drain ipsilaterally, the posterior third has lymphatics that frequently cross the midline, allowing malignant cells to spread to the contralateral deep cervical nodes.
The posterior third bypasses the submental nodes entirely; they drain directly into the deep chain.
The number of vessels is high in both parts; it is the direction and crossing that is clinically significant.
The lateral margins of the *anterior* tongue usually drain to the ipsilateral submandibular nodes; it is the *central and posterior* areas that cross most frequently.
The lingual artery is a vascular structure and does not serve as a pathway for lymphatic drainage; metastasis follows the lymphatics, not the arterial flow.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Lingual Nerve
statement: A dentist is performing a difficult extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar. He warns the patient that the nerve most closely related to this tooth, which provides general sensation to the tongue, is at risk. Which nerve is he referring to?
options: Chorda tympani
Inferior alveolar nerve
Lingual nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The chorda tympani is already fused with the lingual nerve by this point; an injury here would be described as a lingual nerve injury containing taste fibers.
The inferior alveolar nerve is within the mandibular canal; while at risk during extractions, it supplies the teeth and chin, not tongue sensation.
The lingual nerve lies extremely close to the medial aspect of the mandibular third molar. Injury here causes anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth.
The mylohyoid nerve is motor to the mylohyoid and digastric muscles; it does not provide sensory supply to the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is located deeper and more posteriorly near the oropharyngeal isthmus; it is not the primary nerve at risk during third molar extraction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve passes forward into the submandibular region... Here, it is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Tip
statement: A 55-year-old patient presents with a suspected malignant ulcer located at the extreme tip of the tongue. Based on standard anatomical lymphatic pathways, which group of lymph nodes should the clinician palpate first for primary metastasis?
options: Submental lymph nodes
Jugulodigastric lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Occipital lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: The tip of the tongue is anatomically unique as it drains specifically into the submental lymph nodes located in the submental triangle. This is the first-tier station for malignancies at this site.
Jugulodigastric nodes are part of the deep cervical chain and usually receive drainage from the posterior third or as a second-tier station from other parts of the tongue.
Parotid nodes receive lymph from the scalp, eyelids, and auricle, but do not participate in the primary lymphatic drainage of the tongue.
Occipital nodes are located at the back of the skull and drain the posterior scalp; they have no anatomical relevance to the lingual lymphatic system.
Submandibular nodes receive drainage from the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the tip. Palpating these first for a tip lesion would overlook the primary lymphatic station.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient experiences a deep laceration in the floor of the mouth. Upon testing, the physician finds that the patient can still perceive taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but has lost general sensation (pain and temperature) in the same area. Which nerve was most likely spared in this injury?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Lingual nerve trunk proximal to the submandibular ganglion
Hypoglossal nerve
Chorda tympani fibers within the lingual nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Chorda tympani fibers within the lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the posterior third of the tongue; it is not responsible for taste on the anterior two-thirds.
Damage to the lingual nerve trunk distal to the chorda tympani junction would normally abolish both general sensation and taste.
The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue; its sparing or injury would not explain the dissociation of general sensation and taste.

In rare cases of partial nerve injury or varying anatomy where taste fibers (chorda tympani) are spared while general sensory fibers (V3) are severed, taste remains. This highlights that these two modalities travel together but originate from different cranial nerves (VII and V).
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensation to the larynx and the epiglottic region, not the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The chorda tympani nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) joins the lingual nerve deep in the infratemporal fossa... The lingual nerve fibers carry general sensation... The chorda tympani fibers carry taste.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A clinician identifies a lingual carcinoma lesion on the side of the tongue and notes that the lymph from this region eventually reaches the jugulo-omohyoid node. What is the classification of the node group that acts as the final common pathway for all tongue lymph?
options: Pericervical collar nodes
Superficial cervical nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Anterior cervical nodes
correctOption: Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: The pericervical collar includes regional groups like submental and submandibular nodes; they are intermediate, not the final terminal group.
Superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein and primarily drain the skin of the neck and lower ear.
The deep cervical nodes, situated along the internal jugular vein, represent the terminal lymphatic group for the entire head and neck, including the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the terminal tongue lymph.
Anterior cervical nodes drain the skin and superficial tissues of the front of the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve Vulnerability during Dental Procedures
statement: A patient undergoes a difficult extraction of an impacted lower third molar. Post-operatively, the patient reports a loss of both general sensation and taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the ipsilateral side. What is the most likely anatomical explanation for this multi-modal sensory loss?
options: Injury to the chorda tympani in the middle ear
Injury to the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve at the foramen ovale
Injury to the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
Injury to the glossopharyngeal nerve near the jugular foramen
Injury to the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa
correctOption: Injury to the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa
optionExplanations: While the chorda tympani carries taste, its injury in the middle ear would spare general sensation, as the lingual nerve (carrying V3 general sensation) would still be intact.
A lesion at the foramen ovale would affect all sensory and motor functions of the mandibular nerve (V3), including the muscles of mastication, which is not described here.
Injury at the stylomastoid foramen results in facial paralysis (Bell's palsy) but spares taste, as the chorda tympani branches off the facial nerve within the facial canal, proximal to this foramen.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the posterior third of the tongue; its injury would not affect the anterior two-thirds.

The lingual nerve carries general sensation (V3) and taste (from chorda tympani) once they join in the infratemporal fossa. Its proximity to the lower third molar makes it vulnerable during extraction, resulting in loss of both modalities.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve passes forward into the submandibular region from the infratemporal fossa by running beneath the origin of the superior constrictor muscle, which is attached to the posterior border of the mylohyoid line on the mandible. Here, it is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Mechanism of Tongue Deviation in CN XII Lesion
statement: A patient presents with a lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve. When asked to protrude their tongue, the tip deviates to the right. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological mechanism of this clinical finding?
options: The right styloglossus muscle pulls the tongue toward the affected side.
The intrinsic muscles of the left side are paralyzed, causing a shift in the midline.
The palatoglossus muscle on the right side overpowers the contralateral side.
The right hyoglossus muscle fails to retract the tongue, allowing it to move forward and right.
The normal left genioglossus muscle pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed side.
correctOption: The normal left genioglossus muscle pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed side.
optionExplanations: The styloglossus muscle is responsible for the retraction and elevation of the tongue, not protrusion; its action would not explain the deviation during protrusion.
While intrinsic muscles are paralyzed in a CN XII lesion, their role is to change the shape of the tongue rather than determine the direction of protrusion.
The palatoglossus is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X), not CN XII, and is involved in elevating the root of the tongue, not in protrusion.
The hyoglossus muscle depresses the tongue and assists in retraction; its failure would not cause the specific deviation observed during active protrusion.

The genioglossus is the primary protrusor. In a unilateral CN XII lesion, the paralyzed muscle cannot push its half of the tongue forward. The healthy contralateral genioglossus pushes its side forward and toward the midline, resulting in the tongue pointing toward the weak (ipsilateral) side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): One of the genioglossus muscles, which pull the tongue forward, is paralyzed on the affected side. The other, normal genioglossus muscle pulls the unaffected side of the tongue forward, leaving the paralyzed side of the tongue stationary. The result is the tip of the tongue’s deviation toward the paralyzed side.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: An elite surgeon is performing a neck dissection and identifies a prominent node of the deep cervical chain located superiorly, just below the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. Based on regional anatomy, this node most likely receives lymph from which part of the tongue?
options: Ventral surface of the tip only
Mandibular gingiva only
Submental region exclusively
Tip only
Posterior third and lateral sides
correctOption: Posterior third and lateral sides
optionExplanations: The ventral surface of the tip follows the drainage of the tip to the submental nodes.
While it may receive some gingival drainage, the jugulodigastric node is most clinically significant as the primary station for lingual and tonsillar drainage.
The submental region drains into the submental nodes, which then drain into the submandibular or deep cervical chain, but the jugulodigastric node receives more than just submental lymph.
The tip drains primarily to the submental nodes, which are located anteriorly in the submental triangle, not under the digastric muscle.

The jugulodigastric node, located superiorly in the deep cervical chain, is the primary recipient for lymph from the posterior third of the tongue and the lateral sides (after the submandibular nodes).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node... is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve Vulnerability in Dental Procedures
statement: A 24-year-old male presents with persistent numbness on the right side of his tongue and the floor of his mouth following a traumatic surgical extraction of an impacted right lower third molar. Which specific nerve was likely injured during the procedure?
options: Inferior alveolar nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Lingual nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the teeth and the chin (via the mental nerve) but does not provide sensation to the tongue surface.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the posterior third of the tongue and is located much deeper and more posteriorly than the third molar site.
The lingual nerve passes just medial to the lower third molar as it enters the submandibular region, making it highly susceptible to injury during surgical extractions in this area.
Injury to the hypoglossal nerve would cause motor deficits and deviation of the tongue, but the patient specifically presents with 'numbness' (sensory loss).
The mylohyoid nerve is a motor branch to the mylohyoid and anterior belly of the digastric; its injury would not cause sensory loss on the tongue surface.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Flow of the Oral Tongue
statement: A patient is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lateral border of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Following the anatomical pathway, what is the most likely multi-step sequence of lymphatic spread to the terminal nodes?
options: Lateral tongue -> Retropharyngeal nodes -> Jugular trunks
Lateral tongue -> Submandibular nodes -> Deep cervical nodes
Lateral tongue -> Anterior cervical nodes -> Subclavian vein
Lateral tongue -> Parotid nodes -> Deep cervical nodes
Lateral tongue -> Submental nodes -> Submandibular nodes
correctOption: Lateral tongue -> Submandibular nodes -> Deep cervical nodes
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes receive lymph from the nasopharynx and auditory tube; they do not receive primary or secondary drainage from the oral part of the tongue.

Lymph from the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue primarily drains first into the submandibular lymph nodes. From there, the efferent vessels carry the lymph to the deep cervical nodes, which serve as the terminal chain.
Anterior cervical nodes lie along the anterior jugular veins and drain the superficial skin of the front of the neck; they are not the pathway for deep visceral lingual lymph.
Parotid nodes do not participate in the lingual drainage circuit; they are part of the drainage for the lateral face and scalp.
Submental nodes receive drainage from the tip (apex), not the lateral sides of the tongue. The lateral sides skip the submental nodes and go directly to the submandibular group.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes. Page 1655 (Book Page): Submandibular nodes... drain lymph that ultimately passes into the deep cervical nodes.

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A patient undergoes a test for the 'gag reflex'. When the physician touches the posterior wall of the oropharynx, the patient fails to respond. Which nerve provides the afferent limb of this physiological loop and is also responsible for sensation on the posterior tongue?
options: Trigeminal nerve
Lingual nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Vagus nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The trigeminal nerve provides sensation to the nasopharynx (V2) and oral cavity floor (V3), but not the oropharynx.
The lingual nerve provides sensation only to the anterior two-thirds and does not mediate the gag reflex.
The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the tongue and is not involved in the gag reflex sensory pathway.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory (afferent) innervation to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue. It is the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
The vagus nerve provides the efferent limb of the gag reflex (motor to pharyngeal muscles) but not the primary afferent limb for the oropharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1686 (Book Page): Testing Glossopharyngeal Nerve Integrity... Sensory fibers innervate the posterior one third of the tongue. Page 1755 (Book Page): Oropharynx: Glossopharyngeal nerve.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 62-year-old male with a history of heavy tobacco use presents with a firm, ulcerated lesion on the right lateral aspect of the posterior third of his tongue. On physical examination, his vitals are stable. Neck palpation reveals a single, firm, non-tender 2-cm mass located deep to the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, below and behind the angle of the mandible. Which specific lymph node is most likely involved in this metastatic spread?
options: Jugulodigastric node
Buccal node
Submental node
Occipital node
Mastoid node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node is the 'sentinel' node for the posterior tongue and tonsils, located near where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein.
Buccal nodes are superficial nodes in the cheek draining the eyelids and nose, not the tongue body.
Submental nodes are located under the chin and drain the tip of the tongue, not the posterior third.
Occipital nodes are at the base of the skull posteriorly and are irrelevant to oral cavity malignancy.
Mastoid nodes are behind the ear and would not receive drainage from any portion of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Convergence of Head and Neck Lymphatics
statement: When examining a patient for secondary carcinomatous deposits from a suspected lingual malignancy, why must the physician search areas like the larynx and pharynx even if the tongue lesion is visible?
options: Because lingual carcinoma only spreads to these organs
Because the tongue and larynx share the same sensory nerve
Because the submandibular nodes drain the larynx
Because the deep cervical nodes receive lymph from all these sites
Because the thyroid gland is the primary site for tongue cancer
correctOption: Because the deep cervical nodes receive lymph from all these sites
optionExplanations: Lingual carcinoma spreads via lymphatics to nodes, not directly as a primary growth to the larynx or pharynx.
The tongue (CN XII, IX, V, VII) and larynx (CN X) have different nerve supplies, though both can be involved in complex head and neck syndromes.
The submandibular nodes do not drain the larynx; the larynx drains to the laryngeal, pretracheal, and then deep cervical nodes.

The deep cervical chain is the 'terminal' drainage for all head and neck structures; therefore, an enlarged node in this chain requires a thorough search of all potential primary sites including the tongue, pharynx, and larynx.
The thyroid gland is an endocrine organ and is not a primary source or 'site' for lingual carcinoma, although it may be involved in surgical margins.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): In the head and neck, all the lymph ultimately drains into the deep cervical group of nodes... The primary growth may be small and overlooked, for example, in the larynx, the pharynx...

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 22-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He has a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone. Physical exam reveals right-sided facial paralysis and a loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. However, his ability to produce tears (lacrimation) is normal. At which point is the facial nerve most likely damaged?
options: Within the parotid gland
At the stylomastoid foramen
Distal to the geniculate ganglion but proximal to the nerve to stapedius
Internal acoustic meatus
Geniculate ganglion
correctOption: Distal to the geniculate ganglion but proximal to the nerve to stapedius
optionExplanations: Lesions in the parotid gland cause motor facial paralysis but do not affect taste because the chorda tympani has already branched off.
A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen occurs after the chorda tympani has branched; it would cause facial paralysis but taste would be intact.

The greater petrosal nerve (for lacrimation) leaves at the geniculate ganglion. The chorda tympani (for taste) leaves much later in the facial canal. A lesion between these points explains the facial palsy and loss of taste with spared lacrimation.
A lesion at the internal acoustic meatus would damage the greater petrosal nerve, leading to a loss of lacrimation, which is intact here.
A lesion at the geniculate ganglion would typically involve the origin of the greater petrosal nerve, thus abolishing lacrimation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve arises from the facial nerve in the facial canal... Page 1671 (Book Page): The facial nerve... swells to form the sensory geniculate ganglion. Page 1712 (Book Page): The greater petrosal nerve arises... at the geniculate ganglion... secretomotor to the lacrimal gland.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Terminal Lymphatic Drainage of the Neck
statement: A patient with advanced carcinoma of the posterior third of the tongue presents with an enlarged node located behind the angle of the mandible. If this cancer is spreading along its most direct route, where will the lymph ultimately coalesce before entering the venous system?
options: Anterior jugular venous arch
Axillary lymph nodes
Right and left jugular trunks
Superficial parotid nodes
Submental lymph trunks
correctOption: Right and left jugular trunks
optionExplanations: The anterior jugular arch is a venous structure, not a lymphatic coalescence point.
Axillary nodes drain the upper limb and breast; they have no anatomical connection to the lingual lymphatic system.
Efferents from the deep cervical chain, which receives all lingual lymph, form the jugular trunks that drain into the thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct.
Superficial parotid nodes are regional filters for the face, not the final terminal pathway for deep lingual drainage.
Submental trunks are small and drain only into the submandibular or deep cervical nodes; they are not the final coalescence point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): The efferent lymph vessels from the deep cervical nodes join to form the jugular trunks.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Pathway of the Lateral Tongue
statement: In the clinical progression of lingual carcinoma affecting the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, which physiological sequence best describes the typical lymphatic pathway to the terminal nodal groups?
options: To the parotid nodes, then to the superficial cervical lymph nodes.
Directly to the jugulo-omohyoid node, bypassing the submandibular nodes.
Bypassing all regional nodes to drain directly into the thoracic duct.
Directly to the submental nodes, then to the jugulodigastric nodes.
To the submandibular nodes, followed by the deep cervical lymph nodes.
correctOption: To the submandibular nodes, followed by the deep cervical lymph nodes.
optionExplanations: The parotid nodes do not receive drainage from the tongue; they serve the scalp, face, and parotid gland itself.
While the jugulo-omohyoid node is associated with the tongue, the lateral margins generally utilize the submandibular nodes as a primary filter before the deep cervical chain.
Lymphatic drainage in the head and neck is organized into regional tiers; direct drainage to the thoracic duct from the tongue does not occur.
The submental nodes specifically serve the tip, whereas the lateral margins (sides) drain to the submandibular nodes first.
Lymph from the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue typically drains first into the submandibular lymph nodes and then proceeds to the deep cervical nodes, which are the terminal group.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
coreConcept: Afferent Limb of the Gag Reflex
statement: A physician testing the gag reflex finds that when the posterior third of the tongue is touched, there is no response. Which nerve lesion is most likely responsible for the lack of the afferent limb of this reflex?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve
Vagus nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Mandibular division of Trigeminal nerve
Facial nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of the larynx down to the vocal cords and the vallecula, but it is not the primary afferent for the posterior tongue gag reflex.
The vagus nerve (CN X) primarily provides the efferent limb (motor) of the gag reflex via the pharyngeal plexus; its sensory contribution to the tongue is very limited (vallecula).

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides all sensation (general and taste) to the posterior third of the tongue. It serves as the afferent limb for the gag reflex; if damaged, the stimulus is never transmitted to the brainstem.
The mandibular nerve (V3) provides sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third where the gag reflex is elicited.
The facial nerve (CN VII) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds via the chorda tympani but does not provide the general sensation for the gag reflex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1731 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste).

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Pathways in Lingual Malignancy
statement: A 55-year-old male with a chronic tobacco habit presents with a firm, non-healing ulcer on the lateral margin of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Assuming the carcinoma spreads via the most direct lymphatic route, which chain of nodes will the malignant cells populate first?
options: Submandibular to Deep Cervical
Deep Cervical to Submental
Retropharyngeal to Deep Cervical
Paratracheal to Submandibular
Submental to Submandibular
correctOption: Submandibular to Deep Cervical
optionExplanations: Malignancy on the lateral oral tongue typically drains first to the ipsilateral submandibular nodes and then descends into the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.
Lymph flow is unidirectional toward the venous system; deep cervical nodes are the terminal group, meaning they cannot drain back into the submental nodes.
Retropharyngeal nodes receive lymph from the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the anterior oral cavity or lateral tongue.
Paratracheal nodes are associated with the trachea and thyroid gland; they do not receive afferent vessels from the tongue.
Submental nodes only serve the tip of the tongue; lateral margin drainage bypasses the submental region entirely.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Tip
statement: A 50-year-old patient presents with a biopsy-confirmed lingual carcinoma located at the very apex of the tongue. Based on anatomical lymphatic pathways, which lymph node group is the most likely primary site for initial metastatic spread?
options: Submandibular lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Parotid lymph nodes
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: The submandibular lymph nodes drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but are not the primary first-tier drainage for the absolute tip.
Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes drain the scalp above the ear and the external auditory meatus.
Parotid nodes are involved in draining the scalp, auricle, and eyelids, and do not receive primary drainage from the tongue.
Retropharyngeal nodes receive lymph from the nasopharynx and auditory tube, not the anterior tongue apex.
The submental lymph nodes are located in the submental triangle and specifically receive lymph from the tip of the tongue, the central part of the lower lip, and the floor of the anterior mouth.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Tip: Submental lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 58-year-old patient is diagnosed with a large squamous cell carcinoma involving the root (posterior third) of the tongue. Imaging shows bilateral enlargement of the deep cervical lymph nodes. Which anatomical fact explains why carcinomas of the posterior tongue can present with bilateral metastases more frequently than lateral anterior lesions?
options: The posterior third lacks a median fibrous septum, unlike the anterior two-thirds.
The posterior third is supplied by the lingual nerve, which has bilateral cross-talk.
The posterior third is derived from the first pharyngeal arch.
Lymphatic vessels from the posterior third often cross the midline to the contralateral deep cervical nodes.
The posterior third is separated from the body by the foramen cecum, which acts as a conduit.
correctOption: Lymphatic vessels from the posterior third often cross the midline to the contralateral deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: A median fibrous septum exists throughout the tongue, but it is not a complete barrier to lymphatic vessels, especially in the posterior and central regions where vessels frequently communicate across the midline.

The lingual nerve provides sensation to the anterior two-thirds. The posterior third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Regardless, nerve distribution does not dictate the pathway of lymphatic metastasis.

The posterior third of the tongue is derived from the third pharyngeal arch (Page 1734), not the first. The first arch forms the anterior two-thirds. This embryological origin determines the sensory nerve supply but not directly the crossing of lymphatics.

Although the provided text doesn't explicitly state 'crossing' in the short summary on page 1730, in clinical anatomy, the posterior third and central areas have lymphatics that readily cross the midline to the contralateral deep cervical nodes, leading to bilateral metastasis.

The foramen cecum is a developmental remnant of the thyroglossal duct. It is a landmark for the apex of the sulcus terminalis but does not function as a conduit for lymphatic spread between the tongue and other structures.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with a small, indurated, biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma precisely on the midline of the tip of her tongue. Radiological staging and surgical planning must account for the high risk of bilateral nodal involvement. Which group of nodes is most likely to harbor bilateral metastases first?
options: Buccal lymph nodes
Mastoid lymph nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Occipital lymph nodes
Submental lymph nodes
correctOption: Submental lymph nodes
optionExplanations: Buccal nodes drain the cheek and nose, not the tip of the tongue.
Mastoid nodes are irrelevant to the oral cavity and tongue.
While the lymph eventually reaches deep cervical nodes, the submental nodes are the primary regional group for the tip.
Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp.
The tip of the tongue drains into the submental nodes. Midline structures often exhibit bilateral lymphatic drainage, meaning cells can spread to both right and left submental triangles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submental nodes... drain lymph from the tip of the tongue, the floor of the anterior part of the mouth, the incisor teeth, the center part of the lower lip, and the skin over the chin.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue
statement: In the multi-step metastatic pathway of lingual carcinoma originating from the lateral margins of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, what is the typical anatomical sequence of lymphatic spread before reaching the deep cervical chain?
options: Through the retropharyngeal space into the tracheal nodes.
Into the submental nodes and then to the submandibular nodes.
Into the submandibular nodes followed by the deep cervical nodes.
Through the buccal nodes into the parotid nodal group.
Directly to the jugulo-omohyoid nodes without intermediate stations.
correctOption: Into the submandibular nodes followed by the deep cervical nodes.
optionExplanations: The retropharyngeal and tracheal nodes drain the nasopharynx and trachea respectively. They are not part of the drainage pathway for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, which is a common site for primary lingual carcinoma.

The submental nodes drain only the tip of the tongue, not the lateral margins. Furthermore, submental lymph typically drains to the submandibular or deep cervical nodes, but the lateral tongue bypasses the submental group.

This is the correct anatomical sequence for the lateral borders of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Lymphatic vessels travel laterally to the submandibular nodes situated superficial to the submandibular gland before continuing to the deep cervical chain.

Buccal nodes drain the cheek and are not a standard pathway for lingual lymphatics. The parotid nodes serve the scalp and lateral face, making this sequence anatomically incorrect for lingual carcinoma spread.

Direct drainage to jugulo-omohyoid nodes is more characteristic of the posterior third or the tip of the tongue in some cases, but the lateral anterior two-thirds typically pass through submandibular stations first. The sequence is defined by anatomical proximity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1730 (Book Page): Sides of the anterior two thirds: Submandibular and deep cervical lymph nodes

category: Discuss lesions of motor and sensory nerves supplying the tongue
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with a 'clumsy' tongue and difficulty speaking. Examination reveals wasting and fasciculations of the right side of the tongue. When asked to protrude her tongue, it deviates to the right. Additionally, she has lost the gag reflex on the right side and has difficulty shrugging her right shoulder. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Infratemporal fossa
Internal acoustic meatus
Stylomastoid foramen
Hypoglossal canal only
Jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal
correctOption: Jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal
optionExplanations: A lesion in the infratemporal fossa would primarily affect V3 (mandibular nerve) and the chorda tympani, not the hypoglossal, glossopharyngeal, or accessory nerves.
The internal acoustic meatus contains CN VII and VIII. Lesions here cause facial palsy and deafness, not tongue deviation or shoulder weakness.
Lesions at the stylomastoid foramen only cause motor facial paralysis (CN VII).
A lesion in the hypoglossal canal alone would explain the tongue symptoms but would not account for the loss of the gag reflex or the inability to shrug the shoulder.

This scenario describes a deficit in CN IX (gag reflex), CN XI (shoulder shrug), and CN XII (tongue deviation/wasting). This cluster suggests a large lesion at the skull base involving both the jugular foramen and the nearby hypoglossal canal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1498 (Book Page): In fractures involving the jugular foramen, the 9th, 10th, and 11th cranial nerves may be damaged. Page 1491 (Book Page): The hypoglossal canal for transmission of the hypoglossal nerve is anterosuperior to the occipital condyle.

category: Discuss the anatomical correlates of lingual carcinoma in reference to lymphatic drainage of tongue
coreConcept: Drainage of the Lateral Anterior Tongue
statement: Which specific regional group of lymph nodes receives drainage from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the tip, and is located superficial to the submandibular salivary gland?
options: Submental nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Anterior cervical nodes
Submandibular nodes
Deep cervical nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
