While the orbicularis oculi is supplied by the facial nerve, it acts as a sphincter to close the eyes; it does not raise the eyebrows. Furthermore, it is not supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
The corrugator supercilii pulls the eyebrows medially and inferiorly (frowning), but it is supplied by the facial nerve, not the ophthalmic nerve (which is sensory only).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1517 (Book Page): The frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis can raise the eyebrows in expressions of surprise or horror... Page 1535 (Book Page): All the facial muscles develop from the second pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the facial nerve.

category: Define modiolus
coreConcept: Internal Acoustic Meatus and Modiolus Base
statement: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) occupying the internal acoustic meatus. As the tumor enlarges, it compresses the neurovascular structures entering the base of the modiolus. Which clinical finding would be most directly related to the compromise of these specific fibers?
options: Inability to close the eye on the affected side (lagophthalmos)
Anesthesia of the skin over the angle of the mandible
Sensorineural hearing loss due to damage of fibers perforating the modiolus
Loss of taste from the posterior one-third of the tongue
Hyperacusis due to paralysis of the tensor tympani muscle
correctOption: Sensorineural hearing loss due to damage of fibers perforating the modiolus
optionExplanations: Eye closure is controlled by the facial nerve (CN VII). While CN VII is in the internal acoustic meatus, the question asks specifically about fibers entering the modiolus (cochlear nerve).
Sensation over the angle of the jaw is provided by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), which does not pass through the internal acoustic meatus.
The cochlear nerve enters the cochlea by perforating the base of the modiolus. Compression here results in sensorineural hearing loss.
Taste from the posterior third of the tongue is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which exits via the jugular foramen, not the internal acoustic meatus.
Hyperacusis results from stapedius muscle paralysis (CN VII). The tensor tympani is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3), which is not in the internal acoustic meatus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page)-1716: The modiolus has a broad base, which is situated at the bottom of the internal acoustic meatus. Branches of the cochlear nerve perforate it. ... The cochlear nerve divides into branches, which enter the foramina at the base of the modiolus.

category: Define modiolus
statement: The hollow bony tube of the cochlea follows a specific helical path. Exactly how many spiral turns does this tube make as it winds around the central modiolus?
options: Three and one-half
Two and one-half
One and one-half
Four
Five
correctOption: Two and one-half
optionExplanations: Three and one-half turns is an overestimation of the standard anatomical spiral of the cochlea.
The human cochlea typically consists of approximately 2.5 (two and a half) turns around the central axis of the modiolus.
One and one-half turns is fewer than the standard anatomical count for the human cochlea.
Four turns is significantly more than the 2.5 turns described in human anatomy.
Five turns is incorrect; the cochlea is a compact structure of only two and one-half turns.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): Basically, it consists of a central pillar, the modiolus, around which a hollow bony tube makes two and one-half spiral turns.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A patient is unable to whistle and finds that food accumulates in the vestibule of the mouth during chewing. On examination, they can close their eyes and frown normally. Which nerve branch is most likely dysfunctional?
options: Temporal branch of the facial nerve
Mandibular branch of the facial nerve
Buccal nerve of the mandibular division (V3)
Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Zygomatic branch of the facial nerve
correctOption: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
optionExplanations: The temporal branch supplies the forehead and eyebrows; its dysfunction would cause an inability to frown or raise the eyebrows.
The mandibular branch supplies the muscles of the lower lip; its dysfunction would cause sagging of the lower lip.
The buccal nerve (from V3) is entirely sensory to the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek and does not provide motor supply to the buccinator.
The buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the buccinator muscle, which keeps the cheek taut to prevent food accumulation in the vestibule and allows for blowing/whistling.
The zygomatic branch supplies the orbicularis oculi; its dysfunction would cause an inability to close the eye.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): The buccal branch emerges from the anterior border of the gland below the parotid duct and supplies the buccinator muscle and the muscles of the upper lip and nostril.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: During the initial phase of opening the mouth, the mandible must be depressed and simultaneously pulled forward to prevent the angle of the jaw from impinging on the parotid gland and sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which muscle is primarily responsible for this coordinated protrusion and depression?
options: Masseter
Digastric (posterior belly)
Temporalis
Medial pterygoid
Lateral pterygoid
correctOption: Lateral pterygoid
optionExplanations: The masseter is a powerful elevator of the mandible and does not participate in the opening or depression of the mouth.

The posterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII) and assists in depressing the mandible, but it does not provide the protrusive force characteristic of the lateral pterygoid.
The temporalis muscle primarily elevates the mandible; its posterior fibers are responsible for retraction of the jaw, not depression.
The medial pterygoid muscle acts to elevate the mandible (closing the mouth) and assists in protrusion, but it does not depress the jaw.

The lateral pterygoid is unique among the masticatory muscles because its contraction pulls the mandibular neck and articular disc forward (protrusion), facilitating the rotation required for depression (opening).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1509 (Book Page): Depression of the mandible is brought about by contraction of the digastrics, the geniohyoids, and the mylohyoids. The lateral pterygoids play an important role by pulling the mandible forward.

category: Define modiolus
coreConcept: Anatomic Orientation of the Modiolus Base
statement: The cochlear nerve fibers must traverse the central axis of the cochlea to reach the brainstem. What is the specific anatomical relationship between the modiolus and the internal acoustic meatus?
options: The apex of the modiolus forms the floor of the internal acoustic meatus.
The modiolus is located laterally to the internal acoustic meatus and is not in contact with it.
The modiolus arises from the roof of the internal acoustic meatus via the spiral lamina.
The modiolus acts as the lateral wall of the internal acoustic meatus for the facial nerve.
The broad base of the modiolus is situated at the bottom of the internal acoustic meatus.
correctOption: The broad base of the modiolus is situated at the bottom of the internal acoustic meatus.
optionExplanations: The apex of the modiolus faces anterolaterally towards the tympanic cavity, while the base is directed posteromedially toward the internal acoustic meatus.
The modiolus is directly continuous with the internal acoustic meatus, as its base serves as the entry point for the cochlear nerve fibers.
The spiral lamina projects from the modiolus into the cochlear canal; it does not connect the modiolus to the roof of the meatus.
The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial nerve, but the modiolus is specifically related to the cochlear division of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).
The broad base of the modiolus is anatomically positioned at the fundus (bottom) of the internal acoustic meatus, where it is perforated by cochlear nerve branches.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): The modiolus has a broad base, which is situated at the bottom of the internal acoustic meatus. Branches of the cochlear nerve perforate it.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of Facial Nerve Branches
statement: A 45-year-old male undergoes a deep parotidectomy for a malignant tumor. Post-operatively, the surgeon notes that the patient is unable to compress the cheek on the operated side, leading to food accumulation in the oral vestibule, and shows significant drooping of the upper lip. Which terminal branch of the facial nerve was most likely sacrificed during the procedure?
options: Mandibular branch
Cervical branch
Buccal branch
Zygomatic branch
Temporal branch
correctOption: Buccal branch
optionExplanations: The mandibular branch supplies the muscles of the lower lip (e.g., depressor anguli oris). A lesion here would cause drooping of the corner of the mouth and asymmetry of the lower lip, not the upper lip or cheek compression.
The cervical branch supplies the platysma muscle in the neck; its paralysis would not result in the specific oral vestibule or upper lip deficits described in the scenario.

The buccal branch innervates the buccinator muscle (responsible for cheek compression) and the muscles of the upper lip and nostril. Loss of this branch leads to food accumulating in the vestibule (buccinator paralysis) and drooping of the upper lip.

The zygomatic branch primarily supplies the orbicularis oculi; damage would result in inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos) but would not affect the buccinator or the muscles of the upper lip.

The temporal branch supplies the muscles of the forehead (frontal belly of occipitofrontalis) and the superior part of the orbicularis oculi; its lesion would cause inability to wrinkle the forehead, not cheek or upper lip issues.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): [The buccal branch emerges from the anterior border of the gland below the parotid duct and supplies the buccinator muscle and the muscles of the upper lip and nostril.]

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A patient presents with a limited ability to protrude the mandible. Anatomical analysis of the muscles of mastication reveals that protrusion requires a coordinated forward pull of the mandibular condyle. Which specific muscle is responsible for pulling the neck of the mandible and the articular disc forward onto the articular tubercle?
options: Medial pterygoid
Temporalis (posterior fibers)
Mylohyoid
Lateral pterygoid
Masseter
correctOption: Lateral pterygoid
optionExplanations: The medial pterygoid assists in protrusion, but its primary role is elevation and lateral movement; it does not have the direct attachment to the disc required for the initial glide.
The posterior fibers of the temporalis are the primary retractors of the mandible, pulling the condyle backward into the fossa.
The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that assists in depression of the mandible once the condyle has been translated forward, but it does not initiate protrusion.

The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that originates anterior to its insertion in a way that allows it to pull the condyle and disc forward, facilitating both protrusion and the start of depression.
The masseter is primarily an elevator of the mandible and does not contribute to the forward translation (protrusion) of the condyle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1509 (Book Page): [Mandible Depression] This is accomplished by the contraction of the lateral pterygoid muscle, which pulls forward the neck of the mandible and the articular disc so that the latter moves onto the articular tubercle.

category: Define modiolus
statement: Where is the spiral ganglion of the cochlear nerve specifically located in relation to the modiolus?
options: On the lateral surface of the bony labyrinth.
Within the internal acoustic meatus proper.
At the very apex of the modiolus (helicotrema).
In a canal winding around the modiolus at the base of the spiral lamina.
In the vestibule, posterior to the modiolus.
correctOption: In a canal winding around the modiolus at the base of the spiral lamina.
optionExplanations: The ganglion is internal, within the bony pillar of the modiolus.
The vestibular ganglion is in the IAM; the spiral ganglion is specifically within the cochlea itself.
The helicotrema is the apex of the cochlear turns, not the site of the spiral ganglion.
The spiral ganglion is housed in the spiral canal of the modiolus, located where the spiral lamina meets the modiolus.
The spiral ganglion is exclusively related to the cochlear modiolus, not the vestibule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1716 (Book Page): The sensory ganglion of this nerve takes the form of an elongated spiral ganglion that is lodged in a canal winding around the modiolus in the base of the spiral lamina.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Lower Motor Neuron Facial Nerve Lesion
statement: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for an inability to express emotion on the left side of her face after a traumatic injury at the base of the skull involving the stylomastoid foramen. She cannot whistle, her left cheek accumulates food while eating, and her left eye remains open even during sleep. However, her jaw movements and ability to chew remain perfectly symmetrical. Which nerve lesion and resulting muscle paralysis explain these findings?
options: Facial nerve lesion, paralyzing the lateral pterygoid and medial pterygoid.
Hypoglossal nerve lesion, paralyzing the intrinsic muscles of the tongue.
Trigeminal nerve (V3) lesion, paralyzing the buccinator and masseter.
Facial nerve (CN VII) lesion at the stylomastoid foramen, paralyzing the orbicularis oris, buccinator, and orbicularis oculi.
Glossopharyngeal nerve lesion, paralyzing the stylopharyngeus and parotid secretion.
correctOption: Facial nerve (CN VII) lesion at the stylomastoid foramen, paralyzing the orbicularis oris, buccinator, and orbicularis oculi.
optionExplanations: The facial nerve does not supply the pterygoids; these are muscles of mastication supplied by the mandibular nerve.
A hypoglossal lesion would cause tongue deviation and atrophy, not facial expression paralysis or food accumulation in the cheek.
The trigeminal nerve (V3) does not pass through the stylomastoid foramen; its lesion would cause chewing weakness and deviation of the jaw.

The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the stylomastoid foramen. A lesion here causes paralysis of all muscles of facial expression on that side. This includes the orbicularis oris (whistling), buccinator (food accumulation), and orbicularis oculi (eye closure), while sparing muscles of mastication (chewing).
The glossopharyngeal nerve is not involved in facial expression; its lesion would affect taste on the posterior third of the tongue and swallowing.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): Damage to the facial nerve ... causes distortion of the face. Inability to close the eyelids ... sagging of the angle of the mouth ... The patient ... commonly dribbles ... when attempting to eat or drink. ... The facial nerve ... emerges from the temporal bone through the stylomastoid foramen. ... Page 1536 (Book Page): The buccinator is a significant muscle in food processing in that it compresses the cheeks ... positioning food for efficient chewing.

category: Define modiolus
statement: A 68-year-old female with progressive sensorineural hearing loss undergoes advanced temporal bone imaging. The report mentions 'significant sclerosis of the central pillar of the cochlea,' implying damage to the modiolus. Based on its anatomical structure, which physiological process would be most directly hindered by this sclerosis?
options: The rotation of the malleus around its anteroposterior axis
The equalization of pressure via the pharyngotympanic tube
The movement of the stapes footplate within the fenestra vestibuli
The drainage of endolymph into the saccus endolymphaticus
The passage of cochlear nerve branches through their respective foramina
correctOption: The passage of cochlear nerve branches through their respective foramina
optionExplanations: Malleus rotation is a middle ear mechanical event involving the tympanic membrane and ligaments, unrelated to the internal ear's modiolus.
Pressure equalization via the auditory tube is a function of the middle ear and nasopharynx, completely independent of the cochlear modiolus.
Stapes movement is a middle ear/vestibule interface function, not a function of the internal cochlear pillar (modiolus).
Endolymph drainage involves the ductus endolymphaticus and saccus endolymphaticus, which are part of the membranous labyrinth and not housed within the modiolus.
The modiolus contains the foramina through which the cochlear nerve fibers must pass. Sclerosis (hardening or overgrowth) of this bone would compress or obstruct these nerve fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): The modiolus has a broad base, which is situated at the bottom of the internal acoustic meatus. Branches of the cochlear nerve perforate it.

category: Define modiolus
coreConcept: Anatomical Relationship of the Modiolus and Spiral Lamina
statement: Regarding the structural organization of the cochlea, what is the precise mechanical relationship between the modiolus and the spiral lamina?
options: The spiral lamina is a continuation of the outer bony wall that meets the modiolus in the midline.
The spiral lamina is a bony ledge that winds around the modiolus and projects into the cochlear canal.
The spiral lamina is a vertical septum that divides the modiolus into anterior and posterior halves.
The spiral lamina is a ligament that attaches the modiolus to the tympanic membrane.
The spiral lamina serves as the base of the modiolus within the internal acoustic meatus.
correctOption: The spiral lamina is a bony ledge that winds around the modiolus and projects into the cochlear canal.
optionExplanations: The spiral lamina originates from the modiolus and projects outward, rather than being a continuation of the outer wall meeting the center.
The spiral lamina is a critical bony projection from the modiolus that provides the structural support for the basilar membrane and divides the cochlear duct.
The spiral lamina is a horizontal/spiral ledge, not a vertical septum, and it divides the cochlear canal, not the modiolus itself.
The spiral lamina is a bony feature of the internal ear, whereas the tympanic membrane is the lateral boundary of the middle ear; they do not attach via a ligament.
The base of the modiolus is at the internal acoustic meatus, but the spiral lamina is a projection along its length, not its base.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): A spiral ledge, the spiral lamina, winds around the modiolus and projects into the interior of the canal and partially divides it.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A 22-year-old male presents to the clinic after his jaw 'locked' while he was yawning. On examination, the patient is unable to close his mouth, and his chin is protruded. A diagnosis of bilateral temporomandibular joint dislocation is made. Which of the following muscles, by sudden contraction, was primarily responsible for pulling the head of the mandible and the articular disc anteriorly beyond the summit of the articular tubercle?
options: Temporalis (posterior fibers)
Medial pterygoid
Lateral pterygoid
Masseter
Digastric (posterior belly)
correctOption: Lateral pterygoid
optionExplanations: The posterior fibers of the temporalis are the primary retractors of the mandible; their contraction would pull the jaw backward, potentially helping to reduce a dislocation rather than causing one.
The medial pterygoid assists in protrusion and elevation, but it is not the primary muscle whose spasm causes the mandibular head to jump over the articular tubercle.

The lateral pterygoid pulls the neck of the mandible and the articular disc forward; over-contraction during wide opening (like yawning) can pull these structures past the articular tubercle, locking the jaw.
The masseter is a powerful elevator; while its spasm (trismus) can make reduction of a dislocation difficult, it does not provide the anterior vector required for the initial dislocation.
The posterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the facial nerve and acts on the hyoid bone; it does not participate in the anterior translation of the mandibular head within the TMJ.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1511 (Book Page): Temporomandibular Joint Dislocation... a sudden contraction of the lateral pterygoid muscles, as in yawning, may be sufficient to pull the disc forward beyond the summit.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Motor Distribution of Facial Nerve Branches
statement: In the complex coordination of facial expressions, the 'modiolus' serves as a critical anatomical landmark. If a surgeon accidentally damages the motor nerve supply to the muscle that pulls the angle of the mouth laterally and upward during a broad smile, which specific branch and muscle are most likely involved?
options: Cervical branch; Platysma
Zygomatic branch; Orbicularis oculi
Temporal branch; Occipitofrontalis
Buccal branch; Zygomaticus major
Mandibular branch; Mentalis
correctOption: Buccal branch; Zygomaticus major
optionExplanations: The cervical branch primarily supplies the platysma in the neck; while it may sometimes assist with the depressor anguli oris, it is not the nerve for the zygomaticus major.
The zygomatic branch specifically targets the orbicularis oculi for eyelid closure; it does not provide the primary motor drive for the zygomaticus major during smiling.

The temporal branch supplies the forehead (occipitofrontalis) and the upper part of the orbicularis oculi, but it does not descend low enough to supply the zygomaticus major or the angle of the mouth.

The zygomaticus major, which pulls the angle of the mouth upward and laterally to smile, is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which innervates the muscles radiating from the oral aperture.
The mandibular branch supplies the muscles of the lower lip and chin, such as the mentalis and depressor labii inferioris; it does not supply the elevators of the angle of the mouth.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1536 (Book Page): [Lip and Cheek Muscles] Traced from the side of the nose to the angle of the mouth... Zygomaticus major... [Page 1537 (Book Page): Facial Nerve] The buccal branch... supplies... the muscles of the upper lip.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Pathophysiology of TMJ Dislocation and Reduction
statement: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a violent yawn, unable to close his mouth. He is in significant distress with his chin protruding forward. Physical examination reveals both heads of the mandible are located anterior to the articular tubercles. Which muscle's involuntary contraction is the primary obstacle preventing the manual reduction of this dislocation?
options: Digastric
Lateral pterygoid
Medial pterygoid
Masseter
Temporalis
correctOption: Lateral pterygoid
optionExplanations: The digastric muscle is a depressor of the mandible; its action would actually assist in opening the mouth further and is not the source of the resistance to repositioning the jaw into the closed position.

The lateral pterygoid muscle, when in spasm, pulls the mandibular head forward beyond the summit of the articular tubercle; backward pressure during reduction is specifically designed to overcome this spasm to return the head to the mandibular fossa.
The medial pterygoid assists in protrusion and elevation, but the primary spasm that fixes the mandible in the anteriorly displaced position in a dislocation is the lateral pterygoid.
The masseter, like the temporalis, exerts tension that must be overcome by downward pressure, but it does not cause the initial protraction into the dislocated state.

The temporalis muscle undergoes tension that resists downward displacement during reduction, but it is not the muscle that actively holds the mandible in the protruded, dislocated position anterior to the tubercle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1511 (Book Page): [Temporomandibular Joint Dislocation] The downward pressure overcomes the tension of the temporalis and masseter muscles, and the backward pressure overcomes the spasm of the lateral pterygoid muscles.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A patient is unable to frown or produce vertical wrinkles in the forehead. This clinical finding indicates a loss of function in which specific muscle, and which nerve is responsible for its action?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris; Oculomotor nerve
Orbicularis oculi; Trigeminal nerve
Occipitofrontalis (frontal belly); Mandibular nerve
Corrugator supercilii; Facial nerve
Procerus; Facial nerve
correctOption: Corrugator supercilii; Facial nerve
optionExplanations: The levator palpebrae superioris elevates the upper eyelid. While its paralysis causes ptosis, it does not produce wrinkles in the forehead skin.
Orbicularis oculi closes the eye. It is innervated by the facial nerve, whereas the trigeminal nerve provides sensory supply to the face, not motor supply to the orbicularis oculi.

While the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis is innervated by the facial nerve, it produces horizontal wrinkles (expression of surprise), not vertical ones, and is not supplied by the mandibular nerve.

The corrugator supercilii muscle pulls the eyebrows medially and inferiorly, creating vertical wrinkles in the forehead typically associated with frowning. It is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
The procerus muscle is responsible for horizontal wrinkles over the bridge of the nose, not vertical wrinkles of the forehead.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1518 (Book Page): Table 12.3... Corrugator... Action: Vertical wrinkles of forehead as in frowning... Nerve supply: Facial nerve.

category: Define modiolus
coreConcept: Functional Deficit of the Facial Modiolus
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with severe unilateral sagging of the right side of her face. Clinical examination reveals she cannot whistle, and food persistently accumulates in her right oral vestibule during meals. Based on the anatomical role of the modiolus and its associated muscles, which clinical sign would most likely be present on the affected side?
options: An increase in the depth of the right nasolabial fold.
Inability to stabilize the oral commissure, leading to the dribbling of saliva.
Excessive tension in the right masseter muscle.
Numbness over the skin of the angle of the mandible.
A hyper-active gag reflex due to glossopharyngeal irritation.
correctOption: Inability to stabilize the oral commissure, leading to the dribbling of saliva.
optionExplanations: In facial palsy, the nasolabial fold typically flattens or disappears due to the loss of muscle tone; it does not increase in depth.

The modiolus serves as the intersection that keeps the oral commissure competent. Paralysis of the muscles forming this hub (Bell's palsy) leads to sagging and a failure to contain fluids, causing dribbling.
Masseter tension would be related to the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), not the facial nerve which supplies the mimetic muscles of the modiolus.
Numbness at the angle of the mandible involves the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), which is not a part of the motor paralysis involving the facial modiolus.
The gag reflex is mediated by CN IX and CN X, which are unrelated to the superficial facial muscles of the modiolus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): Inability to close the eyelids, drooping of the lower eyelid, and sagging of the angle of the mouth on the affected side are characteristic sequelae. The patient has an expressionless, masklike side of the face and commonly dribbles from the corner of the mouth when attempting to eat or drink.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: All the muscles of facial expression share a common embryological origin and a primary motor nerve supply. Which pharyngeal arch and cranial nerve are responsible for these muscles?
options: First pharyngeal arch; Trigeminal nerve (V)
Third pharyngeal arch; Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)
Fourth pharyngeal arch; Vagus nerve (X)
Second pharyngeal arch; Facial nerve (VII)
Sixth pharyngeal arch; Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Second pharyngeal arch; Facial nerve (VII)
optionExplanations: The first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the muscles of mastication, supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
The third arch gives rise to the stylopharyngeus muscle, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The fourth arch gives rise to the cricothyroid and pharyngeal constrictors, supplied by the superior laryngeal branch of the vagus.
The second arch (hyoid arch) gives rise to all mimetic muscles, the stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric, all supplied by the facial nerve.
The sixth arch gives rise to the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1535 (Book Page): All the facial muscles develop from the second pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the facial nerve.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Nerve Distribution Relative to the Parotid Gland
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with a deep, invasive malignant tumor in the right parotid gland. Physical examination reveals a total right-sided facial paralysis including an inability to close the right eye and a sagging angle of the mouth. However, when the patient is asked to clench his teeth, the masseter and temporalis muscles on the right side feel firm and appear to contract normally. Which anatomical fact explains this clinical discrepancy?
options: The muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, which does not pass through the parotid gland.
The muscles of mastication are located in the infratemporal fossa, which is never involved in parotid pathology.
The tumor has selectively spared the cervical branch of the facial nerve while destroying the buccal and temporal branches.
The facial nerve only supplies the superficial part of the masseter, leaving the deep part functional.
The parotid gland only contains the sensory branches of the trigeminal nerve, which are unrelated to motor function.
correctOption: The muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, which does not pass through the parotid gland.
optionExplanations: The facial nerve (CN VII) passes through the parotid gland and supplies the muscles of facial expression. The mandibular nerve (V3), which supplies the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis), does not pass through the parotid gland and remains intact.
The infratemporal fossa can be involved in advanced parotid tumors, but the primary reason the muscles work is the nerve supply, not just location.
Sparing one branch would not explain why the masseter (a non-facial expression muscle) is functional; clencing the teeth involves muscles supplied by V3.
The facial nerve does not supply any part of the masseter; the masseter is entirely supplied by the masseteric branch of V3.
The parotid gland contains the motor branches of the facial nerve, not the trigeminal nerve. Trigeminal branches provide sensory innervation to the overlying skin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): Damage to the facial nerve ... in the parotid gland (by a tumor) ... causes distortion of the face. Inability to close the eyelids ... and sagging of the angle of the mouth on the affected side are characteristic. ... Page 1508 (Book Page): Table 12.2 Mastication Muscles: Temporalis and Masseter: Nerve Supply: Mandibular nerve (V3). Page 1637 (Book Page): The external carotid artery ... terminates in the substance of the parotid gland ... by dividing into the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. The facial nerve divides into its five terminal branches as it runs forward within the substance of the parotid salivary gland.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A patient presents with a limited ability to retract their mandible after it has been protruded. Which muscle and specific fiber group are primarily responsible for the posterior movement of the head of the mandible into the mandibular fossa?
options: Medial pterygoid
Superior fibers of the masseter
Anterior fibers of the temporalis
Posterior fibers of the temporalis
Lateral pterygoid
correctOption: Posterior fibers of the temporalis
optionExplanations: The medial pterygoid muscle acts to elevate the mandible and assists the lateral pterygoid in protrusion; it is not a muscle of retraction.
The masseter is primarily an elevator of the mandible. While it has some slight protrusive component, it does not contribute significantly to the retraction of the mandible into the fossa.
The anterior fibers of the temporalis are vertically oriented and primarily function to elevate the mandible (close the mouth) rather than pulling it posteriorly.

The posterior fibers of the temporalis muscle are oriented horizontally. When they contract, they pull the head of the mandible backward from the articular tubercle into the mandibular fossa, effecting retraction.
The lateral pterygoid is the primary muscle of protrusion (pulling the mandible forward); therefore, its action is directly antagonistic to the retraction needed in this scenario.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1510 (Book Page): [Retraction is brought about by contraction of the posterior fibers of the temporalis.]

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A 25-year-old patient is unable to compress the cheeks against the teeth to prevent food from accumulating in the vestibule during mastication. Which nerve and muscle are most likely involved?
options: Facial nerve and orbicularis oris muscle
Facial nerve and buccinator muscle
Mandibular nerve and masseter muscle
Maxillary nerve and zygomaticus major muscle
Mandibular nerve and buccinator muscle
correctOption: Facial nerve and buccinator muscle
optionExplanations: While the orbicularis oris is supplied by the facial nerve, it acts as a sphincter for the lips (closing the mouth) rather than compressing the cheeks for food positioning.

The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression (mimetic) and is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Its action is to compress the cheeks against the teeth, preventing food accumulation in the vestibule.
The masseter is a muscle of mastication supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3); its primary action is the elevation of the mandible, not cheek compression.

The maxillary nerve (V2) is primarily sensory to the face and does not provide motor innervation to the zygomaticus major; the zygomaticus major is a mimetic muscle supplied by the facial nerve for smiling.
The mandibular nerve (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication, not the buccinator. The buccal branch of V3 is sensory to the cheek, but the motor supply to the buccinator is from the facial nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1536 (Book Page): The buccinator is a significant muscle in food processing in that it compresses the cheeks and lips against the teeth, thus positioning food for efficient chewing... All the facial muscles develop from the second pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the facial nerve.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Mechanics of Mandibular Depression and Protrusion
statement: During a clinical demonstration of mandibular movements, the instructor explains that for the mouth to open wide, the mandible must be protracted. Which muscle is primarily responsible for pulling the neck of the mandible and the articular disc forward onto the articular tubercle?
options: Lateral pterygoid
Medial pterygoid
Mylohyoid
Temporalis
Masseter
correctOption: Lateral pterygoid
optionExplanations: The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that assists in depressing the mandible. It functions by pulling the neck of the mandible and the articular disc forward, facilitating the rotation and gliding necessary for opening the mouth.
The medial pterygoid muscle primarily elevates the mandible and assists in protrusion, but it does not play the leading role in the initial forward pull of the disc during depression.

The mylohyoid muscle contributes to the depression of the mandible once the lateral pterygoid has initiated the forward movement, but it does not act on the articular disc or the neck of the mandible directly.
The temporalis elevates the mandible. Its posterior fibers are specifically noted for the retraction of the mandible, which is the opposite of the movement required to open the mouth wide.
The masseter is a powerful elevator of the mandible used for closing the mouth; it does not assist in opening or protraction of the articular disc.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1509 (Book Page): This is accomplished by the contraction of the lateral pterygoid muscle, which pulls forward the neck of the mandible and the articular disc so that the latter moves onto the articular tubercle.

category: Define modiolus
statement: A 62-year-old male presents with a deep-seated malignant tumor in the parotid gland. Following a radical parotidectomy, he develops drooping at the right corner of his mouth and finds it difficult to prevent saliva and food from leaking while eating. Damage to which specific neural structure has most likely led to the loss of stability at the facial modiolus?
options: The greater petrosal nerve at the geniculate ganglion.
The buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
The infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (V2).
The auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve (V3).
correctOption: The buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
optionExplanations: The greater petrosal nerve is involved in lacrimation and is located deep within the petrous bone, far from the parotid-facial nerve terminal branches.
The buccal branch of the facial nerve innervates the buccinator and muscles of the upper lip, which are central to the modiolus; its damage causes sagging of the mouth angle.
The cervical branch supplies the platysma in the neck; while it can affect the depressor anguli oris, the primary stability of the modiolus is via the buccal and mandibular branches.
The infraorbital nerve (V2) is purely sensory to the skin of the cheek and upper lip; it does not provide motor innervation to the modiolus muscles.
The auriculotemporal nerve provides sensory supply to the temple and parotid region, and parasympathetic fibers to the gland, but not motor control to the modiolus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): "The buccal branch emerges from the anterior border of the gland below the parotid duct and supplies the buccinator muscle and the muscles of the upper lip and nostril." Page 1537 (Book Page): "drooping of the lower eyelid, and sagging of the angle of the mouth on the affected side are characteristic sequelae."

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Facial Nerve Course and Clinical Paralysis
statement: A 48-year-old patient presents with a deep-seated malignant tumor in the parotid gland. On examination, the patient is unable to close their right eye and the right corner of their mouth sagged, with saliva dribbling out. Which anatomical fact explains this clinical presentation?
options: The masseter muscle is paralyzed, preventing proper lip closure and saliva control.
The tumor has invaded the mandibular nerve (V3) within the infratemporal fossa.
The tumor has blocked the parotid duct, causing pressure-induced sensory loss of the facial skin.
The facial nerve (CN VII) divides into five terminal branches within the substance of the parotid gland.
The tumor has compressed the auriculotemporal nerve as it leaves the parotid.
correctOption: The facial nerve (CN VII) divides into five terminal branches within the substance of the parotid gland.
optionExplanations: The masseter is a muscle of mastication; its paralysis would affect jaw closure but not the ability to close the eyelids or the subtle movements of the facial orifices.
The mandibular nerve does not pass through the parotid gland; it is located deeper in the infratemporal fossa and supplies muscles of mastication, not facial expression.
Parotid duct obstruction causes painful swelling (parotitis) but does not lead to the muscular paralysis of the eyelid and mouth angle seen in facial nerve damage.

The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland, separating it into superficial and deep lobes. A malignant tumor here often invades the nerve, causing lower motor neuron paralysis of the muscles of facial expression.
The auriculotemporal nerve is sensory and secretomotor; its compression would not cause the widespread motor paralysis (inability to close eye/mouth) seen in this case.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): The facial nerve divides into its five terminal branches as it runs forward within the substance of the parotid salivary gland. ... Page 1537 (Book Page): Inability to close the eyelids, drooping of the lower eyelid, and sagging of the angle of the mouth on the affected side are characteristic sequelae.

category: Define modiolus
statement: A 55-year-old patient presents with right-sided facial nerve palsy. During the evaluation, the physician notes that the patient is unable to compress the cheek against the teeth and frequently dribbles saliva from the right corner of the mouth. This clinical finding results from the loss of motor control over which structure?
options: The facial modiolus hub and its contributing muscles.
The ciliary ganglion in the orbit.
The sensory fibers of the auriculotemporal nerve.
The motor root of the trigeminal nerve.
The temporomandibular joint ligaments.
correctOption: The facial modiolus hub and its contributing muscles.
optionExplanations: Paralysis of the facial nerve affects muscles that meet at the modiolus (like the buccinator and orbicularis oris). Loss of tone at this hub causes sagging and the inability to contain saliva or position food.
The ciliary ganglion is parasympathetic and controls the pupil, not the mouth.
The auriculotemporal nerve provides sensation, not the motor control required for oral competence.
The motor root of CN V supplies muscles of mastication, not the muscles of facial expression at the modiolus.
TMJ ligaments provide joint stability but do not control lip/cheek tone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): Damage to the facial nerve... causes distortion of the face. Inability to close the eyelids, drooping of the lower eyelid, and sagging of the angle of the mouth on the affected side are characteristic sequelae. The patient... commonly dribbles from the corner of the mouth.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A 32-year-old patient presents with difficulty keeping food between their teeth while chewing, frequently biting the inner lining of their cheek. Which of the following nerves is responsible for the motor innervation of the muscle primarily involved in compressing the cheeks against the teeth to prevent this occurrence?
options: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
Buccal nerve (branch of mandibular nerve)
Zygomatic branch of the facial nerve
Buccal branch of the facial nerve
correctOption: Buccal branch of the facial nerve
optionExplanations: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) is primarily sensory to the middle third of the face and does not provide motor innervation to the skeletal muscles of facial expression or mastication.

The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, and pterygoids), but it does not provide motor supply to the buccinator, which is a muscle of facial expression.

The buccal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division (V3) and provides sensory innervation to the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek. It is frequently confused with the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which is motor.

The zygomatic branch of the facial nerve primarily supplies the orbicularis oculi muscle and does not innervate the buccinator, which is located more inferiorly in the cheek region and supplied by the buccal branch of CN VII.

The buccinator muscle is a muscle of facial expression derived from the second pharyngeal arch; thus, it is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically its buccal branch. Its action is to compress the cheeks against the teeth, which assists in positioning food during mastication.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): [The buccal branch emerges from the anterior border of the gland below the parotid duct and supplies the buccinator muscle and the muscles of the upper lip and nostril.]

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Distinction between CN VII and CN V3 Lesions
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with a suspected neurological lesion. Clinical findings include: 1. Normal jaw-closing strength, 2. No deviation of the mandible on opening, 3. Inability to compress the cheek to prevent food from spilling out of the mouth, and 4. Sagging of the lower eyelid. Which functional group of muscles and which cranial nerve are predominantly involved?
options: Muscles of mastication; Mandibular nerve
Pharyngeal constrictors; Vagus nerve
Extraocular muscles; Oculomotor nerve
Muscles of facial expression; Facial nerve
Suprahyoid muscles; Mylohyoid nerve
correctOption: Muscles of facial expression; Facial nerve
optionExplanations: A lesion of the mandibular nerve (V3) would result in weakness of jaw-closing and deviation of the mandible toward the paralyzed side on opening, which are not present here.
The pharyngeal constrictors are involved in swallowing once the bolus has entered the pharynx, but they do not control facial orifices or the accumulation of food in the cheek vestibule.

Extraocular muscles move the eyeball itself; although the oculomotor nerve supplies the levator palpebrae superioris to raise the lid, it does not supply the muscles of the cheek or those that close the eyelid.

The combination of cheek weakness (buccinator) and eyelid sagging (orbicularis oculi) with spared jaw strength confirms that the muscles of facial expression (CN VII) are involved while mastication (CN V3) is intact.
The suprahyoid muscles (like mylohyoid) assist in opening the mouth and moving the hyoid; they do not control the eyelid or cheek compression for food containment.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): Facial Muscle Paralysis... Inability to close the eyelids, drooping of the lower eyelid, and sagging of the angle of the mouth on the affected side are characteristic sequelae... This is essentially a lower motor neuron lesion.

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Parotid Gland and Facial Nerve
statement: A 45-year-old female undergoes a parotidectomy for a tumor in the deep lobe of the parotid gland. Post-operatively, she presents with an inability to whistle and reports that food constantly gets trapped between her teeth and the cheek on the operated side. Which muscle and nerve branch were likely compromised during the surgery?
options: Masseter muscle; Masseteric branch of the mandibular nerve
Buccinator muscle; Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Levator labii superioris; Temporal branch of the facial nerve
Risorius muscle; Zygomatic branch of the facial nerve
Orbicularis oris; Mandibular branch of the facial nerve
correctOption: Buccinator muscle; Buccal branch of the facial nerve
optionExplanations: The masseter is a muscle of mastication supplied by the trigeminal nerve. It is located deep to the parotid but its paralysis would result in weak jaw closure, not food entrapment in the cheek.

The buccinator muscle is responsible for compressing the cheek against the teeth to keep the food bolus on the occlusal surfaces. It is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which passes through the parotid gland and is at risk during parotid surgery.
Levator labii superioris is supplied by the zygomatic and buccal branches, not the temporal branch. Its paralysis would affect the ability to elevate the upper lip.
While the risorius is supplied by the facial nerve, its primary action is retracting the corner of the mouth; it does not prevent food from trapping in the cheek vestibule.
Orbicularis oris is the sphincter of the mouth. While its paralysis would cause drooling and inability to whistle, it is primarily the buccinator that prevents food trapping in the vestibule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): The facial nerve divides into its five terminal branches as it runs forward within the substance of the parotid salivary gland... The buccal branch... supplies the buccinator muscle and the muscles of the upper lip and nostril.

category: Define modiolus
statement: A 42-year-old male is admitted following a high-impact motor vehicle accident. CT imaging reveals a longitudinal fracture of the petrous temporal bone that passes through the internal acoustic meatus and the adjacent central axis of the cochlea. If the modiolus is fractured at its base, which clinical finding is most expected?
options: Loss of taste from the posterior third of the tongue
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle on the ipsilateral side
Conductive hearing loss due to stapes footplate fixation
Inability to close the eye due to damage to the temporal branch of the facial nerve
Profound sensorineural hearing loss due to destruction of cochlear nerve entry points
correctOption: Profound sensorineural hearing loss due to destruction of cochlear nerve entry points
optionExplanations: Taste from the posterior third of the tongue is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which exits via the jugular foramen, not the internal acoustic meatus.
The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X), which does not pass through the petrous part of the temporal bone.
Conductive hearing loss involves the external or middle ear (ossicles); a modiolus fracture is an internal ear injury resulting in sensorineural hearing loss.

While the facial nerve also passes through the internal acoustic meatus, its temporal branch arises outside the skull in the parotid gland; facial palsy would be a lower motor neuron sign involving all facial muscles, not just eye closure via a specific branch distal to the fracture site.
Because the cochlear nerve branches enter the internal ear through foramina at the base of the modiolus, a fracture at this specific site will sever or compress the auditory pathway at its origin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1716 (Book Page): The cochlear nerve divides into branches, which enter the foramina at the base of the modiolus. The sensory ganglion of this nerve takes the form of an elongated spiral ganglion that is lodged in a canal winding around the modiolus

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
statement: A 52-year-old patient presents with a complete loss of the ability to wrinkle the forehead, close the eye tightly, and whistle on the right side. On examination, the patient also reports that sounds seem abnormally loud in the right ear. Which nerve lesion and associated muscle paralysis best explain these findings?
options: Mandibular nerve lesion affecting the masseter and tensor tympani.
Facial nerve lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius.
Oculomotor nerve lesion affecting the levator palpebrae superioris.
Trigeminal nerve lesion at the foramen ovale affecting the buccinator.
Facial nerve lesion at the stylomastoid foramen affecting only mimetic muscles.
correctOption: Facial nerve lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius.
optionExplanations: A mandibular nerve lesion would cause masticatory weakness and jaw deviation, but not the widespread facial expression paralysis or hyperacusis.
A lesion of the facial nerve proximal to the nerve to stapedius explains both the paralysis of facial expression (mimetic muscles) and the hyperacusis (paralysis of the stapedius).
An oculomotor lesion would cause ptosis (drooping) rather than the inability to close the eye (which is an orbicularis oculi/facial nerve function).
The trigeminal nerve does not innervate the buccinator (which is facial nerve) or the muscles of the forehead and eye closure.
A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen would cause facial paralysis but would spare the stapedius, so hyperacusis would not be present.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1685 (Book Page): "If the patient is excessively sensitive to sound in one ear (hyperacusis), the lesion probably involves the nerve to the stapedius."

category: Enlist in tabulated manner the muscles of facial expression and mastication, giving their nerve supply and actions
coreConcept: Differential diagnosis of CN VII vs. CN V3 lesions
statement: A 52-year-old male presents with a sudden onset of facial asymmetry. Examination reveals he cannot close his right eye, his right nasolabial fold is flattened, and saliva dribbles from the right corner of his mouth. However, he can still clench his teeth firmly and move his jaw side-to-side. Which anatomical conclusion is most accurate?
options: The Trigeminal nerve (CN V) is damaged, affecting the Masseter and Temporalis.
The Oculomotor nerve (CN III) is damaged, preventing eyelid closure.
The Mandibular division (V3) is damaged, affecting the Pterygoid muscles.
The Facial nerve (CN VII) is damaged, while the Mandibular division (V3) is intact.
The Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is damaged, affecting the Buccinator muscle.
correctOption: The Facial nerve (CN VII) is damaged, while the Mandibular division (V3) is intact.
optionExplanations: A Trigeminal nerve lesion would result in weakness of jaw clenching (mastication) and sensory loss, which are not present here as the patient can clench his teeth.
CN III (Oculomotor) opens the eye (levator palpebrae superioris). Closing the eye is the function of the Orbicularis oculi, which is supplied by the Facial nerve (CN VII).
The Pterygoid muscles are responsible for side-to-side jaw movement; since he can still perform this, V3 (motor) must be functional.
The patient exhibits classic symptoms of Bell's Palsy (CN VII lesion: drooping mouth, inability to close eye). The retention of mastication (clenching) and jaw movement proves CN V3 is intact.
The Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus and parotid gland (parasympathetic); it does not innervate the buccinator or muscles of facial expression.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): Damage to the facial nerve ... causes distortion of the face. Inability to close the eyelids ... and sagging of the angle of the mouth ... clench his or her jaws firmly [is platysma/masseter]. Page 1508 (Book Page): Muscles of mastication are summarized in Table 12.2 [supplied by mandibular nerve].

category: Define modiolus
statement: A 58-year-old male presents with severe sensorineural hearing loss following a temporal bone fracture. High-resolution CT shows a comminuted fracture specifically involving the central bony axis of the cochlea. Which physiological process is most directly compromised by damage to the modiolus?
options: The drainage of endolymph through the ductus endolymphaticus
Transmission of mechanical vibrations from the stapes to the perilymph
The rotation of the head as sensed by the semicircular ducts
The equalization of pressure between the middle ear and the nasopharynx
The passage of cochlear nerve branches to the spiral organ of Corti
correctOption: The passage of cochlear nerve branches to the spiral organ of Corti
optionExplanations: Endolymph drainage occurs via the ductus endolymphaticus to the saccus endolymphaticus on the posterior surface of the petrous bone.
Vibration transmission is a function of the ossicles and the fenestra vestibuli, not the modiolus.
Rotational sense is a function of the semicircular canals and their ampullae, which are posterior to the cochlea and independent of the modiolus.
Pressure equalization is the function of the auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube.
Correct. The modiolus houses the spiral ganglion and provides the conduits for the cochlear nerve fibers to reach the organ of Corti. Damage here interrupts neural transmission.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): The modiolus has a broad base... Branches of the cochlear nerve perforate it.

category: Define modiolus
coreConcept: Identification of the Modiolus in Clinical Context
statement: A 55-year-old patient with an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) is undergoing surgical evaluation. The tumor is located at the internal acoustic meatus. The surgeon notes that the tumor is compressing the nerve fibers just as they emerge from the base of the central pillar of the cochlea. Which anatomical structure is the surgeon referring to as the 'central pillar'?
options: Modiolus
Tegmen Tympani
Cochlear Duct
Spiral Lamina
Promontory
correctOption: Modiolus
optionExplanations: The modiolus is defined explicitly as the central bony pillar of the cochlea.
The tegmen tympani is the roof of the middle ear, located far superior to the cochlear modiolus.
The cochlear duct is the membranous labyrinth (scala media) containing endolymph, not a bony pillar.
The spiral lamina is a ledge projecting from the central pillar, not the pillar itself.
The promontory is the projection on the medial wall of the middle ear caused by the first turn of the cochlea, not the central pillar.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): Basically, it consists of a central pillar, the modiolus, around which a hollow bony tube makes two and one-half spiral turns.

category: Define modiolus
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Internal Acoustic Meatus and Modiolus
statement: A 52-year-old patient presents with total sensorineural hearing loss. An MRI reveals an osteoma (bony tumor) obstructing the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus. Given the anatomical relationship of this site to the cochlea, which part of the central support system is most likely compromised, preventing the passage of nerve branches?
options: The spiral organ of Corti
The apex of the modiolus
The base of the modiolus
The promontory
The cupula
correctOption: The base of the modiolus
optionExplanations: The spiral organ of Corti is the sensory receptor located within the cochlear duct, not the bony support at the meatus.
The apex of the modiolus faces anterolaterally toward the end of the cochlear spiral and is not located at the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus.
The broad base of the modiolus is directly situated at the bottom (fundus) of the internal acoustic meatus where cochlear nerve fibers must pass through its foramina.
The promontory is the external bulge seen in the middle ear and is not involved in the nerve entry at the internal acoustic meatus.
The cupula is part of the vestibular system (ampulla of semicircular ducts) or the term for the apex of the cochlea, but not the primary site of nerve entry into the pillar.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1715 (Book Page): The modiolus has a broad base, which is situated at the bottom of the internal acoustic meatus. Branches of the cochlear nerve perforate it.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
coreConcept: Trigeminal Nerve Divisions and Mental Nerve
statement: A 55-year-old male presents with excruciating, shock-like pain in his right lower lip and chin, triggered by shaving. The pain is limited to the distribution of the mental nerve. This nerve is a direct terminal branch of which structure, and where does it exit the skull?
options: Nerve to mylohyoid; Stylomastoid foramen
Buccal nerve; Pterygomaxillary fissure
Inferior alveolar nerve; Mental foramen
Lingual nerve; Mandibular foramen
Maxillary nerve; Foramen rotundum
correctOption: Inferior alveolar nerve; Mental foramen
optionExplanations: The nerve to mylohyoid is a motor branch of the inferior alveolar nerve that supplies the mylohyoid muscle and anterior digastric; it does not provide cutaneous sensation to the chin.
The buccal nerve (from V3) supplies the cheek's skin and mucous membrane but does not supply the chin or exit the mental foramen.
The mental nerve is the terminal continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve (a branch of V3). It exits through the mental foramen of the mandible to provide sensory supply to the chin and lower lip.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation to the tongue and does not supply the skin of the chin or exit the mental foramen.
The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the foramen rotundum but supplies the midface, not the chin or lower lip.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1531 (Book Page): The mental nerve emerges from the mental foramen of the mandible and supplies the skin of the lower lip and chin. Page 1669 (Book Page): Inferior alveolar nerve... emerges through the mental foramen (mental nerve) to supply the skin of the chin.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Terminal branching of the facial artery
statement: Which specific arterial branch represents the terminal portion of the facial artery as it reaches the medial angle of the eye?
options: Superior labial artery
Submental artery
Infraorbital artery
Angular artery
Lateral nasal artery
correctOption: Angular artery
optionExplanations: The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth to supply the upper lip and nasal septum; it is a major branch but not the termination of the vessel.
The submental artery is a branch that arises from the facial artery specifically at the lower border of the body of the mandible, supplying the chin and lower lip, not the terminal end.
The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery, not the facial artery, although it does supply parts of the face and accompanies the infraorbital nerve.
The angular artery is correctly identified as the terminal part of the facial artery, located between the nose and the medial canthus, where it anastomoses with the ophthalmic artery.
The lateral nasal artery arises alongside the nose to supply the skin of the dorsum and side of the nose; it precedes the final angular segment.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery. It runs in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: During a surgical repair of a deep laceration on the upper lip, an anesthetist performs a regional nerve block by injecting lidocaine into the infraorbital foramen. This pharmacological intervention successfully anesthetizes which group of structures?
options: The temple, auricle, and external auditory meatus.
The lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose, and upper lip.
The angle of the jaw and the parotid region.
The forehead, scalp, and frontal sinus.
The chin, lower lip, and lower gums.
correctOption: The lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose, and upper lip.
optionExplanations: The temple and auricle are primarily supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve (V3) and the great auricular nerve, not the infraorbital nerve.
Correct. The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits the infraorbital foramen and radiates to supply the lower eyelid, cheek, lateral nose, and upper lip.
The angle of the jaw and parotid region are supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), which originates from the cervical plexus.
The forehead and scalp are supplied by the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (V1), which exit at the superior orbital margin.
The chin and lower lip are supplied by the mental nerve (V3), which is blocked at the mental foramen, not the infraorbital foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The infraorbital nerve... appears on the face through the infraorbital foramen. It immediately divides into numerous small branches... and supply the skin of the lower eyelid and cheek, the side of the nose, and the upper lip.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
coreConcept: Sensory vs Motor Innervation of the Cheek
statement: During a physical examination, a clinician notes that a patient has lost general sensation from the skin of the cheek but retains the ability to puff out the cheeks against resistance. Which of the following best explains this diagnostic contrast?
options: Lesion of the buccal branch of the facial nerve
Lesion of the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve
Lesion of the buccal nerve of the mandibular division (V3)
Lesion of the motor root of the trigeminal nerve
Lesion of the infraorbital nerve of the maxillary division (V2)
correctOption: Lesion of the buccal nerve of the mandibular division (V3)
optionExplanations: A lesion of the buccal branch of the facial nerve would cause motor paralysis of the buccinator muscle, preventing the patient from puffing out their cheeks, but would not affect sensation.
The zygomatic branch of the facial nerve supplies the orbicularis oculi; a lesion here would affect eye closure rather than cheek function.
The buccal nerve of V3 is purely sensory to the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek. Losing it results in sensory loss while sparing the motor-innervated buccinator (supplied by CN VII).
The motor root of the trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication; its loss would affect chewing rather than cheek sensation.
The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid, side of the nose, and upper lip, but not the primary sensory area of the lower cheek.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1668 (Book Page): Buccal nerve to the skin and the mucous membrane of the cheek. The buccal nerve does not supply the buccinator muscle (which is supplied by the facial nerve), and it is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Clinical Palpation Points of the Face
statement: An anesthetist is preparing a patient for surgery and wishes to monitor the pulse using the facial artery. Following standard clinical procedure, where is the most appropriate anatomical landmark to palpate this vessel?
options: Against the mastoid process behind the ear
At the medial angle of the eye against the nasal bone
Against the maxilla just below the infraorbital foramen
Against the lower margin of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter
Against the zygomatic arch in front of the ear
correctOption: Against the lower margin of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter
optionExplanations: This location is used to find the occipital or posterior auricular arteries; it is not the location for the facial artery pulse.
While the angular artery is here, it is too small and lacks a hard bony backing suitable for reliable pulse palpation compared to the mandible.
The infraorbital artery emerges here, but it is small and its pulse is not typically palpable or used for routine monitoring.
The facial artery is easily compressed against the inferior border of the mandible just anterior to the masseter muscle, providing a robust clinical pulse point.
This point identifies the superficial temporal artery pulse, which is also used by anesthetists but is distinct from the facial artery pulse.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1533 (Book Page): and the facial artery, as it winds around the lower margin of the mandible level with the anterior border of the masseter, are commonly used by the anesthetist to take the patient’s pulse.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
statement: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) provides sensory innervation to several structures through various branches. Which of its branches is responsible for the sensation on the tip of the nose?
options: Supraorbital nerve
Lacrimal nerve
Infratrochlear nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
External nasal nerve
correctOption: External nasal nerve
optionExplanations: The supraorbital nerve supplies the skin of the forehead and the upper eyelid, not the nose.
The lacrimal nerve supplies the conjunctiva and skin of the lateral part of the upper eyelid.
The infratrochlear nerve supplies the skin of the medial upper eyelid and the adjacent part of the side of the nose, but not the tip.
The zygomaticofacial nerve is a branch of V2 (maxillary) and supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheek.
The external nasal nerve (a branch of the nasociliary nerve, V1) emerges to supply the skin on the dorsum and the tip of the nose.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The external nasal nerve leaves the nose by emerging between the nasal bone and the upper nasal cartilage. It supplies the skin on the side of the nose down as far as the tip.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Vascular relations within the parotid gland
statement: A 45-year-old female undergoes a total parotidectomy for a suspected malignancy. Deep within the substance of the gland, the surgeon must identify a large venous vessel formed by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins. An injury here would result in significant hemorrhage from which vessel?
options: Anterior jugular vein
External jugular vein
Retromandibular vein
Internal jugular vein
Facial vein
correctOption: Retromandibular vein
optionExplanations: The anterior jugular vein begins below the chin and descends in the front of the neck, having no direct origin from the temporal or maxillary veins.
The external jugular vein is formed outside/below the parotid gland by the union of the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein.
The retromandibular vein is the specific vessel formed by these two tributaries within the parotid gland, and it is a key landmark during parotid surgery.
The internal jugular vein is located deep to the parotid gland and carotid sheath; it is not formed by the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.
The facial vein is formed at the medial angle of the eye and descends across the face; it does not originate within the parotid gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1645 (Book Page): The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the superficial temporal and the maxillary veins. On leaving the parotid salivary gland, it divides into an anterior branch... and a posterior branch.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: In the physiological mapping of facial dermatomes, how does the degree of overlap between the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve compare to the spinal dermatomes of the trunk?
options: The overlap is identical in both regions.
The overlap is slight in the face.
There is no overlap at all in the face.
The overlap only occurs between V1 and V2, never V2 and V3.
The overlap is significantly greater in the face.
correctOption: The overlap is slight in the face.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The face differs from the trunk in this specific clinical characteristic.
Clinical mapping of the face is more precise because the V1, V2, and V3 territories have very little (slight) overlap compared to the nerves of the trunk.
Incorrect. While slight, some overlap does exist; it is not 'zero'.
Incorrect. There is no such specific restriction mentioned; slight overlap occurs generally between all adjacent divisions.
Incorrect. Overlap is described as slight, whereas trunk dermatomes have significant overlap.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1527 (Book Page): The overlap of the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve is slight compared with the considerable overlap of dermatomes of the trunk and limbs.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Venous communications and the Danger Triangle
statement: A patient presents with an infected furuncle on the lateral aspect of the nose. Understanding the 'danger triangle' of the face, what is the primary pathophysiological mechanism that allows this superficial infection to cause intracranial cavernous sinus thrombosis?
options: Retrograde flow through the valveless facial vein into the superior ophthalmic vein
Spread of organisms via the deep facial vein into the pterygoid venous plexus
Hematogenous seeding via the infraorbital artery into the maxillary sinus
Direct extension of infection through the ethmoid air sinuses to the meninges
Lymphatic spread through the submandibular nodes into the jugular trunk
correctOption: Retrograde flow through the valveless facial vein into the superior ophthalmic vein
optionExplanations: The facial vein is valveless, and its connection to the superior ophthalmic vein allows for retrograde flow of infected emboli directly into the cavernous sinus, especially when the area is manipulated.

The facial vein does join the pterygoid plexus via the deep facial vein, and the plexus connects to the cavernous sinus, but the superior ophthalmic vein is the more direct and classically described clinical route for this specific pathology.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; hematogenous seeding via the infraorbital artery would take infection away from the brain toward the face, making this mechanism impossible for intracranial spread.

While the ethmoid sinuses are separated from the orbit by a thin plate, direct extension to the meninges is a mechanism of meningitis, not primarily cavernous sinus thrombosis from a nasal skin infection.
Lymphatic drainage from the nose goes to submandibular nodes; however, this system filters through nodes and does not provide the direct, rapid venous access required for sinus thrombosis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1534 (Book Page): The facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus by way of the superior ophthalmic vein. This anastomosis is of great clinical importance because it provides a pathway for the spread of infection from the face to the cavernous sinus.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
statement: Which muscle of the face, essential for compressing the cheeks against the teeth to prevent food from accumulating in the vestibule, is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve?
options: Risorius
Masseter
Zygomaticus major
Temporalis
Buccinator
correctOption: Buccinator
optionExplanations: The risorius is a muscle that pulls the angle of the mouth laterally; while innervated by the facial nerve, it does not compress the cheek against the teeth.
The masseter is a muscle of mastication innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
The zygomaticus major is a muscle used for smiling; it is innervated by the facial nerve but is not the primary muscle for cheek compression.
The temporalis is a muscle of mastication innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Its loss leads to food accumulation in the cheek.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1536 (Book Page): The buccinator muscle thus blends with and forms part of the orbicularis oris muscle... is a significant muscle in food processing in that it compresses the cheeks and lips against the teeth... Page 1537 (Book Page): The buccal branch... supplies the buccinator muscle.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: While illustrating the cutaneous innervation of the face, an examiner points to the small foramen on the lateral side of the zygomatic bone. Which nerve emerges here to supply the skin over the prominence of the cheek?
options: Zygomaticotemporal nerve
Infraorbital nerve
Buccal nerve
Supratrochlear nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
correctOption: Zygomaticofacial nerve
optionExplanations: The zygomaticotemporal nerve emerges in the temporal fossa on the posterior surface of the zygomatic bone to supply the temple.
