At the anterior border of the masseter muscle on the lower margin of the mandible
One fingerbreadth below the zygomatic arch
On the bridge of the nose
Just anterior to the tragus of the ear
correctOption: At the anterior border of the masseter muscle on the lower margin of the mandible
optionExplanations: The mental foramen transmits the mental nerve and vessels; the main facial artery passes well posterior to this point at the edge of the masseter.
The facial artery winds around the lower border of the mandible just anterior to the masseter muscle. This provides a hard surface to compress the artery for pulse detection.
This location describes the transverse facial artery or parotid duct region, where the facial artery is too deep to reliably palpate.
The terminal branches (angular artery) are found here, but they are too small and the surface is too soft for a reliable pulse palpation compared to the mandible.
This is the location for palpating the superficial temporal artery pulse, not the facial artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): [The facial artery] curves around the inferior margin of the body of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle. Its pulse can be easily felt here.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
coreConcept: Cutaneous Innervation Boundary of the Face
statement: A clinician is testing the cutaneous integrity of the face in a patient with suspected Trigeminal Nerve injury. Which specific region of the face must be identified as an exception to Trigeminal innervation and is instead supplied by the cervical plexus?
options: Prominence of the cheek
Skin over the parotid gland and angle of the jaw
Skin over the mental protuberance
Temporal region above the zygomatic arch
Lateral side of the orbital opening
correctOption: Skin over the parotid gland and angle of the jaw
optionExplanations: The skin over the cheek prominence is supplied by the zygomaticofacial nerve, a branch of the maxillary division (V2).
The area over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland is the classic exception to trigeminal facial supply; it is innervated by the Great Auricular nerve (C2-C3) from the cervical plexus.
The mental protuberance (chin) is supplied by the mental nerve, a terminal branch of the mandibular division (V3).
The temporal region is supplied by the zygomaticotemporal (V2) and auriculotemporal (V3) nerves.
The lateral side of the orbital opening is supplied by the maxillary nerve (V2) branches.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1527 (Book Page): The skin of the face is supplied by branches of the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve, except for the small area over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland (Figs. 12.19A and 12.20), which is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2 and 3).

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: A 32-year-old patient presents with a deep laceration over the mental foramen following a mandibular fracture. Evaluation reveals a complete loss of sensation over the skin of the lower lip and chin. Which nerve is most likely transected?
options: Buccal nerve
Mandibular branch of the facial nerve
Nerve to the mylohyoid
Mental nerve
Lingual nerve
correctOption: Mental nerve
optionExplanations: The buccal nerve supplies the skin of the cheek, further posterior and superior to the chin area.
The mandibular branch of the facial nerve is a motor nerve supplying the muscles of the lower lip, not the skin sensation.
The nerve to the mylohyoid is a motor nerve supplying the mylohyoid and the anterior belly of the digastric; it does not supply the skin of the lip.
The mental nerve is the cutaneous continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3) and is responsible for sensation to the chin and lower lip skin.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the floor of the mouth, not the external skin of the chin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1531 (Book Page): The mental nerve emerges from the mental foramen of the mandible and supplies the skin of the lower lip and chin.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: A 24-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a facial injury with significant bleeding. To control the hemorrhage, the physician attempts to compress the facial artery against the mandible. Based on the anatomical relationship of this vessel to the muscles of mastication, where is the pulse best palpated?
options: At the anterior border of the masseter muscle
Deep to the zygomaticus major muscle on the cheek
At the posterior border of the masseter muscle
Superior to the zygomatic arch in the temple
Inferior to the angle of the mandible in the carotid triangle
correctOption: At the anterior border of the masseter muscle
optionExplanations: The facial artery enters the face by crossing the lower border of the mandible just anterior to the masseter, where it can be compressed against the bone.
While the facial artery runs deep to the zygomaticus muscles, it is too deep and the tissue is too soft here to effectively compress it for pulse palpation.
The posterior border of the masseter is related to the parotid gland and the retromandibular vein; the facial artery does not cross here.
The vessel palpated superior to the zygomatic arch is the superficial temporal artery, not the facial artery.
While the facial artery originates in the neck, its landmark for compression to control facial bleeding is specifically where it crosses the mandible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): It [facial artery] curves around the inferior margin of the body of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle. Its pulse can be easily felt here.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: The zygomaticofacial nerve, a branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, exits onto the face through a small foramen to supply which specific region?
options: The temple
The philtrum of the upper lip
The side of the nose
The prominence of the cheek
The lateral part of the upper eyelid
correctOption: The prominence of the cheek
optionExplanations: The temple is supplied by the zygomaticotemporal nerve (V2) and the auriculotemporal nerve (V3).
The philtrum of the upper lip is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2).
The side of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) and the external nasal nerve (V1).
The zygomaticofacial nerve is the specific branch of V2 that provides sensation to the skin overlying the malar eminence (cheekbone).
The lateral part of the upper eyelid is supplied by the lacrimal nerve (V1).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The zygomaticofacial nerve passes onto the face through a small foramen on the lateral side of the zygomatic bone. It supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheek.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: A patient suffers a laceration on the skin directly over the prominence of the cheekbone. Which cutaneous nerve is most likely severed in this specific anatomical location?
options: Zygomaticofacial nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Infraorbital nerve
Buccal nerve
Zygomaticotemporal nerve
correctOption: Zygomaticofacial nerve
optionExplanations: The zygomaticofacial nerve (a branch of V2) emerges from its eponymous foramen on the lateral surface of the zygomatic bone to supply the skin over the 'prominence of the cheek'.
The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the skin of the auricle and the temple region anterior to the ear.
The infraorbital nerve supplies the cheek lower and more medially, primarily between the lower eyelid and the upper lip.
The buccal nerve (V3) supplies a small area of skin over the buccinator muscle in the lower cheek, but not the malar prominence.
The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the skin of the temple, not the cheekbone prominence.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The zygomaticofacial nerve passes onto the face through a small foramen on the lateral side of the zygomatic bone. It supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheek.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Branching Pattern of the Facial Artery
statement: A 52-year-old patient undergoes an emergency procedure for a deep laceration on the face. The surgeon notes profuse bleeding from an artery running medially in the upper lip. This vessel is a branch of which of the following?
options: Superficial temporal artery
Facial artery
Ophthalmic artery
Transverse facial artery
Maxillary artery
correctOption: Facial artery
optionExplanations: The superficial temporal artery supplies the scalp and temporal regions; its only facial branch is the transverse facial artery, which is superior to the lip.
The facial artery gives off several branches in the face, including the inferior labial and superior labial arteries, which run in the substance of the lips and anastomose with their counterparts.
The ophthalmic artery supplies the orbit and forehead (supratrochlear/supraorbital) but does not extend branches down to the upper lip.
The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery that runs across the cheek above the parotid duct, not within the upper lip.

The maxillary artery provides the infraorbital artery, which supplies the cheek and lower eyelid, but the specific vessel in the substance of the upper lip is the superior labial artery, a branch of the facial artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth. It runs medially in the upper lip and gives branches to the septum and ala of the nose.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: During a dissection at the medial angle of the eye, a student identifies a significant anastomosis between the terminal part of the facial artery and a branch of the internal carotid system. Which specific vessels are participating in this critical communication?
options: Angular artery and terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery
Lateral nasal artery and infraorbital artery
Superior labial artery and zygomaticofacial artery
Inferior labial artery and mental artery
Submental artery and supratrochlear artery
correctOption: Angular artery and terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery
optionExplanations: The angular artery is the terminal segment of the facial artery (External Carotid) and it forms a vital anastomosis with the ophthalmic artery (Internal Carotid) at the medial angle of the eye, providing collateral flow.

The lateral nasal artery is a branch of the facial artery, but the infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery; while they supply the region, they are not the primary vessels forming the facial-internal carotid link at the medial canthus.

The superior labial artery supplies the lip and septum, and the zygomaticofacial artery is a branch of the maxillary nerve/artery system; they do not form the specific medial canthal anastomosis described.

The inferior labial artery is a facial branch in the lower lip, and the mental artery is a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery (maxillary); they do not participate in the medial eye anastomosis.

The submental artery is a branch of the facial artery in the neck/chin region, and the supratrochlear artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery on the forehead; they do not meet at the medial angle of the eye.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): It then ascends deep to the zygomaticus muscles and the levator labii superioris muscle and runs along the side of the nose to the medial angle of the eye, where it anastomoses with the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery (see Fig. 12.19C).

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: A 24-year-old boxer sustains a severe blow to the lateral aspect of the orbit, resulting in a fractured zygomatic bone. On examination, he has numbness over the prominence of his cheek but normal sensation over the temple and lower eyelid. Which nerve was most likely damaged as it emerged from its specific foramen?
options: Infraorbital nerve; Infraorbital foramen
Zygomaticotemporal nerve; Zygomaticotemporal foramen
Zygomaticofacial nerve; Zygomaticofacial foramen
Maxillary nerve; Foramen rotundum
Buccal nerve; Mandibular foramen
correctOption: Zygomaticofacial nerve; Zygomaticofacial foramen
optionExplanations: The infraorbital nerve supplies the lower eyelid; since lower eyelid sensation is normal, this nerve is likely intact.
The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the temple; since temple sensation is normal, this nerve is likely intact.
Correct. The zygomaticofacial nerve exits a foramen on the lateral zygomatic bone and specifically supplies the 'malar' prominence. Its isolated injury fits the described sensory deficit.
A lesion at the foramen rotundum would affect the entire Maxillary nerve distribution, including the teeth, palate, and lower eyelid, which is not the case here.
The buccal nerve (V3) supplies the lower cheek/buccal area and does not exit through the zygomatic bone or supply the malar prominence.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The zygomaticofacial nerve passes onto the face through a small foramen on the lateral side of the zygomatic bone. It supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheek.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: To palpate the facial artery pulse against the mandible, where should the physician place their fingers?
options: At the lower margin of the mandible, level with the anterior border of the masseter
Superior to the zygomatic arch, anterior to the ear
At the symphysis menti, inferior to the incisors
At the mental foramen, inferior to the premolars
At the angle of the mandible, posterior to the masseter
correctOption: At the lower margin of the mandible, level with the anterior border of the masseter
optionExplanations: The facial artery is easily felt where it crosses the lower border of the mandible, immediately anterior to the masseter muscle. This is a standard clinical site for pulse assessment.
The area superior to the zygomatic arch and anterior to the ear is the site for palpating the superficial temporal artery, not the facial artery.
The symphysis menti is the midline of the chin; the facial artery is lateral to this, winding over the body of the mandible.
The mental foramen is where the mental nerve and vessels emerge; it is on the lateral surface of the mandible, not the lower margin where the main facial artery trunk is palpated.
The area posterior to the masseter at the angle of the mandible is where the parotid gland and external carotid artery are located deeper; the facial artery is anterior to the masseter.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1533 (Book Page): [The] facial artery, as it winds around the lower margin of the mandible level with the anterior border of the masseter, [is] commonly used by the anesthetist to take the patient’s pulse.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: A 65-year-old female with chronic hypertension presents with uncontrollable epistaxis. The bleeding is localized to the anterior portion of the nasal septum (Kiesselbach’s plexus). Which branch of the facial artery is a major participant in the arterial anastomosis in this area?
options: Supratrochlear artery
Angular artery
Superior labial artery
Infraorbital artery
Lateral nasal artery
correctOption: Superior labial artery
optionExplanations: The supratrochlear artery is a branch of the ophthalmic (internal carotid) and supplies the forehead.
The angular artery is the terminal branch on the face and does not reach the internal nasal septum.
Correct. The superior labial artery (from the facial) gives off a septal branch that enters the nose and anastomoses with the sphenopalatine and ethmoidal arteries on the anterior septum.
The infraorbital artery (maxillary) supplies the cheek and lower eyelid, and while it gives nasal branches, it is not the primary facial contributor to Kiesselbach's plexus.
The lateral nasal artery supplies the side and dorsum of the nose but is not the primary facial branch in the septal anastomosis (Little's area).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1768 (Book Page): The sphenopalatine artery anastomoses with the septal branch of the superior labial branch of the facial artery in the region of the vestibule.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: A clinician is evaluating a patient for a potential vascular reconstruction of the face. Which anatomical contrast distinguishes the facial artery from its terminal anastomotic partner, the ophthalmic artery?
options: The facial artery is an end-artery with no anastomoses, unlike the ophthalmic artery.
The facial artery is a branch of the internal carotid, while the ophthalmic is from the external carotid.
The facial artery supplies the retina, whereas the ophthalmic supplies only the skin.
The facial artery originates in the neck from the external carotid, whereas the ophthalmic arises from the internal carotid within the cranium.
The facial artery passes through the optic canal, whereas the ophthalmic artery passes over the masseter muscle.
correctOption: The facial artery originates in the neck from the external carotid, whereas the ophthalmic arises from the internal carotid within the cranium.
optionExplanations: Both arteries have extensive anastomoses; specifically, they meet at the medial canthus of the eye (angular with supratrochlear/supraorbital branches).
This is incorrect; the facial artery is a branch of the External Carotid Artery (ECA), and the ophthalmic artery is a branch of the Internal Carotid Artery (ICA).
The opposite is true: the ophthalmic artery (via the central artery of the retina) is the sole supply to the retina, while the facial artery primarily supplies the skin and muscles of the face.

The facial artery is a major branch of the external carotid system originating in the carotid triangle of the neck. In contrast, the ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery, providing a vital bridge between the intracranial and extracranial circulations.
The ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal with the optic nerve, whereas the facial artery winds around the lower margin of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1531 (Book Page)-1532: The face receives a rich blood supply from two main vessels, the facial and superficial temporal arteries... The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery in the upper neck. Page 1584 (Book Page): The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery after that vessel emerges from the cavernous sinus.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: A 24-year-old male is evaluated in the emergency department after being struck by a baseball in the right orbit. Physical examination reveals limited upward gaze and enophthalmos. Vitals: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, RR 16/min. He reports a loss of sensation (anesthesia) specifically over the right cheek, right upper lip, and the right upper gum. Radiographic imaging reveals a 'blowout' fracture of the orbital floor. Which nerve was most likely compressed or damaged?
options: Supraorbital nerve
Infraorbital nerve
Lacrimal nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Mental nerve
correctOption: Infraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: The supraorbital nerve passes through the orbital roof (frontal bone); its damage would cause numbness in the forehead, not the cheek or upper lip.

The infraorbital nerve runs in the infraorbital groove and canal in the orbital floor (maxilla). A blowout fracture of the floor directly impacts this nerve, causing sensory loss in its distribution: cheek, upper lip, and gums.
The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper eyelid and conjunctiva; it is not located on the orbital floor and its damage wouldn't affect the lip.
The zygomaticofacial nerve supplies only the prominence of the cheek; it does not innervate the upper lip or gums.
The mental nerve is located on the mandible; it has no relation to orbital floor fractures.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1501 (Book Page): Blowout fractures of the orbital floor... Damage to the infraorbital nerve may occur, resulting in altered sensation in the skin of the cheek, upper lip, and gum.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Origin and Course of the Transverse Facial Artery
statement: The transverse facial artery, which contributes to the arterial supply of the cheek, is a branch of which vessel?
options: Maxillary artery
Infraorbital artery
Superficial temporal artery
Internal carotid artery
Facial artery
correctOption: Superficial temporal artery
optionExplanations: The maxillary artery provides the infraorbital artery and branches to the muscles of mastication, but the transverse facial is not one of its branches.
The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery; it is a separate vessel from the transverse facial artery.
The transverse facial artery is a specific branch of the superficial temporal artery (the terminal branch of the external carotid) that emerges within the parotid gland.
The internal carotid artery provides the ophthalmic artery; it does not directly supply the cheek via the transverse facial artery.
The facial artery supplies the face through the labial and nasal branches but does not give rise to the transverse facial artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The superficial temporal artery... Branches: The transverse facial artery arises within the parotid gland. It runs forward across the cheek just above the parotid duct and below the zygomatic arch.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
coreConcept: ECA-ICA Junction at the Medial Canthus
statement: A patient presents with an infection in the 'danger triangle' of the face. While the primary concern is venous spread, the physician notes that the facial artery's terminal anastomosis at this site also provides a route for potential complications. Which specific anatomical junction is located at the apex of this triangle?
options: The lateral nasal artery and the buccal artery.
The transverse facial artery and the zygomaticofacial artery.
The submental artery and the mental artery.
The superior labial artery and the infraorbital artery.
The angular artery and the supratrochlear/supraorbital arteries.
correctOption: The angular artery and the supratrochlear/supraorbital arteries.
optionExplanations: The lateral nasal and buccal arteries are located lower on the face and do not form the critical ECA-ICA junction at the medial canthus.
The transverse facial and zygomaticofacial arteries anastomose more laterally over the zygomatic bone.
The submental and mental arteries anastomose near the chin/mandible, which is the base of the face, not the apex of the danger triangle.
The superior labial and infraorbital arteries anastomose on the cheek/upper lip area, which is lower than the medial canthus junction.

The angular artery (terminal facial/ECA) meets the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (terminal ophthalmic/ICA) at the medial angle of the eye, which corresponds to the apex of the danger triangle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1520 (Book Page): The supratrochlear and the supraorbital arteries, branches of the ophthalmic artery (a branch of the internal carotid artery), ascend over the forehead... Page 1532 (Book Page): [The facial artery] runs along the side of the nose to the medial angle of the eye, where it anastomoses with the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
statement: A 60-year-old male presents with sudden, recurring paroxysms of excruciating, 'lightning-like' pain on the right side of his face, triggered by shaving or light touch. The pain is localized to the area of the cheek and upper lip. There is no evidence of sensory loss or muscle weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bell's palsy
Glossopharyngeal neuralgia
Mandibular nerve compression
Trigeminal neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) of the maxillary division
Herpes Zoster of the ophthalmic division
correctOption: Trigeminal neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) of the maxillary division
optionExplanations: Bell's palsy is a motor disorder characterized by facial muscle paralysis, not sensory paroxysms of pain.
Glossopharyngeal neuralgia causes pain in the throat, tonsil, and ear, triggered by swallowing, rather than facial skin triggers.
Mandibular nerve compression would usually lead to sensory loss (anesthesia) or motor weakness in the muscles of mastication, rather than paroxysmal pain.
Trigeminal neuralgia characteristically causes brief, severe pain in the V2 (maxillary) or V3 (mandibular) distributions, often without objective sensory deficits.
Herpes Zoster (Shingles) in the ophthalmic division (V1) would typically involve the forehead and scalp and be accompanied by a vesicular rash and steady pain, not just triggers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1531 (Book Page): Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) is a relatively common (often idiopathic) condition in which the patient experiences sudden attacks of excruciating pain in the distribution of the mandibular or maxillary division...

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: The facial artery is a direct branch of which major vascular trunk?
options: Brachiocephalic artery
External carotid artery
Maxillary artery
Internal carotid artery
Thyrocervical trunk
correctOption: External carotid artery
optionExplanations: The brachiocephalic artery is a large trunk from the aortic arch that divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
The facial artery is one of the anterior branches of the external carotid artery, arising just above the lingual artery.
The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, but it does not give rise to the facial artery; it is a peer vessel.
The internal carotid artery provides no branches in the neck and primarily supplies the brain and the contents of the orbit.
The thyrocervical trunk is a branch of the subclavian artery, supplying the thyroid gland and structures in the lower neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery in the upper neck.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: The infraorbital nerve is the primary sensory supply to the mid-face. After emerging from the infraorbital foramen, it immediately divides into a plexus of branches. Which specific combination of areas represents the cutaneous territory of these radiating branches?
options: Lower lip, chin, and mucous membrane of the cheek
Temple, cheek prominence, and lower lip
Lower eyelid, side of the nose, and upper lip
Lower eyelid, prominence of the cheek, and upper lip
Upper eyelid, bridge of the nose, and forehead
correctOption: Lower eyelid, side of the nose, and upper lip
optionExplanations: The lower lip and chin are supplied by the mental nerve (V3), and the mucous membrane of the cheek by the buccal nerve (V3).
The temple is supplied by the zygomaticotemporal and auriculotemporal nerves, and the lower lip by the mental nerve.
The infraorbital nerve (V2) provides sensory innervation to the skin of the lower eyelid, the lateral side of the nose, the anterior cheek, and the entire upper lip.
The prominence of the cheek is primarily supplied by the zygomaticofacial nerve, not the infraorbital nerve.
This territory (upper eyelid, bridge of nose, forehead) is served by the branches of the ophthalmic nerve (V1).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): [The infraorbital nerve] immediately divides into numerous small branches, which radiate out from the foramen and supply the skin of the lower eyelid and cheek, the side of the nose, and the upper lip.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: A 68-year-old female with a history of long-standing hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus presents with sudden, transient loss of vision in her right eye (amaurosis fugax). Carotid doppler reveals a 95% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery proximal to the ophthalmic branch. Despite the stenosis, the retina appears perfused on ophthalmoscopy. Retrograde flow is detected in the right supratrochlear artery. This compensatory circulation is most likely facilitated by an anastomosis with which vessel?
options: Infraorbital artery via the maxillary artery
Greater palatine artery via the pterygopalatine fossa
Transverse facial artery via the superficial temporal artery
Deep temporal artery via the mandibular division
Angular artery via the facial artery
correctOption: Angular artery via the facial artery
optionExplanations: The infraorbital artery does supply the face but is not the primary terminal vessel forming the classic external-to-internal carotid shunt at the medial canthus.
The greater palatine artery supplies the hard palate and does not contribute to the superficial orbital anastomosis described in the scenario.
The transverse facial artery crosses the cheek below the zygomatic arch and does not typically reach the medial canthus to provide retrograde ophthalmic flow.
The deep temporal arteries supply the temporalis muscle in the temporal fossa and are not part of the superficial facial anastomosis with the ophthalmic system.

In the setting of ICA stenosis, blood from the External Carotid Artery can travel through the facial artery into the angular artery. At the medial canthus, it anastomoses with the ophthalmic system (supratrochlear/supraorbital), allowing retrograde flow to maintain retinal perfusion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1584 (Book Page): The ophthalmic artery forms a notable facial anastomosis with the angular artery (the terminal end of the facial artery) and the frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: A physician intends to assess the pulse of the facial artery. Based on its anatomical course, at which location is the artery most superficial and easily palpated against a bony surface?
options: At the anterior border of the masseter muscle on the mandible
Along the superior border of the zygomatic arch
At the posterior border of the ramus of the mandible
Between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Directly over the mental protuberance
correctOption: At the anterior border of the masseter muscle on the mandible
optionExplanations: The facial artery is easily palpated as it crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of the masseter muscle, where it is relatively superficial.
The zygomatic arch is the landmark for palpating the superficial temporal artery, not the facial artery.
The posterior border of the ramus of the mandible is related to the parotid gland and the retromandibular vein, not the facial artery's main palpable segment.
The region between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid is the site for assessing the internal jugular vein or carotid pulse, not the facial artery pulse.
The mental protuberance is the site of the mental nerve and artery (terminal branches), but the main facial artery trunk is lateral to this point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): [The facial artery] curves around the inferior margin of the body of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle. Its pulse can be easily felt here.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
coreConcept: Cervical Plexus Contribution to Facial Innervation
statement: A 24-year-old medical student is studying a diagram of the cutaneous innervation of the face. She notes a specific region over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland that is surprisingly not supplied by the trigeminal nerve. Which nerve provides sensation to this area?
options: Buccal nerve
Mental nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Great auricular nerve
Transverse cutaneous nerve of the neck
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The buccal nerve is a sensory branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) that supplies the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek, but not the posterior angle of the mandible.
The mental nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) and supplies the skin of the lower lip and chin, not the angle of the mandible.
The zygomaticofacial nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) supplying the skin over the prominence of the cheekbone (zygomatic bone).

The great auricular nerve, derived from the C2 and C3 spinal nerves of the cervical plexus, is the only non-trigeminal nerve providing cutaneous sensation to the face, specifically at the angle of the jaw and over the parotid gland.
The transverse cutaneous nerve of the neck (C2, 3) supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, not the face or the angle of the mandible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1527 (Book Page): The skin of the face is supplied by branches of the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve, except for the small area over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland (Figs. 12.19A and 12.20), which is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2 and 3).

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
coreConcept: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Facial Lesions
statement: During a neurological examination, a physician notes that a patient has paralysis of the muscles of the lower right half of the face, but is still able to wrinkle their forehead and close their eye on the same side. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: Geniculate ganglion of the right facial nerve
Left motor cortex or its descending pyramidal tracts
Right facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
Facial nerve nucleus in the pons
Right facial nerve in the internal acoustic meatus
correctOption: Left motor cortex or its descending pyramidal tracts
optionExplanations: The geniculate ganglion is part of the LMN pathway; its damage results in complete facial paralysis on the affected side along with potential loss of taste and lacrimation.

The forehead muscles are supplied by neurons receiving bilateral corticobulbar innervation. Thus, a unilateral Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion only paralyzes the lower face, as the forehead still receives signals from the contralateral cortex.
A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen is a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion, which would cause complete ipsilateral paralysis of both the upper and lower face.
The facial nerve nucleus itself is part of the LMN pathway; a lesion here would cause total ipsilateral facial paralysis, not sparing the forehead.
A lesion in the internal acoustic meatus is an LMN lesion affecting all branches of the facial nerve, causing total ipsilateral facial paralysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1537 (Book Page): An upper motor neuron lesion (involvement of the pyramidal tracts) will leave the upper part of the face normal because the neurons supplying this part of the face receive corticobulbar fibers from both cerebral cortices.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
coreConcept: Terminal Branch of the Facial Artery
statement: When examining the branches of the facial artery, which specific vessel is identified as the final terminal segment located in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus?
options: Lateral nasal artery
Submental artery
Angular artery
Inferior labial artery
Superior labial artery
correctOption: Angular artery
optionExplanations: The lateral nasal artery arises alongside the nose but is not the terminal segment; the angular artery continues superiorly from it.
The submental artery is an early branch arising in the neck at the lower border of the mandible.
The angular artery is the definitive terminal branch of the facial artery, reaching the medial angle of the eye.
The inferior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth to supply the lower lip.
The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth to supply the upper lip and is not the terminal branch.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery. It runs in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: A 60-year-old female presents with a deep-seated malignant parotid tumor. She reports a loss of sensation on the skin of her auricle, the external auditory meatus, and the scalp just above her ear. Which nerve, which typically communicates with the facial nerve but provides sensory supply to these regions, is likely involved?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Buccal nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
correctOption: Auriculotemporal nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp posterior to the ear and the medial surface of the auricle, but not the meatus or the temporal scalp.
The great auricular nerve supplies the angle of the jaw and the lower part of the ear, but not the external auditory meatus or the scalp above the ear.

The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) passes through the parotid gland and ascends in front of the auricle. It is the primary sensory supply to the external auditory meatus, tympanic membrane, auricle, and temporal scalp.
The buccal nerve supplies the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek, not the ear or scalp.
The zygomaticofacial nerve supplies the malar (cheek) prominence.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1531 (Book Page): The auriculotemporal nerve... supplies the skin of the auricle, the external auditory meatus, the outer surface of the tympanic membrane, and the skin of the scalp above the auricle.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: The facial artery is described as having a tortuous course. Which physiological reason and anatomical branch match this description to ensure the blood supply remains constant during mandibular movement?
options: The lateral nasal artery's lack of branches to prevent kinking.
Reduced pressure in the Submental artery during swallowing.
The angular artery's straight path to resist torsion from the eye muscles.
Increased diameter of the occipital artery during head rotation.
Elasticity for mouth opening provided by the tortuous facial artery and its labial branches.
correctOption: Elasticity for mouth opening provided by the tortuous facial artery and its labial branches.
optionExplanations: The lateral nasal artery is a branch that supplies the nose and is part of the overall flexible facial network.
The submental artery's role is to supply the chin/floor of the mouth; its tortuosity is less significant than the main facial trunk.
The angular artery is also part of the tortuous facial system; it is not straight, as it must accommodate movements of the nose and eyelids.
The occipital artery is not a branch of the facial artery; it is a separate branch of the External Carotid artery supplying the back of the scalp.
The facial artery is remarkably tortuous to allow for the wide range of movements of the mandible and the lips (opening the mouth, smiling) without stretching or occluding the vessel.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): It next runs upward in a tortuous course toward the angle of the mouth and is covered by the platysma and the risorius muscles... The inferior labial artery... runs medially in the lower lip and anastomoses with its fellow of the opposite side.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
coreConcept: Terminal branch of the facial artery
statement: Which specific vessel represents the terminal portion of the facial artery and serves as a primary site for anastomosis with branches of the internal carotid artery?
options: Lateral nasal artery
Superior labial artery
Infraorbital artery
Transverse facial artery
Angular artery
correctOption: Angular artery
optionExplanations: The lateral nasal artery arises from the facial artery alongside the nose to supply the dorsum and skin, but it is not the terminal segment.
The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth and supplies the upper lip and nasal septum; it does not represent the termination of the facial artery.
The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid), not the facial artery, although it does supply facial skin.
The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery, not the facial artery, and is found running across the cheek above the parotid duct.

The angular artery is the final segment of the facial artery, located at the medial canthus of the eye, where it establishes a critical collateral link between the external and internal carotid systems.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery. It runs in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
statement: A 60-year-old woman describes 'lightning-like' stabs of pain in her face. The pain is triggered whenever she touches her upper lip or the side of her nose. In a diagram of cutaneous innervation, which division of the trigeminal nerve and specific branch are mapped to this 'trigger zone'?
options: Mandibular division; Mental nerve
Maxillary division; Infraorbital nerve
Ophthalmic division; Infratrochlear nerve
Maxillary division; Zygomaticofacial nerve
Mandibular division; Buccal nerve
correctOption: Maxillary division; Infraorbital nerve
optionExplanations: The mental nerve (V3) supplies the lower lip and chin; pain in the upper lip excludes this as the primary branch.
The symptoms describe trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux). The upper lip and side of the nose are classic cutaneous territories of the infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary division (V2).
The infratrochlear nerve (V1) supplies the medial eye area and upper side of the nose, but trigeminal neuralgia more commonly affects V2 and V3.
The zygomaticofacial nerve (V2) supplies the prominence of the cheek, not the upper lip or side of the nose.
The buccal nerve (V3) supplies the cheek skin and mucosa, but the side of the nose is definitively V2 territory.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The infraorbital nerve is a direct continuation of the maxillary nerve... It immediately divides into numerous small branches, which radiate out from the foramen and supply the skin of the lower eyelid and cheek, the side of the nose, and the upper lip.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Deep Venous Connections of the Face
statement: A 30-year-old female presents with a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the cheek. Physical examination reveals edema that obscures the nasolabial fold and tenderness along the course of the facial vein. Considering the anatomical connections of the facial vein, which of the following is the most significant deep tributary that links the facial vein to the pterygoid venous plexus?
options: Deep facial vein
Transverse facial vein
Retromandibular vein
Superior ophthalmic vein
Maxillary vein
correctOption: Deep facial vein
optionExplanations: The deep facial vein is the specific anatomical bridge that allows venous blood (and infection) to pass from the facial vein into the infratemporal fossa and the pterygoid plexus.
The transverse facial vein drains the cheek into the superficial temporal vein within the parotid gland and is not the primary link to the deep plexus.
The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins; it joins the facial vein but does not primarily connect it to the pterygoid plexus.
The superior ophthalmic vein connects the facial vein directly to the cavernous sinus, providing a different route than the pterygoid plexus.
The maxillary vein is a tributary that helps form the retromandibular vein; it originates from the pterygoid plexus but is not a branch *off* the facial vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1534 (Book Page): It [the facial vein] joins the pterygoid venous plexus by the deep facial vein and the cavernous sinus by the superior ophthalmic vein.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
coreConcept: Terminal branch of the Facial Artery
statement: Which specific branch of the facial artery serves as its terminal portion, concluding its course at the medial angle of the eye?
options: Submental artery
Infraorbital artery
Angular artery
Lateral nasal artery
Superior labial artery
correctOption: Angular artery
optionExplanations: The submental artery arises in the neck near the submandibular gland, supplying the chin and lower lip; it is one of the earliest branches of the facial artery.
The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (not the facial artery), though it contributes to the face via the infraorbital foramen.
The angular artery is the final segment of the facial artery, reaching the medial canthus of the eye where it establishes a key anastomosis with internal carotid branches.
The lateral nasal artery arises from the facial artery alongside the nose to supply the skin on the side and dorsum; it is not the terminal branch.
The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth to supply the upper lip and nasal septum; it occurs much earlier in the facial artery's course.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery. It runs in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
statement: A 45-year-old male undergoes a mandibular biopsy near the second premolar. Post-operatively, he reports complete numbness of the skin of his lower lip and chin on that side. No other deficits are noted. Which specific branch of the trigeminal nerve was likely compromised?
options: Infratrochlear nerve
Mental nerve
Infraorbital nerve
Buccal nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
correctOption: Mental nerve
optionExplanations: The infratrochlear nerve is a branch of V1 (ophthalmic) and supplies the skin of the upper eyelid and bridge of the nose.
The mental nerve is the terminal cutaneous continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3); it exits the mental foramen (located near the second premolar) to supply the chin and lower lip.
The infraorbital nerve is the terminal branch of V2 (maxillary) and supplies the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper lip.
The buccal nerve of V3 supplies the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek, not the lower lip or chin.
The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the auricle, external auditory meatus, and the temple, far superior to the mandible's mental foramen.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1531 (Book Page): The mental nerve emerges from the mental foramen of the mandible and supplies the skin of the lower lip and chin.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
coreConcept: Functional Modalities of the Chorda Tympani
statement: A patient presents with a loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and reduced submandibular salivary secretion. However, the muscles of facial expression are functioning normally. A lesion is most likely involving which component of the facial nerve pathway?
options: The greater petrosal nerve
The facial nerve at the internal acoustic meatus
The facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
The nerve to the stapedius
The chorda tympani nerve after it joins the lingual nerve
correctOption: The chorda tympani nerve after it joins the lingual nerve
optionExplanations: The greater petrosal nerve carries secretomotor fibers for the lacrimal gland; its loss would affect tearing, not tongue taste.
A lesion at the internal acoustic meatus would involve both motor and sensory/parasympathetic roots, causing total facial paralysis and hearing/balance issues.

At the stylomastoid foramen, the nerve is purely motor to the face; taste and secretomotor fibers have already branched off within the facial canal/middle ear cavity via the chorda tympani and greater petrosal nerves. Thus, facial expression would be lost but taste would be spared if the lesion was here only for the motor trunk (though Bell's palsy often occurs higher). Regardless, the prompt states facial expressions are normal, ruling this out as the primary site of a trunk lesion and focusing it on the specific chorda tympani branch distribution distal to the motor divisions if it were isolated or combined with lingual nerve injury distal to the junction but proximal to the tongue distribution as specified by common clinical correlates of nerve junction anatomy described in the source text and clinical note section (Page 1669). If facial expressions are normal, the main trunk and its internal motor branches are intact; the specific sensory/secretomotor loss points to the isolated chorda tympani or its post-junction lingual nerve distribution as the vulnerable site mentioned in surgical extraction notes (Page 1669). Given the prompt, option C is the most anatomically precise regarding the sensory/parasympathetic loss in isolation from motor deficits as it joins the lingual nerve distal to the middle ear exit point but before reaching the target tissue described in the source text under functional course distribution on page 1673 and 1609-1610 regarding the infratemporal fossa contents and nerve junctions as distinct functional pathways and their vulnerability mentioned on 1669 regarding third molar extraction as a specific mechanism of injury for this segment which matches the clinical presentation exactly. Note: Page 1669 specifies lingual nerve injury at the third molar leads to sensory/taste loss as it contains the chorda tympani fibers at that point. Since the motor trunk is spared, the lesion is isolated to the V3-VII communication segment or its distal path (Lingual nerve containing Chorda Tympani). C is the most correct anatomic choice based on the descriptions in chapters 12-45 through 12-46 for the infratemporal fossa and the lingual/chorda tympani relationship as the specific vector for these modalities after they leave the facial trunk properly properly as described on 1673 and 1609-1610.
The nerve to stapedius is purely motor to the stapedius muscle in the middle ear; its injury causes hyperacusis, not loss of taste.

The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa. A lesion here or in the lingual nerve distal to this junction spares the facial motor fibers (which exited earlier) while causing loss of taste and salivary secretion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): The chorda tympani contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth. ... it joins the lingual nerve. ... preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that reach the submandibular ganglion.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Terminal Branch of the Facial Artery
statement: What is the name of the terminal branch of the facial artery that is found in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye?
options: Angular artery
Submental artery
Infraorbital artery
Superior labial artery
Lateral nasal artery
correctOption: Angular artery
optionExplanations: The angular artery is the final segment of the facial artery, reaching the medial angle of the eye where it completes the external-internal carotid anastomosis.
The submental artery arises from the facial artery in the neck, near the submandibular gland, and supplies the chin; it is one of the first branches, not the terminal one.
The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (from the external carotid) that emerges through the infraorbital foramen, not a terminal part of the facial artery.
The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth and supplies the upper lip and nasal septum; it is not the terminal part of the vessel.
The lateral nasal artery arises from the facial artery alongside the nose but is not the terminal branch; it supplies the dorsum and side of the nose.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery. It runs in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
coreConcept: Contralateral Arterial Anastomosis of the Face
statement: A 25-year-old patient undergoes an emergency repair of a deep midline laceration of the upper lip. The surgeon observes that hemostasis requires ligation of vessels coming from both the left and right sides of the lip. Which physiological characteristic of the facial artery's branching pattern explains this clinical finding and the general resilience of facial skin flaps to necrosis?
options: The terminal transition into the angular vein
Minimal overlap of dermatomes in the trigeminal system
The absence of deep fascia allowing for rapid diffusion
High density of sweat glands facilitating thermoregulation
Extensive anastomosis with contralateral fellow vessels
correctOption: Extensive anastomosis with contralateral fellow vessels
optionExplanations: The facial artery terminates as the angular artery, not a vein; while it eventually drains into the facial vein, the arterial anastomosis described is responsible for the clinical finding of bilateral bleeding.
Trigeminal dermatomes have very little overlap, but this relates to sensory innervation and does not explain the vascular resilience or the profuse bleeding from contralateral arterial sources.
While the absence of deep fascia is a characteristic of the face that allows muscles to insert into skin, it does not provide the vascular mechanism for flap survival or contralateral bleeding.

The skin of the face does have many sweat and sebaceous glands, but these contribute to skin health and oil production rather than provide the robust collateral circulation required for flap survival.

Correct. The facial artery's labial branches (superior and inferior) anastomose freely with their counterparts from the opposite side in the midline. This profuse, interconnected supply ensures that facial skin flaps rarely necrose and that midline injuries involve bleeding from both sides.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The superior labial artery arises near the angle of the mouth. It runs medially in the upper lip and anastomoses with its fellow of the opposite side.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
statement: While testing the cutaneous sensation of the face, a student notes that the area over the angle of the mandible remains sensitive despite a complete block of the trigeminal nerve. Which nerve is responsible for the sensory supply to this specific region?
options: Great auricular nerve
Buccal nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Mental nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve (from the cervical plexus, C2-C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the jaw and the parotid gland, marking a boundary with the trigeminal territory.
The buccal nerve (V3) supplies the skin over the cheek (long buccal).
The zygomaticofacial nerve (V2) supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheekbone.
The mental nerve (V3) supplies the skin of the chin and lower lip.
The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the temple, part of the auricle, and the external auditory meatus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1527 (Book Page): The skin of the face is supplied by branches of the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve, except for the small area over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland (Figs. 12.19A and 12.20), which is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2 and 3).

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Terminal Branches of the Facial Artery
statement: In the terminal distribution of the facial artery, which branch is found in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye?
options: Superior labial artery
Angular artery
Supratrochlear artery
Infraorbital artery
Lateral nasal artery
correctOption: Angular artery
optionExplanations: The superior labial artery is a branch of the facial artery that supplies the upper lip and nasal septum.
The angular artery represents the final segment of the facial artery where it anastomoses with branches of the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system).
The supratrochlear artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, not the facial artery.
The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (from the infraorbital foramen), not the facial artery.
The lateral nasal artery arises lower along the side of the nose, before the artery reaches the medial canthus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The angular artery is the terminal part of the facial artery. It runs in the narrow gap between the side of the nose and the medial canthus of the eye.

category: Describe the functional modalities, course, branches, and distribution of cranial nerves innervating the face (sensory and motor): trigeminal and facial nerves
statement: A 32-year-old female presents with ipsilateral facial muscle paralysis, loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and hyperacusis (excessive sensitivity to sound). However, her lacrimation (tear production) is normal. At which specific point is the facial nerve (CN VII) most likely damaged?
options: Distal to the stylomastoid foramen
Distal to the chorda tympani nerve origin
Proximal to the geniculate ganglion
At the internal acoustic meatus
Within the facial canal, distal to the geniculate ganglion but proximal to the nerve to stapedius
correctOption: Within the facial canal, distal to the geniculate ganglion but proximal to the nerve to stapedius
optionExplanations: A lesion distal to the stylomastoid foramen only affects the motor branches to facial expression muscles, sparing taste, salivation, and the stapedius reflex.
A lesion distal to the chorda tympani would cause facial paralysis but would spare taste and the stapedius reflex (no hyperacusis).
A lesion proximal to the geniculate ganglion would result in loss of lacrimation (dry eye), which is not present in this patient.
A lesion in the internal acoustic meatus would typically involve CN VIII (hearing/balance) and affect lacrimation, as it is proximal to the geniculate ganglion.

Normal lacrimation implies the geniculate ganglion and greater petrosal nerve are intact. Hyperacusis and loss of taste indicate the lesion is proximal to the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani, respectively.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1685 (Book Page): If the patient is excessively sensitive to sound in one ear (hyperacusis), the lesion probably involves the nerve to the stapedius. Loss of taste over the anterior two thirds of the tongue implies that the seventh nerve is damaged proximal to the point where it gives off the chorda tympani.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: When comparing the vascular pathways of the face, which specific anatomical characteristic distinguishes the facial vein from its corresponding arterial counterpart, the facial artery?
options: The facial vein is situated significantly deeper than the facial artery
The facial vein lacks any communications with intracranial venous sinuses
The facial vein follows a much straighter course than the artery
The facial vein arises from the internal jugular vein in the parotid gland
The facial vein contains numerous valves to prevent retrograde flow
correctOption: The facial vein follows a much straighter course than the artery
optionExplanations: The facial vein is generally superficial to the muscles it crosses and often lies posterior and more superficial than the tortuous facial artery.
The facial vein has critical communications with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein, making it a major pathway for intracranial infection spread.
Unlike the tortuous facial artery, the facial vein follows a relatively straight course as it descends from the medial angle of the eye toward the mandible.
The facial vein does not arise in the parotid; it is formed at the medial angle of the eye and eventually drains into the internal jugular vein, whereas the retromandibular vein forms in the parotid.
The facial vein is clinically significant because it is largely valveless, which allows for the retrograde spread of infection to the cavernous sinus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1533 (Book Page): The facial vein descends behind the facial artery to the lower margin of the body of the mandible. [Comparison to Page 1532 (Book Page): runs upward in a tortuous course].

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: Anatomy students are asked to identify the origin of the facial artery during a dissection. Which vessel gives rise to the facial artery in the neck?
options: Common carotid artery bifurcation
Maxillary artery
External carotid artery
Internal carotid artery
Thyrocervical trunk
correctOption: External carotid artery
optionExplanations: The bifurcation is the point where the common carotid splits into internal and external; it is not a vessel that 'gives rise' to the facial artery directly as a branch.
The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid, arising much higher (within the parotid gland) than the facial artery.
The external carotid artery provides several branches in the neck, including the superior thyroid, lingual, and facial arteries.
The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck; it supplies the brain and the orbit.
The thyrocervical trunk is a branch of the subclavian artery, supplying the lower neck and shoulder region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery in the upper neck.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
coreConcept: Hutchinson's Sign and Nasociliary Nerve Path
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with painful, vesicular eruptions following a dermatomal pattern on his right forehead and the bridge of his nose. Notably, a small vesicle is present on the absolute tip of his nose (Hutchinson's sign). Which specific nerve branch mediates the sensation at the tip of the nose, and what is its parent branch within the orbit?
options: Infratrochlear nerve; branch of Frontal nerve
Supraorbital nerve; branch of Frontal nerve
Lacrimal nerve; branch of Ophthalmic nerve
External nasal nerve; branch of Nasociliary nerve
Infraorbital nerve; branch of Maxillary nerve
correctOption: External nasal nerve; branch of Nasociliary nerve
optionExplanations: The infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial part of the upper eyelid and adjoining side of the nose, but it does not reach the tip of the nose.
The supraorbital nerve supplies the central upper eyelid and the forehead as far as the vertex, not the tip of the nose.
The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral part of the upper eyelid and conjunctiva, having no role in nasal tip innervation.

Correct. The external nasal nerve is a continuation of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (from the nasociliary nerve, V1). Vesicles at the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicate nasociliary involvement, which often correlates with ocular shingles complications.
The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid, cheek, and side of the nose, but the tip of the nose is specifically V1 (external nasal).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1530 (Book Page): The external nasal nerve leaves the nose by emerging between the nasal bone and the upper nasal cartilage. It supplies the skin on the side of the nose down as far as the tip.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: A 72-year-old patient with severe atherosclerosis of the left internal carotid artery (ICA) undergoes a Doppler study. The study reveals retrograde flow in the ophthalmic artery. Which vessel is the most likely source of this collateral blood supply via the angular artery?
options: Ascending pharyngeal artery
Maxillary artery
Inferior thyroid artery
Transverse facial artery
Facial artery
correctOption: Facial artery
optionExplanations: The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharynx and prevertebral muscles; it does not reach the medial canthus of the eye to provide orbital collateralization.
The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid, but it enters the pterygopalatine fossa; it is not the direct precursor of the angular artery.
The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk (subclavian system) and is located in the lower neck; it does not contribute to facial-orbital anastomoses.
The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery; while it supplies the cheek, it does not terminate as the angular artery at the medial canthus.

The facial artery terminates as the angular artery at the medial angle of the eye. In the presence of ICA occlusion, high pressure in the facial artery (ECA) can push blood through the angular-ophthalmic anastomosis in a retrograde fashion to reach the ICA territory.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): [The facial artery] ascends deep to the zygomaticus muscles... and runs along the side of the nose to the medial angle of the eye, where it anastomoses with the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the primary origin of the facial artery during a cadaveric dissection of the neck. Which vessel should the student trace the facial artery back to for its direct origin?
options: Superficial temporal artery
External carotid artery
Maxillary artery
Internal carotid artery
Common carotid artery
correctOption: External carotid artery
optionExplanations: The superficial temporal artery is the smaller terminal branch of the external carotid artery; while it supplies the scalp and transverse facial region, it does not give rise to the facial artery.

The external carotid artery is the source of the facial artery, which arises in the carotid triangle and arches over the submandibular gland before reaching the face at the anterior border of the masseter.

The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, arising within the parotid gland, and supplies the deeper structures like the jaws and meninges, rather than originating the facial artery.
The internal carotid artery provides no branches in the neck; it enters the cranium via the carotid canal to supply the brain and the orbit via the ophthalmic artery, not the superficial face.

The common carotid artery bifurcates at the level of the superior border of the thyroid cartilage into internal and external carotid arteries but does not directly give off the facial artery as a branch.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery in the upper neck.

category: Draw a diagram to illustrate cutaneous innervation of face
coreConcept: Buccal Nerve vs. Buccal Branch of Facial Nerve
statement: During a neurological exam, a physician compares sensory and motor functions of the cheek. Which nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the skin over the buccinator muscle, and which nerve provides the motor supply to the muscle itself, respectively?
options: Buccal nerve (V3); Buccal branch of Facial nerve (VII)
Buccal branch of VII; Buccal nerve (V3)
Infraorbital nerve (V2); Buccal nerve (V3)
Mental nerve (V3); Zygomatic branch of VII
Mandibular nerve (V3); Cervical branch of VII
correctOption: Buccal nerve (V3); Buccal branch of Facial nerve (VII)
optionExplanations: The Buccal nerve (a branch of the Mandibular division, V3) provides sensory innervation to the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek. The Buccal branch of the Facial nerve (VII) provides motor innervation to the buccinator muscle.
This is the reverse of the correct functional assignment.
While the infraorbital nerve supplies some cheek skin, the buccal nerve (V3) is the primary sensory nerve for the mid-cheek skin, and V3 is never motor to facial expression muscles.
The mental nerve supplies the chin, and the zygomatic branch supplies the orbicularis oculi, not the buccinator.
The mandibular nerve is the division that contains the buccal sensory nerve, but the cervical branch of VII supplies the platysma, not the buccinator.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1668 (Book Page): Buccal nerve to the skin and the mucous membrane of the cheek. The buccal nerve does not supply the buccinator muscle (which is supplied by the facial nerve).

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: A 62-year-old male presents with a persistent, ulcerated lesion on the center of his lower lip. Vitals: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 80 bpm. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Upon palpation of the neck, a single firm node is found in the submental triangle. Based on the lymphatic drainage patterns of the face, why is this node the most likely site for metastasis?
options: The submental nodes are the terminal drainage group for all facial lymph.
Lateral parts of the lower lip drain into the submental nodes before the submandibular nodes.
The lesion has likely spread through the buccal nodes into the submental group.
All lymph from the lips drains directly to the submandibular nodes.
The center part of the lower lip and the chin drain specifically into the submental nodes.
correctOption: The center part of the lower lip and the chin drain specifically into the submental nodes.
optionExplanations: The deep cervical lymph nodes are the terminal group for all head and neck lymph; the submental nodes are regional regional nodes that drain into them.
Incorrect; lateral parts of the lower lip bypass the submental nodes and drain directly into the submandibular nodes located beneath the body of the mandible.
Buccal nodes are found on the cheek along the facial vein and drain toward the submandibular nodes, not the submental nodes which are further inferior and medial.
This is incorrect; while the lateral parts of the lips drain to the submandibular nodes, the central lower lip has a unique drainage pathway to the submental nodes.

The lymphatic vessels from the central portion of the lower lip and the chin pass downward to the submental nodes in the submental triangle, making them the primary site for metastases from midline lip cancers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1534 (Book Page): The central part of the lower lip and the skin of the chin drain into the submental lymph nodes.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
statement: A 25-year-old medical student is asked to identify the specific anatomical origin of the facial artery during a dissection of the submandibular region. Which of the following vessels directly gives rise to this artery?
options: Internal carotid artery
Superficial temporal artery
External carotid artery
Common carotid artery
Maxillary artery
correctOption: External carotid artery
optionExplanations: The internal carotid artery does not give off branches in the neck; it enters the skull to supply the brain and orbit.
The superficial temporal artery is the other terminal branch of the external carotid artery, supplying the scalp and parotid region.
The facial artery is a major anterior branch of the external carotid artery, arising just above the lingual artery in the carotid triangle.
The common carotid artery bifurcates into the internal and external carotids but does not directly give rise to the facial artery.
The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, not the source of the facial artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery in the upper neck

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
statement: A patient suffers a deep laceration at the medial angle of the eye. Despite ligation of the terminal angular artery, persistent arterial bleeding occurs. Anatomically, which vessel is providing the collateral flow from the internal carotid system?
options: Infraorbital artery
Middle meningeal artery
Dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery
Superior labial artery
Transverse facial artery
correctOption: Dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery
optionExplanations: The infraorbital artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (ECA) and while it supplies the cheek, it is not the primary internal carotid collateral source at the medial canthus.
The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery that enters the cranium; it does not contribute to the superficial facial anastomosis at the eye.

The ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery, sends terminal branches (like the dorsal nasal) to the medial angle of the eye to anastomose with the angular artery, providing a vital ECA-ICA communication.
The superior labial artery is a more proximal branch of the facial artery and would not provide retrograde high-pressure collateral flow if the angular artery itself is the ligated vessel.
The transverse facial artery is a branch of the superficial temporal artery and supplies the cheek area laterally, not the medial canthus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1532 (Book Page): It [facial artery] then ascends deep to the zygomaticus muscles and the levator labii superioris muscle and runs along the side of the nose to the medial angle of the eye, where it anastomoses with the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery.

category: Discuss anastomoses of facial artery with contralateral vessels and branches of internal carotid artery with their clinical significance
coreConcept: Vascular Path of Intracranial Infection Spread
statement: A 25-year-old patient develops a severe furuncle (boil) on the upper lip. Three days later, he presents with high fever, chemosis (swelling of the conjunctiva), and paralysis of the extraocular muscles. This clinical presentation is most likely due to the spread of infection through which vascular connection?
options: The facial vein to the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein.
The angular artery to the vertebral artery.
The submental artery to the jugular bulb.
The facial artery to the internal carotid artery.
The labial veins to the pterygoid plexus via the maxillary artery.
correctOption: The facial vein to the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein.
optionExplanations: The 'danger triangle' of the face (nose, eye, upper lip) has venous drainage (facial vein) that communicates with the superior ophthalmic vein. Because these veins are valveless, infection (like a boil) can travel into the cavernous sinus, causing life-threatening cavernous sinus thrombosis.
The angular artery does not communicate with the vertebral artery; its significant connection is with the ophthalmic system.
The submental vessels drain toward the submandibular region and do not have a direct, valveless route to the jugular bulb that would explain orbital/cavernous symptoms.
Infections primarily spread through the venous system due to lower pressure and lack of valves, not through the high-pressure arterial system.
Veins do not join the cavernous sinus via arteries; the spread is through a continuous venous pathway from the facial vein to the ophthalmic veins.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1533 (Book Page): The facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus by way of the superior ophthalmic vein. This anastomosis is of great clinical importance because it provides a pathway for the spread of infection from the face to the cavernous sinus... often referred to the danger triangle of the face.

category: Describe the vascular supply and lymphatic drainage of face
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of Facial Artery Pulse
