category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Functional classification of the Submandibular Ganglion
statement: The submandibular ganglion is classified as which type of functional neurological structure based on its roots and location?
options: Sympathetic chain ganglion
Somatic motor ganglion
Special visceral afferent ganglion
Sensory (dorsal root) ganglion
Parasympathetic ganglion
correctOption: Parasympathetic ganglion
optionExplanations: Sympathetic chain ganglia (like the superior cervical ganglion) are part of the thoracolumbar outflow, whereas the submandibular is part of the cranial parasympathetic outflow.
There is no such thing as a 'somatic motor ganglion' in this context; somatic motor fibers (like to the tongue) do not synapse in peripheral ganglia.
Special visceral afferent refers to taste fibers (which pass through but do not synapse in the ganglion); the ganglion itself is functionally parasympathetic (efferent).
Sensory ganglia (like the trigeminal or geniculate ganglia) contain cell bodies of afferent fibers and do not involve synapses; the submandibular ganglion is a motor (autonomic) relay.
The submandibular ganglion is one of the four peripheral parasympathetic ganglia of the head, where preganglionic fibers from the facial nerve synapse with postganglionic neurons.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The submandibular ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that lies deep to the submandibular salivary gland and is attached to the lingual nerve by small nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: During the physiological salivary reflex, stimulation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue leads to increased submandibular gland secretion. Which specific counter-regulatory loop component ensures the relay of this parasympathetic signal to the submandibular ganglion?
options: The maxillary nerve provides the motor root to the submandibular ganglion.
The deep petrosal nerve provides sympathetic inhibition to the ganglion.
The lingual nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion.
The lesser petrosal nerve synapses in the otic ganglion.
The chorda tympani nerve joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa.
correctOption: The chorda tympani nerve joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa.
optionExplanations: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve, V3), not the maxillary nerve (V2).
The deep petrosal nerve is sympathetic (vasoconstrictor) and does not serve as the primary preganglionic relay for the salivary reflex to the submandibular ganglion.

Postganglionic sympathetic fibers for the head originate in the superior cervical ganglion, but they do not form the 'parasympathetic signal' relay that defines the secretomotor salivation reflex at the submandibular ganglion.
The lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion are part of the parotid salivation pathway, not the submandibular pathway triggered by the anterior tongue.

The reflex loop involves sensory input (taste) via chorda tympani, processed in the brainstem, and then motor output via the same chorda tympani (parasympathetic fibers) which joins the lingual nerve to reach the submandibular ganglion.

The chorda tympani fibers... give off preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular ganglion.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia

Both ganglia are parasympathetic relay stations, though sympathetic fibers may pass through them without synapsing.
The submandibular ganglion targets the submandibular and sublingual glands; the otic ganglion exclusively provides secretomotor postganglionic fibers to the parotid gland.
Neither ganglion supplies the lacrimal gland (which is supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion).

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Anatomic Relations of the Otic Ganglion
statement: A patient presents with a deep infection in the infratemporal fossa. Petrotympanic fissure
Stylomastoid foramen
Mandibular foramen
Pterygopalatine fossa
correctOption: Nerve to the medial pterygoid
optionExplanations: The otic ganglion (parotid secretion) is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid (which supplies tensor veli palatini). A lesion here explains both findings.
The petrotympanic fissure is the exit for the chorda tympani, which would affect submandibular/sublingual glands, not the parotid.
The stylomastoid foramen is the exit of the facial nerve; damage here would cause facial paralysis, not tensor veli palatini paralysis or parotid dryness.
The mandibular foramen is the entry for the inferior alveolar nerve into the mandible and is distal to the otic ganglion and tensor veli palatini supply.
The pterygopalatine fossa involves the maxillary nerve and lacrimal/nasal glands, not the tensor veli palatini or parotid secretion.

optionExplanations: The vagus nerve does not provide the parasympathetic supply to the parotid gland; its cranial parasympathetic outflow does not involve the otic ganglion.
This sequence describes the preganglionic parasympathetic pathway to the submandibular and sublingual glands via the submandibular ganglion.

Correct. The otic ganglion receives its parasympathetic input from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve, while the submandibular ganglion receives input from the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani.

Inferior alveolar nerve
Lingual nerve

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia

statement: In the anatomy of the infratemporal fossa, where is the otic ganglion precisely situated relative to the mandibular nerve?

Superior to the mandibular nerve, in the middle cranial fossa.

Lingual nerve at the posterior end of the mylohyoid line
Chorda tympani in the middle ear
Inferior alveolar nerve at the mandibular foramen
Auriculotemporal nerve at the neck of the mandible
correctOption: Lingual nerve at the posterior end of the mylohyoid line
optionExplanations: The lesser petrosal nerve damage would only affect parotid secretion via the otic ganglion.

The lingual nerve carries general sensation and the chorda tympani fibers (taste/parasympathetic). Damage here, especially near the third molar, destroys general sensation and the preganglionic fibers/ganglion attachments required for sublingual and submandibular salivation.
Damage to the chorda tympani would cause loss of taste and salivary flow but would not affect general sensation (which is carried by the lingual nerve).
The inferior alveolar nerve damage would cause loss of sensation to the teeth and chin, not the tongue or salivary glands.
The auriculotemporal nerve damage would affect parotid secretion and sensation to the temple/auricle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar. ... Page 1670 (Book Page): The submandibular ganglion... is attached to the lingual nerve by small nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Branch of CN VII for Submandibular Secretion
statement: Regarding the distribution of the facial nerve (CN VII) within the petrous temporal bone, which branch eventually delivers preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion via the lingual nerve?
options: Greater petrosal nerve
Nerve to stapedius
Deep petrosal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
Posterior auricular nerve
correctOption: Chorda tympani nerve
optionExplanations: The greater petrosal nerve carries fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimation and nasal secretion.
The nerve to stapedius is a motor branch supplying the stapedius muscle in the middle ear and has no secretomotor role.
The deep petrosal nerve is a sympathetic nerve and is not a branch of the facial nerve.
The chorda tympani emerges from the facial nerve, crosses the tympanic membrane, and joins the lingual nerve to reach the submandibular ganglion.
The posterior auricular nerve is a mixed branch given off after the facial nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen, supplying the auricle and occipitofrontalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve... contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of the Otic Ganglion
statement: Regarding the topographical anatomy of the infratemporal fossa, which specific structure is the otic ganglion most intimately adherent to?
options: The chorda tympani nerve
The nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle
The inferior alveolar nerve
The main trunk of the maxillary nerve
The nerve to the lateral pterygoid muscle
correctOption: The nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa but is associated with the submandibular ganglion, not the otic ganglion.

Correct. Anatomically, the otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic ganglion located medial to the mandibular nerve trunk, immediately below the foramen ovale, and is specifically adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

Incorrect. The inferior alveolar nerve is a branch of the posterior division of V3; while it is nearby, the otic ganglion is more proximal and adherent to the medial pterygoid nerve branch of the main trunk.
Incorrect. The maxillary nerve (V2) is located in the pterygopalatine fossa, not the infratemporal fossa, and is associated with the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Incorrect. The nerve to the lateral pterygoid is a branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve, whereas the otic ganglion is located medial to the main trunk of V3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that is located medial to the mandibular nerve just below the skull, and it is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Pathway of the Parotid Gland
statement: A researcher is tracing the secretomotor pathway to the parotid gland. Which sequence accurately describes the preganglionic parasympathetic root of the otic ganglion starting from the brainstem?
options: Lacrimatory nucleus -> Facial nerve -> Chorda tympani
Edinger-Westphal nucleus -> Oculomotor nerve -> Short ciliary nerves
Inferior salivary nucleus -> Mandibular nerve -> Auriculotemporal nerve
Inferior salivary nucleus -> Glossopharyngeal nerve -> Lesser petrosal nerve
Superior salivary nucleus -> Facial nerve -> Greater petrosal nerve
correctOption: Inferior salivary nucleus -> Glossopharyngeal nerve -> Lesser petrosal nerve
optionExplanations: The lacrimatory nucleus and chorda tympani (CN VII) provide the preganglionic supply to the submandibular ganglion for the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus and CN III are involved in the pathway to the ciliary ganglion for pupillary constriction and accommodation, not the parotid gland.
The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic, not preganglionic, parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland; the mandibular nerve itself does not contain preganglionic parasympathetic fibers.

The inferior salivary nucleus (medulla) sends preganglionic fibers via CN IX, which then travel through the tympanic branch and tympanic plexus to become the lesser petrosal nerve, synapsing in the otic ganglion.
The superior salivary nucleus and greater petrosal nerve (branch of CN VII) are part of the pathway to the pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimation and nasal glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Hitchhiking Mechanism of Parasympathetic Postganglionic Fibers
statement: When contrasting the distribution of the otic and submandibular ganglia, which statement accurately distinguishes the postganglionic hitchhiking mechanism used to reach their respective target glands?
options: The otic ganglion utilizes the zygomaticotemporal nerve, while the submandibular ganglion utilizes the inferior alveolar nerve.
Both ganglia send fibers exclusively through the facial nerve's terminal branches (temporal and zygomatic).
Postganglionics from the otic ganglion hitchhike on the lingual nerve, whereas submandibular fibers use the auriculotemporal nerve.
Both ganglia utilize the buccal nerve of the mandibular division (V3) to reach the oral vestibule.
Postganglionics from the otic ganglion hitchhike on the auriculotemporal nerve, whereas submandibular fibers pass directly to the glands or hitchhike on the lingual nerve.
correctOption: Postganglionics from the otic ganglion hitchhike on the auriculotemporal nerve, whereas submandibular fibers pass directly to the glands or hitchhike on the lingual nerve.
optionExplanations: The zygomaticotemporal nerve is used by fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion (to reach the lacrimal gland), not the otic. The inferior alveolar nerve is motor to the mylohyoid and sensory to the teeth, not secretomotor to the submandibular gland.
Terminal branches of the facial nerve are somatic motor to the muscles of facial expression and do not carry parasympathetic postganglionic secretomotor fibers.
This is a direct reversal of the correct nerves. The otic uses the auriculotemporal nerve, and the submandibular ganglion is associated with the lingual nerve.
The buccal nerve of V3 is purely sensory to the cheek and does not serve as the primary hitchhiking route for these specific salivary postganglionics.

Snell's Anatomy specifies that postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion join the auriculotemporal nerve to reach the parotid. Fibers from the submandibular ganglion are located deep to the gland and pass directly to the submandibular gland or follow the lingual nerve to reach the sublingual gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The postganglionic secretomotor fibers [from the otic ganglion] reach the parotid salivary gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. ... Postganglionic secretomotor fibers [from the submandibular ganglion] pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: A patient presents with a deep infection in the submandibular space (Ludwig's angina). If the submandibular ganglion is involved, which of the following glands would lose its secretomotor stimulation?
options: Sublingual gland
Parotid gland
Glands of the nasal septum
Lacrimal gland
Sweat glands of the temple
correctOption: Sublingual gland
optionExplanations: The submandibular ganglion provides postganglionic secretomotor fibers to both the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.
The parotid gland is supplied by the otic ganglion.
Nasal glands are supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion.
The lacrimal gland is supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Sweat glands of the temple are supplied by sympathetic fibers or misdirected auriculotemporal fibers (Frey's), but not the submandibular ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Postganglionic secretomotor fibers [from the submandibular ganglion] pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Anatomical Location and Adhesion of the Otic Ganglion
statement: An anatomical dissection reveals a small, pinhead-sized parasympathetic ganglion located in the infratemporal fossa, specifically situated medial to the mandibular nerve just below the foramen ovale. To which specific motor nerve is this ganglion typically adherent?
options: Nerve to the lateral pterygoid
Inferior alveolar nerve
Nerve to the medial pterygoid
Masseteric nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
correctOption: Nerve to the medial pterygoid
optionExplanations: The nerve to the lateral pterygoid is a branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve and does not possess a physical adherence to the otic ganglion. It primarily provides motor innervation to the lateral pterygoid muscle for mandibular protrusion.

The inferior alveolar nerve is a large sensory and motor branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve. It enters the mandibular foramen and is distinct from the more superiorly located otic ganglion.

The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic structure located in the infratemporal fossa. It is classically described as being adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle, a branch from the main trunk of the mandibular nerve.

The masseteric nerve is a motor branch that passes through the mandibular notch to reach the masseter muscle. While it is a branch of the mandibular nerve, it is not the structure to which the otic ganglion is adherent.

The auriculotemporal nerve is closely related to the otic ganglion as it carries its postganglionic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland, but the ganglion is not adherent to it; it is adherent to the medial pterygoid nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that is located medial to the mandibular nerve just below the skull, and it is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: Regarding the physiological regulation of salivation, which cranial nerve nucleus serves as the origin for the preganglionic fibers that relay in the otic ganglion?
options: Dorsal nucleus of the vagus
Superior salivary nucleus
Inferior salivary nucleus
Nucleus solitarius
Edinger–Westphal nucleus
correctOption: Inferior salivary nucleus
optionExplanations: The dorsal nucleus of the vagus provides parasympathetic supply to the thoracic and abdominal viscera.
The superior salivary nucleus (associated with CN VII) provides fibers for the submandibular and pterygopalatine ganglia.

The inferior salivary nucleus (associated with CN IX) sends fibers that travel with the glossopharyngeal nerve, through the tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve, to relay in the otic ganglion for the parotid gland.
The nucleus solitarius is a sensory nucleus for taste and visceral afferents.
The Edinger–Westphal nucleus is the parasympathetic nucleus for the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1696 (Book Page): ...that of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus. ... Page 1697 (Book Page): The glossopharyngeal nerve projects to the otic ganglion in the infratemporal fossa via its tympanic and lesser petrosal branches.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: When comparing the parasympathetic roots of the otic and submandibular ganglia, which of the following provides the correct anatomical contrast in their preganglionic supply?
options: Otic: Greater petrosal nerve; Submandibular: Deep petrosal nerve
Otic: Nerve to medial pterygoid; Submandibular: Lingual nerve
Otic: Chorda tympani; Submandibular: Lesser petrosal nerve
Otic: Lesser petrosal nerve; Submandibular: Chorda tympani
Otic: Auriculotemporal nerve; Submandibular: Mylohyoid nerve
correctOption: Otic: Lesser petrosal nerve; Submandibular: Chorda tympani
optionExplanations: The greater petrosal nerve supplies the pterygopalatine ganglion. The deep petrosal nerve is sympathetic, not parasympathetic.

The nerve to the medial pterygoid is motor and merely adherent to the otic ganglion. The lingual nerve carries the fibers to the submandibular ganglion, but the root itself originates from the chorda tympani.
This is reversed. The chorda tympani supplies the submandibular ganglion, while the lesser petrosal supplies the otic ganglion.

The otic ganglion receives its preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve. The submandibular ganglion receives its preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani.
The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion, not preganglionic. The mylohyoid nerve is motor to the mylohyoid and digastric muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers [for the otic ganglion] originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve... Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers [for the submandibular ganglion] reach the ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: Regarding the distribution of the submandibular ganglion, which of the following is its primary functional output?
options: General sensory to the posterior third of the tongue
Vasoconstriction of the maxillary artery
Secretomotor to the submandibular and sublingual glands
Dilation of the pupil (mydriasis)
Somatomotor to the mylohyoid muscle
correctOption: Secretomotor to the submandibular and sublingual glands
optionExplanations: General sensation to the posterior third of the tongue is provided by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the submandibular ganglion.
Vasoconstriction is a sympathetic function; the submandibular ganglion is primarily a parasympathetic (secretomotor) relay.
The submandibular ganglion is the peripheral parasympathetic relay for the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, facilitating saliva production.
Pupillary dilation is mediated by sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion via the long ciliary nerves, not the submandibular ganglion.
The mylohyoid muscle is supplied by the mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, which is somatomotor (V3), not autonomic.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Postganglionic secretomotor fibers pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Anatomic Location of the Otic Ganglion
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with a tumor at the base of the skull, specifically involving the foramen ovale. Anatomically, which parasympathetic ganglion is located immediately medial to the mandibular nerve (V3) at this exit point and is most likely to be affected?
options: Submandibular ganglion
Ciliary ganglion
Trigeminal ganglion
Pterygopalatine ganglion
Otic ganglion
correctOption: Otic ganglion
optionExplanations: The submandibular ganglion is located in the submandibular region, suspended from the lingual nerve as it passes deep to the submandibular gland.
The ciliary ganglion is located in the posterior part of the orbital cavity, far from the foramen ovale and the mandibular nerve's exit point.
The trigeminal ganglion is a sensory ganglion located inside the middle cranial fossa within the trigeminal cave, not a parasympathetic ganglion in the infratemporal fossa.
The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa, associated with the maxillary nerve (V2) as it exits the foramen rotundum.
The otic ganglion is specifically situated in the infratemporal fossa, medial to the mandibular nerve (V3) just after it exits the foramen ovale.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that is located medial to the mandibular nerve just below the skull, and it is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Cranial Nerve Roots of Parasympathetic Ganglia
statement: A comparative study of the cranial parasympathetic ganglia focuses on their preganglionic roots. Which of the following accurately distinguishes the root of the submandibular ganglion from the root of the otic ganglion?
options: Submandibular: Maxillary nerve; Otic: Mandibular nerve
Submandibular: Facial nerve via chorda tympani; Otic: Glossopharyngeal nerve via lesser petrosal nerve
Submandibular: Glossopharyngeal nerve; Otic: Facial nerve
Submandibular: Vagus nerve; Otic: Facial nerve
Submandibular: Oculomotor nerve; Otic: Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Submandibular: Facial nerve via chorda tympani; Otic: Glossopharyngeal nerve via lesser petrosal nerve
optionExplanations: The maxillary and mandibular nerves provide the physical framework and sensory pathways for these ganglia but are not the source of the preganglionic parasympathetic roots.

The submandibular ganglion's preganglionic input is from the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani, whereas the otic ganglion's input is from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve.
This option reverses the actual nerve origins; the facial nerve supplies the submandibular ganglion and the glossopharyngeal supplies the otic.
The vagus nerve does not relate to the cranial parasympathetic ganglia like the otic or submandibular; it projects to postcranial plexuses instead.
The oculomotor nerve supplies the ciliary ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the [submandibular] ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves... [Otic ganglion] preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: During a surgical procedure to remove an impacted third molar, the lingual nerve is accidentally transected proximal to its connection with the submandibular ganglion. What is the expected deficit regarding the distribution of this ganglion?
options: Loss of taste to the posterior third of the tongue.
Inability to constrict the pupil in response to light.
Paralysis of the mylohyoid and the anterior belly of the digastric.
Loss of secretomotor function to the parotid gland only.
Loss of secretomotor function to both the submandibular and sublingual glands.
correctOption: Loss of secretomotor function to both the submandibular and sublingual glands.
optionExplanations: The posterior third of the tongue is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); the lingual nerve (with chorda tympani) supplies the anterior two-thirds.
Pupillary constriction is mediated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III) and the ciliary ganglion, entirely separate from the submandibular ganglion.
These muscles are supplied by the nerve to the mylohyoid (a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve), not the lingual nerve.
The parotid gland is supplied by the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve; it is unaffected by lingual nerve injury.

The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve and distributes postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to both the sublingual and submandibular salivary glands. Transecting the lingual nerve proximal to the ganglion disrupts the preganglionic input (from chorda tympani), leading to secretomotor loss in both glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Postganglionic secretomotor fibers pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with gustatory sweating, where beads of perspiration appear on the skin over his parotid gland while eating. This condition, Frey’s syndrome, involves aberrant reinnervation following damage to which nerve carrying postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion?
options: Great auricular nerve
Facial nerve
Lingual nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Zygomaticotemporal nerve
correctOption: Auriculotemporal nerve
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve is a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus that normally supplies skin sensation; it is the recipient of the aberrant fibers, not the source of the parasympathetics.
While the facial nerve is associated with the parotid gland anatomically, the parasympathetic secretomotor supply to the parotid is mediated via CN IX and the auriculotemporal nerve.
The lingual nerve carries fibers to the submandibular ganglion and the tongue; it is not involved in parotid secretomotor distribution.
The auriculotemporal nerve normally carries parasympathetic postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. In Frey's syndrome, these fibers misdirect to sweat glands.
The zygomaticotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion to the lacrimal gland, not the parotid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1747 (Book Page): Frey’s syndrome... is caused by damage to the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves. During the process of healing, the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Pathway of the Lesser Petrosal Nerve and Otic Ganglion
statement: A patient suffers from a deep infection in the middle ear that damages the tympanic plexus. Which of the following autonomic functions is most likely to be impaired due to the interruption of preganglionic fibers bound for a ganglion in the infratemporal fossa?
options: Constriction of the pupil (miosis)
Salivation from the parotid gland
Tension of the tympanic membrane
Secretory activity of the sublingual gland
Salivation from the submandibular gland
correctOption: Salivation from the parotid gland
optionExplanations: Pupillary constriction is managed by the ciliary ganglion, which receives input from the oculomotor nerve, not the glossopharyngeal/tympanic plexus.
The lesser petrosal nerve arises from the tympanic plexus in the middle ear and carries preganglionic fibers to the otic ganglion, which controls parotid salivation.
Tension of the tympanic membrane is a motor function of the tensor tympani muscle (V3), not a parasympathetic function of the otic ganglion.
The sublingual gland shares the same pathway as the submandibular gland and is not linked to the tympanic plexus or otic ganglion.
The submandibular gland's secretomotor pathway (chorda tympani) passes through the middle ear but does not involve the tympanic plexus or the otic ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the [otic] ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve... the lesser petrosal nerve... is a parasympathetic component of the glossopharyngeal nerve. It runs from the middle ear into the infratemporal fossa, where it joins the otic ganglion.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: When distinguishing between the parasympathetic roots of the cranial ganglia, which of the following correctly matches the ganglion to its specific preganglionic root and cranial nerve origin?
options: Otic ganglion: Chorda tympani (CN VII); Submandibular ganglion: Lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX).
Otic ganglion: Lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX); Submandibular ganglion: Lingual nerve (CN V3).
Otic ganglion: Deep petrosal nerve (Sympathetic); Submandibular ganglion: Facial nerve (CN VII).
Otic ganglion: Greater petrosal nerve (CN VII); Submandibular ganglion: Chorda tympani (CN VII).
Otic ganglion: Lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX); Submandibular ganglion: Chorda tympani (CN VII).
correctOption: Otic ganglion: Lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX); Submandibular ganglion: Chorda tympani (CN VII).
optionExplanations: This option incorrectly swaps the roots of the two ganglia; the chorda tympani is for the submandibular/sublingual relay and the lesser petrosal is for the parotid relay.
The lingual nerve (V3) is the physical carrier for the chorda tympani fibers, but the fibers themselves originate from the facial nerve (CN VII).
The deep petrosal nerve is a sympathetic bundle from the carotid plexus and does not serve as a preganglionic parasympathetic root for the otic ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve (CN VII) provides preganglionic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion.

The otic ganglion receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve, while the submandibular ganglion receives them from the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1697 (Book Page): [The facial nerve projects to the pterygopalatine ganglion in the pterygopalatine fossa and to the submandibular ganglion in the oral floor... The glossopharyngeal nerve projects to the otic ganglion in the infratemporal fossa via its tympanic and lesser petrosal branches.]

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Postganglionic Delivery Mechanism of the Submandibular Ganglion
statement: In the physiological regulation of salivation, which nerve is responsible for carrying the postganglionic fibers from the submandibular ganglion to the glands in the oral floor?
options: Mental nerve
Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Direct branches from the ganglion
correctOption: Direct branches from the ganglion
optionExplanations: The mental nerve is a sensory branch to the chin/lip.
The buccal branch of the facial nerve is motor to the buccinator and upper lip muscles.
The mylohyoid nerve is motor to the mylohyoid and anterior digastric muscles.
The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers for the otic ganglion/parotid gland, not the submandibular.
Unlike the otic ganglion which 'hitchhikes' on the auriculotemporal nerve, the submandibular ganglion sends postganglionic fibers directly to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Postganglionic secretomotor fibers [from the submandibular ganglion] pass directly to the gland.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Frey's Syndrome and Otic Ganglion Distribution
statement: A 45-year-old patient who previously underwent a parotidectomy presents with beads of perspiration over the skin of the parotid region whenever he eats. This clinical condition, known as Frey's syndrome, is most likely caused by which anatomical misdirection of fibers?
options: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the chorda tympani joining the great auricular nerve
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve growing to join the great auricular nerve sweat gland branches
Motor fibers of the facial nerve re-innervating the masseter muscle
Sensory fibers of the trigeminal nerve re-innervating the parotid capsule
Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion joining the lingual nerve
correctOption: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve growing to join the great auricular nerve sweat gland branches
optionExplanations: The chorda tympani is related to the submandibular and sublingual glands, not the parotid or Frey's syndrome.

Frey's syndrome occurs when parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion (originally intended for the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve) regenerate and incorrectly join sympathetic pathways to sweat glands via the great auricular nerve.
The facial nerve provides motor supply to the muscles of facial expression; misdirection of motor fibers causes synkinesis, not localized sweating.
Sensory re-innervation would not lead to an autonomic response such as sweating (gustatory sweating).
Frey's syndrome is a parasympathetic-to-sympathetic misdirection, not a purely sympathetic phenomenon involving the lingual nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1747 (Book Page): During the process of healing, the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve. Eventually, these fibers reach the sweat glands in the facial skin.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: Contrast the physiological origins of the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the otic and submandibular ganglia. Which nuclei are correctly matched to their respective ganglia?
options: Otic: Superior salivary nucleus; Submandibular: Inferior salivary nucleus
Otic: Inferior salivary nucleus; Submandibular: Superior salivary nucleus
Otic: Inferior salivary nucleus; Submandibular: Nucleus ambiguus
Otic: Dorsal nucleus of vagus; Submandibular: Lacrimatory nucleus
Otic: Edinger-Westphal nucleus; Submandibular: Superior salivary nucleus
correctOption: Otic: Inferior salivary nucleus; Submandibular: Superior salivary nucleus
optionExplanations: This is the reverse of the correct physiological arrangement.
The otic ganglion receives fibers from the inferior salivary nucleus (via CN IX), while the submandibular ganglion receives fibers from the superior salivary nucleus (via CN VII).
The nucleus ambiguus provides motor fibers to the muscles of the pharynx and larynx, not parasympathetic secretomotor fibers.
The dorsal nucleus of the vagus provides parasympathetic fibers for thoracic and abdominal viscera, not for the otic or submandibular ganglia.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides fibers for the ciliary ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1696 (Book Page): those of the facial nerve are the lacrimatory and the superior salivary nuclei, that of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Submandibular Ganglion Roots
statement: A 22-year-old female undergoes a difficult extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar. Postoperatively, she complains of a 'dry mouth' and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the ipsilateral side. Damage to the lingual nerve near the posterior border of the mylohyoid line has interrupted the preganglionic supply to which ganglion?
options: Submandibular ganglion
Inferior cervical ganglion
Pterygopalatine ganglion
Otic ganglion
Ciliary ganglion
correctOption: Submandibular ganglion
optionExplanations: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve. The lingual nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (from the chorda tympani) to this ganglion. Injury at the 3rd molar site interrupts these fibers, causing xerostomia (dry mouth) and ageusia (loss of taste).
The inferior cervical ganglion is a sympathetic structure in the neck; its damage leads to Horner's syndrome, not loss of taste or specific salivary deficit.
The pterygopalatine ganglion is related to the maxillary nerve and handles lacrimation and nasal secretion, which are unaffected by lingual nerve injury.
The otic ganglion is located higher in the infratemporal fossa and receives its root from the lesser petrosal nerve, which is independent of the lingual nerve.
The ciliary ganglion is intraorbital; its supply is derived from the oculomotor nerve, not the mandibular or lingual nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): [The lingual nerve] is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction... Page 1670 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the [submandibular] ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Otic Ganglion Distribution and Frey's Syndrome
statement: In the clinical context of Frey's syndrome, misdirected regeneration involves fibers originally destined for parotid secretion. These postganglionic fibers were originally distributed from which ganglion and via which specific nerve?
options: Pterygopalatine ganglion via the lacrimal nerve
Submandibular ganglion via the lingual nerve
Ciliary ganglion via the short ciliary nerves
Otic ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve
Otic ganglion via the auriculotemporal nerve
correctOption: Otic ganglion via the auriculotemporal nerve
optionExplanations: The pterygopalatine ganglion regulates tears and nasal mucus, not parotid salivation.
The submandibular ganglion and lingual nerve are not involved in parotid secretion or the pathophysiology of Frey's syndrome.
The ciliary ganglion is involved in ocular functions (pupil constriction and accommodation), not parotid secretion or gustatory sweating.
The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic fibers to the otic ganglion; it does not carry postganglionic fibers to the parotid gland.

Frey's syndrome occurs when postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion, which normally travel in the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid, misregenerate to supply sweat glands in the skin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1746 (Book Page): This condition is caused by damage to the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves... the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve. Page 1670 (Book Page): The postganglionic secretomotor fibers reach the parotid salivary gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Function of the Lesser Petrosal Nerve
statement: A neurosurgeon accidentally lesions the lesser petrosal nerve as it exits the skull. Based on the anatomical connections of the otic ganglion, which physiological function will be most impaired?
options: General sensation from the skin over the angle of the mandible.
Secretion of tears from the lacrimal gland.
Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Production of mucous saliva from the sublingual gland.
Production of serous saliva from the parotid gland.
correctOption: Production of serous saliva from the parotid gland.
optionExplanations: Sensation over the angle of the mandible is provided by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not by cranial parasympathetic pathways.
Tear secretion is mediated by the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion, not the lesser petrosal and otic ganglion.
Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani (VII), not the lesser petrosal nerve (IX).
The sublingual gland is supplied by the submandibular ganglion (via the chorda tympani), which is unaffected by a lesser petrosal nerve lesion.
The lesser petrosal nerve is the preganglionic parasympathetic root for the otic ganglion; lesioning it prevents the relay of signals for parotid salivation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1610 (Book Page): [The lesser petrosal nerve... joins the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then join the auriculotemporal branch... The lesser petrosal nerve provides the secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland.]

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Submandibular Ganglion Roots
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and significantly reduced salivation following a traumatic extraction of an impacted mandibular third molar. Which anatomical relationship explains this combined sensory and autonomic deficit?
options: The facial nerve was damaged at the stylomastoid foramen, affecting the greater petrosal nerve distribution.
The auriculotemporal nerve was crushed, interrupting the otic ganglion fibers to the sublingual gland.
The lingual nerve, carrying chorda tympani fibers, was damaged as it passed beneath the superior constrictor muscle near the last molar.
The inferior alveolar nerve was severed, preventing sympathetic supply to the submandibular ganglion.
The glossopharyngeal nerve was injured, blocking preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
correctOption: The lingual nerve, carrying chorda tympani fibers, was damaged as it passed beneath the superior constrictor muscle near the last molar.
optionExplanations: Damage at the stylomastoid foramen would cause facial muscle paralysis but would not affect the chorda tympani or greater petrosal nerves, as they branch off higher up in the facial canal.
The auriculotemporal nerve is related to the parotid gland and the otic ganglion, not the tongue or submandibular gland.

The lingual nerve is very close to the lower third molar. It carries taste (from chorda tympani) and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers destined for the submandibular ganglion. Damage here causes loss of taste and salivary dysfunction.
The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the teeth and chin; it does not carry taste or parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides taste and sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar. ... The chorda tympani fibers carry taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and also give off preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular ganglion.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Pathway of the Otic Ganglion
statement: The secretomotor pathway for the parotid gland involves a complex multi-step relay. Which of the following describes the correct physiological sequence of the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers?
options: Vagus nerve → Pharyngeal plexus → Auriculotemporal nerve → Otic ganglion
Facial nerve → Greater petrosal nerve → Nerve of the pterygoid canal → Otic ganglion
Glossopharyngeal nerve → Tympanic nerve → Tympanic plexus → Lesser petrosal nerve → Otic ganglion
Mandibular nerve → Buccal nerve → Otic ganglion → Auriculotemporal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve → Chorda tympani → Lingual nerve → Otic ganglion
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve → Tympanic nerve → Tympanic plexus → Lesser petrosal nerve → Otic ganglion
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve (CN X) does not provide the secretomotor supply to the parotid gland; its cranial parasympathetic outflow does not involve the otic ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that targets the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion.

Preganglionic fibers originate in the inferior salivary nucleus of CN IX, pass through the tympanic nerve to the tympanic plexus, and then exit as the lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion.
The mandibular nerve (V3) provides the carrier for the postganglionic fibers (auriculotemporal nerve) but the preganglionic fibers are from CN IX.
The chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) and joins the lingual nerve to reach the submandibular ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): The preganglionic parasympathetic fibers for the parotid salivary gland leave the plexus as the lesser petrosal nerve ; they synapse in the otic ganglion .

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: In comparing the roots of the otic and submandibular ganglia, which statement accurately distinguishes their preganglionic inputs?
options: Both receive preganglionic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve
The otic root arises from CN VII, while the submandibular root arises from CN IX
The otic root is the greater petrosal nerve, and the submandibular root is the lesser petrosal nerve
Both receive preganglionic fibers from the facial nerve
The otic root arises from CN IX, while the submandibular root arises from CN VII
correctOption: The otic root arises from CN IX, while the submandibular root arises from CN VII
optionExplanations: Only the otic ganglion receives fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve.
This statement incorrectly swaps the origins of the two ganglia's roots.
The greater petrosal nerve is for the pterygopalatine ganglion; the lesser petrosal is for the otic ganglion. The submandibular root is the chorda tympani.
Only the submandibular ganglion receives fibers from the facial nerve.
The otic ganglion receives preganglionic input from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and the submandibular ganglion receives input from the facial nerve (CN VII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Otic Ganglion... Preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve... Submandibular Ganglion... Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: A student identifies a small ganglion attached to the lingual nerve while dissecting the submandibular region. Based on the anatomical location, which salivary glands receive postganglionic secretomotor distribution from this specific ganglion?
options: Parotid and submandibular salivary glands
Parotid gland only
Submandibular and sublingual salivary glands
Sublingual gland and lacrimal gland
Glands of the nose and palate
correctOption: Submandibular and sublingual salivary glands
optionExplanations: The parotid is supplied by the otic ganglion; the submandibular is supplied by the submandibular ganglion.
The parotid gland is supplied by the otic ganglion.
The submandibular ganglion, attached to the lingual nerve, provides secretomotor fibers to both the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The lacrimal gland is supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Glands of the nose and palate are supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Submandibular Ganglion... Postganglionic secretomotor fibers pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Otic Ganglion
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with reduced salivation from the parotid gland following a deep facial trauma. Sensation in the anterior tongue and taste are completely preserved, and facial muscle movements are symmetrical. Which nerve lesion, occurring between the skull base and the otic ganglion, explains this isolated autonomic deficit?
options: Lesser petrosal nerve
Lingual nerve
Mental nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
correctOption: Lesser petrosal nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser petrosal nerve specifically carries preganglionic secretomotor fibers for the parotid gland to the otic ganglion. Its isolated injury would spare taste and facial expression.
Damage to the lingual nerve would result in loss of general sensation and taste (if distal to chorda tympani junction) on the tongue, not isolated parotid dry mouth.
The mental nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the chin and lower lip; it has no parasympathetic or secretomotor function.
Damage to the greater petrosal nerve would affect lacrimation and nasal secretions, not parotid gland salivation.
Damage to the chorda tympani would cause loss of taste and reduced submandibular/sublingual secretion, but not parotid secretion deficits.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers for the parotid salivary gland leave the plexus as the lesser petrosal nerve; they synapse in the otic ganglion.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: During a pharmacological study on salivary regulation, an agonist specifically acting on the postganglionic output of the submandibular ganglion is administered. Through which anatomical structures do these postganglionic fibers reach the sublingual gland?
options: By traveling with the facial artery's sympathetic plexus
Through the nerve to the medial pterygoid
Directly from the otic ganglion via the mandibular division
Via the chorda tympani within the middle ear
Direct branches from the lingual nerve
correctOption: Direct branches from the lingual nerve
optionExplanations: While the facial artery has a sympathetic plexus, the parasympathetic postganglionic secretomotor fibers of the submandibular gland arise from the submandibular ganglion, not a vascular plexus.
The nerve to the medial pterygoid is anatomically adherent to the otic ganglion but does not serve as a distribution pathway for submandibular postganglionic fibers.
The otic ganglion is responsible for parotid secretion, not the sublingual or submandibular glands.
The chorda tympani carries preganglionic fibers to the ganglion; it does not carry postganglionic fibers to the glands.

The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve; its postganglionic fibers reach their targets (submandibular and sublingual glands) either directly or by re-entering and traveling via the lingual nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The submandibular ganglion... is attached to the lingual nerve by small nerves... Postganglionic secretomotor fibers pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: An anatomist is demonstrating the infratemporal fossa to medical students. He identifies a small, pinhead-sized parasympathetic ganglion located immediately medial to the mandibular nerve (V3) as it exits the foramen ovale. Which of the following correctly identifies this structure and its specific anatomical adherence?
options: Submandibular ganglion; adherent to the hyoglossus muscle
Ciliary ganglion; adherent to the ophthalmic nerve
Otic ganglion; adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid
Pterygopalatine ganglion; adherent to the maxillary nerve
Geniculate ganglion; adherent to the facial canal
correctOption: Otic ganglion; adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid
optionExplanations: The submandibular ganglion is located in the submandibular region, suspended from the lingual nerve, not the main trunk of V3.
The ciliary ganglion is located in the posterior orbit, not the infratemporal fossa, and is associated with the oculomotor nerve branches rather than the mandibular nerve.

The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic relay station specifically found in the infratemporal fossa, medial to V3 and just below the foramen ovale, and is noted for being adherent to the nerve that supplies the medial pterygoid muscle.
The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa, suspended from the maxillary nerve (V2), not the mandibular nerve (V3).
The geniculate ganglion is a sensory ganglion located on the facial nerve within the petrous part of the temporal bone, not in the infratemporal fossa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that is located medial to the mandibular nerve just below the skull, and it is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Chorda Tympani and Submandibular Ganglion Distribution
statement: A surgeon is performing a mastoidectomy to treat chronic cholesteatoma. During the dissection of the posterior wall of the middle ear, the chorda tympani nerve is accidentally sacrificed. Which of the following accurately describes the long-term deficit related to the distribution of the submandibular ganglion?
options: Anesthesia of the skin over the angle of the mandible
Loss of secretomotor function to the parotid gland
Paralysis of the mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric
Loss of secretomotor function to the submandibular and sublingual glands
Inability to constrict the pupil on the affected side
correctOption: Loss of secretomotor function to the submandibular and sublingual glands
optionExplanations: Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not the chorda tympani.
Secretomotor function to the parotid is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve and otic ganglion; it does not involve the chorda tympani.
The mylohyoid and digastric muscles are supplied by the mylohyoid nerve (branch of V3), not the chorda tympani.

The chorda tympani carries preganglionic fibers that synapse in the submandibular ganglion. Damage to these fibers results in a loss of secretomotor supply to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.
Pupillary constriction is mediated by the ciliary ganglion and CN III; it is unaffected by chorda tympani injury.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1713 (Book Page): The chorda tympani... carries preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that reach the submandibular ganglion and are there relayed to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Roots of the Otic Ganglion
statement: The otic ganglion receives its preganglionic parasympathetic fibers through which specific nervous structure?
options: Deep petrosal nerve
Lesser petrosal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Chorda tympani nerve
External laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Lesser petrosal nerve
optionExplanations: The deep petrosal nerve consists of postganglionic sympathetic fibers derived from the internal carotid plexus and does not carry the parasympathetic roots required for the otic ganglion.
The lesser petrosal nerve is the continuation of the tympanic plexus, carrying preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the otic ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve is a branch of the facial nerve that carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
The chorda tympani nerve is a branch of the facial nerve that provides the preganglionic parasympathetic root for the submandibular ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
The external laryngeal nerve is a motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X) that supplies the cricothyroid muscle and has no relation to the otic ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve (see glossopharyngeal nerve below).

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: Where is the submandibular ganglion anatomically situated in relation to the major salivary glands and surrounding nerves?
options: In the pterygopalatine fossa, suspended from the maxillary nerve
Medial to the mandibular nerve, adherent to the medial pterygoid
Deep to the submandibular salivary gland, attached to the lingual nerve
Lateral to the parotid gland and superficial to the masseter
Within the carotid sheath, lateral to the internal jugular vein
correctOption: Deep to the submandibular salivary gland, attached to the lingual nerve
optionExplanations: This describes the location and suspension of the pterygopalatine (sphenopalatine) ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.
This describes the exact location of the otic ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.
The submandibular ganglion is found in the submandibular region, specifically deep to the submandibular gland, where it is physically suspended by roots from the lingual nerve.
This describes the location of the parotid gland or the terminal branches of the facial nerve, not the submandibular ganglion.
The carotid sheath contains the carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve, but no parasympathetic ganglia like the submandibular are found there.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The submandibular ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that lies deep to the submandibular salivary gland and is attached to the lingual nerve by small nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Postganglionic Distribution of Otic Ganglion via Auriculotemporal Nerve
statement: A 52-year-old woman presents with gustatory sweating (Frey's syndrome) following a surgical procedure on the lateral aspect of her face. Vitals: BP 135/82 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, Temp 36.8°C. This condition arises because fibers that normally distribute from the otic ganglion to a specific gland have misdirected their growth to sweat glands. Which nerve carried these fibers before the injury?
options: Nerve to the medial pterygoid
Auriculotemporal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Lingual nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
correctOption: Auriculotemporal nerve
optionExplanations: The nerve to the medial pterygoid is motor and provide the physical point of adherence for the otic ganglion, but it does not carry the secretomotor distribution to the parotid gland.

The auriculotemporal nerve normally carries postganglionic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. In Frey's syndrome, these fibers are damaged and inappropriately reinnervate sweat glands in the skin over the parotid.
The greater petrosal nerve is preganglionic and leads to the pterygopalatine ganglion; it is not involved in the postganglionic distribution of the otic ganglion.
The lingual nerve carries fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands via the submandibular ganglion, not fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid.

The mylohyoid nerve is a motor branch of the inferior alveolar nerve supplying the mylohyoid and anterior belly of the digastric; it has no role in the parasympathetic distribution to salivary glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1746 (Book Page): During the process of healing, the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve. Eventually, these fibers reach the sweat glands in the facial skin.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: During a dissection of the floor of the mouth, a student identifies a small ganglion suspended from the lingual nerve. What are the 'roots' of this ganglion that provide the preganglionic parasympathetic input?
options: Lesser petrosal nerve and nerve to medial pterygoid.
Mylohyoid nerve and nerve to geniohyoid.
Mental nerve and inferior alveolar nerve.
Chorda tympani nerve via the lingual nerve.
Greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve.
correctOption: Chorda tympani nerve via the lingual nerve.
optionExplanations: The lesser petrosal nerve is the preganglionic root for the otic ganglion.
The mylohyoid nerve is motor to the mylohyoid and digastric muscles; the nerve to the geniohyoid is C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.
The mental and inferior alveolar nerves are branches of V3 involved in sensory supply to the teeth and chin, not parasympathetic roots.
The submandibular ganglion receives its preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani, which hitchhikes with the lingual nerve (V3).
These form the nerve of the pterygoid canal, which goes to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the [submandibular] ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of the Otic Ganglion
statement: A 28-year-old dental student is reviewing the anatomy of the infratemporal fossa. Regarding the otic ganglion, which anatomical relationship correctly describes its precise location in this region?
options: It lies within the pterygopalatine fossa, suspended by the maxillary nerve.
It is attached to the lingual nerve in the floor of the submandibular triangle.
It is located lateral to the mandibular nerve as it exits the foramen rotundum.
It is found within the substance of the parotid gland, superficial to the facial nerve.
It is situated medial to the mandibular nerve just below the foramen ovale.
correctOption: It is situated medial to the mandibular nerve just below the foramen ovale.
optionExplanations: The pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion, is located in the pterygopalatine fossa and is suspended by the maxillary nerve (V2).
The ganglion attached to the lingual nerve in the submandibular region is the submandibular ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2), not the mandibular nerve, and is located in the pterygopalatine fossa, whereas the otic ganglion is in the infratemporal fossa.

While the otic ganglion provides secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland, it is not located within the gland itself; the facial nerve (CN VII) passes through the parotid gland but does not synapse in the otic ganglion.

The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic relay station located in the infratemporal fossa, specifically positioned on the medial aspect of the mandibular nerve (V3) immediately after its exit from the foramen ovale, and is often adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that is located medial to the mandibular nerve just below the skull, and it is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Submandibular Ganglion Clinical Relation
statement: A 24-year-old male undergoes a difficult extraction of an impacted right lower third molar. Post-operatively, he reports a loss of taste and a persistent 'numb' feeling on the right side of his tongue. Additionally, he feels that the floor of his mouth is drier than usual. Examination reveals loss of general sensation and taste on the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and absent salivary flow from the right sublingual fold. Where is the most likely site of the nerve injury?
options: Right mandibular nerve (V3) at the foramen ovale.
Right chorda tympani in the middle ear cavity.
Right lingual nerve proximal to the submandibular ganglion.
Right auriculotemporal nerve in the infratemporal fossa.
Right glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen.
correctOption: Right lingual nerve proximal to the submandibular ganglion.
optionExplanations: Injury at the foramen ovale would cause extensive facial anesthesia and paralysis of the muscles of mastication, which are not mentioned.
Injury to the chorda tympani in the middle ear would cause loss of taste and secretion but would spare general sensation to the tongue (which travels via the lingual nerve).

The lingual nerve carries general sensation (V3), taste (VII), and preganglionic secretomotor (VII) fibers near the third molar. A lesion here explains the combined loss of tongue sensation, taste, and sublingual/submandibular secretion.
The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the parotid and scalp; its injury would not cause loss of tongue sensation or taste.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the posterior 1/3 of the tongue; the patient's deficits are specifically in the anterior 2/3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): [The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction... The chorda tympani fibers carry taste... and also give off preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular ganglion.]

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Secretomotor Pathway to the Parotid Gland
statement: In the physiological pathway of parotid gland secretion, which nerve provides the definitive preganglionic parasympathetic relay to the otic ganglion?
options: Auriculotemporal nerve
Nerve of the pterygoid canal
Deep petrosal nerve
Lesser petrosal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
correctOption: Lesser petrosal nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland; it is the distribution nerve, not the preganglionic root.
Incorrect. The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) is formed by the union of the greater and deep petrosal nerves and supplies the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Incorrect. The deep petrosal nerve carries postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the internal carotid plexus, not preganglionic parasympathetic fibers.

Correct. The secretory pathway begins in the inferior salivary nucleus; fibers travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), its tympanic branch (Jacobson’s nerve), and finally the lesser petrosal nerve to synapse at the otic ganglion.
Incorrect. The greater petrosal nerve is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) and provides preganglionic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Lingual Nerve and Submandibular Ganglion Roots
statement: A 32-year-old male undergoes a traumatic extraction of an impacted lower third molar. Post-operatively, he reports a loss of general sensation and taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, alongside a noticeable reduction in saliva on that side. Based on the anatomical distribution of the submandibular ganglion's roots, which nerve was most likely damaged?
options: Inferior alveolar nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Lingual nerve
correctOption: Lingual nerve
optionExplanations: Damage to the inferior alveolar nerve would cause numbness of the lower teeth and chin (mental nerve distribution) but would not affect the tongue or salivation from the submandibular/sublingual glands.

The mylohyoid nerve is a motor branch of the inferior alveolar nerve supplying the mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric; it does not carry sensory or secretomotor fibers to the tongue or salivary glands.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides taste and sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue. Damage here would not affect the anterior two-thirds or the submandibular ganglion.
Damage to the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) would cause motor paralysis and wasting of the tongue muscles but would not affect taste, general sensation, or salivation.

The lingual nerve carries general sensation (V3), taste (from chorda tympani), and the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion. Its proximity to the lower third molar makes it vulnerable; damage results in loss of all three modalities.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): The lingual nerve... is closely related to the last molar tooth and is liable to be damaged in cases of clumsy extraction of an impacted third molar.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Comparative Distribution of Cranial Parasympathetic Ganglia
statement: In contrasting the distribution of postganglionic fibers between the otic and submandibular ganglia, which statement is accurate?
options: Both ganglia primarily distribute fibers via the infraorbital nerve to reach the facial skin.
The otic ganglion supplies the lacrimal gland, whereas the submandibular supplies the nasal glands.
The submandibular ganglion supplies only the submandibular gland, while the otic supplies all other salivary glands.
The otic ganglion supplies the sublingual gland, whereas the submandibular supplies the parotid.
The otic ganglion supplies the parotid gland, whereas the submandibular supplies the sublingual and submandibular glands.
correctOption: The otic ganglion supplies the parotid gland, whereas the submandibular supplies the sublingual and submandibular glands.
optionExplanations: The infraorbital nerve (V2) is primarily sensory to the face and does not serve as the primary distribution route for these specific ganglia.
The lacrimal and nasal glands are supplied by the pterygopalatine ganglion.
The submandibular ganglion supplies both the submandibular and sublingual glands, as well as small glands in the oral floor.
This is incorrect; the targets are reversed.
The otic ganglion is the relay station for the parotid gland (via the auriculotemporal nerve), while the submandibular ganglion serves both the submandibular and sublingual glands.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Postganglionic secretomotor fibers [from the submandibular ganglion] pass to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. ... The postganglionic secretomotor fibers [from the otic ganglion] reach the parotid salivary gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: Which of the following describes the specific origin of the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that eventually reach the submandibular ganglion?
options: The facial nerve via the chorda tympani
The trigeminal nerve via the lingual branch
The glossopharyngeal nerve via the tympanic branch
The vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus
The facial nerve via the greater petrosal nerve
correctOption: The facial nerve via the chorda tympani
optionExplanations: Preganglionic fibers for the submandibular ganglion originate in the superior salivary nucleus and travel with the facial nerve, leaving it via the chorda tympani to join the lingual nerve.
The trigeminal nerve is primarily sensory to the head and neck; it does not have a parasympathetic nucleus of its own, though its branches (like the lingual nerve) act as conduits for other nerves.
The glossopharyngeal nerve and its tympanic branch provide preganglionic fibers for the otic ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.
The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic supply to the thoracic and abdominal viscera but does not project to the cranial parasympathetic ganglia like the submandibular ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve (CN VII) carries preganglionic fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimation and nasal secretions.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Frey's Syndrome and the Otic Ganglion Pathway
statement: A 52-year-old female presents with sweating and flushing on the skin over her parotid gland whenever she eats (Frey's Syndrome) following a prior parotidectomy. This pathology involves the misdirection of postganglionic fibers originally intended for the parotid gland. Which nerve and ganglion are central to this diverted secretomotor pathway?
options: Auriculotemporal nerve and otic ganglion
Greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion
Chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion
Facial nerve and geniculate ganglion
Lingual nerve and submandibular ganglion
correctOption: Auriculotemporal nerve and otic ganglion
optionExplanations: In Frey's syndrome, postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion, which normally travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid gland, are damaged. During regeneration, these fibers erroneously join sympathetic pathways in the great auricular nerve to reach sweat glands in the skin. Consequently, a salivary stimulus (eating) results in localized sweating and flushing.
The greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion are involved in lacrimation and nasal secretion, not parotid secretion or the cutaneous area over the parotid.
The chorda tympani relates to the submandibular ganglion and salivary glands in the floor of the mouth, not the parotid or the auriculotemporal nerve.

The facial nerve provides the primary motor supply to the face. While the geniculate ganglion contains taste cell bodies, it is not the relay station for the postganglionic fibers that cause Frey's syndrome. The fibers in Frey's syndrome are parasympathetic postganglionics from the otic ganglion that originally reached the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.
The lingual nerve and submandibular ganglion serve the floor of the mouth and the submandibular/sublingual glands, not the parotid region or the auriculotemporal distribution.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1746 (Book Page): Frey’s syndrome is an interesting complication that sometimes develops after penetrating wounds of the parotid gland... caused by damage to the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves. During the process of healing, the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Submandibular Ganglion
statement: The submandibular ganglion is anatomically characterized by its relationship to which muscle and gland?
options: Superficial to the masseter and lateral to the parotid gland
Deep to the mylohyoid and superior to the digastric muscle
Lateral to the hyoglossus and inferior to the hypoglossal nerve
Medial to the medial pterygoid and lateral to the pharynx
Deep to the submandibular gland and suspended from the lingual nerve
correctOption: Deep to the submandibular gland and suspended from the lingual nerve
