correctOption: Otic ganglion postganglionic fibers joining the auriculotemporal nerve.
optionExplanations: The pterygopalatine ganglion distribution is to the lacrimal and nasal glands; it does not supply the skin overlying the parotid gland.
The submandibular ganglion supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands; its injury would not result in sweating over the parotid region.
Ciliary ganglion fibers are involved in the pupillary light reflex and accommodation; they do not have a distribution to facial sweat glands.

In Frey's syndrome, parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion, which normally travel in the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid gland, are damaged and mistakenly regrow to innervate sweat glands in the overlying skin. Thus, the stimulus for salivation (eating) causes localized sweating.

The superior cervical ganglion provides sympathetic fibers which normally stimulate sweating, but Frey's syndrome is specifically a parasympathetic-to-sympathetic miswiring following trauma to the parotid area.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1747 (Book Page): During the process of healing, the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve. Eventually, these fibers reach the sweat glands in the facial skin.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Chorda Tympani Vulnerability in the Middle Ear
statement: A patient with a history of chronic middle ear infections undergoes a tympanoplasty. Post-operatively, the patient notes a loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and significantly reduced salivation from the floor of the mouth. Which neuro-ganglionic pathway was likely compromised?
options: Auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid gland
Chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion
Deep petrosal nerve to the internal carotid plexus
Greater petrosal nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion
Lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion
correctOption: Chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion
optionExplanations: The auriculotemporal nerve is in the infratemporal fossa; it doesn't pass through the middle ear, and its loss wouldn't affect taste.
The chorda tympani passes through the middle ear; injury here interrupts taste to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and the preganglionic parasympathetic supply to the submandibular/sublingual glands.
The deep petrosal nerve is sympathetic and its loss would not cause the specific loss of taste or major secretomotor deficit in the oral floor.
The greater petrosal nerve leaves the facial nerve at the geniculate ganglion and doesn't cross the tympanic membrane; it regulates lacrimation.
The lesser petrosal nerve does pass through the middle ear but only regulates the parotid gland; its loss wouldn't cause taste loss on the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve arises from the facial nerve in the facial canal in the posterior wall of the middle ear. It runs forward over the medial surface of the upper part of the tympanic membrane... It also contains taste fibers from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Parasympathetic Origin of the Otic Ganglion
statement: The preganglionic fibers for the otic ganglion originate from a specific brainstem nucleus. Which nucleus and which cranial nerve provide this functional 'root' to the ganglion?
options: Inferior salivary nucleus via the glossopharyngeal nerve
Dorsal nucleus of the vagus via the vagus nerve
Lacrimatory nucleus via the facial nerve
Edinger-Westphal nucleus via the oculomotor nerve
Superior salivary nucleus via the facial nerve
correctOption: Inferior salivary nucleus via the glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The inferior salivary nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) sends preganglionic fibers that form the lesser petrosal nerve, which is the preganglionic root for the otic ganglion.
The dorsal nucleus of the vagus provides fibers to thoracic and abdominal viscera, not to the cranial parasympathetic ganglia (otic/submandibular).
The lacrimatory nucleus provides fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion (for lacrimation), not the otic ganglion.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides fibers to the ciliary ganglion for the eye.
The superior salivary nucleus provides preganglionic fibers for the submandibular and sublingual glands via the facial nerve and submandibular ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1696 (Book Page): that of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus... Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Clinical Correlation of Lingual Nerve and Submandibular Ganglion
statement: A 28-year-old patient undergoes a surgical extraction of a deeply impacted right mandibular third molar. Postoperatively, the patient reports a loss of taste on the right anterior tongue and a noticeable decrease in salivation. If the lingual nerve was damaged at the site of the tooth (distal to the chorda tympani junction), which autonomic structure is most likely deprived of its primary regulatory input?
options: Superior cervical ganglion
Submandibular ganglion
Otic ganglion
Ciliary ganglion
Pterygopalatine ganglion
correctOption: Submandibular ganglion
optionExplanations: The superior cervical ganglion provides sympathetic fibers; the symptoms described (loss of taste and salivation) are related to parasympathetic and sensory pathways of CN VII/V3.

The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve. Since the chorda tympani (carrying preganglionic fibers) joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa, a lesion of the lingual nerve near the third molar destroys the preganglionic input to the submandibular ganglion, resulting in xerostomia of the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The otic ganglion receives fibers from the lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX) and is not associated with the lingual nerve.
The ciliary ganglion is located in the orbit and handles pupillary constriction and accommodation.
The pterygopalatine ganglion is associated with the maxillary nerve (V2) and handles lacrimation and nasal secretion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The submandibular ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that lies deep to the submandibular salivary gland and is attached to the lingual nerve by small nerves. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Topographical Relations of the Otic Ganglion
statement: Topographically, the otic ganglion is described as being adherent to which specific nerve branch within the infratemporal fossa?
options: Deep temporal nerves
Nerve to the masseter
Chorda tympani
Nerve to the lateral pterygoid
Nerve to the medial pterygoid
correctOption: Nerve to the medial pterygoid
optionExplanations: The deep temporal nerves supply the temporalis muscle and are located in the temporal and infratemporal fossae but do not carry the otic ganglion.
The masseteric nerve is a branch of the anterior division of V3 and is not related to the otic ganglion's location.
The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve and is associated with the submandibular ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
The nerve to the lateral pterygoid is a branch of the anterior division of V3 and is not adherent to the otic ganglion.
The otic ganglion is located medial to the mandibular nerve and is specifically adherent to the nerve that supplies the medial pterygoid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion that is located medial to the mandibular nerve just below the skull, and it is adherent to the nerve to the medial pterygoid muscle.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: In the physiological regulation of the parotid gland, the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that eventually reach the otic ganglion originate from which brainstem nucleus?
options: Edinger–Westphal nucleus
Superior salivary nucleus
Nucleus ambiguus
Lacrimatory nucleus
Inferior salivary nucleus
correctOption: Inferior salivary nucleus
optionExplanations: The Edinger–Westphal nucleus is the source for the oculomotor nerve's (CN III) parasympathetic fibers for the eye.
The superior salivary nucleus belongs to the facial nerve (CN VII) and provides fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The nucleus ambiguus provides motor innervation to the muscles of the pharynx and larynx, not parasympathetic secretomotor output.
The lacrimatory nucleus provides fibers to the lacrimal gland via the facial nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion.
The inferior salivary nucleus belongs to the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and provides the preganglionic fibers for parotid secretion via the otic ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1696 (Book Page): that of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus... The glossopharyngeal nerve projects to the otic ganglion... via its tympanic and lesser petrosal branches.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Differential parasympathetic roots of head ganglia
statement: A patient suffers a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone, resulting in a lesion of the facial nerve proximal to the origin of the chorda tympani but distal to the geniculate ganglion. How would this specifically affect the autonomic 'roots' of the submandibular and otic ganglia?
options: The otic ganglion root would be lost, but the submandibular root remains intact.
Only the sympathetic supply to both ganglia would be interrupted.
Both ganglia would lose their preganglionic parasympathetic roots.
Neither ganglion would be affected as their roots originate from the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The submandibular ganglion root would be lost, but the otic root remains intact.
correctOption: The submandibular ganglion root would be lost, but the otic root remains intact.
optionExplanations: This is incorrect because the otic ganglion's preganglionic root is the lesser petrosal nerve (from CN IX), which would be unaffected by a facial nerve lesion.
Sympathetic fibers originate from the superior cervical ganglion and follow arterial plexuses; they are not the primary preganglionic roots of these parasympathetic ganglia.
The otic ganglion root comes from CN IX, while the submandibular comes from CN VII. A facial nerve lesion does not affect CN IX.
Only the otic ganglion root originates from the glossopharyngeal nerve; the submandibular ganglion root definitely originates from the facial nerve.

The submandibular ganglion receives its preganglionic 'root' from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani. A lesion of the facial nerve in the facial canal would interrupt this. The otic ganglion's root (CN IX) remains functional.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Chorda tympani nerve arises from the facial nerve in the facial canal... contains preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the submandibular and the sublingual salivary glands. ... Page 1670 (Book Page): [Otic] preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: In the physiological regulation of parotid gland secretion, what is the precise sequential pathway taken by the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers before they synapse in the otic ganglion?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve -> deep petrosal nerve -> nerve of the pterygoid canal
Glossopharyngeal nerve -> tympanic nerve -> lesser petrosal nerve
Mandibular nerve -> auriculotemporal nerve -> parotid plexus
Facial nerve -> greater petrosal nerve -> nerve of the pterygoid canal
Facial nerve -> chorda tympani -> lingual nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve -> tympanic nerve -> lesser petrosal nerve
optionExplanations: The deep petrosal nerve is sympathetic and the nerve of the pterygoid canal leads to the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion.

Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers for the parotid gland originate in the inferior salivary nucleus (CN IX), travel through the tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve), form the tympanic plexus, and exit as the lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion.
The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion; it does not carry preganglionic fibers from the brainstem.
The greater petrosal nerve is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that leads to the pterygopalatine ganglion for lacrimation and nasal secretions.
The facial nerve-chorda tympani-lingual nerve pathway is the secretomotor route for the submandibular and sublingual glands, not the parotid gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The preganglionic fibers originate in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and they reach the ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve (see glossopharyngeal nerve below). Page 1676 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers for the parotid salivary gland leave the plexus as the lesser petrosal nerve; they synapse in the otic ganglion.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Preganglionic Roots of the Submandibular Ganglion
statement: The secretomotor pathway to the submandibular and sublingual glands involves a specific synaptic relay. Which nerve carries the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that serve as the functional root of the ganglion responsible for this distribution?
options: Chorda tympani nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Lesser petrosal nerve
Deep petrosal nerve
correctOption: Chorda tympani nerve
optionExplanations: The chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that joins the lingual nerve to provide the preganglionic 'root' for the submandibular ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic fibers from the facial nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.
The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion; it does not carry preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the otic ganglion.
The deep petrosal nerve carries postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the internal carotid plexus, not parasympathetic preganglionic fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Frey's Syndrome and Otic Ganglion Distribution
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with beads of perspiration appearing on the skin covering the parotid gland whenever they eat (Frey's Syndrome) following a previous parotidectomy. Based on the distribution of the otic ganglion, what is the pathophysiological mechanism for this condition?
options: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the internal carotid plexus misdirected to the parotid duct.
Regeneration of the chorda tympani nerve into the greater occipital nerve fibers.
Misdirection of the lesser petrosal nerve into the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve misdirected to skin sweat glands.
Preganglionic fibers from the greater petrosal nerve misdirected to the facial skin.
correctOption: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve misdirected to skin sweat glands.
optionExplanations: Frey's syndrome involves the misdirection of parasympathetic (not sympathetic) fibers originally intended for salivation.
The chorda tympani is related to the submandibular ganglion and taste; it is not involved in the parotid/auriculotemporal misdirection seen in Frey's syndrome.
The lesser petrosal nerve is preganglionic; Frey's syndrome involves the postganglionic fibers misdirecting after the otic ganglion synapse.

Frey's syndrome occurs when parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (from the otic ganglion) that normally travel in the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid gland mistakenly regenerate to follow cutaneous nerves (like the great auricular) to sweat glands.
The greater petrosal nerve does not supply the parotid gland or the auriculotemporal nerve; it is part of the lacrimation pathway.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1746 (Book Page): During the process of healing, the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve grow out and join the distal end of the great auricular nerve. Eventually, these fibers reach the sweat glands in the facial skin.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
coreConcept: Preganglionic Pathway of the Submandibular Ganglion
statement: Which mechanistic pathway correctly describes the transmission of preganglionic parasympathetic impulses to the submandibular ganglion?
options: Via the auriculotemporal nerve arising from the posterior division of V3
Via the greater petrosal nerve joining the nerve of the pterygoid canal
Via the chorda tympani nerve joining the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa
Via direct branches from the glossopharyngeal nerve in the jugular foramen
Via the lesser petrosal nerve passing through the foramen ovale
correctOption: Via the chorda tympani nerve joining the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa
optionExplanations: The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland; it is not a preganglionic root for the submandibular ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve carries fibers to the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.

Preganglionic fibers for the submandibular ganglion originate in the superior salivary nucleus (CN VII), travel via the chorda tympani, exit the petrotympanic fissure, and join the lingual nerve (V3) to reach the ganglion.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides preganglionic fibers to the otic ganglion (via the lesser petrosal nerve), not the submandibular ganglion.
The lesser petrosal nerve is the preganglionic root for the otic ganglion, not the submandibular ganglion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the ganglion from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and the lingual nerves.

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: The 'glossopharyngeal-otic-parotid' pathway represents a specific physiological circuit for salivary regulation. Which structure carries the postganglionic fibers from the otic ganglion to complete this circuit at the target organ?
options: Lesser petrosal nerve.
Chorda tympani.
Buccal nerve.
Nerve to the medial pterygoid.
Auriculotemporal nerve.
correctOption: Auriculotemporal nerve.
optionExplanations: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic fibers *to* the otic ganglion, not postganglionic fibers *from* it.
The chorda tympani is part of the facial nerve (CN VII) pathway for the submandibular and sublingual glands, not the parotid.
The buccal nerve is sensory to the cheek and does not carry secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland.
The nerve to the medial pterygoid is a motor branch of V3; while the otic ganglion is adherent to it, the secretomotor fibers use the auriculotemporal nerve for distribution.
After synapsing in the otic ganglion, the postganglionic secretomotor fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve, which then carries them to the parotid gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): [The postganglionic secretomotor fibers reach the parotid salivary gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.]

category: Describe the location, roots and distribution of otic and submandibular ganglia
statement: The postganglionic parasympathetic distribution from the otic ganglion to its target gland 'hitchhikes' along which specific nerve?
options: Maxillary nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Nerve to stapedius
Chorda tympani
Lingual nerve
correctOption: Auriculotemporal nerve
optionExplanations: The maxillary nerve (V2) is the conduit for postganglionic fibers from the pterygopalatine ganglion, not the otic ganglion.
The auriculotemporal nerve (a branch of V3) passes very close to the otic ganglion and picks up the postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to carry them to the parotid gland.
The nerve to stapedius is a motor branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) within the temporal bone; it has no role in carrying fibers from the otic ganglion.
The chorda tympani carries preganglionic fibers for the submandibular ganglion; it is not the postganglionic distribution carrier for the otic ganglion.
The lingual nerve carries preganglionic fibers to the submandibular ganglion and postganglionic fibers to the tongue, but is not the carrier for otic ganglion distribution.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1670 (Book Page): The postganglionic secretomotor fibers reach the parotid salivary gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Diagnostic Contrast of Hyoid Muscle Attachments
statement: The hyoid bone acts as a critical anchor for several 'strap muscles' of the neck. Which of these muscles, arising from the scapula, attaches to the hyoid bone and acts to depress it?
options: Sternohyoid muscle
Mylohyoid muscle
Omohyoid muscle
Geniohyoid muscle
Thyrohyoid muscle
correctOption: Omohyoid muscle
optionExplanations: The sternohyoid muscle originates from the manubrium of the sternum and the medial end of the clavicle, not the scapula.
The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that forms the floor of the mouth and arises from the mandible, acting to elevate the hyoid during swallowing.

The omohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle consisting of two bellies; its inferior belly arises from the superior border of the scapula and its superior belly attaches to the lower border of the hyoid bone, serving to depress the bone.
The geniohyoid muscle is a suprahyoid muscle that arises from the inferior mental spines of the mandible and attaches to the hyoid, acting to pull the hyoid forward and upward.
The thyrohyoid muscle is a short muscle that connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone; it acts to elevate the larynx or depress the hyoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): The hyoid bone forms a base for the tongue and is suspended in position by muscles that connect it to the mandible, to the styloid process of the temporal bone, to the thyroid cartilage, to the sternum, and to the scapula.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The middle constrictor muscle of the pharynx is fan-shaped and arises from which specific combination of structures associated with the hyoid bone?
options: The body and the thyrohyoid membrane
The inferior border of the body and the thyroid cartilage
The midline raphe and the lesser cornu
The lesser cornu, greater cornu, and stylohyoid ligament
The greater cornu and the epiglottic cartilage
correctOption: The lesser cornu, greater cornu, and stylohyoid ligament
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The body of the hyoid is largely occupied by the geniohyoid, mylohyoid, and sternohyoid muscles.
Incorrect. This describes the region for the infrahyoid muscles and the thyrohyoid membrane.
Incorrect. The midline raphe is the insertion of the constrictors, not the origin.
Correct. The middle constrictor arises from the whole length of the upper border of the greater cornu, the lesser cornu, and the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament.
Incorrect. The epiglottic cartilage does not serve as an origin for the pharyngeal constrictor muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The muscles in the wall of the pharynx are the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles... [Table 12.11 Page 1758 (Book Page): Middle constrictor origin: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater cornua of the hyoid bone].

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Neurovascular Relations of the Thyrohyoid Membrane
statement: During a dissection of the anterior triangle of the neck, a surgeon identifies the thyrohyoid membrane. Which neurovascular bundle must be carefully preserved as it pierces this membrane to enter the larynx?
options: Superior thyroid artery and external laryngeal nerve
Inferior laryngeal artery and recurrent laryngeal nerve
Occipital artery and greater occipital nerve
Superior laryngeal artery and internal laryngeal nerve
Facial artery and glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Superior laryngeal artery and internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The superior thyroid artery and external laryngeal nerve descend together, but the external laryngeal nerve remains external to the larynx to supply the cricothyroid muscle; it does not pierce this membrane.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal artery enter the larynx near the cricothyroid joint, not through the thyrohyoid membrane.
The occipital artery and greater occipital nerve are located in the posterior aspect of the scalp and neck and are not involved in laryngeal structures.

The thyrohyoid membrane, which connects the hyoid to the thyroid cartilage, is pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve (sensory to the upper larynx) and the superior laryngeal vessels. This is a critical landmark in neck surgery.
The facial artery and glossopharyngeal nerve are located higher in the submandibular and oropharyngeal regions and do not relate to the thyrohyoid membrane.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1781 (Book Page): The superior laryngeal vessels and the internal laryngeal nerve pierce the membrane on each side (see Fig. 12.82).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: A 6-year-old child presents with a painless, fluctuant midline mass that moves upward when the child swallows and when the tongue is protruded. If surgical excision (Sistrunk procedure) is required, why must the central portion of the hyoid bone be removed?
options: The bone prevents the surgeon from visualizing the lingual artery.
The hyoid bone acts as a reservoir for the mucus-secreting cells of the duct.
The thyroglossal duct often traverses or is intimately wrapped around the body of the bone.
The hyoid bone is the primary source of the ectopic thyroid tissue.
The greater cornua of the hyoid bone compress the duct, preventing spontaneous closure.
correctOption: The thyroglossal duct often traverses or is intimately wrapped around the body of the bone.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While visualization is important, the primary anatomical reason for removing the bone is the duct's path through or around it.
Incorrect. The bone itself does not secrete mucus; the epithelial lining of the persistent duct remnants does.

Correct. During development, the thyroglossal duct migrates inferiorly and may pass anterior, posterior, or through the hyoid bone's body. Excision of the central hyoid is necessary to remove all ductal remnants and prevent recurrence of cysts.
Incorrect. The ectopic tissue originates from the thyroid diverticulum, not the hyoid bone itself.
Incorrect. It is the body of the bone, not the greater cornua, that is anatomically related to the thyroglossal duct's path.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1818 (Book Page): Because remnants of the duct often traverse the body of the hyoid bone, this may have to be excised also to prevent recurrence.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Unique articulation status of the Hyoid bone
statement: The hyoid bone is described as being exceptionally mobile and maintains its position through a complex network of soft tissue rather than skeletal junctions. Which anatomical feature most accurately defines this lack of direct skeletal connectivity?
options: It is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck that does not articulate with any other bones.
It maintains a rigid attachment to the third cervical vertebra through a short fibrous ligament.
It articulates only with the thyroid cartilage via the thyrohyoid membrane.
It forms a synchondrosis with the mandible and a syndesmosis with the styloid process.
It is fused to the thyroid cartilage during early adolescence to provide laryngeal stability.
correctOption: It is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck that does not articulate with any other bones.
optionExplanations: The hyoid bone is famously the only bone in the human body that does not articulate directly with any other bone. It is suspended by muscles and the stylohyoid ligaments, allowing it to move dynamically during speech, swallowing, and respiration.
There is no direct ligamentous or bony attachment between the hyoid bone and the third cervical vertebra. It is separated from the vertebrae by the pharynx and prevertebral muscles.

While the hyoid is connected to the thyroid cartilage by the thyrohyoid membrane, this is a membranous/ligamentous connection, not a skeletal articulation. Membranes do not constitute true bony articulations.

This option is incorrect as there are no synchondroses or syndesmoses between the hyoid and the mandible. Its relationship with the styloid process is via a long, flexible stylohyoid ligament, not a joint.
The hyoid bone remains separate from the thyroid cartilage throughout life. Fusion would severely restrict the mobility required for laryngeal elevation and tongue movement.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): It does not articulate with any other bones. . . The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: An anatomical study focuses on the superficial-to-deep arrangement of muscles on the anterior surface of the hyoid body. Which muscle's attachment site is found superior to the mylohyoid attachment on the medial aspect of the body?
options: Sternohyoid
Geniohyoid
Thyrohyoid
Omohyoid
Stylohyoid
correctOption: Geniohyoid
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The sternohyoid attaches to the lower border of the body, inferior to the mylohyoid.
Correct. In the hierarchical arrangement of the hyoid body, the geniohyoid muscle attaches superiorly to the mylohyoid attachment.
Incorrect. The thyrohyoid attaches to the lower border/greater cornu, not superior to the mylohyoid on the body.
Incorrect. The omohyoid attaches to the lower border of the body, inferior to the mylohyoid.
Incorrect. The stylohyoid attaches to the junction of the body and greater cornu, lateral to the midline muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1503 (Book Page): The mental spines (genial tubercles) are on the midline medial surface of the body of the mandible; these give origin to the genioglossus muscles above and the geniohyoid muscles below. [Page 1515 (Book Page), Fig 12.13 shows Geniohyoid superior to Mylohyoid on the hyoid body].

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: When an elite vocalist produces a high-pitched note, the tension of the vocal folds is increased. This involves the tilting of the thyroid cartilage, which is influenced by its connection to the hyoid. What is the name of the fibrous sheet connecting the hyoid to the laryngeal framework?
options: Stylohyoid ligament
Cricothyroid ligament
Cricotracheal ligament
Thyrohyoid membrane
Quadrangular membrane
correctOption: Thyrohyoid membrane
optionExplanations: The stylohyoid ligament connects the hyoid to the skull, not to the laryngeal framework.
The cricothyroid ligament connects the cricoid and thyroid cartilages; it is the site used for emergency cricothyroidotomy.
The cricotracheal ligament is located lower in the neck, connecting the laryngeal base (cricoid) to the start of the trachea.
The thyrohyoid membrane is the principal extrinsic membrane of the larynx, spanning the gap between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage, allowing them to move as a functional unit.
The quadrangular membrane is an internal laryngeal membrane extending between the epiglottis and arytenoid cartilages.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): It attaches... to the thyroid cartilage by the thyrohyoid membrane.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The middle constrictor muscle of the pharynx is a fan-shaped muscle. Where does it specifically attach on the hyoid bone to facilitate the narrowing of the pharyngeal lumen during swallowing?
options: The inferior surface of the body only
The whole length of the greater cornu and the lesser cornu
The upper border of the body
The posterior aspect of the greater cornu only
The junction of the body and the lesser cornu only
correctOption: The whole length of the greater cornu and the lesser cornu
optionExplanations: The inferior surface of the body is the primary site for the sternohyoid and omohyoid muscles.
The middle constrictor originates from the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and both the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone, allowing it to constrict the oropharynx effectively.
The upper border of the body is largely occupied by the mylohyoid and geniohyoid muscles.
While it attaches to the greater cornu, it also involves the lesser cornu and the stylohyoid ligament.
The attachment is more extensive than just the junction; it involves both cornua and the associated ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): Pharyngeal Muscles... The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe)... Table 12.11 [Pharynx Muscles]: Middle constrictor... Origin: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and lesser and greater cornua of hyoid bone.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: In terms of surface anatomy and local relations, at which level is the hyoid bone typically situated in the adult neck?
options: Inferior to the cricoid cartilage at the level of C6
Opposite the angle of the mandible at the level of C2
At the level of the suprasternal notch
Directly posterior to the symphysis menti of the mandible
Opposite the third cervical vertebra, superior to the laryngeal prominence
correctOption: Opposite the third cervical vertebra, superior to the laryngeal prominence
optionExplanations: The cricoid cartilage lies at the level of C6; the hyoid is significantly more superior (C3).
The angle of the mandible and the axis (C2) are superior to the hyoid bone, which is level with C3.
The suprasternal notch is at the base of the neck (T2 level), far below the hyoid bone.
The hyoid is well inferior to the symphysis menti; the submental triangle and various muscles separate them.
In the neutral anatomical position, the hyoid bone lies at the level of the third cervical vertebra (C3), tucked under the mandible and situated just above the thyroid cartilage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx... (Related to Fig 12.13 and Fig 12.57).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: Which of the following muscles, when acting alone on the hyoid bone, results in the depression of the bone toward the scapula?
options: Genioglossus
Digastric
Omohyoid
Geniohyoid
Stylohyoid
correctOption: Omohyoid
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue that can pull the hyoid forward/upward, but not depress it toward the scapula.
Incorrect. The digastric is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid or depresses the mandible.
Correct. The omohyoid muscle consists of two bellies and connects the hyoid bone to the scapula. Its contraction depresses the hyoid.
Incorrect. The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid bone.
Incorrect. The stylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates and retracts the hyoid bone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1784 (Book Page): Depression: The sternothyroid, the sternohyoid, and the omohyoid muscles.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Functional relationship between the Hyoid and the Tongue
statement: A patient with a tumor of the posterior third of the tongue requires a surgical procedure. The surgeon considers the muscular attachments of the hyoid to provide access. Which muscle, arising from the hyoid, forms the lateral boundary of the tongue and is crucial to its depression?
options: Geniohyoid
Palatoglossus
Genioglossus
Hyoglossus
Styloglossus
correctOption: Hyoglossus
optionExplanations: The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid bone; it does not form the lateral boundary of the tongue or depress it.
The palatoglossus arises from the soft palate and elevates the posterior tongue; it is not attached to the hyoid bone.
The genioglossus arises from the mental spines of the mandible and acts to protrude the tongue, though some fibers attach to the hyoid.
The hyoglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue that originates from the body and greater cornu of the hyoid bone and acts to depress the tongue.
The styloglossus arises from the styloid process and acts to retract and elevate the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Table 12.9... Hyoglossus... Origin: Body and greater cornu of hyoid bone... Action: Depresses tongue.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of Thyroglossal Duct Remnants
statement: A 4-year-old child is scheduled for a Sistrunk procedure to remove a recurrent thyroglossal cyst. Based on the embryological path of the thyroglossal duct, which part of the hyoid bone must be surgically excised to ensure complete removal of the duct remnants?
options: The right greater cornu
The junction of the body and greater cornu
The left lesser cornu
The central body
The entire bone and its stylohyoid ligaments
correctOption: The central body
optionExplanations: The thyroglossal duct descends in the midline; therefore, lateral structures like the greater cornu are rarely involved in the duct's path.
The duct remains in the midline; the junction of the body and greater cornu is too lateral to be the primary site of duct remnants.
While the duct passes near the hyoid, it is the midline body that is embryologically associated with the descent of the thyroid primordium, not the lesser cornu.

The thyroid gland descends from the foramen cecum. The thyroglossal duct often passes anterior to, posterior to, or even through the hyoid body; thus, the central part of the body must be removed to prevent recurrence of cysts.
Excising the entire hyoid bone would severely destabilize the larynx and tongue, as it serves as a vital anchor; only the central body portion is required for the Sistrunk procedure.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1819 (Book Page): Because remnants of the duct often traverse the body of the hyoid bone, this may have to be excised also to prevent recurrence.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Laryngeal Suspension via the Hyoid Bone
statement: What is the specific anatomical relationship between the hyoid bone and the thyrohyoid membrane?
options: The membrane is a continuation of the investing fascia that skips the hyoid
The membrane is reinforced by the stylohyoid ligament at the midline
The membrane attaches only to the lesser cornua
The membrane attaches the hyoid bone to the cricoid cartilage
The membrane connects the upper margin of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone
correctOption: The membrane connects the upper margin of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid membrane is a distinct laryngeal ligamentous structure, not merely a facial continuation; it specifically attaches to the hyoid.
The stylohyoid ligament is a lateral structure connecting to the lesser cornu; the thyrohyoid membrane is reinforced in the midline by the median thyrohyoid ligament.
The thyrohyoid membrane attaches to the body and greater cornua of the hyoid, not just the lesser cornua.
The membrane connects to the thyroid cartilage, not the cricoid. The cricoid is connected to the thyroid via the cricothyroid ligament.
Correct. This membrane provides a vital structural link between the hyoid bone and the laryngeal skeleton (thyroid cartilage).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1781 (Book Page): Thyrohyoid membrane: This connects the upper margin of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. Page 1514 (Book Page): It attaches... to the thyroid cartilage by the thyrohyoid membrane.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: Which muscle of the pharynx utilizes the greater cornu of the hyoid bone as a site of origin, helping to form the middle portion of the pharyngeal wall?
options: Middle constrictor
Inferior constrictor
Superior constrictor
Salpingopharyngeus
Palatopharyngeus
correctOption: Middle constrictor
optionExplanations: Correct. The middle constrictor muscle of the pharynx originates from the greater cornu of the hyoid bone (and the stylohyoid ligament) before fanning out to the pharyngeal raphe.
Incorrect. The inferior constrictor originates from the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
Incorrect. The superior constrictor attaches to the pterygomandibular raphe and the mandible, not the hyoid.
Incorrect. The salpingopharyngeus originates from the auditory tube.
Incorrect. The palatopharyngeus originates from the soft palate and inserts into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and pharyngeal wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): The major muscles that attach to the hyoid bone are shown in Figure 12.13. [Figure 12.13 identifies the Middle constrictor attachment on the greater cornu].

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: In relation to the surrounding landmarks of the neck, where is the hyoid bone typically located?
options: In the midline, inferior to the mandible and superior to the larynx
Posterior to the cervical vertebrae at the level of C3
Superior to the mandible and inferior to the tongue
Deep to the thyroid gland isthmus
Lateral to the carotid sheath and medial to the sternocleidomastoid
correctOption: In the midline, inferior to the mandible and superior to the larynx
optionExplanations: The hyoid is a midline structure situated in the neck, specifically positioned below the mandible and above the thyroid cartilage of the larynx.
The hyoid is an anterior structure, not posterior to the vertebrae. It lies at the level of the C3 vertebra but is located anteriorly.
The hyoid is inferior to the mandible, not superior to it.
The hyoid is superior to the thyroid gland; the thyroid isthmus typically lies in front of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings.
The hyoid is medial to the carotid sheath; the sheath and sternocleidomastoid are lateral to the midline structures like the hyoid and larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: During the second stage of deglutition (swallowing), the hyoid bone is elevated to facilitate laryngeal closure. Which of the following muscles acts directly to elevate the hyoid bone by pulling it towards the mandible?
options: Mylohyoid
Omohyoid
Thyrohyoid
Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
correctOption: Mylohyoid
optionExplanations: Correct. The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that forms the floor of the mouth and connects the mandible to the body of the hyoid; its contraction elevates the hyoid.
Incorrect. The omohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that originates from the scapula and acts to depress the hyoid bone, not elevate it.

Incorrect. The thyrohyoid connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid. While it can elevate the larynx towards the hyoid, it is generally grouped with muscles that act on the larynx rather than pulling the hyoid to the mandible.
Incorrect. The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that originates from the sternum and acts to depress the hyoid bone.
Incorrect. The sternothyroid attaches to the thyroid cartilage (not the hyoid) and acts as a laryngeal depressor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): The hyoid bone forms a base for the tongue and is suspended in position by muscles that connect it to the mandible, to the styloid process of the temporal bone, to the thyroid cartilage, to the sternum, and to the scapula.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Skeletal Articulation Characteristics of the Hyoid
statement: Regarding its skeletal organization, which feature uniquely distinguishes the hyoid bone from all other bones in the human body?
options: It is the only bone in the skeleton that does not articulate with any other bone.
It is the only bone that develops entirely from the fourth pharyngeal arch mesenchyme.
It is the only bone in the neck that is not derived from the paraxial mesoderm.
It is the only bone that possesses both hyaline and elastic cartilage components in adulthood.
It is the only bone that lacks a periosteal covering on its anterior surface.
correctOption: It is the only bone in the skeleton that does not articulate with any other bone.
optionExplanations: This is correct; the hyoid is unique because it is suspended by muscles and ligaments and lacks a direct synovial or fibrous articulation with any other skeletal element.
This is incorrect; the hyoid bone develops from the second and third pharyngeal arches, not exclusively the fourth.
This is incorrect; several bones in the head and neck are derived from the neural crest (ectomesenchyme) rather than paraxial mesoderm, so the hyoid is not unique in this regard.
This is incorrect; while it is held by ligaments, the hyoid bone itself is a single bone and does not contain elastic cartilage within its structure.
This is incorrect; like other bones, the hyoid bone is covered by periosteum, which serves as a site for muscular and ligamentous attachments.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx. It does not articulate with any other bones.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Functional Significance of the Hyoid as a Base for the Tongue
statement: A 45-year-old male is brought to the morgue following a suspected manual strangulation. The forensic pathologist identifies a fracture of the hyoid bone. Which physiological function was most likely compromised immediately preceding the fracture due to the hyoid's role as a 'base'?
options: Structural integrity of the vertebral column
Transmission of sound through the middle ear
Mobility and stability of the tongue
Regulation of intracranial pressure
Primary protection of the spinal cord roots
correctOption: Mobility and stability of the tongue
optionExplanations: The hyoid is not part of the vertebral column and does not contribute to its structural integrity.
Sound transmission is the function of the auditory ossicles in the middle ear, not the hyoid bone.
The hyoid bone acts as a mobile anchor and base for the tongue. Its fracture disrupts the stable platform required for tongue movements used in speech and swallowing.
The hyoid bone has no role in regulating intracranial pressure, which is managed by CSF and venous drainage.
The spinal cord is protected by the vertebrae; the hyoid is located anteriorly in the neck and provides no protection to the cord.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): The hyoid bone forms a base for the tongue and is suspended in position by muscles that connect it to the mandible, to the styloid process of the temporal bone, to the thyroid cartilage, to the sternum, and to the scapula.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Suspension Apparatus of the Hyoid Bone
statement: The stylohyoid ligament, which can occasionally undergo ossification, serves as a critical suspensory structure for the hyoid bone. To which specific part of the hyoid bone does this ligament attach?
options: The inferior border of the body
The lesser cornu
The superior border of the body
The lateral-most tip of the greater cornu
The junction of the body and greater cornu
correctOption: The lesser cornu
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The inferior border of the body is the attachment site for infrahyoid 'strap' muscles like the sternohyoid.
Correct. The stylohyoid ligament connects the styloid process of the temporal bone specifically to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone, aiding in its suspension.
Incorrect. The superior border of the body is largely associated with the attachments of the suprahyoid muscles such as the mylohyoid and geniohyoid.
Incorrect. The greater cornu primarily serves as the attachment point for the thyrohyoid and hyoglossus muscles and the thyrohyoid membrane.
Incorrect. While this is a dense area of the bone, the specific ligamentous attachment for the styloid process is the lesser cornu.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): It attaches to the skull by the stylohyoid ligament and to the thyroid cartilage by the thyrohyoid membrane. ... The hyoid bone is U-shaped and consists of a body and two greater and two lesser cornua (Fig. 12.13).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The middle constrictor muscle of the pharynx is essential for the involuntary propulsion of food. Which parts of the hyoid bone provide the origin for this muscle?
options: The thyrohyoid membrane interface only
Anterior surface of the body only
Inferior border of the body only
Greater and lesser cornua
The stylohyoid ligament junction only
correctOption: Greater and lesser cornua
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid membrane is a connective tissue sheet, not a muscular origin site for the pharyngeal constrictors.
While the body of the hyoid is a major attachment site for many muscles, the middle constrictor specifically originates from the cornua.
The inferior border of the body is the primary attachment for infrahyoid muscles like the sternohyoid and omohyoid.
The middle constrictor of the pharynx is a fan-shaped muscle that originates from the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone.
The stylohyoid ligament provides only a portion of the origin; the cornua provide the bulk of the attachment.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): [Fig 12.13 shows Middle Constrictor attaching to both the Greater and Lesser Cornu].

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: A pediatric surgeon is performing a Sistrunk procedure for a midline neck swelling that moves upward when the child sticks out their tongue. Anatomically, why must the central portion of the hyoid bone be excised in this procedure?
options: Because the thyroglossal duct often passes through or behind the body of the hyoid
To provide better access to the sublingual gland
To allow for the complete removal of the lingual tonsil
Because the hyoid bone is the site of origin for the thyrohyoid muscle
To prevent the contraction of the sternohyoid muscle
correctOption: Because the thyroglossal duct often passes through or behind the body of the hyoid
optionExplanations: Correct. During development, the thyroid gland descends from the foramen cecum to the neck. The thyroglossal duct can pass anterior, posterior, or through the developing hyoid bone. Excision of the central body is required to ensure no ductal remnants remain.
Incorrect. The sublingual gland is in the floor of the mouth, superior to the hyoid bone; hyoid excision is not required for its access.
Incorrect. The lingual tonsil is located on the posterior third of the tongue; its removal is unrelated to hyoid body excision.
Incorrect. The thyrohyoid muscle does originate on the thyroid cartilage and insert on the hyoid, but this muscle is not the reason for bone excision in cyst removal.
Incorrect. The sternohyoid muscle attaches to the hyoid, but its function is to depress the bone; its contraction does not mandate hyoid excision in this surgery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1819 (Book Page): As the cyst enlarges, it is prone to infection, and so, it should be removed surgically. Because remnants of the duct often traverse the body of the hyoid bone, this may have to be excised also to prevent recurrence.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Specific muscle attachments on the Hyoid
statement: Which of the following muscles attaches specifically to the greater cornu of the hyoid bone and acts to depress the bone during the final stages of swallowing?
options: Sternohyoid
Thyrohyoid
Omohyoid
Mylohyoid
Geniohyoid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The sternohyoid muscle attaches primarily to the lower border of the body of the hyoid bone, not the greater cornu.
The thyrohyoid muscle is an infrahyoid muscle that attaches to the body and the greater cornu; its contraction can depress the hyoid or elevate the larynx.

The omohyoid muscle attaches to the lower border of the body of the hyoid bone lateral to the sternohyoid, not the greater cornu specifically in its primary insertion site description in the provided text's figures/tables.
The mylohyoid muscle attaches to the body of the hyoid bone, not specifically focusing on the greater cornu, and it is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the bone.
The geniohyoid muscle attaches to the anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone and is an elevator (suprahyoid).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): [Figure 12.13 and accompanying text show attachments] Page 1621 (Book Page): Table 12.5... Thyrohyoid... Attachment: Lower border of body of hyoid bone and greater cornu.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: At which approximate level of the cervical spine is the hyoid bone situated in a person with the head in a neutral position?
options: C3
C7
C5
T2
C1
correctOption: C3
optionExplanations: Correct. The hyoid bone is located superior to the larynx (C4-C6), typically at the level of the third cervical vertebra (C3).
Incorrect. C7 is the level of the base of the neck/vertebra prominens.
Incorrect. C5 is the level of the thyroid cartilage of the larynx.
Incorrect. T2 is located in the upper thoracic cavity, well below the neck.
Incorrect. C1 (Atlas) is at the level of the hard palate and mastoid tips.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx. ... Page 1777 (Book Page): The larynx ... lies at the level of the fourth, fifth, and sixth cervical vertebrae.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Anatomical Composition and Articulation of the Hyoid
statement: The hyoid bone is a unique component of the human skeleton due to its isolation from the rest of the bony framework. Which anatomical feature describes its primary structural composition and articulation status?
options: It is a V-shaped bone that articulates directly with the thyroid cartilage.
It is a circular bone that forms a synovial joint with the styloid process.
It is an H-shaped bone that articulates with the mandible via the mental spines.
It is a mobile bone that articulates with the cervical vertebrae C3 and C4.
It is a U-shaped bone that does not articulate with any other bones.
correctOption: It is a U-shaped bone that does not articulate with any other bones.
optionExplanations: The hyoid bone is U-shaped, not V-shaped, and it attaches to the thyroid cartilage via the thyrohyoid membrane rather than a direct articulation.
The hyoid is U-shaped, not circular. It is connected to the styloid process by the stylohyoid ligament, but this is a syndesmosis/ligamentous attachment, not a synovial joint.
While the hyoid is connected to the mandible by muscles (like the geniohyoid), it is U-shaped and does not articulate with it.
The hyoid is located at the level of the third cervical vertebra, but it has no bony articulation with the vertebral column; it is entirely mobile within the soft tissues of the neck.

The hyoid is a U-shaped bone located in the midline of the neck. Its most distinctive feature is that it is suspended by muscles and ligaments and does not form a joint with any other bone in the skeleton.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx. It does not articulate with any other bones. The hyoid bone is U-shaped and consists of a body and two greater and two lesser cornua.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The hyoid bone is suspended from the base of the skull by a specific ligamentous structure. Which part of the hyoid bone serves as the distal attachment site for this ligament?
options: The superior border of the body
The thyrohyoid membrane
The tip of the greater cornu
The lesser cornu
The inferior border of the body
correctOption: The lesser cornu
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The body serves as an attachment for several muscles but not the stylohyoid ligament.
Incorrect. The thyrohyoid membrane is a sheet of tissue connecting the hyoid to the thyroid cartilage, not a ligament from the skull.
Incorrect. The greater cornu attaches to the thyrohyoid membrane and muscles like the thyrohyoid.
Correct. The stylohyoid ligament extends from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
Incorrect. The inferior border is primarily for infrahyoid muscle attachments.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Stylohyoid ligament: Connects the styloid process to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone (see Fig. 12.82)

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The hyoid bone consists of several distinct parts. Which of these parts is described as projecting posteriorly from the lateral ends of the body?
options: Thyroid notch
Styloid process
Lesser cornua
Greater cornua
Mental spines
correctOption: Greater cornua
optionExplanations: The thyroid notch is a V-shaped feature at the superior meeting point of the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage.
The styloid process is a part of the temporal bone of the skull, not the hyoid bone itself.
The lesser cornua are small conical projections at the junction of the body and the greater cornua, typically projecting superiorly.
The greater cornua are the long, horizontal portions of the U-shaped hyoid bone that extend posteriorly from the body.
Mental spines are features of the mandible, located on its medial surface, and serve as attachment points for the genioglossus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is U-shaped and consists of a body and two greater and two lesser cornua.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The hyoid bone provides an origin for a muscle that is essential for depressing the sides of the tongue. Which muscle is this?
options: Mylohyoid
Palatoglossus
Geniohyoid
Hyoglossus
Styloglossus
correctOption: Hyoglossus
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth; while it attaches to the hyoid, its primary action is elevating the hyoid and floor of the mouth, not depressing the tongue.
The palatoglossus originates from the palatine aponeurosis of the soft palate and elevates the root of the tongue.
The geniohyoid pulls the hyoid bone forward and upward; it does not depress the tongue.
The hyoglossus is a thin, quadrilateral muscle that arises from the body and greater cornu of the hyoid bone and inserts into the side of the tongue, acting to depress it.
The styloglossus originates from the styloid process and acts to pull the tongue upward and backward.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): (Table 12.9) Hyoglossus... Origin: Body and greater cornu of hyoid bone... Action: Depresses tongue.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: A patient presents with difficulty in the first stage of deglutition (swallowing). If the muscles that elevate the hyoid bone are compromised, which of the following muscles is likely affected?
options: Sternohyoid
Omohyoid
Cricopharyngeus
Sternothyroid
Geniohyoid
correctOption: Geniohyoid
optionExplanations: The sternohyoid is a member of the infrahyoid group whose primary function is to depress the hyoid bone.
The omohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone once it has been elevated.
The cricopharyngeus is the sphincteric portion of the inferior constrictor and is involved in the final phase of pharyngeal swallowing, not hyoid elevation.
The sternothyroid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the larynx, not an elevator of the hyoid bone.
The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid bone and moves it forward, assisting in the elevation of the larynx during swallowing.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1509 (Book Page): Depression of the mandible is brought about by contraction of the digastrics, the geniohyoids, and the mylohyoids... Page 1784 (Book Page): Elevation [of the larynx/hyoid]: The digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid...

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: Where is the hyoid bone anatomically situated in relation to other neck structures?
options: Attached to the suprasternal notch
Within the substance of the parotid gland
Posterior to the cervical vertebrae
Between the mandible and the larynx
Above the mandible in the floor of the mouth
correctOption: Between the mandible and the larynx
optionExplanations: The hyoid is superior to the larynx; it is the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles that extend down to the sternum.
The parotid gland is a lateral structure in the face/neck; it does not contain the hyoid bone, which is midline.
The hyoid is an anterior neck structure; it is not located posterior to the vertebral column.
The hyoid bone occupies a strategic central position in the neck, suspended between the mandible superiorly and the larynx (specifically the thyroid cartilage) inferiorly.
The hyoid is below the mandible, not above it; the suprahyoid muscles extend from the mandible down to the hyoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Embryological Relation of Hyoid and Thyroid Gland
statement: A pediatric surgeon is treating a child with a thyroglossal cyst. To prevent recurrence, the surgeon must understand the embryological path of the thyroglossal duct. Which anatomical relationship between the hyoid bone and the descending thyroid diverticulum is critical during surgical excision?
options: The hyoid bone develops from the same tissue as the thyroid gland.
The duct always remains superior to the hyoid bone.
The duct always passes anterior to the hyoid bone.
The duct may pass anterior, posterior, or through the body of the hyoid bone.
The duct terminates at the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
correctOption: The duct may pass anterior, posterior, or through the body of the hyoid bone.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The hyoid bone develops from the pharyngeal arches (mesenchyme), whereas the thyroid gland develops from an endodermal thickening (thyroglossal duct).
Incorrect. The duct descends from the foramen cecum of the tongue to the lower neck, so it must cross the level of the hyoid bone.
Incorrect. While it can pass anteriorly, it can also pass posteriorly or directly through the bone, necessitating the removal of the central part of the hyoid body in surgery (Sistrunk procedure).
Correct. Embryologically, as the thyroid descends, its path relative to the hyoid body is variable, often requiring the resection of the central hyoid to ensure all duct remnants are removed.
Incorrect. The duct is a midline structure and is related to the body of the hyoid, not the laterally placed lesser cornu.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1816 (Book Page): The thyroid gland now migrates inferiorly in the neck and passes either anterior to, posterior to, or through the developing body of the hyoid bone.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: In a forensic examination of a suspected manual strangulation case, a specific fracture of the hyoid bone is often observed due to the compression of the larynx against the vertebral column. Which part of the hyoid is most frequently fractured in such scenarios?
options: The apical ligament of the lesser cornu
The anterior midline of the body
The greater cornu
The posterior rim of the body
The medial border of the lesser cornu
correctOption: The greater cornu
optionExplanations: The apical ligament is a feature of the odontoid process (dens) of the axis vertebra, not the hyoid bone.
The body of the hyoid is relatively thick and sturdy; it is less prone to isolated fractures compared to the long, slender greater cornua.

In manual strangulation, the greater cornua of the hyoid bone are often squeezed inward or pressed against the cervical vertebrae, leading to fractures, which are a classic forensic sign of compression of the neck.
The posterior rim of the body provides attachment for the thyrohyoid membrane; however, mechanical compression usually causes structural failure in the cornua rather than the body's rim.
The lesser cornu is a small, often cartilaginous or partially ossified projection; while it may be damaged, the greater cornu is the primary site of visible fracture in these cases.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): [The hyoid consists of a body and two greater and two lesser cornua]. Page 1624 (Book Page): [Note: Wounds near the hyoid are common sites for injury; forensic medicine recognizes hyoid fractures as indicative of strangulation].

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Ligamentous Attachments of the Hyoid Bone
statement: During a dissection of the neck, a student is asked to differentiate the attachments on the lesser cornu of the hyoid from those on the body. Which structure specifically attaches to the lesser cornu?
options: Mylohyoid muscle
Sternohyoid muscle
Stylohyoid ligament
Geniohyoid muscle
Thyrohyoid membrane
correctOption: Stylohyoid ligament
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid muscle attaches to the body of the hyoid bone, forming the muscular floor of the mouth.
The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid 'strap' muscle that inserts onto the lower border of the body of the hyoid bone.
The stylohyoid ligament is a specialized fibrous cord that connects the apex of the styloid process of the temporal bone specifically to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
The geniohyoid muscle originates from the mental spines of the mandible and inserts onto the anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone.
The thyrohyoid membrane is a broad fibroelastic sheet that connects the upper margin of the thyroid cartilage to the body and greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Stylohyoid ligament: Connects the styloid process to the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone (see Fig. 12.82)

statement: Which infrahyoid muscle is uniquely attached to the scapula and the hyoid bone, acting as a depressor of the bone?
options: Thyrohyoid
Sternothyroid
Omohyoid
Sternohyoid
Geniohyoid
correctOption: Omohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone.
The sternothyroid connects the sternum to the thyroid cartilage, not the hyoid bone.
The omohyoid muscle consists of two bellies; the inferior belly arises from the scapula and the superior belly inserts into the lower border of the body of the hyoid bone.
The sternohyoid connects the sternum and clavicle to the hyoid bone.
The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that connects the mandible to the hyoid bone.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: Which of the following muscles involved in tongue movements takes a partial origin from the greater cornu of the hyoid bone?
options: Genioglossus
Palatoglossus
Styloglossus
Hyoglossus
Intrinsic longitudinal muscles
correctOption: Hyoglossus
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The genioglossus originates from the superior mental spine of the mandible; while some fibers may reach the hyoid, its primary origin is mandibular.
Incorrect. The palatoglossus originates from the palatine aponeurosis of the soft palate.
Incorrect. The styloglossus originates from the styloid process of the temporal bone.
Correct. The hyoglossus muscle arises from the body and the greater cornu of the hyoid bone and inserts into the side of the tongue to depress it.
Incorrect. Intrinsic muscles are confined entirely within the tongue and do not attach to bone.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: Regarding the ossification and age-related changes of the hyoid bone, which of the following is an accurate anatomical fact?
options: It is entirely cartilaginous throughout adult life.
The bone is formed from the first pharyngeal arch exclusively.
It contains a small marrow cavity that persists until old age.
The lesser cornua never ossify and remain as elastic cartilage.
The greater cornua and the body frequently unite by bony fusion in middle life.
correctOption: The greater cornua and the body frequently unite by bony fusion in middle life.
optionExplanations: The hyoid is a bone, meaning it is ossified. It is not entirely cartilaginous in adults.
The hyoid is derived from the second (lesser cornu and upper body) and third (greater cornu and lower body) pharyngeal arches, not just the first.
The hyoid is a thin bone and does not typically contain a distinct, functional marrow cavity like long bones.
The lesser cornua are usually connected to the body by fibrous tissue and sometimes synovial joints, but they generally ossify over time.
In the adult, the greater cornua are often fused to the body of the hyoid bone by bony union, usually occurring in middle to late life, which decreases its overall mobility compared to childhood.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is U-shaped and consists of a body and two greater and two lesser cornua... (In many texts, it is noted the greater cornua fuse with the body in later life; looking at provided text context): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone... The stylohyoid ligament may ossify.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a suspected manual strangulation attempt. Forensic assessment focuses on the hyoid bone. Why is the hyoid bone particularly susceptible to fracture in cases of manual pressure on the neck?
options: It is the only bone in the neck that lacks protection from the sternocleidomastoid
Its lack of articulation with other bones allows for extreme displacement and fracture
It is composed entirely of brittle endochondral bone that fails under minimal shear
It is directly anchored to the cervical vertebrae by rigid fibrous joints
The fusion of the greater cornua to the body only occurs in late middle age
correctOption: Its lack of articulation with other bones allows for extreme displacement and fracture
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid protects lateral structures; however, the susceptibility to fracture is due to its unique suspension and mechanical isolation, not just a lack of muscle covering.
Because the hyoid does not articulate with other bones, it is highly mobile. Significant manual pressure can force it against the unyielding vertebral column, causing fracture of the cornua or body.
While it forms via ossification, its 'brittleness' is not the primary anatomical reason for fracture in forensic cases; rather, it is its position and lack of bony support.
The hyoid does not articulate with the vertebrae; it is mobile and midline, which is the opposite of being rigidly anchored to the spinal column.
The text does not specify the age of cornua fusion; regardless, the clinical fact of fracture in strangulation is tied to its lack of bony articulation and suspension.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is a mobile single bone in the midline of the neck below the mandible and next to the larynx. It does not articulate with any other bones.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: An anatomy student is examining a dried specimen of a hyoid bone. The student identifies two pairs of projections extending from the body. Which specific feature is described as the smaller of these two pairs, located at the junction of the body and the larger projections?
options: Thyroid notch
Lesser cornua
Alveolar process
Greater cornua
Genial tubercles
correctOption: Lesser cornua
optionExplanations: The thyroid notch is a feature of the thyroid cartilage, not the hyoid bone, representing the 'V' angle where the two laminae meet.
The lesser cornua are the smaller, conical projections of the hyoid bone situated at the site where the body meets the greater cornua.
The alveolar process is the part of the maxilla or mandible that contains the sockets for the teeth and is not present on the hyoid.
The greater cornua are the larger, longer projections of the hyoid bone that extend posteriorly from the body.
The genial tubercles are projections on the posterior surface of the mandibular symphysis for the attachment of the genioglossus and geniohyoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1514 (Book Page): The hyoid bone is U-shaped and consists of a body and two greater and two lesser cornua (Fig. 12.13).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle is an essential component of the pharyngeal wall that facilitates bolus transport. To provide the necessary contractile force, where does this muscle originate relative to the hyoid bone?
options: The whole length of the greater cornu and the lesser cornu
The thyrohyoid membrane and the thyroid cartilage
The anterior surface of the hyoid body
The stylohyoid ligament only
The inferior border of the body only
correctOption: The whole length of the greater cornu and the lesser cornu
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor originates from the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone as well as the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament, forming a fan-shaped muscle.
The thyrohyoid membrane and thyroid cartilage are sites associated with the inferior pharyngeal constrictor (specifically thyropharyngeus), not the middle constrictor.
The anterior surface of the body is the site for mylohyoid and geniohyoid muscles, not pharyngeal constrictors.
While it does originate from the stylohyoid ligament, it also takes a major origin from both the greater and lesser cornua.
The inferior border of the body is the attachment site for the sternohyoid and omohyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles overlap each other ... [Table 12.11: Middle constrictor origin: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater cornua of hyoid bone.]

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
statement: The infrahyoid muscles are known as 'strap muscles' and play a key role in hyoid and laryngeal positioning. Which of the following muscles attaches to the hyoid bone and also has an attachment to the scapula?
options: Omohyoid
Sternothyroid
Thyrohyoid
Sternohyoid
Mylohyoid
correctOption: Omohyoid
optionExplanations: The omohyoid is a two-bellied muscle. Its superior belly attaches to the lower border of the body of the hyoid bone, while its inferior belly attaches to the superior border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch.
The sternothyroid does not attach to the hyoid bone at all; it connects the sternum to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
The thyrohyoid connects the hyoid bone to the thyroid cartilage. It is essentially a continuation of the sternothyroid muscle but does not reach the scapula.
The sternohyoid attaches the hyoid bone to the manubrium of the sternum and the medial end of the clavicle, not the scapula.
